picks.bull_thesis:
Jet2 is the best-run leisure travel business in the United Kingdom, trading at roughly seven times its earnings and about six times its free cash flow. The bull case is that the market is pricing a cyclical squeeze as if it were permanent.

The evidence: revenue reached a record 7.48 billion pounds in the year to March 2026 (up 4.3%), passengers passed 20 million, and free cash flow was 495 million pounds - 2.6 billion pounds since the pandemic (FY26 results call, 8 July 2026). Management has a high-credibility record: it flagged its own small miss on flight-only pricing early (November 2025) and landed full-year operating profit inside its 435-440 million pound guide. The September 2026 trading statement showed booked passengers up 8.8% on capacity up 7.6%, with Gatwick ahead of plan.

Three drivers can lift profit from here. First, the newer bases (Bournemouth, Luton and from March 2026 Gatwick) carry start-up costs today and should mature into profit; Gatwick is guided to break even by the year to March 2029. Second, the A321neo fleet (232 seats against 189, lower cost per seat, about 22% of the summer 2026 fleet) lowers unit costs as it grows. Third, the buyback shrinks the share count: about 22 million shares were bought back in the year to March 2026 and a further 250 million pounds runs to 31 May 2027, roughly 9% of today's market value of about 2.7 billion pounds.

Consensus, as cited in the committee's prior record, expects earnings per share to recover toward 188p for the year to March 2028 and 243p for the year to March 2029. On those numbers the stock trades at about eight and six times earnings respectively, with a balance sheet that carries roughly break-even own net debt and an undrawn 500 million pound credit line. If flight-only pricing stabilises and Gatwick scales, a multiple of nine to ten times recovery earnings gives 1,700-2,150p.

Conditions: flight-only yields stop falling, hotel cost inflation moderates toward package price growth, and no large demand shock (conflict, recession) hits the 2027 summer booking season.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that Jet2's profit has stopped growing even as it adds capacity, and that the cheap multiple reflects a narrowing moat in a crowded market rather than a mispricing.

The evidence: net income fell from 447 million pounds (FY25) to 410 million pounds (FY26) while seat capacity grew about 8%. Flight-only ticket yield fell 7% in both the November 2025 and July 2026 calls; management calls this 'investing in price' and 'investing in load factor', which is another way of saying it cannot hold fares. Hotel costs, 45% of the cost base, rose about 6.5% while package prices rose 3%, of which about one point was customers trading up. Return on capital employed slipped from a 17% three-year average to 14.4%, and our scan's return on invested capital of 6.4% is near the cost of capital. Free cash flow fell about 25% year on year as bookings moved closer to departure.

The headline net cash of about 2.0 billion pounds is mostly customer deposits; the CFO himself put own cash at about 1.2 billion pounds, roughly equal to the 1.28 billion pounds of debt including leases. In a shock those deposits become a refund liability, not a cushion, and the new 2 times leverage target signals more borrowing to fund the Airbus order book. Consensus earnings for the year to March 2027 of about 136p (cited in the prior record) imply the stock is not cheap on this year's numbers at about 11 times.

What would confirm the bear case: the 18 November 2026 interim results showing summer 2026 profit flat or down despite higher passenger numbers, winter flight-only yields still falling, or capacity guidance for summer 2027 that again outruns the market. The business is also exposed to inflation: its gross margin fell from 13.8% to a loss through the 2021-22 period (largely pandemic-driven), and it has shown only partial pass-through of hotel cost increases.
picks.consensus_delta: The street is not pricing terminal decline; it is pricing a profit plateau. The street may also be too relaxed about flight-only yield, which has fallen 7% in two reporting periods running. We do not see a large expectations gap at 1,525p.

Hotel cost inflation, sustainable aviation fuel mandates (32 million pounds of extra premium in FY26) and employment-tax rises all pressure margins. That is why the wait is tied to a sector or style sell-off rather than to mechanical selling.

Wait for a better price: we buy near 1,250p, which a sector-wide sell-off of UK consumer and airline shares could deliver.

At 1,250p the trade becomes attractive: about 38% upside to fair value against little downside to the adverse case. The shares were near 980p as recently as March 2026, so a sector-wide sell-off of that kind is not far-fetched.

# Jet2 plc (JET2.L) - a deep dive on management and the setup

Debate date: 16 November 2026. Live price 1,525p (FMP quote, London listing, pence). Transcripts read: interim results call of 19 November 2025 (half year to 30 September 2025) and full-year results call of 8 July 2026 (year to 31 March 2026). The next dated release is the interim results for the half year to 30 September 2026, scheduled for 18 November 2026 (FMP earnings calendar), two days after this debate.

The short version: management is credible and conservative, the balance sheet is strong, and the cash returns are real. But the last eighteen months show a business that is growing passengers by giving away price, with profit flat to slightly down while capacity grows about 8% a year. That is a narrow moat that is being tested, not a widening one.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

In November 2025 the story was "record numbers" and expansion: passengers up 6%, the new bases at Bournemouth and Luton, and the launch of London Gatwick, described as "a once-in-a-generation opportunity to accelerate our growth" (H1 FY26 call). The Gatwick base was explicitly not expected to make money until the year to March 2029.

By July 2026 the emphasis had shifted from growth to resilience. The words used most were "resilient", "robust" and "controlled": operating profit "remained resilient even after absorbing Gatwick startup investment costs and wider industry cost pressures" (FY26 call). The growth story is still there (over 20 million passengers, up 5%), but the profit story has become one of absorbing costs. Capital returns moved to the centre: 363 million pounds returned in the year, "more than ever before", and a further 250 million pound buyback to run to 31 May 2027.

A new strand appeared in July 2026: a medium-term leverage target of 2 times net debt to EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) on an own-cash basis. That is a quiet signal that management intends to use more of the balance sheet over time, mainly to finance the Airbus fleet.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record revenue" (FY26) | Revenue 7.48 billion pounds, up 4.3%; three-year growth about 14% a year, flattered by the post-pandemic rebound from 1.23 billion in 2022 | True, but growth has slowed sharply |
| Operating profit "resilient" | Net income fell from 447 million pounds (FY25) to 410 million (FY26); FY26 operating profit guided at 435-440 million against 446.5 million the year before (29 April 2026 trading update) | Profit fell while capacity grew about 8%. "Resilient" is generous |
| Package price "resilient, up 3%" | About 1 point of the 3% came from customers trading up to four- and five-star hotels; hotel costs, 45% of the cost base, rose about 6.5% | Partial pass-through only; the cost of the holiday rose faster than its price |
| Flight-only demand strong (+15% passengers) | Flight-only ticket yield down 7% in both calls | Volume bought with price |
| "Over 2 billion pounds of net cash" | True on the headline basis, but most of it is customer deposits. The CFO himself split out "1.2 billion pounds of our own cash, excluding customer advances"; against about 1.28 billion pounds of debt including leases, own cash is roughly break-even | The headline overstates distributable cash |
| Free cash flow 495 million pounds; 2.6 billion since the pandemic | Consistent with the trailing figures; free cash flow fell about 25% year on year as customers booked later | True, but declining and timing-sensitive |
| Earnings per share "stable" | Earnings per share roughly 208-211p in both FY25 and FY26 - stable only because about 22 million shares were bought back | Per-share stability is buyback-supported |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Trajectory: stable, with a defensive tilt.

- November 2025: confident, expansionary - "Further growth in the first half across all our key metrics." The CFO was candid about uncertainty: "there's a lot of moving parts ... I'm not being evasive, but there are."
- July 2026: still upbeat ("I hope you're as excited about the future as we are"), but the vocabulary moved to cost absorption, "investing in price" and capital returns. On the Middle East conflict, management described later bookings and a bounce-back in eastern Mediterranean destinations rather than a lasting hit.

There is no sign of panic and no sign of rising ambition either. The language is that of a well-run operator in a tougher market.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Reliability: high.

- The November 2025 guide for flight-only pricing was "mid-single digits down"; the CFO volunteered that the outcome was "slightly worse" at minus 7%. Flagging a small miss early is a good sign.
- FY26 operating profit landed inside the 435-440 million pound range guided in April 2026.
- The beat rate in our data is 50% (one of two quarters), and FMP shows the November 2025 half-year earnings per share at 300p against a 281p estimate.
- The July 2026 capital spending cut of about 350 million pounds for the following year was explained as Airbus delivery timing, "timing only, it doesn't undermine any of our growth plans". That is plausible given industry-wide Airbus delays, but it also flatters near-term free cash flow.

No sandbagging pattern, and no pattern of over-promising.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- Capacity versus price: analysts asked in both calls whether growing capacity 8-9% when competitors grow less would force further fare cuts. Management answered with flexibility ("we can make adjustments") rather than with yield guidance. This is the central unresolved question.
- Cost per seat: management repeatedly declined to give unit-cost guidance before Eurocontrol fees and slot declarations were known.
- Booking curve: later bookings came up in both calls; management treats them as a timing effect, but they reduce visibility and the customer-deposit float.
- AI distribution (July 2026): asked whether large language models would change how holidays are booked, management said "We've not seen a big impact from LLMs at the moment" and that direct bookings are steady at just under 80% for holidays. Honest, but untested.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Red flags:
- Profit falling while capacity grows about 8% a year (April 2026 trading update; FY26 results, July 2026).
- Flight-only yield down 7% two reporting periods running (November 2025, July 2026).
- Return on capital employed down from 17% (three-year average quoted in November 2025) to 14.4% in FY26.
- Hotel cost inflation (about 6.5%) running ahead of package price (3%, of which 1 point is mix).
- Gatwick start-up costs, with profitability not expected until the year to March 2029.

Green flags:
- Strong own-cash position, an undrawn 500 million pound revolving credit facility extended to October 2030.
- Shareholder returns at record levels, with the share count falling: about 22 million shares bought back in FY26 and a further 250 million pounds under way to May 2027.
- Fleet renewal to the A321neo (232 seats against 189, lower seat cost; about 22% of the summer 2026 fleet).
- Industry-leading customer service and low cancellation rates, which support the package-holiday brand.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "Investing in price" and "investing in load factor" have become standing phrases. When a company describes price cuts as investments, it is telling you that it does not have the pricing power to hold fares.
- The new 2 times leverage target signals a shift from a cash-rich to a more geared capital structure as the Airbus order book is financed.
- The CFO's own-cash framing (1.2 billion pounds excluding customer advances) is a welcome bit of honesty that the headline net-cash figure hides.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: stable. Capital allocation is disciplined (buybacks at single-digit earnings multiples, fleet renewal, no acquisitions), and management is credible.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: Jet2's profit has stopped growing even as capacity grows. The investment case depends on Gatwick and the newer bases maturing into profit and on flight-only pricing stabilising. The interim results on 18 November 2026 are the next test of whether summer 2026 converted bookings into profit.

Moat: scale-cost plus brand (the integrated package-holiday model, about 80% direct distribution, customer-service reputation). It is real but narrow, and the evidence - return on capital falling from 17% to 14.4%, yields given away to fill seats - says it is being tested rather than widening. Our scan's return on invested capital of 6.4% sits near the cost of capital. Secular threat: manageable. AI-led travel search could change distribution over time, but management reports no impact so far and the direct-booking share is steady. The cheapness looks like a cyclical fear-print on a competitive, cost-inflated leisure market, not a structurally shrinking base - but the moat needs proof that pricing can hold.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

# CECONOMY AG (CEC.DE, Xetra, EUR) - forensic dossier, 2026-11-09

Price used: EUR 4.53 on Xetra (FMP live quote, 9 November 2026; 52-week range EUR 3.51-4.59; market value about EUR 2.20 billion on about 485 million shares). Latest call transcript: second fiscal quarter, 13 May 2026.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
CECONOMY runs MediaMarkt and Saturn, Europe's largest consumer-electronics chain (about 1,000 stores, 11 countries, roughly EUR 24 billion of sales). The story management tells has moved from "turnaround retailer" to "platform": retail media (selling advertising to suppliers against store and app traffic), services, a third-party marketplace and rented floor space, now about 40% of gross profit. Since late 2025 the story has been overtaken by ownership: JD.com's 2025 tender at EUR 4.60 left JD.com and partner Convergenta with 85.2% on completion. The European Commission conditionally approved the purchase under the foreign-subsidies rules on 3 November 2026, and closing is expected by 12 November 2026, inside the 10 November-area long-stop the chief financial officer flagged on 13 May 2026.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
- Claim: twelve-plus straight quarters of adjusted operating profit growth. Preliminary fiscal 2025/26 figures reported in October 2026 put adjusted operating profit (EBIT, earnings before interest and tax) at about EUR 515 million versus a EUR 500 million target and EUR 406 million restated a year earlier; sales about EUR 23.9 billion, up about 5%. Final figures are due 14 December 2026. Corroborated, though from trade press, not the company release.
- Reported profit does not match adjusted profit: net income was negative in fiscal 2023 (EUR -39 million) and 2025 (EUR -35 million); trailing earnings per share EUR -0.03 at 30 June 2026. The gap of roughly EUR 300 million a year between adjusted and reported profit recurs with a differently named one-off each year.
- The screen's 3.2 times price to free cash flow counts trailing free cash flow of EUR 731 million before about EUR 524 million a year of store rent, which lease accounting books in financing. After rent, owner free cash flow is about EUR 200 million, in line with management's own guide: about 11 times at today's price.
- Return on invested capital 1.8%; gross margin 15.1% and contracting. Net debt EUR 1.51 billion at 30 June 2026 (borrowings EUR 2.60 billion less cash EUR 1.09 billion), a seasonal high; near nil at the December peak.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Confident on operations, deliberately vague on the minority. On 13 May 2026 the finance chief confirmed closing "in the second half of the calendar year" before the November long-stop and declined to give a precise delisting date. Tone on Germany and Austria, the core markets, was guarded across both reported 2026 quarters.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Good on the adjusted line: the EUR 500 million target was met and beaten (about EUR 515 million, preliminary, October 2026). Weaker on reported profit, where guidance is not given and one-offs recur. Credibility on deal timing was adequate: the timetable slipped from first half to second half of calendar 2026, but the regulatory path closed before the long-stop.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
Analysts pressed on deal timing and delisting mechanics (13 May 2026), not on the adjusted-versus-reported gap or rent-adjusted cash flow. No current analyst price targets could be found with a dated source; the stock is effectively a controlled company with thin coverage.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
Red: recurring one-offs; 1.8% return on capital; contracting gross margin; JD.com committed in its 2025 offer to no domination or profit-transfer agreement (a contract that would force an appraised cash exit) for at least three years; a German delisting offer must only meet the six-month average price (about EUR 4.15-4.30 on the 200- and 50-day averages) and the bidder's qualifying pre-acquisitions; free float about 14.8% and thin.
Green: adjusted profit beat (October 2026); mix shift to higher-margin income; supplier-funded working capital; no refinancing pressure; EU approval obtained 3 November 2026.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
The share price (EUR 4.53, 94% up its range) has converged to within 1.5% of JD.com's EUR 4.60 tender price, above the statutory six-month-average floor. The market is pricing a delisting offer struck at or near EUR 4.60, not the business. Volume is low (about 5,000 shares on the quote day), so the marginal buyer is an event trader.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
A better business than its reputation, held inside a security whose payout is set by the controlling shareholder's delisting decision. Today's price already discounts the most likely minority exit; the upside case (an appraised exit under a domination agreement) is contractually ruled out for about three years. Nothing here for a value book.

# G-III Apparel Group (GIII) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Prepared 2026-10-26. Price used: $29.67 (NASDAQ, US dollars, live quote 2026-10-26). Transcripts covered: five calls from 2025-09-04 (second quarter of fiscal 2026) to 2026-09-02 (second quarter of fiscal 2027). G-III's fiscal year ends 31 January, so "fiscal 2027" is roughly calendar 2026.*

**Bottom line:** management has done what it said it would do. It has replaced most of the revenue lost when PVH took back the Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger licences, it has lifted gross margin through a tariff shock, and it has kept the balance sheet clean. The open question is no longer execution on the old plan; it is whether the roughly $500 million Marc Jacobs purchase, closed on 1 September 2026, earns its keep. Two cautions for the reader: the trailing twelve-month (TTM) earnings and free-cash-flow figures are flattered by a one-off tariff refund, and insiders have been net sellers on the open market.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **September 2025 (Q2 fiscal 2026):** a defensive call. Tariffs hit gross margin harder than planned ("higher-than-expected tariff costs"), retailers were "increasingly cautious on their inventory buys", and management said it was "prioritizing margin over sales". The story was survival through the licence exit.
- **December 2025 (Q3 fiscal 2026):** earnings beat the top of guidance "despite the impacts of tariffs"; inventory held nearly flat. The owned-brand story (DKNY, Donna Karan, Karl Lagerfeld, Vilebrequin) moved to the front.
- **March 2026 (Q4 fiscal 2026):** a full-year miss on earnings explained almost entirely by the Saks bankruptcy (a roughly $17.5 million bad-debt charge, about $0.30 a share). Owned brands reached "close to 60% of revenue, up from roughly 50% last year"; Donna Karan grew about 40%. Management openly said it was hunting for "an amazing acquisition".
- **June 2026 (Q1 fiscal 2027):** the Marc Jacobs deal was announced - G-III buys 100% of the operating company and 50% of the brand's intellectual property in a joint venture with WHP Global, for about $500 million funded by cash and the revolving credit line. Management called it "dilutive in the first year" with accretion thereafter. First gross-margin expansion "since fiscal 2025" (+350 basis points).
- **September 2026 (Q2 fiscal 2027):** the deal closed on 1 September. Gross margin up 440 basis points; non-GAAP earnings of $0.26 a share against $0.15-0.25 guidance; full-year earnings guidance raised (excluding Marc Jacobs). The target is now a "$1 billion" long-term Marc Jacobs revenue line and a "brand-led global apparel powerhouse".

The arc runs from defence (licence exit, tariffs) to offence (acquisition, global licensing). The language of scale has returned, which is the thing to watch.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Gross margin expanding 440 basis points" (2026-09-02) | Q2 fiscal 2027 gross profit $250.4M on $554.1M sales = 45.2%, versus 39.6% a year earlier | Matches |
| Go-forward portfolio growing "high single digits" | Total sales still falling: $554M vs $613M (-9.6%) in Q2; fiscal 2026 sales $2.96B (-7%) | Plausible - the decline is the planned PVH run-off; the go-forward figure is not separately audited |
| "Replaced $700 million" of the ~$1.2B lost PVH revenue | Revenue fell from $3.23B (fiscal 2024) to $2.96B (fiscal 2026), a far smaller drop than $1.2B | Broadly corroborated |
| Strong cash position, "nearly $530 million in cash" | Balance sheet 2026-07-31: cash $529M vs total debt $341M, of which $333M is lease liabilities - net cash about $188M | Matches, but the $134M tariff refund received in Q2 is in that cash |
| Strong profitability | Q1 fiscal 2027 GAAP net income $66.5M while non-GAAP was a loss of $0.21 a share; GAAP gross margin of about 65% in Q1 shows a large one-off credit (the tariff refund) inside cost of goods | Caution: TTM GAAP earnings of $3.04 a share and the 5x price-to-free-cash-flow are inflated by a non-repeatable refund |
| Marc Jacobs "dilutive in the first year" | Not yet in the numbers; first quarter with Marc Jacobs reports around 8 December 2026 | Untested |

The underlying business is better than the headline sales decline suggests, but worse than the TTM earnings suggest. The honest earnings base is the non-GAAP run-rate: fiscal 2026 non-GAAP earnings of $2.61 a share and fiscal 2027 consensus of about $2.25.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising.** September 2025 was hedged and tariff-heavy. By March 2026 Morris Goldfarb (chairman and CEO) was comparing Donna Karan favourably with the early Calvin Klein build ("We're bigger and further along in 18 months"). By September 2026 the tone was expansive - "transformational", "powerhouse" - and less specific: he declined to give Marc Jacobs detail and said LVMH gave "not a lot of access to the existing strategy" before close. Rising confidence paired with falling specificity is the pattern that usually precedes integration disappointments, so it deserves a watch, not a penalty yet.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** Quarterly guidance was met or beaten in five of the six quarters checked: Q2 fiscal 2026 sales "well ahead of our guidance"; Q3 fiscal 2026 earnings above the high end; Q1 fiscal 2027 a loss of $0.21 against an expected $0.30 loss; Q2 fiscal 2027 $0.26 against $0.15-0.25. The one miss, Q4 fiscal 2026 ($0.30 against a $0.57 estimate), was driven by the Saks bankruptcy, which management quantified ($0.30 a share). This lines up with the screener's 6-of-7 beat rate. There is a mild sandbagging pattern (conservative quarterly ranges), which is a feature, not a flaw.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Europe:** raised on every 2026 call; management concedes "Europe continues to be more challenged" (2026-09-02) and has no fix beyond waiting.
- **Second-half shape:** KeyBanc (2026-09-02) pushed on third-quarter declines from the PVH run-off and a possible warm winter. Outerwear is still "a little more than 25%" of sales - the weather exposure is smaller than it was, not gone.
- **Tariff modelling:** guidance switched from prior IEEPA rates to "current tariffs" in September 2026 - the refund tailwind is behind them and the go-forward cost base is what it is.
- **Marc Jacobs detail:** analysts asked twice for synergy and seasonality detail; management deferred to "next quarter". This is the deflected topic that matters.
- **Price targets have been cut:** UBS to $27 (2026-10-02), Telsey to $32 (2026-09-03), from $38-40 in June.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: TTM earnings and free cash flow flattered by a ~$134M tariff refund (Q1-Q2 fiscal 2027) - the 5x price-to-free-cash-flow is not a run-rate number.
- Red: insiders sold on the open market - 8 sales (324,193 shares) against 3 purchases (68,076 shares).
- Red: a roughly $500M acquisition into a brand where the buyer had limited pre-close access (2026-09-02), funded partly by the revolver, while sales are still shrinking.
- Red: department-store distribution remains the core channel, and Goldfarb himself talks of "diminishing door count" (2026-06-05).
- Green: gross margin up 350 then 440 basis points in consecutive quarters (2026-06-05, 2026-09-02) straight through tariffs - pricing is sticking.
- Green: inventory down 13% year on year (Q2 fiscal 2027) - clean working capital.
- Green: owned brands near 60% of revenue (fiscal 2026), up from about 50%; owned brands run at "mid-teens up to the upper teens" operating margin versus "low double-digit" for licensed lines (Neal Nackman, CFO, 2026-06-05).
- Green: a new dividend and continued buybacks (more than $50M returned in fiscal 2026).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary moved from "licensee" to "brand builder", "steward" and "global fashion house". Licensing income (royalties from partners) is now pitched as a profit centre - G-III is becoming partly a brand-management company, which deserves a higher multiple only if the royalty line becomes visible in the numbers.
- Goldfarb on Converse (2026-03-12): "Where we have less control, we don't rule. We're guided by the licensor." That is a frank admission of why licences are lower-quality earnings - and why Marc Jacobs is half-owned rather than licensed.
- The Marc Jacobs economics are a "hybrid" paying "essentially a half royalty" (CFO, 2026-06-05) - the operating margin will sit between the licensed and owned portfolios, not at the owned-brand level.
- Follow-up news on 2026-10-26: G-III, WHP and I.T Group announced a Greater China partnership for Marc Jacobs - consistent with the licensing-led international plan, but not yet a number.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: turning.** The company is mid-pivot from licensee to owner, and the pivot is working on margins. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the cheapness is partly an accounting illusion.** On normalised non-GAAP earnings of about $2.25 a share for fiscal 2027 the stock is roughly 13 times earnings, not the single-digit multiple the TTM figures suggest, and the cash cushion that made the balance sheet look rich has largely been spent on Marc Jacobs.

**Moat:** narrow - an intangible-brand moat in the owned labels plus a scale and relationship advantage in US department-store wholesale. Returns are modest (return on invested capital about 8.8%) but the margin trend is improving, so the moat is stable rather than eroding. **Secular threat:** material, not terminal - the shift of apparel spending away from department stores toward direct and online channels is a real, slow headwind; G-III is answering it with direct-to-consumer growth (Donna Karan online sales up about 170% in fiscal 2026) and now Marc Jacobs, which is about two-thirds direct. The discount looks like a fear-print on a business in transition rather than a structurally shrinking base, but the proof is the next two quarters.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

picks.bull_thesis:
Kogeneracja supplies district heating - hot water piped to buildings - and electricity to Wroclaw, a Polish city of about 640,000 people, from plants that make both at once (combined heat and power). At 84.20 zloty the whole company is valued at about 1.25 billion zloty. Over the twelve months to 30 June 2026 it earned about 334 million zloty of net profit (about 22.4 zloty a share) and generated 401 million zloty of free cash flow (cash left after capital spending): about 3.8 times earnings, 3.1 times free cash flow and 0.45 times the 188 zloty of book value (accounting net assets) per share.

The earnings step-up has a specific, finished cause. The 179-megawatt Czechnica-2 gas unit, a roughly 1.4 billion zloty project, was launched on 29 May 2025. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA, a proxy for operating cash earnings) rose from 485 million zloty in 2024 to about 718 million over the twelve months to June 2026, while quarterly capital spending has run below depreciation for three reported quarters. On 29 June 2026 the company also won contracted cogeneration support for its EC Wroclaw gas engines, so part of its revenue is no longer exposed to the power market.

The reporting is clean: a Piotroski score of 8 out of 9 (a nine-point accounting-health checklist) and results pre-announced to the decimal four times running. The June 2026 dividend of 2.58 zloty, the first since the 2021 year, shows the payout channel is open. If PGE, the 58% parent, lifts the payout at the 2027 meeting - the argument for retaining cash to build the plant has expired - or buys out the 42% it does not own, the shares re-rate toward book value.
picks.bear_thesis:
The earnings are real; the problem is that a minority shareholder cannot reach them, and nothing since 12 October has changed that.

At 30 June 2026 Kogeneracja held 16.1 million zloty of cash and 1,349.9 million zloty of 'other receivables' - more than its whole market value - most plausibly a cash-pool balance swept to the parent and lent back on the group's terms. PGE owns 58.06% and decides. On 28 May 2026 a minority pension fund asked for 6.71 zloty a share; the 11 June meeting gave 2.58 zloty, about 14% of profit, and the fund fell below 5% on 2 July.

The earnings are also flattered by a good moment. The June 2026 quarter swung to a 6.2 million zloty loss with gross profit down from 37.1 to 20.8 million. The heat tariff is cost-plus, so a supplier whose winter gross margin rose from 21.7% to 28.0% will share that gain at the next reset; the remaining coal units face rising carbon costs, and the announced full exit from coal plus the boiler tenders now under way mean a second spending wave that competes with dividends.

And the price has done the work: the shares rose from 78.50 zloty on 12 October to 87.90 at the high and 84.20 now with no announcement at all. # Kogeneracja (KGN.WA) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*As of 2 November 2026. Price used: 84.20 zloty (PLN) on the Warsaw exchange (live quote from the paid data feed, 2 November 2026; previous close 87.00, 52-week range 59.40-87.90). All figures in zloty.*

**Source note.** No earnings-call transcript exists in the paid data feed for this listing, and Kogeneracja - a Polish subsidiary of the state-controlled PGE group - does not hold English-language analyst calls. This dossier tests management's actions and public statements (results pre-announcements, the annual-meeting dividend decision, capital spending, regulatory filings) against the reported quarterly statements pulled from the paid feed on 2 November 2026. The paid news feed carries no item for this ticker since 1 October 2026. The company's own announcement list (bankier.pl, checked 2 November 2026) shows nothing after the half-year report of 8 September 2026, and the biznesradar.pl news page shows no company-specific item since then either. The web-search allowance for this run ran out after two searches, so a deeper Polish-language press check was not possible. No quotes are invented below.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story over the last two years has one spine: build gas-fired replacements for coal, switch them on, and harvest the cash. The 179-megawatt Czechnica-2 gas unit (roughly 1.4 billion zloty of investment) was launched on 29 May 2025. Through 2024 and the first half of 2025 the narrative was about spending; since the September 2025 quarter it has been about earnings. In the regulator's cogeneration-premium auction held 22-24 June 2026 the company entered its AK6-10 gas engines at EC Wroclaw (49.9 megawatts of electricity, 50 megawatts of heat) and won support (result announced 29 June 2026) - a correction to our earlier notes, which attached that premium to Czechnica-2. Company material also describes a full exit from coal across its three Wroclaw-area plants (418 megawatts of electricity and 1,080 megawatts of heat in total), and public tenders show gas- and electricity-fired water boilers being procured.

What has not changed is who decides where the cash goes. PGE owns 58.06%. The 11 June 2026 annual meeting approved a dividend of 2.58 zloty a share (about 14% of the 277 million zloty 2025 profit) - the first since the 2021 year - after a minority pension fund had asked for 6.71 zloty. For a minority shareholder the arc is: the earnings arrived, the cash mostly did not.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim / action | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| The new gas unit lifts earnings | Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) over the twelve months to 30 June 2026 were about 718 million zloty, against 485 million in 2024 | Matches |
| The capital programme is over | Quarterly capital spending of 39.2, 45.6 and 33.7 million in the last three reported quarters, below quarterly depreciation of 61-67 million | Matches - but the coal-exit plan and boiler tenders mean a second, smaller spending wave is coming |
| Results pre-announced accurately | Q1 2026 pre-announced at about 213 million, delivered 213.1 million; 2025 at about 277 million, delivered 277.0 million | Matches |
| Free cash flow is real | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow 401 million zloty | Matches, but lumpy and seasonal |
| Cash belongs to shareholders | Cash of 16.1 million zloty at 30 June 2026 against 1,349.9 million of "other receivables" (most plausibly a group cash-pool balance with PGE) | Diverges |

The June 2026 quarter showed revenue of 471.6 million zloty (up 5.7%), gross profit down to 20.8 million from 37.1 million, EBITDA flat at 67.0 million and a net loss of 6.2 million zloty. That is the normal summer trough for a heat supplier, slightly weaker than last year. The September 2026 quarter, due in late November 2026, will also be seasonally weak (a 15.0 million zloty loss a year earlier).

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Stable. Without calls, tone is read from conduct: management pre-announces winter-quarter results weeks early and to the decimal, and the June 2026 dividend - small as it is - was the first in four years. No guidance has been withdrawn and nothing defensive has been published since the half-year report of 8 September 2026.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

High. The company does not issue forward guidance in the usual sense, but its results pre-announcements have matched the final numbers four times running. No evidence of sandbagging or misses.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

No sell-side price target exists in the paid feed for this listing, and none was found on Polish market-data sites. The pressure comes from shareholders: the pension fund that asked on 28 May 2026 for 6.71 zloty got 2.58 and cut its stake below 5% on 2 July 2026. The unanswered question remains what the 1.35 billion zloty receivable is, what rate it earns, and whether it is callable.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- 🔴 (Q2 2026) net loss of 6.2 million zloty and negative operating cash flow in the summer quarter, worse than a year earlier at the gross-profit line.
- 🔴 (30 June 2026) 1,349.9 million zloty of other receivables against 16.1 million of cash - more than the company's market value, held where a minority holder cannot reach it.
- 🔴 (11 June 2026) a payout of about 14% of profit with the main build finished.
- 🔴 (October 2026) the shares rose from 78.50 to a 52-week high of 87.90 with no company announcement - the discount closed on flows, not news.
- 🟢 capital spending below depreciation for three straight reported quarters.
- 🟢 (29 June 2026) contracted cogeneration premium won for the EC Wroclaw gas engines.
- 🟢 Piotroski score of 8 out of 9 (a nine-point accounting-health checklist) and accurate pre-announcements.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

Book value per share keeps compounding - about 188 zloty at 30 June 2026 - so retained profit is kept, not lost. Interest income (13.9 million zloty in the June quarter) is double interest expense (6.7 million), consistent with the receivable being an interest-bearing group loan. Turnover on 2 November 2026 was 20,296 shares, roughly seven times the 2,845 shares of 12 October - unusually heavy for a 19% free float, and the day closed 3.2% lower after touching 81.20. The supply side drives this stock.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: strengthening at the operating level, unchanged at the shareholder level. The single thing to weigh: the value is real but controlled - PGE decides the payout and holds the cash. Size this as an access problem, not an earnings problem, and note that at 84.20 zloty the price already sits slightly above our base-case fair value.

Moat: a regulatory-licence moat - the licensed district-heating supplier to Wroclaw (about 640,000 people), with cost-plus tariffs. Narrow (returns on invested capital of about 6% on the screener's measure, about 11-12% on our post-project EBITDA basis - at or slightly above a Polish cost of capital) and stable. The secular threat is material, not terminal: the remaining coal units face rising carbon costs as free allowances for district heating phase down toward 2030, but dense-city district heat is not being displaced and the gas units are the transition answer. The cheapness is a governance and liquidity discount, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

(a) The outcome of the next tariff review by ARSESP, the São Paulo regulator. The regulated return on the asset base drives everything, and we could not verify the current review's status.
(b) Cash flowing up to the controlling group. The Cosan group is under clear market stress: CSAN3 trades at R$2.77, near its 52-week low of R$2.16 and far below its high of R$6.90. PASS3 trades at R$20.77, against a high of R$35.03. A stressed parent has every reason to pull maximum dividends out of Comgás.
(c) Brazil's high interest rates. Debt costs are high: interest expense ran R$371M in Q2-26, against R$232M in Q2-25.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red flag (Q4-25 to Q2-26): dividends above net income, funded partly by new debt. Net debt is creeping up while the parent group is under stress.
- Red flag (Q2-26): interest expense up about 60% year on year (R$371M vs R$232M). Q2's net interest cost of R$239M was lower than the gross figure only because of an unusually large R$132M of interest income.
- Red flag (live quote, 2026-11-09): CGAS3 traded zero shares. The stock sits at its 52-week low of R$120, which looks like a stale last print. The real exit price for size is unknowable.
- Red flag: the screener's cash-flow and DCF numbers are inflated by FMP's inconsistent capex capture.
- Green flag (2022-2026): gross profit and EBITDA are steady through a large swing in gas costs. The regulated margin model works.
- Green flag: return on invested capital of about 19%, and the effective tax rate fell in Q2-26 (17%). The concession monopoly is intact.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
- Share-count noise: Q2-25 shows 103.9M weighted shares against 132.5M everywhere else. This is an FMP artifact, not dilution.
- Investment is steady at about R$1.5B a year, which grows the asset base and therefore future allowed revenue. That is the real compounding engine of a regulated utility.
- The parent and grandparent re-rated sharply lower while CGAS3/CGAS5 moved much less (CGAS5 is down from R$139.96 to R$115.12, about 18%). The minority line is trading as a bond proxy, not on the parent's distress.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: **stable**. Operating earnings power is flat-to-growing in real terms. Capital allocation is controller-friendly: about 100% payout, partly debt-funded.

The single most important thing to weigh: **this is a fairly priced, illiquid, high-payout bond proxy, not a deep-value mispricing.** The 5.5x free-cash-flow and 70% DCF discount that flagged it are artifacts of missing capex. On consistent numbers it trades at about 10x free cash flow, about 10x earnings and about 6.2x EV/EBITDA (enterprise value, meaning market value plus net debt, divided by EBITDA). That is broadly where Brazil's cost of capital puts a regulated utility. A buyer also cannot easily get in or out of the common line.

**Moat:** a regulatory license, the exclusive São Paulo distribution concession. Width is **narrow but real**: the monopoly is total, but the regulator caps the return, and returns have been stable rather than rising. **Secular threat:** manageable. Electrification is a long-run headwind for gas distribution, but Brazil's gas market is still expanding (industrial and pre-salt supply, biomethane), so it does not impair terminal value in the next decade. The cheapness, such as it is, reflects Brazil rates and the stressed group around it, not a shrinking base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

Earning roughly EUR 1bn of operating profit, this business alone justifies most of the share price at a contractor multiple. Second, APRR (the motorway network, about 52% economically owned) remains a legal monopoly with operating margins above 70% and roughly nine years to run. Even after the proposed levy - Morgan Stanley puts the hit at 9-12% of 2027 earnings for the exposed groups - its remaining cash flow is worth tens of euros per share. Third, there are real hidden assets: a stake in Getlink (the Channel Tunnel operator), airports, other concessions and treasury shares. France has no parliamentary majority; a budget forced through by special constitutional powers can be harsher than the draft, and the next government could revisit the concession contracts themselves. Operationally, light-vehicle traffic is falling on high oil prices tied to the Middle East conflict (2026-08-26) and road-building is down 5% on weaker local-authority spending. Earnings per share were flat in 2025 (+0.6%), free cash flow fell 12.2%, gross margin is contracting (12.9%), return on invested capital is a thin 6.3% and the Altman-Z solvency score is 1.0 because of EUR 10.8bn of net debt (including leases) at 2026-06-30. What would confirm the bear: article 22 passed at or above 12.2%, a second year of surtax, a dividend cut below the 45% payout, or a works margin slipping below 4%.
picks.consensus_delta: The street is not pricing terminal decline - consensus targets sit around EUR 155-158 with a buy rating across about 17 analysts (MarketScreener / ad-hoc-news, October 2026) - but the tape is: the stock sits about 2% above its 52-week low and 22% below its 200-day average. Where we disagree with the market is the size of the political hit. Morgan Stanley's 9-12% cut to 2027 earnings is a one-year earnings figure; for APRR's remaining roughly nine years it is worth about EUR 7 per share in present value on our numbers, against a share-price fall of about EUR 48 from the high. The market is extrapolating the fiscal clawback into the works business, which has no such exposure and a record order book. We also disagree with the bulls: consensus near EUR 155 looks stale on concession value, and Goldman's EUR 127 (2026-10-20) is closer to our EUR 128.
picks.valley_of_death: The next three to nine months: (1) the 2027 finance-law debate - article 22 could be passed at or above 12.2%, by special constitutional powers, possibly with a renewed corporate surtax; (2) Q3 revenue around 2026-11-11/12 could show further light-vehicle traffic declines while oil stays high; (3) full-year results in late February 2027 carry dividend risk - management said the 45% payout is not a floor. picks.positioning_washout: Smart-money score 4/100 and the price 2% up its 52-week range show holders have already been selling. picks.moderator_conclusion: Buy now. Last time we said Eiffage was a genuinely good business at a modestly good price and that we would wait for a wash-out - a sharp sell-off by forced or non-fundamental sellers. It has arrived: the shares fell 10.8% from EUR 109.20 to EUR 97.42 by 2026-10-23 and trade at EUR 99.70 today, about a third below the 52-week high. The thesis holds. The discount is real, the business is clean, and the risk is a lower fair value rather than a broken company. Size it as a deep-value position with a political tail, and re-check after the finance-law vote and the February 2027 results.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Eiffage (FGR.PA) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-10-26. Live price EUR 99.70 on Euronext Paris (FMP quote, 2026-10-26; previous close EUR 97.42; 52-week range EUR 96.26-147.50). All figures in euros.

Short version: management has done what it said it would for three reporting periods running. Contracting (the "works" side: construction, infrastructure, energy systems) keeps growing its order book and margins hold. The concession side (mainly APRR, the motorway network Eiffage controls with about a 52% economic stake) is where the stress is, and that stress comes from outside the company: high oil prices cutting car traffic, and a French government that wants to more than double a special levy on motorway operators. The share price has fallen by about a third from its 52-week high. That fall is a verdict on French politics and on a concession that ends in the mid-2030s, not on the quality of management's execution.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **FY2024 results call (2025-02-27).** The story was scale and visibility. A record order book, up 11% year on year, strengthened by "the two major contracts of the EPR 2 [and] Line 15 East", about EUR 5 billion of new-nuclear work, more than EUR 1.1 billion of offshore-wind orders at Smulders, and a "total change of scale in Germany" through the Salvia and EQOS acquisitions. Management formalised a 45% dividend payout policy. The concession expiry question (what replaces APRR's profits once the concession ends) got a candid "it's still far too early to be able to say".
- **H1 2025 call (2025-08-29).** Same story, more Europe: revenue up 8.4%, growth in Europe outside France of 17.4%, order book up another 4%. A new theme arrived: the French "exceptional contribution" corporate surtax (EUR 135 million booked in the first half, about EUR 200 million for the year). Management called it "temporary" but conceded that "things are pretty unstable right now".
- **H1 2026 call (2026-08-26).** The framing moves to long-term structural demand: "sovereignty of energy, development of new mobilities, necessary adaptation to the climate change". The works side is still advancing (order book up again "on all of the branches lines of business"). For the first time the concessions are described as a drag: "performance is impacted by the decrease of the motorway traffic of the LVs [light vehicles] given the persistence of the oil price, which is high, direct consequence of the Middle East conflict." Road-building (Eiffage Route) is down 5% on weaker local-authority spending. Data centres are framed with deliberate restraint: one hyperscale project under way, perhaps three at most "on a frame of 6 to 12 months".

Net arc: the contracting growth story widened over the period (Germany, nuclear, grid, offshore wind, data-centre power), while the concession story narrowed from "cash machine" to "cash machine under political and traffic pressure".

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Evidence in the financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Very strong year... dynamic growth" (2025-02-27); revenue growth in 2025 and 2026 | Revenue EUR 19.2bn (2021) to 26.1bn (2025), +8.8% in 2025, 3-year compound growth 7.8% | Matches |
| Construction "back to growth" from 2025 (promised 2025-02-27) | H1 2025 construction +3.6% (2025-08-29); H1 2026 "construction line is back to growth" | Delivered |
| Earnings growth | Net income EUR 753m (2021) to 1.04bn (2024), then 1.02bn (2025): earnings per share +0.6% in 2025 | Poorer than the story. The French surtax (about EUR 200m) explains the 2025 stall; underlying growth continued |
| Margins "of good quality... no notion of impairment of the margin level" (2026-08-26) | Gross margin 12.9% and described as contracting; net margin 3.9%; margin 0.25 standard deviations below its historical peak | Broadly matches. The gross-margin drift is mostly mix (more acquired energy-services revenue), not price erosion, but it is a drift |
| Cash generation "extremely good" | Free-cash-flow margin 10.8%, price-to-free-cash-flow about 3.2x; free cash flow fell 12.2% in 2025 | Strong in level. Note that group free cash flow includes 100% of APRR, of which about 48% belongs to minority holders, and concession cash is a wasting asset that runs off at expiry |
| Balance sheet comfort ("cash available is significant", 2025-08-29) | Net debt EUR 10.80bn including leases (EUR 9.66bn excluding leases) at 2026-06-30, mostly concession debt; Altman-Z (a solvency score) 1.0 | Normal for a concession group, but leverage sits on the asset now under fiscal attack |
| Returns | Return on equity 14.6%; return on invested capital 6.3% | Modest. Capital-heavy concessions dilute the high-return contracting business |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: **Stable**, with the confidence shifting from the concessions to the works side.

- 2025-02-27: offensive. "Once again, a very strong year both in terms of earnings as well as order intake."
- 2025-08-29: offensive on operations, defensive on taxation. Results "went very well according to our expectations and confirms our outlook"; on French tax, "we do not have more visibility than you have".
- 2026-08-26: confident on works, matter-of-fact on concessions. Outlook for higher activity and results in 2026 confirmed; organic-growth guidance of 2-3% for energy systems reaffirmed ("the assumption of 2%, 3% organic growth is the right one"). On data centres, notably careful: "do not expect a tremendous jump overnight in activity."

Guidance has stayed qualitative (direction, not numbers) throughout, which is this company's long-standing style rather than a new retreat.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

- Promised a return to construction volume growth in 2025: delivered by H1 2025.
- 2025 outlook "confirmed" in August 2025: full-year revenue +8.8% delivered; net income flat only because of the surtax management had flagged in advance.
- 2026 outlook (growth in activity and results) confirmed on 2026-08-26; press coverage reports half-year profit up 11%.
- Earnings beat rate of 3 of the last 5 quarters (60%): neither sandbagging nor serial misses.

Reliability: **High** on what management controls; it does not and cannot guide French fiscal policy.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **The APRR expiry** (BNP Paribas, 2025-02-27): how will lost concession profit be replaced? The answer was a non-answer ("far too early"), and that remains the single largest unresolved question in the valuation.
- **French tax and the dividend** (Jefferies, 2025-02-27 and 2025-08-29): is the 45% payout a floor? Management: "it's not a floor". The surtax "will have an effect on dividends". Analysts were right to push: French fiscal risk has since escalated (see below).
- **Offshore wind** (Citigroup, 2025-08-29): no US exposure, but caution that European clients are stretched by their US problems.
- **Data-centre opportunity** (2026-08-26): analysts pushed on a large addressable market; management deliberately talked it down.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: Concession traffic falling (2026-08-26) because high oil prices, linked to the Middle East conflict, are cutting light-vehicle trips. Tolls are regulated, so lost volume is lost margin.
- Red: The French 2027 finance bill (article 22, filed at the National Assembly on 2026-10-01 after the government announced it on 2026-09-29) would raise the levy on long-distance transport infrastructure from a flat 4.6% to as much as 12.2% for the most profitable operators, and bars passing it through to tolls. Morgan Stanley estimates a 9-12% hit to 2027 earnings for the exposed groups. As of 2026-10-22 article 22 had not yet been debated.
- Red: The 2025 surtax already showed the state treats concession profits as a fiscal reserve; the dividend policy was explicitly "not a floor".
- Red: Eiffage Route down 5% (2026-08-26) on weaker local-authority orders.
- Green: Order book at a record and growing in every business line (2026-02 and 2026-08-26).
- Green: Long-dated, non-cyclical wins: about EUR 5bn of new-nuclear work (2025-02-27), a 12-year Arabelle Solutions nuclear components partnership, a 25-year Paris district-heating concession, a 5-year RTE grid-buildings contract, EUR 120m of high-voltage work for an AI campus (all 2026-08-26).
- Green: Disciplined mergers and acquisitions in markets it already knows (Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg through Baatz), no adventurism.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary moved from "record order book" to "sovereignty of energy" and "adaptation to the climate change": management is positioning the works business as a European-infrastructure franchise that stands on its own, as it should with APRR's end date approaching.
- The new head of concessions (Camille Bonenfant-Jeanneney, from January 2025, background in EU institutions, RATP and ENGIE) is a regulatory and stakeholder profile, not a traffic engineer: a hint that the next decade of concessions is a negotiation with the state.
- On treasury shares (5.8% of capital in early 2025): "we're not going to cancel". Buybacks are opportunistic and kept as a resource, not returned outright.
- Getlink stake: "prepared to strengthen, but we don't plan to take control". It is a financial option, not an empire-building signal.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **Stable.** The works franchise is strengthening and the concession franchise is being squeezed from outside; together they net to steady.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **how much of today's discount is a permanent transfer of APRR's cash flow to the French state.** If article 22 passes as drafted and traffic stays weak, the concession's remaining roughly nine years of cash flow shrink by a mid-single-digit euro amount per share in present value. If the levy is softened, much of the 2026 sell-off is overdone. The works business, which carries no such political exposure, is on its own worth a large part of the current share price.

Moat: the concessions hold a regulatory-license moat (a legal monopoly on the motorway network), wide while it lasts but finite (APRR and AREA expire in the mid-2030s) and now visibly subject to fiscal clawback. The works business has a scale-and-capability moat (few European contractors can deliver nuclear, high-voltage and hyperscale work), narrow but real, and widening in energy systems. Returns are modest (return on invested capital 6.3%) and stable rather than falling, so this is not an eroding moat in the sense of a melting franchise. On balance: narrow, stable.

Secular threat: none of the listed structural forces (artificial-intelligence displacement, energy transition and so on) threatens the terminal value; the energy transition is a tailwind for the works side. The real terminal question is the concession end date and the regulatory model that replaces it, a known, dated, political risk that is manageable rather than terminal. The cheapness therefore looks more like a fear print on French politics than a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: Geely is one of the few mass-market Chinese carmakers that still makes real money in a price war. In H1 2026 (results call 2026-08-17) it earned close to RMB 10 billion attributable profit at about a 5.6% margin while management put the industry average at 1.6%, and it ranked first in China by retail sales. Two engines are offsetting a shrinking home market: exports (the annual target was hit by mid-year, raised from 640,000 to 920,000, and nine-month exports reached 797,670, up 169%, per CnEVPost on 2026-10-01) and the premium ZEEKR brand (+97% in H1 2026), which lifts revenue per car. The One Geely programme is cutting costs measurably (admin ratio 1.9% to 1.7%, R&D ratio 5.5% to 5.2%, model count down 20%). The balance sheet carries RMB 56.6 billion of net cash at 2026-06-30, roughly 40% of the HK$148 billion market value, and the company pays out 30% of profit. At HK$13.71 the stock trades at roughly 7x annualised core earnings and a low single-digit multiple of free cash flow. If margins merely hold near current levels and the market re-rates toward 10-11x earnings, fair value is in the mid-to-high HK$20s. Conditions: gross margin stays near 16-17%, exports keep growing despite trade barriers, and no large value-destroying acquisition consumes the cash.
picks.bear_thesis: The cheapness may be deserved. Returns on capital are poor (ROIC about 2.5%, ROE 11.6%), reported EPS was flat in 2025 at RMB 1.63, the 2024 jump was about half one-off gains (core profit RMB 8.5 billion vs reported RMB 16.6 billion, per the 2025-03-12 call), the screener shows 0 of 2 recent quarters beating consensus, and latest-quarter EPS fell 22% year on year. The home market shrank by double digits in H1 2026 and domestic sales fell about 25% in August 2026; all of Geely's growth now comes from exports, which are exposed to tariffs and anti-subsidy actions in Europe and elsewhere, and exports slipped 3% month on month in September 2026. Management itself flagged rising chip and raw-material costs on 2026-08-17 and admitted 'a lack of blockbuster product' in the mainstream segment. The headline free cash flow and net cash are flattered by supplier credit (car makers pay suppliers late), so a slowdown could reverse working capital and shrink the cash pile quickly. If net margin falls toward 3% and the market keeps a 6x multiple, the stock could trade near HK$11.
picks.consensus_delta: The market is pricing Geely as if the Chinese price war will crush its margins the way it has crushed most rivals' profits. The numbers so far say otherwise: H1 2026 net margin about 5.6% against an industry average of 1.6% (2026-08-17), gross margin near 16-17%, and growth shifted to exports and the premium ZEEKR brand. At HK$13.71 the stock trades around 7x annualised core earnings with about 40% of its market value in net cash. Where we disagree with the market: we think it extrapolates the sector's losses onto the one large private carmaker that is still profitable. Where the market has a point: reported EPS is flat, the latest quarter fell 22%, and returns on capital are low; so our fair value assumes no margin expansion and a below-peer-leader multiple. No dated analyst consensus target could be verified via FMP (no coverage for this listing), so we cite none.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead): Q4 2026 and Q1 2027. Domestic demand is shrinking (domestic sales -25% in August 2026), input costs (chips, raw materials) are rising, and Beijing's price-war curbs have not stopped discounting. Exports, now the only growth engine, slipped 3% month on month in September 2026 and face tariff and anti-subsidy risk in Europe and emerging markets. A weak October-December sales run or a second-half margin miss at the March 2027 full-year results could push the stock lower before any re-rating; supplier-credit unwinding could also shrink the reported cash pile. picks.bull_thesis: JD Logistics is China's largest self-operated warehouse-and-delivery network (about 1,600 warehouses and more than 34 million square metres, end-2025), anchored by JD.com volume and growing fast with outside customers. Revenue rose from RMB 104.7B in 2021 to RMB 217.2B in 2025, and first-half 2026 revenue was RMB 124.7B, up 26.5%. Profit is now catching up. Management promised on 2026-03-05 that 2026 profit would improve, and it delivered: IFRS (reported) net income was RMB 0.88B in Q1 and RMB 2.41B in Q2 2026, and adjusted operating profit rose 39.9% in the half. Cost ratios are falling. In Q2 2026 staff costs were 34.2% of revenue (-1.0 point), rent 5.3% (-1.1 points) and operating expenses 6.4% (-0.5 points), as automation (more than 1,000 driverless delivery vehicles and robot-run warehouses) takes cost out. Deppon, the freight subsidiary that dragged on 2025, is 'on the track of recovery' (2026-08-13), and the CFO guided that operating margin 'will be further improved in the second half'. Overseas warehouses (doubled in 2025 to nearly 2 million square metres) and the JoyExpress delivery brand in Europe and Saudi Arabia add a second growth curve. At HK$10.26 the stock trades on about 7.6 times trailing earnings (about RMB 7.4B over the last twelve months), with about RMB 17.3B of net cash before leases, roughly a third of its RMB 53B market value. It sits near the bottom of its 52-week range (HK$9.51 to HK$16.76). Sell-side targets cluster around HK$18.4, though the snapshots date from mid-2026 and are stale. The case needs three things to hold: the second-half margin improvement shows up, Deppon stops dragging, and revenue growth holds in the high teens.
picks.bear_thesis: The cheapness is in the earnings, not the cash or the returns. Return on invested capital is about 1% and the net margin about 3%, so a scale network that protects volume has not shown pricing power. Gross margin fell 0.9 points to 9.7% in Q2 2026 even as revenue grew 24%. More of the growth now comes from consolidated, low-margin on-demand riders, with outsourcing costs up 40.5% to 37% of revenue, rather than from integrated supply-chain work, where external revenue growth slowed to 12.5%. Free cash flow fell 26.7% in 2025, and the latest trailing figure in our data feed is zero. After about RMB 18.7B of lease liabilities, the 'net cash' becomes about RMB 1.4B of net debt, and automation spending will be 'higher than that of 2025' (2026-03-05) with no payback disclosed. Dependence on the parent is rising, not falling: JD Group supplied RMB 19.88B of RMB 30.17B integrated supply-chain revenue in Q2 2026. That means related-party pricing, not market pricing, sets much of the profit, and a parent pushing a European retail venture (Joybuy) can lean on its logistics arm. Chinese express pricing is competitive and the industry is maturing (management conceded the slowdown on 2026-08-13). Energy and wage costs are rising, and margins dipped in the 2021-22 inflation (gross margin 6.9% to 5.5%). If the 2026-11-17 third-quarter results show margins stalling, the stock can stay a low-multiple, low-return logistics utility at 6 to 7 times earnings, with no discount closing.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market: the sell side is more bullish than we are. Mid-2026 snapshots show about 18 of 19 analysts at buy, with targets around HK$18.4 (JPMorgan HK$17 on 2026-07-22, Macquarie HK$16 on 2026-07-08, Nomura HK$20 and Citi HK$18 in May 2026). Those are stale and were set when the stock was HK$13-15. The tape has gone the other way: the stock fell from a HK$16.76 high to HK$10.26, 18% below its 200-day average. Reported profit is recovering on schedule, so 7.6 times is too low for earnings growing in the mid-teens. But the street's HK$18 assumes margin expansion that the Q2 gross margin (-0.9 points) has not yet shown, and it ignores the lease burden. We underwrite HK$13.86, not HK$18.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) starts tomorrow with the Q3 2026 results (2026-11-17). # JD Logistics (2618.HK) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*As of 2026-11-16. Transcripts read: Q3 2025 (2025-11-13), Q4/FY 2025 (2026-03-05), Q2 2026 (2026-08-13). Figures in RMB unless stated; the stock trades in Hong Kong dollars (HK$10.26 on 2026-11-16, FMP quote). Third-quarter 2026 results are due 2026-11-17 (FMP earnings calendar).*

**Takeaway:** JD Logistics is a fast-growing, thin-margin logistics network whose profits are now rising again after a soft 2025, and management has broadly done what it said it would on profit. The two things to watch are the quality of the growth (much of the 2026 revenue jump is a consolidated, low-margin on-demand delivery business, not the higher-value supply-chain work) and cash conversion, which the latest data feed reports as roughly zero over the trailing twelve months.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-11-13):** the story was integrated supply chain (ISC - running a customer's warehousing, inventory and delivery end to end) growth of 45.8% to RMB 13.1B, "targeted investments" in overseas and timeliness, and the new full-time food-delivery rider force. Profit was the soft spot: non-IFRS (adjusted, excluding items like share-based pay) net profit RMB 2.02B, attributable profit down about 8% year on year.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-03-05):** the CEO framed 2025 around three differentiators - ISC, customer experience, and automation/AI. Overseas warehouse space was doubled as promised (nearly 200 bonded/overseas warehouses, about 2 million square metres) and the JoyExpress delivery brand launched in Saudi Arabia and Europe. Deppon (the freight subsidiary) was conceded as a 2025 margin drag with "positive improvement" promised for 2026.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-08-13):** the CFO led with profit, not growth: revenue RMB 64.1B (+24.3%), adjusted operating profit +11.6% for the quarter and +39.9% for the half. The emphasis has shifted from "capacity building" to "operating leverage", with overseas now called "an important second growth curve" and the Joybuy European retail venture of the parent JD.com a named driver.

The arc is from investment to harvest - but the headline growth has quietly changed composition: ISC revenue growth slowed to 12.1% in Q2 2026, while "other customers" (express, freight and the newly consolidated on-demand riders) grew 37.6%.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| "High-quality revenue growth" (every call) | Revenue RMB 104.7B (2021) to 217.2B (2025); H1 2026 RMB 124.7B, +26.5% | Corroborated on volume. Quality is mixed: Q2 2026 gross margin 9.7%, down 0.9pp year on year; outsourcing costs +40.5% to 37% of revenue on the on-demand consolidation. |
| 2026 profit would show "positive improvement" (2026-03-05) | IFRS net income Q1 2026 RMB 0.88B, Q2 RMB 2.41B; H1 adjusted operating profit +39.9% | Delivered. Trailing-twelve-month IFRS net income about RMB 7.4B (Q3 25 2.03 + Q4 25 2.04 + Q1 26 0.88 + Q2 26 2.41). |
| Core business margins rising, Deppon the drag (2026-08-13) | Group gross margin fell; management says the "original core business" margin rose | Plausible but unaudited in the transcript - no segment margin given. Cannot verify the split. |
| Overseas warehouse doubling by end-2025 (2025-11-13) | Confirmed achieved on 2026-03-05 | Delivered. |
| Strong cash generation (implied by the cheap price-to-free-cash-flow) | FY 2025 price/FCF about 5x; FMP trailing FCF reported as 0; FCF growth -26.7% in 2025 | Unclear. A "0" trailing figure may be a data gap, but the falling 2025 FCF is real. Lease payments (RMB 18.7B of lease liabilities) sit below operating cash flow and make FCF look better than owner cash. |
| Balance sheet strength | Cash RMB 22.47B vs borrowings RMB 5.17B (2026-06-30) | Corroborated: about RMB 17.3B net cash before leases; about RMB 1.4B net debt once RMB 18.7B of leases are counted. |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable, edging up.** Q3 2025 was defensive on profit ("lay the foundation for long-term business growth"; "In 2026, still I'm not in the right time to make the forecast"). Q4 2025 was more assertive on 2026 profit but vague on numbers. Q2 2026 is the most confident: "The operating margin will be further improved in the second half" and express growth "more than double the industry average". The shift is from offensive investment language to an operating-leverage message - a healthy direction - but specifics remain thin: no margin targets, no capex number, and no Deppon figures.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Management gives qualitative, not numeric, guidance. What they promised, they delivered: the overseas-warehouse doubling (promised 2025-11-13, confirmed 2026-03-05) and the 2026 profit recovery (promised 2026-03-05, H1 operating profit +39.9%). The screener records 4 of the last 5 quarters beating estimates. Because the targets are soft, sandbagging is hard to detect. **Reliability: Medium-High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Deppon's profitability** (asked 2026-03-05 and 2026-08-13): answered only with "on the track of recovery", never numbers.
- **Automation capex and returns** (2025-11-13, 2026-03-05): management says investment will be "higher than that of 2025" but gives no figure or payback.
- **Express industry slowdown** (2026-08-13): answered with relative growth claims, not unit pricing.
- **2026 revenue outlook** (2025-11-13): explicitly declined.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: gross margin down 0.9pp in Q2 2026 even as revenue grew 24%.
- Red: growth mix shifting toward consolidated, low-margin on-demand delivery (outsourcing costs +40.5%, Q2 2026).
- Red: free cash flow fell 26.7% in 2025 and the latest trailing figure is reported as zero; lease burden is large.
- Red: external ISC growth slowed to 12.5% in Q2 2026 from much higher rates in 2025.
- Green: profit recovery delivered on schedule (H1 2026 adjusted operating profit +39.9%).
- Green: cost ratios improving - staff costs 34.2% of revenue (-1.0pp), rent 5.3% (-1.1pp), operating expenses 6.4% (-0.5pp) in Q2 2026.
- Green: about RMB 17.3B of net cash before leases - roughly a third of the market value.
- Green: overseas build-out delivered to target.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The CFO, not the CEO, opened the Q2 2026 call and led with operating profit - a sign the investor message is now about margins.
- "Technology exports" appeared on 2026-08-13: the company now talks of selling its warehouse robots to outside customers - early, unquantified.
- The dependence on the parent is rising, not falling: JD Group ISC revenue RMB 19.88B of RMB 30.17B in Q2 2026, with Joybuy (JD's European retail) named as a driver. Related-party pricing is a governance lever worth watching.
- Energy-cost language ("fluctuation of the energy industry", 2026-08-13) shows management expects input-cost pressure; vehicle costs nonetheless fell 0.2pp as a share of revenue.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Growth is robust and profit is recovering, but margins are not structurally widening yet, and the mix shift toward on-demand delivery offsets the core ISC improvement.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** whether the cheapness is in the earnings or in the cash. On earnings the stock is about 7.6 times trailing profit with a third of its value in pre-lease net cash; on owner cash (after lease payments and rising automation capex) the case is much thinner. The 2026-11-17 third-quarter results are the next read on both.

**Moat:** scale-cost and network (the densest self-operated warehouse network in China, about 1,600 warehouses and 34 million square metres, plus the JD.com anchor volume). Returns are low (ROIC about 1%, net margin about 3%), so the moat protects volume more than pricing - narrow, stable. **Secular threat:** manageable - automation and autonomous delivery are being adopted by the company itself rather than used against it, and e-commerce channel shift is a tailwind for a logistics provider. The cheapness reads as a fear print on China and thin margins, not a shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

At 9 times (a discount to express peers for about 1% ROIC and parent dependence) that is RMB 66.6B.
