picks.bull_thesis: Petrobras is a low-cost deepwater producer being priced as a political hazard. Production has risen about 37% since May 2024 to roughly 3.5 million barrels of oil equivalent a day, the natural decline of its older fields has been cut from about 10% to about 3% a year, and 11 platforms run above their design capacity without new spending (earnings call, 2026-11-11). Refineries ran at 99% in the third quarter of 2026. That machine produced R$101.8 billion of free cash flow over the trailing twelve months (to 2026-09-30) against a market value of about R$648 billion - a free-cash-flow yield of about 16% at today's price. Net income for the third quarter was R$39.75 billion, up 21.5% year on year, and debt including leases fell by R$33 billion in one quarter. The dividend rule (45% of free cash flow while gross debt sits under the ceiling) was applied to the letter on 2026-11-10, two weeks after the election, which is the single most important proof that the fourth Lula term has not yet bent the payout. Brent near US$93 still sits above the roughly US$65-70 level at which Petrobras covers both its capital spending and the base dividend. The shares have fallen from R$66.49 in mid-October to R$50.31, about 24%, on the election and the oil pullback rather than on anything the business did. If the 2027-2031 strategic plan on 2026-11-23 keeps the payout rule and the debt ceiling, the market has room to re-rate the shares toward our fair value of about R$61, with a further leg toward R$74 if Brent holds near US$90.
picks.bear_thesis: The cash is real but its destination is political. Capital spending rose from R$23.0 billion in the second quarter to R$27.7 billion in the third, lease commitments are R$229 billion and still rising (more support vessels and tankers, earnings call 2026-11-11), and the quarterly payout fell from R$17.4 billion to R$15.3 billion even though the formula did not change. Management openly says it smooths fuel prices rather than following import parity because chasing parity 'lost money and lost market share', so Brazilian consumers are partly shielded from oil spikes at shareholders' expense, and a fourth Lula term (won 2026-10-25) raises the odds this widens. Reported interest in Venezuela (Reuters, 2026-11-11) and in buying BP's stake in a Brazilian discovery (2026-11-12) show capital going where the state wants it. The 2026 free cash flow was earned at Brent well above US$90; at US$65 and a firmer fuel-price cap, normalised free cash flow falls to roughly R$60-65 billion, gross margin (43.7%, already contracting) compresses, and earnings per share would look more like 2024's R$2.84 than today's R$11. Three-year revenue growth is -9.3% a year: there is no growth cushion. If the strategic plan raises capital spending again or loosens the gross-debt ceiling that gates the dividend, the stock can trade back toward the mid-R$30s, where it sat in early 2026 (52-week low R$30.99).
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market: the street is pricing Petrobras as if the fourth Lula term will turn the payout rule into a dead letter. The first post-election data point says otherwise - the 2026-11-10 payout followed the 45%-of-free-cash-flow formula exactly. At R$50.31 the shares sit near a 16% trailing free-cash-flow yield; even on our mid-cycle Brent assumption (about US$75-80) the yield is about 12%. The market is right that capital spending and leases are drifting up and that fuel prices are smoothed, which is why our fair value already carries a political discount (4.6 times EBITDA, not the majors' multiple). Analyst consensus for the preferred shares is about R$57.62 (Clube Acionista, November 2026), and targets have been cut after the election (Bradesco BBI R$62 to R$55) and after results (Itau BBA R$64 to R$58), so the street has already moved toward caution - our edge is modest, not contrarian.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) runs through the 2027-2031 strategic plan on 2026-11-23 and the first months of the new government term. The specific risks: a capital-spending increase or a loosened gross-debt ceiling in the plan (which would shrink the free cash flow that the dividend is computed on); a government push to cap diesel and gasoline prices as Brent swings; and politically directed deals (Venezuela interest, Reuters 2026-11-11; BP stake talks, 2026-11-12). Oil is the other lever: Brent's 50-day average is about US$104 against about US$93 today, so a further retreat to the US$70s would cut free cash flow by roughly a quarter. There is no debt-maturity wall (net debt including leases falling; ex-lease net debt about R$70 billion) and no liquidity risk.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure is modest. The shares fell about 24% from R$66.49 (2026-10-16) to R$50.31 (2026-11-16) on a country-wide sell-off after the 2026-10-25 election and the oil pullback - a sector-wide and country-wide de-rating rather than forced selling by holders who must sell regardless of value. Foreign emerging-market funds trimming Brazil and dividend-focused holders reacting to a smaller quarterly cheque (R$15.3 billion versus R$17.4 billion) are the sellers that could push the price through R$50. If the strategic plan cuts the payout rule outright, yield-focused holders would become mechanical sellers - but that would also change the thesis, and we would re-debate.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near R$50, which the country-wide sell-off after the election and the oil retracement could deliver. The thesis holds, and the price is only about 0.6% above our level (R$50.31 on 2026-11-16). Nothing dated since our last look on 2026-11-09 changes the committee's answer. The third-quarter results on 2026-11-10 backed the thesis - record output, R$31.1 billion of quarterly free cash flow, net debt including leases down to R$299.4 billion, and a R$15.3 billion payout that followed the 45%-of-free-cash-flow rule exactly two weeks after the election - but they also showed capital spending and lease costs rising, which is why we leave fair value at about R$61 rather than raising it. At R$50 the base case sits about 22% above the entry price, enough to clear the 20% bar this market backdrop requires, and the adverse case of about R$36 (Brent near US$65 plus heavier fuel-price interference) is the real risk; there is no structural floor. Conviction stays at 3: the business is cheap and well run operationally, but the value depends on one shared factor (oil) and on a government that now has four more years to direct the cash. The value case alone rates a 4 - the discount is real but not yet large enough for a 5. Watch the 2027-2031 plan on 2026-11-23: a higher capital-spending path or a looser debt ceiling would cut fair value and would be a dated reason to revisit.
picks.forcing_function: The catalyst - what forces the re-rating - is the 2027-2031 strategic plan due 2026-11-23 (per the 2026-11-11 earnings call). If it keeps the 45%-of-free-cash-flow rule and the gross-debt ceiling and holds capital spending near the current run-rate, the post-election discount can narrow toward our R$61 fair value. Beyond that, the quarterly payout announcements (next with fourth-quarter results in early 2027) are the recurring proof points.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# PETR3.SA (Petrobras, common shares, Sao Paulo, Brazilian reais) - deep dive on management and the setup
As of 2026-11-16. Live price R$50.31 (FMP quote, PETR3.SA, Sao Paulo listing). Brent about US$93 (FMP, 2026-11-16), down from a peak near US$119 this year.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
Across the five calls on file (2025-05-14, 2025-08-08, 2026-03-06, 2026-08-06, 2026-11-11) the story moved from defence to offence.
- **Q1-2025 (2025-05-14):** a cost-and-caution call. Brent had fallen from about US$84 to US$75; the president framed the year as "challenging" and promised cost cuts "so that we can have the best results possible for our investors, whether they are in the government or private".
- **Q2-2025 to Q4-2025:** the defence of capital expenditure (capex, money spent on new platforms and wells). Management answered repeated questions on why capex was cut mid-2024 and then raised again, and leaned on the production ramp as proof the spend works. Extraordinary dividends were openly described as harder to pay "with lower revenue".
- **2026 (Q2 and Q3 calls):** with Brent spiking on the US-Iran war, the narrative became production records. On 2026-11-11 the president said output reached about 3.51 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, up 37% from May 2024, with 11 platforms running above nameplate (about 280,000 barrels a day "with no CapEx for the platforms") and refineries at 99% utilisation in Q3-2026.
- What faded: extraordinary dividends. What grew: capex, leased support vessels and the "energy security for Brazil" framing, which arrives just as President Lula won a fourth term (2026-10-25).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Management claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Record production lifts cash generation | Q3-2026 operating cash flow R$58.8B, free cash flow (cash from operations minus capex) R$31.1B; Q2-2026 R$36.7B; trailing-twelve-month (TTM) free cash flow R$101.8B (FMP, period to 2026-09-30) | Matches, but at Brent averaging well above US$90. |
| Profit is growing | Q3-2026 net income R$39.75B, up 21.5% year on year (Reuters, 2026-11-10); TTM diluted earnings per share R$11.03 vs R$8.54 for FY2025 | Matches; 2024's R$2.84 shows how far earnings swing with oil and one-offs. |
| Dividends follow a 45%-of-free-cash-flow rule | Q3-2026 payout approved R$15.3B (R$1.1873 per share, filing 2026-11-10, paid Feb/Mar 2027) vs 45% x R$31.1B = R$14.0B | Matches the formula; the payout is shrinking quarter to quarter because capex is rising, not because the rule moved. |
| Capital discipline | Capex R$27.7B in Q3-2026 vs R$23.0B in Q2-2026; lease liabilities R$229.3B against R$132.6B of borrowings (2026-09-30); the Q3 call revised the lease-cost outlook to the lower band and flagged more support vessels | Mixed. Spend is rising and is increasingly off-balance-sheet-like (leases). |
| Pricing is market-based | The Q3 call says chasing import parity daily "lost money and lost market share", so prices are deliberately smoothed | This is a policy of under-passing oil spikes to Brazilian consumers. |
| Balance sheet is healthy | Net debt incl. leases R$299.4B at 2026-09-30, down from R$332.4B at 2026-06-30; ex-lease net debt about R$70B | Matches; deleveraging is real. |

Gross margin of 43.7% is described as contracting in the scan, and three-year revenue growth is -9.3% a year: the cash flow is an oil-price story, not a growth story.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
**Rising on operations, guarded on payouts.** Q1-2025 was defensive ("redoubled efforts"). By Q3-2026 the president was emphatic ("You can certainly believe me when I say that it is record-breaking numbers"). On dividends the language stayed cautious throughout ("we need to wait now for dividends"). The CFO's closing line on 2026-11-11 that "the specific lags in our results do not change our investment theory" is a defensive tell: the quarter had a cost and lease line that analysts noticed.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Production guidance was met or beaten in 2025 and raised in 2026 (3.3-3.4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, per Q3-2026 coverage). Capex guidance has been raised more than once. Earnings beat in 4 of the last 7 quarters (57%), which is mediocre. Reliability: **Medium** - strong on volumes, weak on cost and capex discipline.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- Lease liabilities and support-vessel charters (BTG, 2026-11-11): the answer was that about 75% of the increase is new support vessels and tankers - a cost that keeps rising.
- Fuel pricing versus import parity: answered with a market-share argument, not a commitment.
- Extraordinary dividends: repeatedly deflected since 2025.
- The 2027-2031 strategic plan (due 2026-11-23 per the call) is where the post-election capex-versus-payout split will be revealed; analysts are clearly worried and management did not pre-announce it.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- 🔴 Capex up (R$23.0B in Q2-2026 to R$27.7B in Q3-2026) while the quarterly payout fell from R$17.4B (Q2) to R$15.3B (Q3).
- 🔴 Lease commitments are large (R$229B) and still rising; equity valuation must deduct them.
- 🔴 Fuel prices smoothed by policy (Q3-2026 call); Lula's fourth term (2026-10-25) raises the risk that this widens.
- 🔴 Reports of interest in Venezuela (Reuters, 2026-11-11) and buying BP's stake in a discovery (2026-11-12): politically flavoured capital use.
- 🟢 Production +37% since May 2024 with decline cut from ~10% to ~3% a year (Q3-2026 call).
- 🟢 Refinery utilisation 99% in Q3-2026.
- 🟢 Net debt including leases down R$33B in one quarter; Piotroski score 9/9.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
"Energy security for Brazil" and "more diesel, more gasoline, more aviation fuel at lower prices" sit next to "create value for our shareholders ... both governmental and private". The ordering matters: the social mandate now leads. The new top bench (governance, logistics directors changed between the 2025 and 2026 calls) speaks of market share rather than parity.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
**Trajectory: STABLE.** Operations strengthen; capital allocation drifts toward capex and the state's priorities, but the 45%-of-free-cash-flow rule is still applied as written (Q3-2026 payout checks to the formula).
The single most important thing: the 2027-2031 strategic plan (2026-11-23) - whether capex rises again and whether the payout rule or the gross-debt ceiling changes. That, not oil, decides whether the discount narrows.

**Moat:** scale and cost - world-class, low-lifting-cost pre-salt reserves plus a near-monopoly on Brazilian refining. Returns (ROIC 14.7%, ROE 30%) are high but swing with oil; there is no structural fall beyond the cycle. Narrow but real, stable.
**Secular threat:** the energy transition is real but slow for a low-cost deepwater producer; ethanol already takes 32% of the gasoline mix (Q3-2026 call). Manageable over our horizon. The cheapness is mostly a political-risk print, not a shrinking base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis:
Dürr is the world's largest maker of automotive paint shops, owns HOMAG (the world's largest woodworking-machinery maker) and owns Schenck, whose balancing machines handle, on the chief executive's account repeated on 12 November 2026, about nine out of ten aircraft engines. At 15.72 euros the equity is worth about 1.09 billion euros and the enterprise value (equity plus net borrowings) about 1.33 billion euros against roughly 4.1 billion euros of revenue: about 0.32 times revenue, below the nearest listed comparison Krones.

The third quarter of 2026 made the operating case more concrete. Automotive sales rose 15% and its margin beat an already high 8.2% prior-year base; group orders rose 5% and sales 3%; the group operating margin before one-off items reached 5.7%, the best of the year, and management expects Q4 to be stronger still, as it typically is. Orders in the Americas are up 10% over nine months as foreign carmakers build US plants behind tariffs, and China is up 17% on domestic customers. The demand mechanism the bull case has rested on since late 2024 held again: a global fleet of 500-plus paint shops, most of them inefficient, and a paint shop is about half of a car plant's energy use, so refurbishment and replacement spending continues whether the plant builds petrol or electric cars. HOMAG's margin is rising sequentially and its new Polish plant (inaugurated October 2026) brings efficiency gains from 2027. Schenck is growing on aerospace and on power-generation equipment for AI data centres.

The portfolio surgery is done, the cash-flow drag in 2026 is made of one-off items (a reversal of 2025 prepayments, tax on the disposal, restructuring cash, a tax-audit settlement), and the 9-10 December Capital Markets Day under an almost entirely new board is the venue for a new 2030 margin target. If 2027 shows operating cash flow covering spending, a business earning roughly 200 to 240 million euros of operating profit will not stay valued at about 1.3 billion euros of enterprise value.
picks.bear_thesis:
The screen calls Dürr extraordinarily cheap (4.3 times free cash flow, 2.92 euros of earnings per share), and both inputs are artifacts. The 2025 earnings came from the 227m euro after-tax gain on selling the environmental business; continuing operations lost about 50m euros that year. Trailing free cash flow included about 100m euros of customer payments the former finance chief said in March 2026 were pulled forward from 2026. That reversal is now in the numbers: FMP quarterly free cash flow fell from +103m in Q4 2025 to +46m, +13m and then -39m in Q3 2026, and the company itself said prepayments were lower because fewer large contracts were signed. Net debt rose from 218m to 240m euros in the quarter, and full-year guidance of -150m to 0 free cash flow implies more to come.

Reported Q3 net income was only 4.9m euros on 1.08 billion of sales once 32m of restructuring and a high tax charge are counted, so the improving operating margin is not yet reaching shareholders. The capital-allocation record is weak: three write-downs on BBS Automation in five quarters and a 25% cut to its 2030 revenue goal in August 2026; group return on invested capital is about 5%. The finance chief retired at end-September and the new one starts weeks before a Capital Markets Day whose first target revision, last time, went down. The big Q4 orders management is counting on may slip into 2027, as it openly allowed. And the macro tape since summer has rewarded companies whose cash flow covers their spending and punished those guiding to burn cash, which is exactly where Dürr sits until March 2027.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market runs both ways. Against the screens: the 4.3 times free cash flow and 2.92 euro earnings figures are a disposal gain and a one-off cash pull-forward; on corrected numbers the business earns roughly 1.10 to 1.25 euros a share and is guided to burn cash in 2026, so it is about half as cheap as advertised. The third quarter made that concrete, with free cash flow at -39m euros and net debt up 22m. In Dürr's favor: the market keeps reading European carmaker distress straight across to Dürr's order book, and the third quarter again contradicted that read. Automotive sales rose 15%, Americas orders are up 10% on foreign carmakers building US plants, China is up 17% on domestic customers, and the demand is driven by an inefficient installed fleet of 500-plus paint shops rather than by new capacity. At 15.72 euros, a new 52-week low reached on a day with no company news, the price is pricing the cash trough as if it were permanent.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window runs from now to the March 2027 full-year report. Q4 2026 must absorb the rest of the guided cash burn (full-year free cash flow -150m to 0 after roughly flat nine months), restructuring cash from Vector and HOMAG, tax on the 2025 disposal and the undisclosed tax-audit settlement; net debt, 240m euros at 30 September including leases, likely ends the year higher. A brand-new finance chief presents for the first time at the 9-10 December Capital Markets Day, where a cautious 2030 target would land on a stock already at its low. If the big Q4 automotive orders slip into 2027, as management allowed they might, the Q4 order number will compare against a very high prior-year base. None of this is a solvency risk; it is a sentiment risk in a tape that pays for cash flow now.
picks.positioning_washout: No forced-selling event is scheduled: the dividend (0.80 euros paid in Q2 2026) was described as sustainable, there is no index deletion, lock-up or spin-off flow in view, and the HOMAG minority is a small, court-fixed claim, not an overhang. What is happening is a slow sector-and-style de-rating: the stock fell 4.1% to 15.72 on 16 November 2026 on no company news, its new 52-week low, about 18% below its 200-day average (19.10) and 37% below the 52-week high of 25.10. picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Dürr AG (DUE.DE) — a deep dive on management and the setup
*Prepared 2026-11-16 from five earnings calls (13 May 2025, 13 November 2025, 5 March 2026, 6 August 2026, 12 November 2026) and FMP quarterly statements through 30 September 2026. Prices in euros on the Frankfurt XETRA listing; live quote 15.72 euros on 16 November 2026.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
Two years ago Dürr told a growth-through-automation story: buy BBS Automation, build "the second largest player in industrial automation", and run five divisions. Across the five calls in this file the story contracted, deliberately, into a simpler one: three divisions (Automotive, Woodworking/HOMAG, Industrial Automation), the environmental-technology business sold (closed 31 October 2025), and "profitability first" as the operating rule. The May 2025 call was still about portfolio reshaping and the held-for-sale process; November 2025 and March 2026 were about the disposal gain, the cash pull-forward and a negative 2026 free-cash-flow guide; August 2026 added the Vector restructuring at BBS Automation and a 25% cut to its 2030 revenue target; the 12 November 2026 call is the first that reads like a steady-state operating report: sales +3%, orders +5%, a 5.7% operating margin before one-off items, guidance confirmed, and a Capital Markets Day on 9-10 December 2026 to reset the 2030 targets.

The growth driver that has quietly grown in importance is Schenck balancing (equipment that balances rotating parts such as aircraft-engine and turbine rotors). In November 2026 management credited it with "high order intake, sales and earnings" on power-generation spending for AI data centres, and repeated that Dürr balances "9 out of 10 aircraft engines globally". The driver quietly dropped is battery-production automation, which no longer features as a growth pillar.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Management claim | Date | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paint-shop demand is replacement and efficiency spending that survives a capacity freeze ("a fleet of roughly 500-plus significant paint shops... at very low efficiency levels") | Nov 2024 to Nov 2026, repeated | Q2 2026 order intake +13%; Q3 2026 +5%; Automotive Q3 sales +15% with margin above the 8.2% prior-year base | Matches |
| Group margin recovers in the second half | 6 Aug 2026 | Q3 2026 operating margin before one-off items 5.7%, the best of the year; nine-month 4.7% | Matches so far; Q4 must carry the year into the 5.0-6.5% range |
| 2025 earnings per share of 2.92 (+107%) | FY2025 | Driven by the 227m euro after-tax disposal gain; continuing operations lost about 50m euros | Headline overstates the business |
| Trailing free cash flow of about 225m euros | to mid-2026 | Included about 100m euros of customer payments pulled into December 2025 (CFO, 5 Mar 2026). FMP quarterly free cash flow: Q4-25 +103m, Q1-26 +46m, Q2-26 +13m, Q3-26 -39m | Overstated; the reversal is now visible |
| "Strong balance sheet... sustainable dividends" | Aug 2026 presentation | FMP net debt (including leases) 218.1m at 30 Jun 2026 rose to 240.1m at 30 Sep 2026; borrowings 987m, cash 747m | Still comfortable, but moving the wrong way |
| BBS Automation "has passed the trough" | 12 Nov 2026 | Industrial Automation "virtually returned to breakeven" in Q3 after a clearly negative Q2; third write-down booked in Q2 2026 (Q2 net loss 89.5m euros) | Unproven; one quarter |

Reported Q3 2026 net income was only 4.9m euros on 1,079m of revenue: 32m of restructuring provisions (Vector plus 17m at HOMAG) and a high tax charge (9.9m on 15.1m pre-tax profit) swallow the operating improvement.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Stable, shifting from defensive to cautiously offensive. In March 2026 the tone was explanatory and defensive (the cash pull-forward, the disputed tax audit whose size "we don't want to mention"). In August 2026 it was candid about BBS ("our expectations in terms of volumes... did not turn out"). On 12 November 2026 the CEO called the performance "very solid" against "an altogether adverse environment", and pointed to Q4 as "the strongest quarter in terms of order intake", while hedging that big orders "which might not be signed in Q4 are highly appreciated also in Q1". On pricing, he was blunt: auto margins are "never good. It's only bad or worse", but "we defend our margins". Confidence is real but carefully bounded.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Medium-High. Delivered: the five-to-three portfolio reduction on schedule; the 2025 margin step-up (4.6% to 5.6%); the H2 2026 margin recovery so far; 2026 guidance confirmed after nine months (orders 3.8-4.2bn, sales 3.9-4.3bn, margin before one-offs 5.0-6.5%, free cash flow -150m to 0). Missed: the BBS Automation plan (three write-downs in five quarters, 2030 revenue target cut 25% on 6 Aug 2026). The screener's 1-of-7 quarterly beat rate reflects consensus models built on polluted earnings more than operating misses. No sandbagging pattern; the group margin is guided "toward the lower end", which it is tracking.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
Recurring: pricing quality on new orders in a weak European auto market (Q3 2026, answered with a general margin-defence argument rather than numbers); the size of the disputed German tax audit (never disclosed); BBS Automation's path and whether M&A resumes (answered: "not... anything soon", a small life-science bolt-on eventually); the tax rate (Q3 2026, answered approximately). What analysts did not press hard: the second-half cash burn and the year-end net-debt figure, which is the single number most likely to disappoint in the March 2027 report.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- 🔴 Three goodwill write-downs on one acquisition (Q2 2025, Q4 2025, Q2 2026).
- 🔴 Free cash flow turned negative in Q3 2026 (-39m euros per FMP) as prepayments fell; net debt rose 22m in the quarter.
- 🔴 CFO Dietmar Heinrich retired end-September 2026; the CEO covered the Q3 call alone; new CFO Alexandra Dambeck starts mid-November, weeks before the Capital Markets Day.
- 🔴 Undisclosed tax-audit liability (March 2026).
- 🟢 Automotive Q3 2026 sales +15% with margin above the 8.2% prior-year base; Americas orders +10% and China +17% in nine months.
- 🟢 HOMAG margin rising sequentially and a new Polish plant inaugurated October 2026, with efficiency effects from 2027.
- 🟢 Schenck balancing growing on aerospace and power-generation demand.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
The shift in vocabulary from "industrial automation leader" (2024) to "sustainable automation" and "profitability first" (2026) is a quiet admission that the BBS growth case failed. The board is almost entirely new (CEO plus three new members, including a new CFO), so the 9-10 December Capital Markets Day will be the first set of targets this team owns. Mercedes hosting part of that event at its Sindelfingen site, the "largest paint shop ever" for Dürr, is a customer-relationship signal, not a financial one. Management now stresses that the European/German news flow is not its whole business, repeated with numbers on regional orders.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: PIVOTING (turning). The portfolio surgery is done and the operating core is improving, but the acquisition record is poor and the 2026 cash line is negative by guidance. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: the cheapness on the screen (4.3 times free cash flow, 2.92 earnings per share) is built on a disposal gain and a one-off cash pull-forward; on corrected numbers the stock is about half as cheap as advertised, and the year-end 2026 net debt and the 2027 cash guide in March 2027 are what will decide whether the market pays for the rest.

Moat: scale-cost and switching costs in automotive paint shops (the largest supplier, an installed base it services, 40%+ return on capital employed in Automotive, prepayment-funded) and an intangible certification niche in Schenck balancing; diluted at group level by HOMAG's cyclicality and BBS Automation's losses. Group return on invested capital of about 5% keeps it narrow; Automotive margins are stable to rising, so not eroding. Secular threat: material but not terminal — the shift to electric cars does not change paint-shop demand, but a prolonged European auto capacity reduction and Chinese domestic competitors can compress pricing. The cheapness is mostly a fear-print on a cyclical, cash-timing trough, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

# CDI.PA - Christian Dior SE - forensic dossier (2026-11-09)

Source note: no earnings-call transcript is bundled and the FMP transcript feed has nothing for this listing. This dossier uses the FMP live quote and price history for Christian Dior (CDI.PA) and LVMH (MC.PA) through 9 November 2026, the FMP news feed (Christian Dior third-quarter release of 12 October 2026; Reuters, Seeking Alpha, WSJ and New York Post coverage of LVMH's third quarter; Reuters on Dior board changes, 7 October 2026), and this committee's own record of 29 September 2026 for the 23 September 2026 restructuring terms. The web search budget for this run was exhausted, so the December meeting date and any update to the offer timetable could not be re-verified independently. All prices in euros on the Paris listing.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
Christian Dior SE is the listed holding company that owns about 42% of LVMH (roughly 1.154 LVMH shares per Dior share) and nothing else of size. For years it traded at an 18-21% discount to that look-through value. On 23 September 2026 the Arnault family announced it would merge its private holding Agache into Christian Dior, convert it into a family-controlled partnership, and offer cash to the 2.44% minority at 95% of look-through asset value, priced off LVMH's one-month volume-weighted average share price five business days before an extraordinary meeting in December 2026. The illustration was EUR 469.05 including a EUR 6.05 interim dividend payable 3 December 2026; offer opening expected in the first quarter of 2027; no squeeze-out. The story is now a formula on LVMH's share price, not a holding-company value case.

Since then: on 7 October 2026 Dior replaced two independent board members ahead of the new structure (Reuters). On 12 October 2026 the Christian Dior group reported nine-month revenue of EUR 57.1 billion, organic growth of 2%; LVMH's third quarter was only very modestly positive organically, with Fashion & Leather Goods down about 5% organically in the quarter (Seeking Alpha, 13 October), and the shares fell toward EUR 380. A broad luxury sell-off followed on 23 October (Kering and Hermes also reported declines). LVMH then rallied from EUR 383 (23 October) to EUR 418.65 (5 November) and closed EUR 402.45 on 9 November.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
- The screen's deep-value signal (P/FCF 5.3x, TTM EPS 50.47, FCF EUR 29.1 billion) is an artifact: Dior consolidates 100% of LVMH's cash flow while owning about 42%, and half-yearly figures appear doubled in the TTM feed. On true 2025 attributable EPS of EUR 25.11 the shares trade near 17x.
- Net debt: the consolidated figure of EUR 29.85 billion (incl. EUR 13.51 billion of leases) is essentially LVMH's own; the parent-level difference was about EUR 40 million at 30 June 2026. For the offer formula, parent net debt is immaterial and LVMH's debt is already inside LVMH's share price. Do not subtract consolidated net debt from Dior's look-through value again.
- Live check of the formula: Dior EUR 432.20 / LVMH EUR 402.45 = 1.074 against the offer's 1.108 times the LVMH average. LVMH's trailing one-month close average is about EUR 393, which implies an offer near EUR 436; at spot LVMH it would be about EUR 446.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Management tone at LVMH has shifted from "recovery under way" (July) to "focused on the next generation, not the next quarter" (Antoine Arnault, CNBC, 16 October). Restructuring signals inside the group (Zenith job cuts, 23 October) point to defensive cost action. The family's own tone on the Dior deal is unchanged; the board refresh on 7 October indicates the process is proceeding.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
LVMH guided in July to a similar currency drag in the second half, a tougher comparison base and slower wines and spirits; the third quarter was in line with that caution rather than better. Guidance has been honest but the hoped-for second-half recovery did not appear in Fashion & Leather Goods. On the Dior transaction, the family has delivered each announced step so far.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- Is the Fashion & Leather Goods decline (about -5% organic in the third quarter) China-specific or brand-specific? Bearish sell-side and independent pieces argue the latter.
- Exact pricing-window dates and the December meeting date, which set the euro offer price.
- The Agache exchange ratio and the independent expert's fairness opinion (not yet published as far as could be verified).

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
Red: LVMH organic growth near zero with its largest division shrinking; luxury peer group at multi-year lows; the minority gets 95% of asset value, set at a five-year LVMH low chosen by the controlling family; no squeeze-out, so non-tendering holders are stranded in a thinner partnership.
Green: no solvency issue at either level; family controls 97.56% of votes so approval is near-certain; LVMH cash generation and gross margin held through the downturn; the spread to the formula is tight and liquidity-supported by event-driven holders.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
The Dior-to-LVMH ratio of 1.074 against a 1.108 formula leaves about 3% of gross spread at spot LVMH, but because the pricing average lags spot, the payout today would be nearer EUR 436, roughly 1% above the Dior price. The market is pricing the deal as near-certain and is effectively lending a holder LVMH exposure with almost no extra return. Dior's volume has normalised to a few thousand shares a day, down from the 139,297 traded on 24 September.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
The family is allocating capital well for itself: buying out a small minority at a 5% discount near the bottom of LVMH's range. For an outside buyer, Christian Dior is now LVMH with a thin spread attached and a hard stop at the pricing window. There is no remaining Dior-specific value edge worth paying for at EUR 432; owning it is a bet on LVMH's share price over the next four weeks, which is better expressed, if at all, by owning LVMH directly.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# EFOR — Everforth, Inc. (formerly ASGN Incorporated) — Forensic Dossier
*Coverage: five earnings calls, Q3 2025 (2025-10-22) through Q3 2026 (2026-10-28). Live price used: $35.64 (NYSE, USD, FMP quote 2026-11-09). Financials cross-checked against FMP quarterly statements filed through 2026-10-30.*

Identity note for the director: EFOR is the old ASGN (IT consulting plus the ECS federal unit, with legacy staffing brands CyberCoders and Creative Circle). It rebranded to Everforth and moved to the new ticker in early 2026 (Q4 2025 call, 2026-02-04: "on Friday, we will officially begin operating as Everforth, and trading under our new stock ticker EFOR"). The peer file for this ticker is unmapped because the new name was not recognised; this dossier fixes the identity.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-22):** a mix-shift story. IT consulting was "approximately 63% of total revenues ... up from 58%", adjusted EBITDA margin (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, excluding one-offs) 11.1%. Financial services, TMT (technology, media and telecom) and business services were all declining year over year. AI was framed as "a fundamental replatforming" that needs IT services partners.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-04):** the pivot quarter. Rebrand to Everforth, the Quinnox acquisition (an India-based application-engineering firm, about $284M cash paid in Q1 2026) and a new $1B buyback authorisation. Management called out a government-shutdown drag on federal awards. The story widened from "consulting mix" to "end-to-end engineering with offshore delivery".
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-22):** the stumble. Revenue in line, but adjusted EBITDA margin of 8.6% "was below our expectations", blamed on "lower-than-expected contribution of some of our higher-margin solutions". Analysts pressed on DSO (days sales outstanding, how long customers take to pay) and on free-cash-flow conversion.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-29):** recovery. Revenue above $1B and above the guided range, 9.6% margin above the top of the range, commercial bookings up double digits. Management said "we're moving to year-over-year growth".
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-28):** confirmation. Revenue $1,031.4M (up about 2% on $1,011.4M a year earlier), adjusted EBITDA $106.3M (10.3%), federal awards $584M (1.9x book-to-bill, meaning new awards divided by revenue, for the quarter), and buybacks paused so the Quinnox debt could be paid down. The story is now AI deployment (Workday, Salesforce, ServiceNow), security (bookings "up over 40% year-to-date") and hyperscaler data-centre work.

Net: the narrative moved from defending a shrinking staffing base to an AI-implementation and federal-mission story, paid for with leverage.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| "Moving to year-over-year growth" (Q2 2026) | Q3 2026 revenue $1,031.4M vs $1,011.4M (+2.0%), part of it from Quinnox | **Partly corroborated**: growth is real but thin, and acquired revenue flatters the organic rate. FY2025 revenue $3.98B was still down 2.9%, with a 3-year compound rate of -4.6% |
| Margin expansion | Adjusted EBITDA margin 8.6% → 9.6% → 10.3% across 2026, but 10.3% is still below Q3 2025's 11.1%. Q4 guide 9.6–10.4% | **Corroborated in sequence, not year over year.** The screener has margins 2.5 standard deviations below their historical peak |
| Earnings power | GAAP EPS (earnings per share under standard accounting) Q3 2026 $0.56 vs $0.87 a year earlier. FY EPS fell from $5.23 (2022) to $2.60 (2025) | **Diverges.** Higher interest (Q3 $20.2M vs $17.4M), deal amortization and a lower margin have roughly halved GAAP earnings. Adjusted EPS of $1.11 beat consensus of $1.02 |
| Cash generation | FMP free cash flow Q4'25 $93.7M, Q1'26 $9.1M, Q2'26 $46.3M, Q3'26 $46.5M; about $196M over the last twelve months, roughly a 13% yield on a $1.46B market value | **Corroborated**, but stock-based pay of about $55M a year is added back. Owner cash flow after that cost is closer to $140–150M |
| Capital return | Diluted shares 43.9M (Q3'25) → 41.1M (Q3'26), about -6% | **Corroborated.** Buybacks then stopped in Q3 2026 to pay down debt |
| Balance sheet | Long-term debt $1.39B, cash about $148M, net debt about $1.24B. Reported net leverage 3.1x against a target of 2.5x or lower | **The weak point.** The Altman-Z (a solvency score) of 1.8 sits in the grey zone; goodwill plus intangibles of $2.86B exceed equity of $1.84B |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
**Rising from a Q1 trough.** Q1 2026 was defensive ("below our expectations"). Q2 and Q3 were offensive ("continued momentum", "AI is not replacing these platforms"). On the Q4 guide, CEO Hanson refused the analyst's word "conservatism": "that's not my word ... I just don't see Q4 as an accelerating quarter". That is measured rather than promotional, which helps credibility. Language on the legacy staffing brands stays guarded: "sequentially stable" but "continued declines" year over year.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
- Q3 2025: at the high end of guidance. Q4 2025: top end of the revenue range.
- Q1 2026: margin miss (8.6%).
- Q2 2026 and Q3 2026: revenue and EBITDA above the top of the range.
- The screener's beat rate is 4 of 7 quarters (57%). Over 2026 the pattern is mild sandbagging (setting guidance low enough to beat) after one miss. **Reliability: Medium-High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- Q4 cadence and whether the guide is conservative (Baird, Q3 2026). Management avoided the question.
- DSO and cash conversion (Q1 2026), answered as seasonality.
- How much of the growth is organic versus Quinnox. Management has not split it out ("we didn't call out the Quinnox numbers"), which is a recurring non-answer.
- The cyclical staffing units are still shrinking year over year.
- Not addressed by management at all: whether AI coding and agent tools cut billable hours per project, the industry's labour-arbitrage deflation risk.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- 🔴 GAAP EPS roughly halved year over year in Q3 2026 ($0.56 vs $0.87). Interest expense is up after the Quinnox debt.
- 🔴 Net leverage of 3.1x, with buybacks suspended (Q3 2026) in a market that rewards cash and punishes borrowing.
- 🔴 Organic growth is not disclosed. Legacy staffing is still declining.
- 🔴 The sell-side consensus target is $29 (high $36, low $22, FMP 2026-11-09), below the price.
- 🟢 Three straight quarters of sequential margin improvement, and Q2 and Q3 both beat the top of guidance.
- 🟢 Federal backlog of $2.9B (2.5x revenue). An NGA (National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency) extension worth potentially over $200M was announced 2026-11-03.
- 🟢 Security bookings are up over 40% year to date, and work with the four largest hyperscalers is accelerating.
- 🟢 The share count fell about 6% in a year, and insider buy ratio is 2.43.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
- "Customer Zero" and "client zero" language (Q2 and Q3 2026): Everforth is deploying AI on its own delivery. That is a margin lever, and also a quiet admission that AI cuts hours per deliverable.
- Federal clients have shifted the vocabulary from "contract backlog" to "mission modernization" and "Enclave Factory". The company is positioning itself as a productised-solutions vendor rather than a body-shop.
- Pausing the buyback right after authorising $1B is the most honest capital-allocation signal: the balance sheet now binds.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT
**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** The business is turning from a shrinking staffing-and-consulting mix into an AI-implementation, offshore-enabled and federal-mission services firm. The 2026 operating trend is improving, but the earnings base has fallen for four years.

**The single thing to weigh:** this is a cash-yield-plus-deleveraging case at about 7x EBITDA, not a growth case. The equity is the residual of a business with about $1.24B of net debt, so a 1-point slip in margin moves equity value by roughly 25%.

**Moat:** narrow. It rests on switching costs in federal contract vehicles and clearances, and on platform-partner certifications (Workday, Salesforce, ServiceNow). Returns are modest (ROIC, return on invested capital, of 7.7%) and margins have trended down since 2022, so the moat trend is eroding rather than stable. **Secular threat: material, not terminal.** AI-driven labour-arbitrage deflation could compress billable hours, but federal mission work and implementation of AI platforms partly hedge that. The cheapness is part fear-print (the stock bottomed near $16.90 inside the last year) and part a real decline in the base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.

picks.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that a genuinely excellent business is being priced as an ordinary one for the length of a self-funded investment programme, and that the programme will eventually pay its owner.

The economics are not in dispute. Dunelm earns about 33% on invested capital, held a 52.5% gross margin in the year to June 2026 (up 10 basis points), spends only about 2.3% of sales on capital (GBP 43m on GBP 1,825m), and carries GBP 95m of debt excluding leases, 0.3 times EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation). Free cash flow on the company's definition rose from GBP 127m to GBP 155m and operating profit conversion to cash improved from 57% to 69% (2026-09-08 results).

It is still winning its market. Share of the GBP 25bn UK homewares and furniture market rose again to 7.9%; digitally enabled sales grew more than 9% and reached 42% of sales; the app produces about 40% higher basket values than web-only customers; customer satisfaction rose for a second year. Made-to-Measure window treatments, which arrive with a fitter and are hard for a marketplace to copy, grew double digits and kept doing so in the 2026-10-15 first-quarter update. That update also confirmed management's September warning was weather, not demand: the first six weeks were about -3%, the last seven about +4%, gross margin +10 basis points, full-year guidance unchanged.

The plan is the right one, badly received: about GBP 100m of cost removed by 2029, GBP 125m of extra capital to reopen the store pipeline (new stores pay back in under three years on the company's own evidence; only two opened last year against five to ten guided), and a target of mid-to-high single-digit sales growth. If the top line moves from about 3% toward 5-6% on a lighter cost base, 2029 earnings power is well above today's 76.8p. The chair and other directors bought in the market at roughly 732p-748p in the week after the September fall, and brokers dated in September 2026 (per the prior record: JPMorgan 1,050p, Deutsche Bank 1,000p, Shore Capital 1,000p, Canaccord 1,185p, Peel Hunt 1,225p; not re-verified this run) all sit above today's price.

Conditions: the cost programme reaches profit rather than being absorbed by wages; gross margin holds above about 52% through a promotional Christmas; store openings accelerate; the UK consumer does not weaken further.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bear case needs nothing to break. It needs only the next three years to look like the last four.

Revenue rose about 15.5% from GBP 1.58bn (FY22) to GBP 1.83bn (FY26) while diluted earnings per share fell from 84p to 76.8p and book value per share shrank about 4.2% a year. The FY26 cost bridge shows why: GBP 15m of productivity was swallowed by more than GBP 20m of inflation (GBP 23m in the results announcement) and about GBP 20m of volume-driven logistics and marketing that grows with digital sales; profit was held flat only with about GBP 10m of help, including GBP 3m of fire-insurance receipts, lower performance pay and GBP 1m of rates relief. Management does not disclose channel profitability.

The moat is narrower than the returns suggest: no switching costs, share gains slowing (about 50bp in 2023, 20bp in 2025, 10bp in 2026), and the FY26 margin gain was attributed to currency, partly offset by promotions; the second half ran near 51.7% against 53.4% in the first. In the last inflation wave gross margin fell from 49.6% to 45.3%.

The plan makes the owner wait: profit before tax guided broadly flat for FY27, GBP 125m of extra capital plus GBP 30-40m of one-off costs, and no special dividends before 2029, which cuts declared distributions from 70.5p to the 45.5p ordinary. If this third efficiency programme is absorbed like the first two, earnings stay near 77p, the market keeps paying 10-12 times, and the shares are worth roughly what they cost today with real downside if Christmas promotions erode the margin: the adverse case is about 577p.

What would confirm it: a weak 14 January 2027 Christmas update, gross margin below 52% at the 10 February 2027 interims, or the cost bridge again showing savings consumed by wage inflation after the April 2027 wage step.
picks.consensus_delta:
This is a deep-value framing question: is the market pricing terminal decline into stable earnings power? It is not. At 906.5p, about 11.8 times flat earnings and about 7 times EBITDA, the market is pricing Dunelm as a stable, ex-growth UK retailer - which is roughly what four years of flat earnings per share say it is. There is no terminal-decline discount left to arbitrage; the September sell-off to 734p-760p has fully reversed.

Where we still differ: the brokers dated in September 2026 (1,000p-1,225p in the prior record, not re-verified) assume the GBP 100m programme reaches profit from FY29. The company's own FY26 cost bridge - productivity fully consumed by inflation and digital variable costs, profit held flat only with about GBP 10m of help - argues that timing is optimistic, and this is at least the third efficiency programme. Where the market may be too cautious: the store pipeline and Made-to-Measure are genuine growth assets that a flat-earnings multiple gives little credit to. On balance the price sits at our base case, so the disagreement is not large enough to trade.
picks.valley_of_death: No solvency or liquidity event exists: net debt excluding leases is GBP 95m, 0.3 times EBITDA, and the 45.5p ordinary dividend is covered. The risky window (the months just ahead) is about earnings, not survival. November-December 2026 peak trading brings back the Black Friday choice management got wrong in FY26 Q2 (growth slowed to about 1.6% when it declined to discount): discount and the margin goes, hold and sales go. Free cash flow falls in FY27 as the GBP 125m extra capital and GBP 30-40m one-off spending begin, against an ordinary dividend that already absorbs most of it. The April 2027 wage step lands just as the cost programme must show up. The dated checks are 14 January 2027 (Christmas trading) and 10 February 2027 (interims, the first cost bridge under the new plan).
picks.positioning_washout: The forced-selling pressure, that is selling by holders who must sell regardless of value, was the income-fund exit after the 2026-09-08 removal of special dividends until 2029, cutting declared distributions from 70.5p to 45.5p. The price action says that wave has largely passed: the shares fell to 734p on 2026-09-09, directors bought at about 732p-748p, and the stock has since climbed back to 906.5p, above both the 50-day (about 828p) and 200-day (about 836p) averages. A renewed wash-out would need a new trigger, most plausibly a weak Christmas update. There is no index-deletion or lock-up overhang.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. The thesis holds - this is a high-return, lightly indebted, well-run UK homewares specialist - but at 906.5p the shares sit at our fair value of about 902p, so there is no margin of safety to buy.

Nothing dated has changed since the committee's 19 October answer: no announcement beyond routine notices, the final dividend went ex on 22 October, and the price has simply recovered the whole of the September fall. The forensic work stays clean (return on invested capital about 33%, gross margin 52.5%, net debt about 0.3 times EBITDA, management that warns early and names its own failures). The problem is the owner's arithmetic: revenue up about 15.5% since FY22 with earnings per share down from 84p to 76.8p, FY27 profit guided flat, and special dividends withdrawn until 2029 while GBP 100m of savings is reinvested.

The value case is real but the discount is gone. The value score stays high because the business qualifies and only the price does not; the price at which our base case would clear the 20% entry bar in this inflation-and-growth backdrop is about 752p, roughly where the September forced selling bottomed and directors bought. A return toward that level, for example on a weak 14 January Christmas update, is the setup this committee would re-examine. The spent strategy catalyst is neither a plus nor a minus here, and the macro backdrop (sticky inflation, a margin history that suffered in the last inflation wave) is context, not a reason.
picks.forcing_function: There is no hard event that forces a re-rating. The calendar items - the 14 January 2027 second-quarter update and the 10 February 2027 interim results - are reporting dates, not binding outcomes. What re-rates Dunelm is arithmetic: sales growth moving from about 3% toward the mid single digits while costs grow slower, so that flat earnings visibly end; on management's own guidance that cannot appear in FY27 profit, so the earliest evidence is the cost bridge at the February 2027 interims. Secondary signals: faster store openings in the interim capital-expenditure line, and any sign the special dividend returns before 2029.

# Dunelm Group (DNLM.L) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-16. Live price 906.5p (London listing, pence sterling, FMP quote). Sources: earnings-call transcripts dated 2024-09-11 (in practice the FY24 interim presentation), 2025-09-09, 2026-02-10 (FY26 interims) and 2026-09-08 (FY26 full-year results plus the new chief executive's strategy session); the screener's financial trajectory; the 2026-10-15 first-quarter trading update as reported in the press.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has moved from "a compounding product company that pays out its surplus" to "a business that must reinvest to grow again, and will pay its owners less while it does".

- **2024 (Nick Wilkinson era).** The pitch was steady compounding: "We're in growth, but our markets are not." First-half profit up 4.8% in line with sales, gross-margin discipline, a 35p special dividend "maintaining our track record in terms of cash generation and distribution". The language was confident and about balance - volume and margin together.
- **2025.** Same frame, weaker numbers. Market-share gains continued but slowed (about 20 basis points in the year), and the special dividend continued at 35p.
- **February 2026 interims.** The first visible strain. Management chose not to match "much deeper levels of discounting" over Black Friday, and second-quarter growth slowed to about 1.6%. A furniture forecasting failure hurt availability. A Bloomberg Intelligence analyst asked for channel profitability and was told it is not disclosed.
- **September 2026 (Clodagh Moriarty, new chief executive).** The pivot. "A solid year" with sales +3.1% to GBP 1,825m, gross margin 52.5% (+10 basis points), profit before tax flat at GBP 211m, and then a three-year plan: about GBP 100m of cost removed by the 2029 financial year and reinvested, GBP 125m of extra capital spending, GBP 30-40m of one-off costs, a return to "mid-to-high single-digit" sales growth, profit guided broadly flat for the 2027 financial year and no special dividends expected before 2029. The new voice is more self-critical ("we have to acknowledge that sometimes we are followers ... weren't on the app"; "We are not satisfied with the number of store openings").

What was dropped: the implicit promise that surplus cash would keep coming back as special dividends. What was added: stores as a growth engine again, Made-to-Measure window treatments as a named growth category, artificial-intelligence shopping (a launch partner for Google's conversational shopping in Europe).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers say | Read |
|---|---|---|
| "We yet again gained share to 7.9%" (2026-09-08) | Share gains of about 50bp (2023), 20bp (2025), 10bp (2026); the reported level has sat near 7.9% across consecutive disclosures | True but decelerating |
| Gross margin "strong ... consistency of our model" | 52.5% in FY26 (+10bp), helped by "a foreign exchange tailwind, partly offset by increased customer participation in promotional events". H1 FY26 was 53.4%, so H2 ran near 51.7% | Headline holds; quality weaker, currency-assisted |
| "Strong inroads covering the on-cost of inflation" | GBP 15m productivity vs more than GBP 20m inflation (skeptic check of the RNS: GBP 23m) plus about GBP 20m of volume-driven logistics and marketing; profit flat only with GBP 10m of "other items" (GBP 3m fire-insurance receipts, lower performance pay, GBP 1m rates relief) | The claim is generous; underlying profit fell |
| Earnings growth over time | Revenue GBP 1.58bn (FY22) to GBP 1.83bn (FY26), about +15.5%; diluted EPS 84p to 76.8p; net income GBP 171m to GBP 156m; book value per share shrinking about 4.2% a year | The key forensic fact: four years of growth with no owner earnings growth |
| "Strong cash generation" | Free cash flow GBP 155m (company definition) vs GBP 127m prior; operating profit conversion 57% to 69%; but dividends paid GBP 141m plus GBP 16m of buybacks for share schemes | True, but there was no headroom before the new capex |
| Balance sheet | Net debt excluding leases GBP 95m (RNS GBP 94.6m), 0.3x EBITDA, inside the 0.2-0.6x target; lease liabilities GBP 268.5m | Clean |
| "Q1 ... normalized" after hot weather (2026-09-08) | 2026-10-15 update: sales +1.1% to about GBP 433m, store like-for-like -0.8%; first six weeks about -3%, last seven about +4%; FY27 guidance unchanged | Borne out |

Data note: the screener's "TTM diluted EPS 1.54" is inconsistent with the 76.8p reported for the year to June 2026 and with flat guidance; it looks like an aggregation artefact and is not used.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-declining on near-term confidence, rising on candour.** 2024: offensive and assured ("We feel we've struck the right balance"). February 2026: defensive, explaining a missed Black Friday and an availability problem. September 2026: more specific and more honest than before, but explicitly guiding to no profit growth next year and naming its own failures. The shift is from distribution language to investment language - from "track record in cash generation and distribution" to "bigger, better, and bolder".

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium-High.** The company delivered the FY26 cost plan it set at the interims ("We delivered to the cost plan that we set out"), warned the market about the weak start to FY27 before it reported, and the 2026-10-15 update matched that warning. Misses are operational rather than financial: two new stores against a guided five to ten, and the furniture forecasting failure. The screener shows one beat in the last three quarters, consistent with a company that guides soberly and does not over-deliver. No sandbagging pattern; no sign of aggressive accounting.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Channel profitability.** Asked directly at the February 2026 interims; not disclosed. Digital is the growth engine and also the source of the volume-driven cost; without the split, investors cannot tell whether mix shift is diluting margins.
- **Black Friday / promotions.** Raised after Q2 FY26 and flagged by management again in September 2026 as "considerations for us looking forward". Unresolved going into this Christmas.
- **Where the GBP 100m of savings goes.** The plan reinvests it; the market's question is when the owner sees any of it. Shares fell about 14% on the day (886.5p to 760p, 2026-09-07 to 09-08).
- **Store openings.** Repeated shortfall against guidance.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Red:
- Flat-to-falling earnings per share over four years despite share gains (FY22-FY26).
- Profit held flat in FY26 only with about GBP 10m of non-recurring or low-quality help (2026-09-08).
- Special dividends withdrawn until 2029; cash returned falls from 70.5p declared in FY26 to the 45.5p ordinary (2026-09-08).
- Gross-margin gain attributed to currency, which reverses (2026-09-08).
- About 8% of salaried support and distribution roles cut ahead of peak trading (per the strategy session coverage).
- Inflation sensitivity: gross margin fell from 49.6% (year to June 2019) to 45.3% (year to June 2023) in the last inflation wave.

Green:
- Return on invested capital about 33%, capital expenditure about 2.3% of sales, net debt 0.3x EBITDA (FY26).
- Digital participation up two points to 42%; the app produces about 40% higher basket values; Click and Collect growing quickly (2026-09-08).
- Made-to-Measure growing double digits, a service-attached category that marketplaces struggle to copy (2026-09-08, reiterated 2026-10-15).
- Directors bought in the open market at roughly 732p-748p in the week after the September fall.
- Customer satisfaction up for a second year from a top-quartile base.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The new chief executive's vocabulary is "customer obsession", "bigger, better, bolder" - growth language that replaces the outgoing team's "cash generation and distribution". Capital allocation has been re-ordered: reinvestment before special dividends.
- The chief financial officer now presents sales as overlapping "store-enabled" and "digitally enabled" figures, a new presentation that makes like-for-like store weakness (just under +1%) less prominent beside digital growth (above +9%).
- Management now says "sometimes we are followers" - an unusual admission that the plan is partly catch-up spending, not optional growth.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: turning.** The most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is an excellent, cash-generative, lightly indebted franchise whose owner earnings have not grown for four years, and management has now told you they will not grow in FY27 either while the surplus is redirected into stores, technology and cost removal. You are buying the probability that the third efficiency programme converts into owner earnings where the previous ones did not.

**Moat.** Scale-cost and brand in UK homewares: the largest specialist at about 7.9% of a GBP 25bn market, own-brand sourcing that supports a 52.5% gross margin, and a store estate that doubles as a fulfilment network. There are no switching costs. The returns are high and stable rather than rising, and share gains are slowing: a narrow but real moat, stable rather than widening.

**Secular threat.** Retail channel shift (online marketplaces and ultra-low-cost cross-border sellers) is real but currently being absorbed: Dunelm is growing digitally faster than the market and gaining share. The threat is manageable rather than terminal, so the cheapness is closer to a fear-print on UK discretionary retail and a re-set income story than a structurally shrinking base. The value-trap argument rests on earnings stagnation, not on a melting revenue base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: Sands China is the largest of Macau's six licensed casino operators and is winning share in a falling market. In the third quarter of 2026 (LVS results, 2026-10-21) Macao net revenue still rose 1.8% to US$1.94B while the overall Macau market was shrinking, its mass-market share reached about 26.1% (the highest in over three years), every property ran 96-99% hotel occupancy, and property EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) recovered from about US$430M in the second quarter to US$529M. At HK$11.07 the stock is down about 50% from its 52-week high of HK$22 and sits about 6% above its 52-week low of HK$10.47. On our numbers the market value is about US$11.5B and enterprise value (market value plus net debt of US$5.58B including leases, at 2026-06-30) about US$17.1B - roughly 8.1x a run-rate EBITDA of about US$2.1B, and roughly a 10% free-cash-flow yield on about US$1.1B of sustainable free cash flow. The bull case needs only two things: Macau gaming revenue stops falling as comparisons ease into 2027 (Jefferies expects a turn in December 2026), and the promotional spending that bought the share stops rising. If margins recover even half of the 4.2 points lost in the past year while share holds, EBITDA returns to the US$2.4-2.5B it earned before the squeeze, and a 10x multiple - in line with where Macau leaders traded through 2024-25 - gives about HK$18.7 a share. The parent, Las Vegas Sands, is an informed buyer: it bought 62M Sands China shares in the third quarter for about US$101M, lifting its stake to 75.56%, and the bond market just lent Sands China US$1.0B (2026-10-27), so refinancing is not a constraint.
picks.bear_thesis: The cheapness is a falling-earnings multiple, not a low one. Property EBITDA fell 12% year on year in the third quarter of 2026 with only about US$11M of that explained by bad luck at the tables; the rest is margin given away to win share - The Londoner's margin dropped from 31.9% to 26.0%, The Venetian's from 35.0% to 31.6%, The Parisian's from 24.3% to 19.9%. Sands China's net income fell 29.8% to US$191M in the quarter. The market itself is shrinking: Macau gaming revenue fell year on year for five straight months to October 2026 (about -10% in October, despite Golden Week), and Seaport expects November down about 6%, with analysts pointing to falling spend per visitor and soft premium-mass demand tied to China tax policy and a choppy consumer. Leverage is meaningful at roughly 2.7x net debt to EBITDA, new debt now costs 6.4-6.7% against a 4.7% group average, and the Altman-Z solvency score is 1.7. Minority holders get little of the cash: the release discloses no Sands China dividend while the parent spends US$950M a quarter buying back its own stock. Finally, the licences run to the end of 2032, so a buyer is paying for about six years of contracted operation plus a renewal that is likely but not guaranteed. If margins keep sliding and EBITDA settles near US$1.8B on a 7x multiple, the shares are worth about HK$6.75.
picks.consensus_delta: On this name the street is not looking the wrong way on direction - forecasts for Macau 2026 gaming revenue have been cut (Jefferies, CLSA) and the stock has halved from HK$22. Where we partly disagree is on permanence: the price, about 8.1x run-rate EBITDA for the market-share leader, already discounts margins staying at today's depressed 27% for good. We do not assume a quick margin rebound, but a market leader gaining share with near-full hotels is unlikely to be a structurally shrinking base. Where we agree with the market: the screener's 7x free cash flow and 66% DCF discount overstate the opportunity because the trailing free-cash-flow input does not reconcile with reported EBITDA. The honest edge is modest, which is why we want a better price.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) holds more weak prints: November gaming revenue (due about 2026-12-01) is expected down about 6% year on year, and LVS fourth-quarter results (late January 2027) will show whether the third-quarter EBITDA recovery held or whether promotions widened again. There is no liquidation event or debt wall: the US$1.0B of notes priced 2026-10-27 extends maturities to 2032-2033, and the parent controls 75.56%. The real risk is a slow grind - another quarter or two of falling margins that takes EBITDA toward US$1.8B, which is our adverse case of HK$6.75. A China policy shock (tighter capital controls or visa rules) is the tail risk.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced selling is limited. The parent owns 75.56% and is a buyer, not a seller (62M shares bought in the third quarter of 2026). The free float is held by Hong Kong and global institutions and sits in Hang Seng index products, so any further fall would come from a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off of Macau and China consumer names on each monthly gaming-revenue miss rather than from holders who must sell regardless of value. With no dividend there is no yield-holder base to flush.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near HK$10.83, which a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off of Macau names on the next weak monthly gaming-revenue print could deliver. The thesis holds: Sands China is still Macau's share leader, its hotels are full, and third-quarter 2026 EBITDA recovered to US$529M from a weak second quarter. But the earnings base is lower than a year ago (EBITDA down 12%, margins down four points as share is bought with promotions), the market has shrunk for five months running, and the company carries about US$5.6B of net debt. On our base case of about US$2.1B of EBITDA at 9x, fair value is HK$13.00, roughly 17% above HK$11.07 - short of the 20% discount we require today, so the right level sits just below the current price. The screener's headline cheapness (7x free cash flow, a HK$31.8 DCF value) rests on a free-cash-flow figure that does not reconcile with reported earnings, so we do not lean on it. The trajectory is deteriorating and management credibility is middling; this is a fairly priced cyclical with a narrow licence moat rather than a deep bargain, and it earns a middling conviction until a quarter shows margins stabilising.
picks.forcing_function: There is no hard-dated corporate event. The re-rating would be forced by data: Macau's monthly gaming-revenue prints turning positive year on year as comparisons ease (Jefferies looks for December 2026), and LVS fourth-quarter 2026 results (late January 2027) showing Macao EBITDA growing again with stable margins. A resumption of Sands China dividends or a minority buy-out proposal from LVS would be stronger catalysts, but neither has been announced.

# Sands China (1928.HK) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Prepared 2026-11-16. Price used: HK$11.07 (FMP live quote, Hong Kong listing, 2026-11-16). Sands China reports in US dollars; converted at about HK$7.78 per US$.*

**Source note.** No earnings-call transcript for Sands China was available: FMP holds none for this listing, and Sands China does not host its own call - management commentary comes through the parent, Las Vegas Sands (LVS), which owns about 75.6% of it. This deep dive therefore rests on the LVS third-quarter 2026 results release (2026-10-21), dated trade-press coverage of the second and third quarters (AGBrief and ASGAM, 2026-07-23 and 2026-10-22), the 2026-10-27 bond pricing release, Macau's October 2026 gaming-revenue print (2026-11-01) and the screener's financial history. Quotes are limited to what the release itself contains. FMP's half-year income statement for 2026 (revenue US$2.32B for the half) conflicts with the LVS segment table and the press reports, so it is treated as a data error and not used.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
The story has moved from "recovery" to "defending share at a cost". In 2023-24 the case was a rebuild: revenue went from US$1.6B in 2022 to US$6.5B in 2023 and US$7.1B in 2024 as Macau reopened, and net income swung from a US$1.6B loss to roughly US$1B. In 2025 revenue still grew about 5% to US$7.4B but net income slipped to about US$0.9B - the first sign that each new dollar of revenue was costing more to win.

2026 has made that the whole story. Macau's market stopped growing (gross gaming revenue fell year on year for five straight months to October 2026, down about 10% in October despite the Golden Week holiday). Sands China held its revenue flat-to-up by taking share - the third-quarter mass-market share of about 26.1% is reported as its highest in more than three years, led by The Londoner Macao - but paid for that share with promotions and reinvestment. LVS's own framing has shifted from growth language to "progress": chief executive Patrick Dumont said the company was "encouraged by our progress in Macao" (Q3 2026 release).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim (source, date) | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Volumes are growing "across all gaming segments" (Dumont, Q3 2026 release, 2026-10-21) | Rolling-chip volume about US$5.7B vs US$4.4B a year earlier; Londoner non-rolling drop US$2.80B vs US$2.27B; Parisian and Sands Macao slot handle up sharply | Matches - volume is up |
| "Progress in Macao" | Macao net revenue US$1,940M vs US$1,906M (+1.8%) but adjusted property EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation at the property level) US$529M vs US$601M (-12%); margin 27.3% vs 31.5%. Hold (the casino's win rate) cost only about US$11M | Richer than the numbers - revenue progress, profit regression |
| Share gains are profitable | Londoner margin fell from 31.9% to 26.0%, Venetian from 35.0% to 31.6%, Parisian from 24.3% to 19.9% | Not supported - share is being bought |
| Sands China profits | Sands China net income US$191M vs US$272M (-29.8%) in Q3 2026; second-quarter Macau EBITDA about US$430M, down about 24% year on year (AGBrief, 2026-07-23, partly blamed on low hold) | Deteriorating, with Q3 better than Q2 sequentially |
| Balance sheet is being managed | US$1.0B of new senior notes priced 2026-10-27 (US$700M 6.40% due 2032, US$300M 6.70% due 2033); bundle balance sheet at 2026-06-30: borrowings US$6.27B, leases US$0.16B, cash US$0.85B, net debt US$5.58B | Refinancing access is intact, but coupons above 6% are well above the group's 4.7% average cost |

The screener's trailing free-cash-flow figure (US$2.53B) looks inconsistent with a business earning about US$2B of property EBITDA and paying about US$0.3B of interest and about US$0.6B of capital spending; I treat sustainable free cash flow as roughly US$1.0-1.2B a year and flag the screener's 7x price-to-free-cash-flow as too flattering. Return on equity of -3,405% in the scan is an artifact of a near-zero or negative equity base, not an operating signal.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Declining, from offensive to defensive. In 2024 the message was capacity (the Londoner rebuild) and growth. Through 2026 the trade press records investors reacting to "margin erosion" (late January 2026, LVS down about 14% on fourth-quarter 2025 results), "higher reinvestment spending" (April 2026) and low hold (July 2026). The October release is measured: "encouraged by our progress", with no margin target given. Specific guidance on Macau margins is absent.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
LVS gives no formal numerical guidance for Macau, so there is little to test. The scan records four beats in the last five reported periods, but with consensus being cut through 2026 (Jefferies and CLSA lowered Macau 2026 gaming-revenue forecasts) beats against falling estimates mean little. Reliability: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- Promotional intensity: how much of the share gain is bought, and when reinvestment normalises. Not answered with a number.
- Premium-mass softness: analysts (Seaport, October 2026) say spend per visitor is falling even as arrivals rise - a mix shift toward lower-spending and non-gaming visitors.
- Capital return: LVS spent US$950M on its own buyback in the quarter and US$101M buying 62M Sands China shares (stake now 75.56%). Minority holders of Sands China are not receiving a comparable return; no Sands China dividend is disclosed in the release.
- Concession tail: the current Macau concessions run to the end of 2032; renewal terms are not yet a market topic but cap the life of any valuation.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red: Macau property margin down 4.2 points year on year in Q3 2026 with only a small hold effect - a cost-of-share problem, not bad luck.
- Red: Macau gaming revenue down for five straight months to October 2026; November expected down again (Seaport about -6%).
- Red: Sands China net income -29.8% in Q3 2026; leverage roughly 2.7x net debt to EBITDA, new money costing over 6%.
- Red: Altman-Z of 1.7 (a solvency score; below about 1.8 is the distress zone) - though for an asset-heavy resort owner with bond-market access this overstates the risk.
- Green: Share at a three-year high (about 26.1% of mass in Q3 2026); hotel occupancy 96-99% at every property.
- Green: EBITDA recovered from about US$430M in Q2 to US$529M in Q3 2026.
- Green: The parent keeps buying Sands China stock in the market (62M shares in Q3 2026) - an informed buyer at these prices.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
LVS creeping up its Sands China stake (to 75.56%) with open-market purchases, while also buying back its own stock, signals it sees value at these prices; it also raises the long-run possibility of a minority buy-out, but the 25% free-float requirement and the absence of any proposal make that speculation, not a catalyst. The 2032/2033 bond maturities sit at or past the 2032 concession end - lenders are implicitly underwriting renewal.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: deteriorating. Revenue is holding through share gains, but profit per dollar of revenue is falling and the market itself is shrinking. The single thing to weigh: whether the 2026 margin loss is cyclical (promotions that fade when Macau demand recovers) or a new, permanently more competitive Macau. Until a quarter shows EBITDA growing again, the cheapness is a falling-earnings multiple, not a low one.

Moat: regulatory licence - one of six Macau concessionaires, with the largest room and convention base on Cotai. That barrier is real, so the moat is narrow but genuine; its width is being worn down by competition among the six (margins falling, return on invested capital about 4.4%). No structural force threatens the terminal value in the sense of a technology or channel shift; the risks are China policy, consumer spending and the 2032 concession renewal - material to the multiple, manageable to the existence of the business. The cheapness is mostly a sector-wide fear print layered on a real, cyclical earnings decline - not a value trap, but not yet a mispricing either.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory weakening · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

picks.bear_thesis: Carrefour has been cheap for a decade and has mostly stayed cheap because the earnings never arrive. Brazil, sold to investors as the growth engine in February 2025, has had falling market volumes since mid-2025 under record interest rates; Argentina is volatile; a group of French franchisees is in dispute.
