# Boyd Gaming (NYSE: BYD) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Covers five earnings calls: Q3 2025 (2025-10-23), Q4 2025 (2026-02-05), Q1 2026 (2026-04-23), Q2 2026 (2026-07-23) and Q3 2026 (2026-10-22), checked against the screener's financials and the FMP quarterly statements through 2026-09-30. Note: this is Boyd Gaming, the US regional and Las Vegas locals casino operator, not the Chinese carmaker BYD Co.*

**Bottom line:** Boyd is a steady, honestly run regional casino operator whose earnings have gone flat. Property margins have held near 38-40% for years and management delivers what it says. But since the July 2025 FanDuel stake sale, almost all per-share progress has come from buybacks, and from 2026 those buybacks are being paid for partly with new debt while free cash flow is squeezed by a heavy building program. The story is credible. The growth is mostly scheduled for 2027-2028.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-23):** The FanDuel transaction dominated. Management had just received about $1.8 billion for its FanDuel stake, cut leverage (debt divided by annual operating earnings) to about 1.5x, and spoke openly about what to do with that balance-sheet room: "could be M&A, could be other things, could tick back up." Core-customer play was "strengthening"; destination (out-of-town visitor) business was soft, mainly at the Orleans.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-05):** A victory lap on 2025: record revenue, roughly $1.4 billion of EBITDAR (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and rent), more than $800 million returned to shareholders and an 11% cut in the share count. The 2026 pitch was a list of projects: Cadence Crossing (opened end of Q1 2026), the Suncoast modernization, the St. Charles convention center, the Sky River expansion, and a tax-bill tailwind for consumers.
- **Q1-Q2 2026:** The message moved from "growth" to "steady." Midwest and South kept delivering; Las Vegas Locals stayed weighed down by the Orleans and Suncoast construction.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-22):** The language now leans on adjustments. Reported revenue and EBITDAR both fell about 1%; management pointed to the Tunica closure (November 2025), the Shreveport sale (2026-08-01), higher Kansas Star property taxes and a lower tax pass-through to say that, adjusted, revenue grew 2% and EBITDAR 1%. Destination softness in Las Vegas is now described as "increased softness," not improving. The growth story has moved out to Norfolk (opening November 2027), Par-A-Dice (construction late 2027) and the Sky River hotel (2028; it was "mid-2027" on the Q3 2025 call).

The arc: from a cash windfall and an open question about how to use it, to a flat operating base where buybacks and future openings carry the per-share story.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Margins consistent" (every call) | Midwest and South adjusted margin 38% in Q3 2026, "consistent with our third quarter margins over the last several years"; company EBITDAR $319.6M vs $321.8M a year earlier on revenue of $990M vs $1,004M | Holds |
| Core customer strength | Las Vegas Locals ex-Orleans/Suncoast revenue and EBITDAR +3% in Q3 2026; Midwest and South EBITDAR $201.6M, flat year on year | Holds, but growth is low single digits |
| Las Vegas Locals recovery | Segment EBITDAR $87.4M in Q3 2026 vs $92.1M (-5%); Downtown $12.9M vs $16.1M (-20%) | Weaker than the story; destination softness widened |
| Capital investments paying off | Sky River fees drive Managed & Other EBITDAR to $29.8M vs $26.3M (+13%); Treasure Chest and St. Charles cited | Holds where the projects have opened |
| "Robust free cash flow" (Q4 2025) | TTM (trailing twelve months) free cash flow to 2026-06-30 only $35M. Q2 2026 operating cash flow was -$24M because of the roughly $360M tax bill on the FanDuel gain (accrued expenses fell from $602M to $342M); capital spending runs about $140-155M a quarter | Distorted by the one-off tax; normalized free cash flow after all building is roughly $250-300M a year, not "robust" against a $600M+ buyback pace |
| Buybacks reduce share count | Diluted shares 73.0M in Q3 2026 vs 80.9M in Q3 2025 (-10%); $164M repurchased in Q3 2026, $387M authorization left | Holds |
| Balance sheet conservatism | Long-term debt rose from $2.27B (2026-03-31) to $2.61B (2026-06-30) to about $2.7B total debt (2026-09-30); cash $297M. Net debt including leases about $3.0B | Leverage is drifting back up from 1.5x as buybacks outrun free cash flow |
| EPS +264% (fiscal 2025) | Fiscal 2025 EPS $22.56 includes the FanDuel gain (Q3 2025 EPS $17.81 alone). Underlying EPS is about $6.6 TTM (Q4 2025 $1.79, Q1 2026 $1.37, Q2 $1.75, Q3 $1.71 GAAP; Q3 adjusted $1.67 vs $1.72 a year earlier) | The headline growth is a one-off; underlying EPS is flat to slightly down |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable, drifting slightly defensive.** Q3 2025 was confident and forward-leaning ("customer trends ... have continued into October"). Q4 2025 was celebratory. By Q3 2026 the prepared remarks spend a full paragraph on adjustments before getting to growth, and the CFO declined to give sequential guidance on the fly: "I have tried to do it in past, and hopefully, I have learned to stop doing that." On M&A, management was disciplined rather than eager: "we are not gonna buy assets just because they are cheap." On online, it played down expectations for new licenses: "not anything that will be a tailwind for us." The tone is measured and candid, not promotional.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Boyd gives little formal guidance, which limits the test. Where it did guide, it delivered: the Online segment guide was raised to $60M of EBITDAR for 2025 and set at about $30M for 2026 after the FanDuel change; Cadence Crossing opened on schedule; Norfolk is "on time and on budget." The screener shows a beat in 6 of 7 recent quarters (86%), and Q3 2026 adjusted EPS of $1.67 beat the $1.65 consensus. One timeline slipped: the Sky River hotel phase moved from "mid-2027" (2025-10-23) to "2028" (2026-10-22), though that is a managed property and a fee stream, not Boyd's own capital. **Reliability: High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Leverage and capital use:** analysts asked repeatedly from Q3 2025 where leverage would settle after the windfall; management said leverage "could tick back up." It has: debt is rising while buybacks run near $150M+ a quarter.
- **Las Vegas destination softness:** raised every quarter since Q3 2025; management has called each bottom ("90-day booking pattern ... much more positive," 2025-10-23) and the softness has instead widened by Q3 2026.
- **Strip and mid-market M&A:** pressed in Q3 2026; management deflected with discipline language.
- **Online growth and new markets:** management answered that it is a small, well-run piece and will not "juice it."

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- 🔴 Las Vegas Locals EBITDAR -5% and Downtown -20% year on year in Q3 2026, after four quarters of being told destination business was close to turning.
- 🔴 Debt-funded buybacks: long-term debt up about $430M in the first nine months of 2026 while operating earnings were flat.
- 🔴 Insiders: 0 open-market buys against 23 sales (about 700,000 shares) in the screener's lookback.
- 🔴 Reported free cash flow is thin because the building program (Norfolk, Suncoast, Orleans, Par-A-Dice) is front-loaded; the payoff is 2027-2028.
- 🟢 Margins steady around 38% in Midwest and South for "the last several years."
- 🟢 Share count down about 10% in a year; dividend maintained at $0.20 a quarter (paid 2026-10-15).
- 🟢 Sky River management fees growing double digits; Online growing double digits on a clean comparison.
- 🟢 Kept its margins through the 2021-22 inflation (gross margin 47.8% in 2019 to 56.0% in 2022).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The shift to "adjusted for these items" framing in Q3 2026 is new; earlier calls led with reported growth.
- "Destination business" has gone from a temporary drag (2025) to a standing caveat attached to every Las Vegas comment.
- Management now says plainly that it does not "have to do anything" on M&A; the excess capital is going to buybacks by default.
- The Sky River hotel slipping from mid-2027 to 2028 is small but is the first timeline slip in the set.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** The operating base is flat; the per-share result depends on buybacks and on the 2027-2028 openings. The single most important thing to weigh: the buyback is now partly funded with debt while operating earnings are not growing, so the equity is getting more levered on a flat base until Norfolk opens in November 2027.

**Moat:** a narrow but real regulatory-license moat. State gaming licenses limit new competition in most of Boyd's regional markets, and its Las Vegas locals network has scale and loyalty-program advantages. Returns are respectable (ROIC, return on invested capital, about 12%) and property margins are stable, though the scan flags gross margin as contracting; the evidence supports a stable, not widening, moat.

**Secular threat:** manageable. Online casino and sports-betting apps could pull some play away from physical casinos, but Boyd participates through Boyd Interactive and its retained FanDuel market-access fees. No terminal-value threat is visible; the cheapness looks like flat earnings plus rising leverage, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that a cash-generating fleet now trades at about 4.4 times trailing operating cash earnings, below its closest Norwegian peer, while the business keeps growing and the newbuild bill is close to fully financed.

The operating record is solid and cash-backed. Over the four quarters to 30 September 2026 Sea1 earned about $155 million of EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) on roughly $300 million of revenue. Third-quarter 2026 revenue of $79.7 million was up about 25% on a year earlier and nine-month revenue of $231.9 million was up 14%. Operating cash flow of $38.4 million in the quarter was nearly double reported net profit of $20.1 million. There is no goodwill to write off and almost no tax charge. The screening data's 'revenue down 18%' and 42% net margin are both distortions from the April 2025 sale of the Sea1 Spearfish and its $45 million one-off gain; the underlying business is growing.

The price has come to the value. At 25.40 kroner (16 November 2026) the market value is about $405 million and enterprise value (market value plus net debt) about $674 million, or 4.4 times trailing EBITDA. DOF Group, the nearest Norwegian subsea and anchor-handling comparator, trades at 4.7 times and Tidewater, the US-listed leader, at 8.7 times (paid feed, 16 November 2026). Book equity is $439 million, or about 27.6 kroner a share, so the shares trade below book value while the fleet earns a return on equity in the high teens.

The newbuild uncertainty is narrowing. The third-quarter report (6 November 2026) disclosed that half of the $50 million of fourth-quarter yard instalments and all later ones are covered by a newbuild loan facility, so the remaining equity outlay is about $25 million. Four high-specification 250-tonne-crane vessels - suited to both deepwater oil and gas and offshore wind, the only tonnage in this sector with genuine pricing power - arrive through 2027. If two are employed at the rates the committee assumed in September they add $25-30 million of annual EBITDA; all four roughly double that. Total backlog, firm plus options, is about $1.08 billion, about seven times quarterly revenue. Management is constructive on deepwater, floating production, South America and West Africa.

The controlling holder is an option, not a cost. Kistefos owns about 52% and has returned capital before (NOK 5, 7 and 4 a share in the last three payments). Once yard payments end, it can restart distributions, sell ships into a firm second-hand market or take the company private.

For this to work: Sea1 Diamond must find work on or soon after its end-January 2027 delivery; North Sea and Brazil rates must hold near current levels; and the market must look through two years of optically falling reported earnings (consensus earnings per share of $0.56 for 2026 and $0.39 for 2027) to the cash the fleet generates.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that Sea1 is about to more than double its exposure to an unproven, unemployed fleet just as part of its market softens, on a balance sheet that has no spare cash.

First, the newbuild bet is larger than it looked. The third-quarter report (6 November 2026) confirms four new vessels under construction, not two, and states that none has a commercial commitment. The first, Sea1 Diamond, arrives at the end of January 2027 - about ten weeks away - and the second at the end of April. The contract price has never been published in two years. If the programme costs in the region of $100-110 million a vessel, as the committee has assumed, it is roughly the size of the company's entire market value, and it is being funded with debt.

Second, the balance sheet is stretched. Cash fell from $111.7 million a year earlier to $35.2 million at 30 September 2026, against $69 million of short-term debt. Net debt is $269.8 million including leases, about 1.7 times trailing EBITDA today; drawing the newbuild facility could take that towards three times before the new ships earn anything. The Altman-Z solvency score is about 1.8, inside the range conventionally flagged as stressed. Free cash flow over the last twelve months is about minus $6 million.

Third, the operating momentum has stalled at the margin. The EBITDA margin slipped to 51% in the third quarter from 52% in the second and 54% a year earlier; utilisation fell to 90% from 93%; the call summary flags near-term pressure on anchor-handler rates; and firm backlog of $572.6 million compares with about $665 million cited for the first quarter. In the fourth quarter of 2024 this same fleet earned only about a quarter of today's operating profit - the earnings base can fall fast.

Fourth, the street expects reported profits to fall two years running (consensus $0.56 a share in 2026, $0.39 in 2027), because the newbuilds bring depreciation and interest before full revenue. Thinly-covered small caps rarely re-rate through that.

Fifth, the register is a permanent discount. Free float is about 22% under a 52% controlling holder; turnover is around 40,000-160,000 shares a day. Minorities have no say on the capital-allocation choices that dominate the case, and no quick exit. The yield that drew income buyers has stopped: nothing has been declared since the April 2026 special dividend.

Finally, there is one driver. Offshore exploration and production budgets key off the oil price; a fall in oil would hit day-rate expectations, the newbuilds' employment prospects and the sector multiple at the same time.
picks.consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is narrower than it was, and runs in Sea1's favour at today's price.

The quantitative consensus in screening data still reads Sea1 as a shrinking company: revenue down 18%, earnings per share down 14%, a 42% net margin. All three are distortions from the April 2025 vessel sale and its $45 million one-off gain. The third-quarter 2026 report (6 November 2026) shows revenue up about 25% year on year and nine-month revenue up 14%. A database-driven reader still sees decline where there is growth.

The published analyst view (four analysts, Strong Buy, 35.73-krone target per S&P Global in September 2026) is directionally right but internally strained: it models earnings per share falling from $0.56 in 2026 to $0.39 in 2027 on flat revenue, which reconciles only if the analysts are valuing ships rather than profit. That is defensible for a shipowner, but it means the 2027 reported numbers will look worse, and a thinly-covered small cap rarely re-rates through falling headline earnings.

Our own view sits between the two: 32.0 kroner, about 26% above today's 25.40, on three lenses that converge - the vessel-by-vessel sum of the parts (32.4 kroner), book value marked up for the operating fleet only (32.0 kroner), and the peer multiple (about 5 times EBITDA, in line with DOF Group). The market has moved from roughly fair at the last look to modestly cheap, mostly because the shares drifted lower after the results and the krone weakened. What the market may be pricing correctly is the employment risk on four uncommitted ships, which no lens above captures until they work.
picks.valley_of_death:
The risky window (the months just ahead) is concentrated in the next three to six months and centres on the newbuilds.

First, delivery without work. Sea1 Diamond arrives at the end of January 2027 and Sea1 Citrine at the end of April, each followed by fitting of underwater robots in Singapore. As of the 6 November 2026 report neither has a commercial commitment. An owner taking delivery of a high-cost ship with no contract starts paying crew, insurance, depreciation and interest immediately; a spot-only start would show up in the first-half 2027 numbers.

Second, leverage rises before earnings do. Cash was $35.2 million at 30 September 2026 against $69 million of short-term debt; $50 million of instalments fall in the fourth quarter, half from the facility; all later instalments are debt-funded. Net debt of $270 million (1.7 times EBITDA) could approach three times before the new ships contribute. The Altman-Z solvency score is about 1.8.

Third, the core market is softening at the margin: the call summary flags near-term pressure on anchor-handler rates, utilisation fell to 90% from 93%, the margin slipped to 51%, and firm backlog appears to have fallen by about $90 million since the first quarter.

Fourth, oil. Offshore exploration budgets key off the barrel; a sharp fall would hit day-rate expectations and the newbuilds' employment at once.

What would confirm the danger: Sea1 Diamond delivered without a contract, a fourth-quarter margin below 48%, or net debt above $350 million with no newbuild employment by the 11 February 2027 report.
picks.positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling opportunity in this register, and that has not changed.

Kistefos holds about 52% and Songa Capital about 10%; free float is about 22% of 153.5 million shares, and turnover runs at roughly 40,000-160,000 shares a day - well under half a million dollars. There is no index membership to lose, no crowded institutional position and no leveraged holder to margin out. The one cohort that could sell is income-seeking retail money attracted by past large dividends; nothing has been declared since the April 2026 special dividend and cash is going to the yard, so that cohort may be drifting out - which is consistent with the slow slide from 27.25 to 25.40 kroner - but it is not large enough to force a deep discount. The practical implication is the reverse of the usual: a position here is slow to build and slow to exit, and the entry the committee wants is an event, not a flush.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Wait for the event: we buy once Sea1 Diamond, the first of four new vessels, is delivered with firm work - which the fourth-quarter report on 11 February 2027 will show.

Two things changed since the committee passed on 26 October. The third-quarter results on 6 November 2026 confirmed the business is doing what we said: revenue up about 25% on a year earlier, a 51% operating cash margin, profits backed by cash, and a newbuild loan facility that now covers half of the fourth-quarter yard bill and all of the later ones. And the price has come to us: at 25.40 kroner, with the krone weaker at 9.64 to the dollar, our fair value of 32.0 kroner sits about 26% above the share price, clearing the 20% discount this backdrop requires.

What keeps us from buying at today's price is one specific fact the same report revealed: the newbuild programme is four ships, not two, and none has a contract. The first arrives in about ten weeks, into a market where anchor-handler rates are softening and firm backlog has slipped. Delivered with work, those ships justify the fair value and more; delivered idle, they push leverage towards three times earnings on a balance sheet with $35 million of cash. That is a question one dated event answers, so we wait for it rather than for a lower price, which in a stock with a 22% free float and no forced sellers may never come.

The thesis holds; there is no wide moat here - this is a cyclical vessel owner - but no structural decline either. Conviction rises from 2 to 3. What would make us buy sooner: a firm contract for any of the newbuilds announced to the exchange. What would make us step back: Diamond delivered without work, a margin below 48%, or net debt above $350 million with no employment by the February report.
picks.forcing_function:
The catalyst - what forces the re-rating - is the newbuilds finding work.

1. Delivery of Sea1 Diamond, end-January 2027, and Sea1 Citrine, end-April 2027 (third-quarter report, 6 November 2026). A firm term contract for either, announced to the exchange, converts the largest unknown in the case into contracted cash flow.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier - Sea1 Offshore Inc. (SEA1.OL, Oslo Stock Exchange)

*Full review, 16 November 2026, continuing coverage from the committee's answer of 26 October 2026. Price used: NOK 25.40 (Oslo, 16 November 2026, paid market-data feed; previous close 25.55; 52-week range 20.45-36.35). The company reports in US dollars and the shares trade in Norwegian kroner; the exchange rate used is 9.6387 kroner to the dollar (16 November 2026). At this price the market value is about NOK 3.90 billion, or $405 million, and enterprise value (market value plus net debt) is about $674 million - roughly 4.4 times trailing operating cash earnings (EBITDA, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation).*

**Sources and limits.** No earnings-call transcript is available in the paid data feed for this listing, and the full third-quarter transcript sits behind a paywall. This review uses: the quarterly income statement, balance sheet and cash-flow statement to 30 September 2026 from the paid feed; the company's 6 November 2026 results notice (Oslo exchange, via Inderes); two third-party summaries of the third-quarter report and call (Quartr and StockAnalysis, both 6 November 2026); and trade-press coverage of the newbuild programme (OE Digital / Marine Link, March 2025 and July 2026). The two results summaries are machine-written, so every figure taken from them was cross-checked against the paid feed's statements where possible; where it could not be, that is said. No management quote below is invented - where a phrase is quoted, it is the summary's wording.

## What is new since the last look (dated)

- **6 November 2026 - third-quarter results.** Revenue $79.7 million, up about 25% on the third quarter of 2025 ($63.4 million on the company's basis; $64.4 million in the paid feed). EBITDA $40.3 million, a 51% margin, against $34.2 million and 54% a year earlier and $41.5 million / 52% in the second quarter. Net profit $20.1 million, or $0.13 a share. Fleet utilisation 90%, down from 93% in the second quarter. The paid feed's statements reconcile: operating profit $26.6 million plus depreciation $13.6 million = $40.3 million.
- **The newbuild programme is four vessels, not two.** The committee's earlier records described two offshore energy support vessels on order. The third-quarter summary states that four 250-tonne-crane offshore energy support vessels are under construction and on schedule, and trade press confirms the sequence: two ordered at Cosco Shipping in November 2024 and two more on 25 March 2025; the first, Sea1 Diamond, floated out on 22 July 2026. This corrects the committee's own record.
- **Delivery and employment.** Sea1 Diamond is due end-January 2027 and Sea1 Citrine end-April 2027, each followed by fitting of underwater robots (ROVs, remotely operated vehicles) in Singapore; Oceaneering has signed for Diamond's ROVs. The summary states the newbuilds have **no commercial commitments yet**.
- **Financing partly disclosed.** Fourth-quarter yard instalments are expected at $50 million, of which $25 million comes from a newbuild loan facility, and later instalments are to be fully financed by that facility. The facility's size is reported inconsistently ($315 million and $350 million in different summaries) and could not be verified against a primary document; the contract price per vessel is still undisclosed.
- **Backlog.** Firm backlog $572.6 million plus $502 million of options, about $1.08 billion in total. A third-party summary of the first quarter cited $665 million firm; if comparable, firm backlog has run down by about $90 million in two quarters.
- **Market commentary.** Management is constructive on deepwater, production, rig and floating-production activity in South America, West Africa and parts of Asia-Pacific (with Asia-Pacific rig activity seen rising from late 2027), but the call summary flags near-term pressure on anchor-handler rates.
- **Balance sheet at 30 September 2026.** Cash $35.2 million (from $39.0 million in June and $111.7 million a year earlier). Borrowings $300.9 million plus $4.1 million of capitalised leases: net debt $269.8 million including leases, $265.6 million excluding them. Equity $439.3 million. Third-quarter capital spending of $45.5 million against operating cash flow of $38.4 million left free cash flow at minus $7.2 million. No dividend was paid in the quarter; the last was the NOK 4.00 special dividend announced 30 March 2026 and paid about 16 April 2026.
- **Price and currency.** The shares have drifted from 27.25 kroner at the last look to 25.40, with no company-specific negative news beyond the results; the krone has weakened from 9.32 to 9.64 per dollar, which lifts every dollar-based value by about 3.4% in kroner terms.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Sea1 Offshore is the company formerly called Siem Offshore, controlled by Christen Sveaas's Kistefos (about 52%). It owns a fleet of offshore support vessels - anchor handlers, platform supply vessels, subsea construction and well-intervention ships, fast crew boats and oil-spill units in Brazil, and a scientific core-drilling ship - and manages a further group of anchor handlers for a fee.

The story over the last two years has had three chapters. First (2024 to mid-2025), a clean-up: the April 2025 sale of the Sea1 Spearfish for roughly $113 million, which inflated 2025 profits with a one-off gain, and a run of large dividends (NOK 5, then 7, then 4 a share). Second (late 2024 onwards), a fleet-renewal pivot: an order for two, then four, high-specification offshore energy support vessels at Cosco, designed to serve both oil-and-gas subsea work and offshore wind. Third (2026), steady operating delivery: revenue and operating cash earnings have risen every quarter this year while the company has quietly shifted cash from dividends to yard instalments.

What has shifted is the weight of the newbuild programme in the story. Four uncommitted ships arriving across 2027 is a much larger bet relative to a $405 million market value than the two the committee had been modelling, and the company now talks about pursuing "favourable long-term contracts or well-paid short-term work" for them - an open-ended employment strategy rather than ships ordered against a charter.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim / narrative | What the numbers show (paid feed, quarter to 30 Sep 2026) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| The operating business is growing | Revenue $68.3m (Q4 25), $72.0m (Q1 26), $80.1m (Q2), $79.7m (Q3); nine-month revenue $231.9m vs $203.3m (+14%) | Matches |
| Margins are strong | Operating profit plus depreciation: $35.4m, $37.6m, $41.5m, $40.3m; margin 51% in Q3, down from 52% in Q2 and 54% a year earlier | Matches, but the expansion run has stopped |
| Earnings are high quality | Q3 operating cash flow $38.4m vs net income $20.1m; no goodwill or intangibles; tax charge small | Matches |
| Newbuilds are financed | Q3 capital spending $45.5m vs operating cash flow $38.4m; net debt rose from $263.9m to $269.8m; facility to fund half of Q4 and all later instalments (summary; size unverified) | Partly verified - financing exists, cost undisclosed |
| The screening data's "revenue -18%, net margin 42%" | Artefacts of the April 2025 vessel-sale gain ($45m non-cash in Q2 2025); trailing earnings per share are $0.55 against the scan's $0.76 fiscal-year figure | Scan headline is misleading, as before |
| Cash generation | Trailing free cash flow about minus $6m after newbuild instalments; cash down $77m in twelve months | The newbuild programme is consuming all the operating cash |

The forensic picture is clean in the sense that matters - the reported profit is backed by cash from operations, with no accounting adjustments doing the work - but the capital programme now absorbs every dollar the fleet earns, and the company has stopped growing its cash cushion.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable.** With no direct transcript access, tone is read from the summaries and the company's own disclosures. The third-quarter commentary is constructive on long-cycle demand (deepwater, floating production, South America, West Africa) but adds a specific near-term caution on anchor-handler rates - a shift from purely offensive to a mixed message. The company has not issued numeric guidance in any quarter reviewed, so there is nothing to grade as more or less specific.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

There is no formal financial guidance to track. The two operational commitments that can be checked have held: the newbuild programme is reported on schedule (Sea1 Diamond floated out 22 July 2026, delivery end-January 2027, consistent with the first-half 2027 window given at order), and the high utilisation claimed through 2026 is reflected in revenue. Analyst coverage is thin (four analysts per S&P Global at September 2026, consensus earnings per share of $0.56 for 2026 and $0.39 for 2027); the company's 2026 delivery so far ($0.46 for nine months) is on track for the 2026 figure. Reliability: **Medium** - nothing missed, but little is promised.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The questions that matter and remain unanswered from the public record: (a) the contract price of the four newbuilds and the total programme cost; (b) the employment plan for four uncommitted ships in a market where anchor-handler rates are softening; (c) the dividend policy once yard payments end - the last three payments run 5, 7, then 4 kroner and nothing has been declared since April; (d) why firm backlog appears to have fallen from about $665 million in the first quarter to $573 million. None of these was answered in the material available.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: four newbuilds with no commercial commitments, the first arriving in about ten weeks (end-January 2027) - Q3 2026 report.
- Red: programme cost still undisclosed after two years; the newbuild loan facility's size is reported inconsistently ($315m vs $350m) - Q4 2025 and Q3 2026 summaries.
- Red: cash $35.2m against $69.0m of short-term debt at 30 September 2026; Altman-Z solvency score about 1.8, inside the range conventionally flagged as stressed.
- Red: near-term pressure on anchor-handler rates (Q3 2026 call summary); utilisation slipped to 90% from 93%.
- Red: firm backlog down by about $90m since the first quarter (if the two summaries are comparable).
- Green: revenue up about 25% year on year in Q3 2026; EBITDA margin 51%; nine-month EBITDA $119.4m vs $114.1m.
- Green: reported profit backed by operating cash; no goodwill; small tax charge.
- Green: half of Q4 instalments and all later ones financed by a committed facility, so the equity outlay on the programme is now bounded at roughly $25m more.
- Green: total backlog including options of about $1.08 billion, roughly seven times quarterly revenue.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The language around the newbuilds has moved from "ordered to serve a tight high-end market" to "pursue favourable long-term contracts or well-paid short-term work" - a hedge that leaves room for spot employment. Dividends have gone quiet: after three large payments, nothing was declared with the half-year or third-quarter results, consistent with cash being redirected to the yard. The board change on 14 October 2026 (Orjan Svanevik in for Rune Magnus Lundetrae) carries no disclosed strategic signal. The controlling holder's behaviour (Kistefos at about 52%) remains the largest unpriced variable: it can restart distributions, sell ships into a firm second-hand market or take the company private, and has disclosed no intention to do any of these.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** The existing fleet is earning more than a year ago, with cash-backed profits, but every dollar of that is going into four ships that are not yet employed.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** whether the four newbuilds find work at rates that justify their (undisclosed) cost. Delivered into firm demand, they could add $25-30 million of annual operating cash earnings each pair and lift the value well above today's price; delivered idle or into spot work while anchor-handler rates soften, they turn a 1.7-times leverage company into a 3-times leverage company with a solvency score already in the cautionary zone. The first test arrives with Sea1 Diamond's delivery at the end of January 2027 and the fourth-quarter report on 11 February 2027.

**Moat.** None in the economic sense. Offshore support vessels are a capital-intensive, cyclical, commodity-like service; competitive advantage comes from fleet specification and customer relationships, not from switching costs or network effects. Returns are currently healthy (return on invested capital roughly 9-13% depending on the measure) but cyclical, not structural. The trend is stable over the last four quarters.

**Secular threat.** Manageable. The energy transition is a long-dated risk to oil-and-gas offshore spending, but the newbuilds are designed for both oil-and-gas subsea work and offshore wind, and the near-term driver is deepwater and floating-production activity, which management describes as firm. The cheapness is a combination of cyclical caution, a controlled shareholder register with a 22% free float, and the newbuild overhang - not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · no real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Maurel & Prom (MAU.PA) - deep dive on management and the setup
*As of 2026-11-09. Paris listing, prices in euros; the company reports in US dollars.*

**Source note.** No earnings-call transcript is available for Maurel & Prom (M&P) - the company reports twice a year and publishes trading updates rather than holding transcribed quarterly calls, and the FMP data feed carries no transcript or press release for this listing. The company's own 22 October 2026 release ("Activity for the first nine months of 2026") is listed on its investor site, but the document could not be retrieved in this session (repeated download timeouts), so we do not quote its figures. This deep dive therefore rests on: the screener's fiscal-year financials; the FMP balance sheet at 30 June 2026; the Gran Tierra Energy (GTE) disclosures about the deal in which M&P is the buyer (signing 5 August 2026, GTE shareholder approval 9 October 2026, GTE third-quarter results 5 November 2026 and its call on 6 November 2026); and live market quotes (M&P EUR 7.10, Brent USD 92.4, both on 9 November 2026). The web-search budget for this run was exhausted, so no broker notes or analyst targets were checked; we cite none.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
For most of 2021-2025 the story was simple: a disciplined, cash-rich producer of Gabonese oil (operated Ezanga permit), with Tanzanian gas, an Angolan interest, a stake of about 20% in Nigeria's Seplat, and a re-entry into Venezuela, controlled by Indonesia's state oil company Pertamina. Net income climbed from $120M (2021) to $233M (2024), and the balance sheet moved to net cash (about $174M at end-2025, $193M at 30 June 2026 on FMP's figures).

In 2026 the story pivoted. On 5 August 2026 M&P signed to buy all of Gran Tierra's Colombian and Ecuadorian business for a total consideration of about $1.33B, structured largely as the assumption of Gran Tierra's debt (its 2029 and 2031 notes, the 9.75% secured amortizing notes) and an oil prepayment. The company went from "net cash, return capital" to "scale up through a levered acquisition in Latin America". It has also joined the SBF 120 index.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim / narrative | What the numbers show |
|---|---|
| Earnings power rising | FY2025 net income $427M on revenue of $602M (a 71% net margin) is inflated by non-recurring items; revenue fell 26% that year. The underlying run-rate is closer to the $210-235M of 2022-2024. |
| Strong cash generation | Free-cash-flow margin was -3.6% in the latest fiscal year and FCF fell 116%; capital spending (including Venezuela and Gabon drilling) absorbed operating cash. |
| Fortress balance sheet | True today (cash and short-term investments $439M vs debt $177M at 30 June 2026), but it is the asset being spent: the Gran Tierra deal swaps it for an estimated $0.8-0.9B of net debt at closing. |
| Accretive acquisition | Gran Tierra's own third quarter (released 5 November 2026) was weak: a $42M net loss, oil sales down 10% on Q2, operating costs up 24% quarter on quarter, and lower realized South American prices. The business M&P is buying is deteriorating into the close. |
| Book value compounding | Book value per share grew about 21.5% a year over five years, and equity was $1.60B at mid-2026 - roughly equal to today's market value of EUR 1.42B (about $1.59B). |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Rating: Stable to rising in ambition, with no call transcript to grade word by word. Management's public framing of the Gran Tierra deal ("a major step" for the group, 5 August 2026) is confident and expansionary. Shifts toward offensive, growth language at a time when the oil price that justified it has been falling (Brent from a 50-day average near $104 to $92 on 9 November 2026) is a mild warning sign.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Historically Medium-High: M&P has generally delivered its production and dividend commitments, and raised the dividend 15% in 2026. The new risk is execution of an acquisition roughly the size of its own market value, in two new countries, closing (per Gran Tierra's CEO on 6 November 2026) "early to mid-December", still subject to regulatory approvals in Colombia and Ecuador. Reliability: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
Without transcripts we cannot quote analyst questions. The obvious pressure points: (a) the acquisition price was set near a $100+ oil tape; (b) what the pro-forma leverage looks like at $80-90 Brent; (c) whether the dividend survives the debt load; (d) Venezuela licence and payment risk; (e) cost inflation in Colombia (Gran Tierra cited a stronger peso and higher power costs).

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red: net cash becomes net debt of roughly $0.8-0.9B at closing (deal terms 5 August 2026).
- Red: the target posted a $42M net loss in the third quarter of 2026 with rising costs (5 November 2026).
- Red: Brent fell 6% on 9 November 2026 alone, to $92; the deal economics were struck at a higher deck.
- Red: Altman Z-score (a bankruptcy-risk gauge) of 1.6 and Piotroski 5/9 - middling quality even before the leverage.
- Red: the 71% net margin and EPS of 2.13 are one-off-inflated; consensus expects EPS to fall about 22%.
- Green: a strong controlling shareholder (Pertamina) that has amended its sponsor support and shareholder-loan agreements (15 October 2026), which lowers refinancing risk.
- Green: book value roughly equal to market value, plus a listed Seplat stake that gives a mark-to-market asset.
- Green: low-cost, long-life Gabon base.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
The 15 October 2026 amendments to the sponsor support agreement with Pertamina and to a shareholder loan suggest the parent is lining up financing support for the acquisition - helpful for solvency, but also a sign the deal leans on parent credit rather than M&P's own cash. Inclusion in the SBF 120 index brings index-tracking holders who may sell mechanically if the shares fall out again.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: PIVOTING - from a net-cash dividend payer to a levered, almost entirely oil-weighted Latin American and African producer. The single most important thing to weigh: the downside support we valued (net cash) is gone at closing, and the acquired cash flows are falling with the oil price, so the equity now carries the full oil beta plus leverage.

Moat: an exploration and production company has no durable moat beyond its cost position; M&P's Gabon assets are low-cost, but Gran Tierra's assets are higher-cost and declining. Moat type: scale-cost, narrow at best - call it NONE in the durable sense. Secular threat: the energy transition is a manageable, long-dated risk for an oil producer with reserve lives of 10-15 years; it is not what drives the next two years, the oil price does.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · no real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.
