The company pays 75% of net profit each quarter - USD 2.40 for Q2 and USD 1.35 for Q3 2026 (ex-dividend in Copenhagen today, 2026-11-16) - and has paid USD 17.45 per share since 2023. Leverage is low: net debt of USD 686m at 2026-09-30 against a broker fleet value of USD 4,333m. The supply side is the durable part of the case and pre-dates the war: management showed on 2026-02-26 that one in four Aframax/LR2 ships is under sanctions and that 2025 sanctions removed almost three years of newbuild deliveries, while LR2s migrating into crude trades have shrunk the fleet actually carrying clean products by about 4% this year even as the nominal fleet grew 7% (Q3 2026 call). Refinery closures in Europe and the US West Coast lengthen voyages, and management estimates inventory rebuilding after the Hormuz disruption adds 1-2% to oil trade volumes over the next year. Clean-product exports out of the Gulf are still only about 1m barrels a day versus 2.5-3m pre-war, so a normalization of those flows is additional cargo entering an already tight market. If rates stay near current levels through 2027, the company earns roughly USD 8-9 per share again, pays most of it out, and net asset value holds or rises - at 0.9x today's NAV the holder is paid to wait. The overhang of the former controlling holder is gone: Oaktree sold its last 6.33m shares around USD 40 on 2026-10-06, so the stock no longer carries a known seller.
picks.bear_thesis: The cheapness is a peak-cycle optical illusion. A trailing price-to-earnings near 4x is meaningless for a shipowner at the top of a war-driven rate spike: pre-war, in Q3 2025, TORM earned USD 78m a quarter; in Q3 2026 it earned USD 199m, and the difference is mostly disruption. The Strait of Hormuz is reopening - management itself says Gulf crude exports are recovering towards pre-conflict levels - and when the inefficiencies (rerouting, ship-to-ship transfers, war-risk avoidance) unwind, spot rates can fall fast; management's own Q3 slide warns that market conditions can change quickly. The anchor for a shipowner is net asset value, and that is marked at peak ship prices: the USD 39.60 per share NAV (2026-09-30), or about USD 38.25 after today's dividend, would fall to about USD 27-31 if vessel values retreat 25-30% toward mid-cycle, and tanker equities historically trade below NAV in a falling-rate market. Meanwhile management is buying and ordering at the top - six MR resales, eight MR newbuildings, an 8-ship LR2 joint venture whose equity cost it declined to disclose (Q3 2026 call) - and has issued about 20m shares since 2023. The best-informed holder, Oaktree, sold out completely at about USD 40 in October. There is no time-charter cover for 2027 (management prefers spot), so the earnings stream is fully exposed. The thesis depends on one shared macro factor - oil-market disruption - that also drives every other tanker name, so it adds little independent return to a book.
picks.consensus_delta: The question for a deep-value name is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into stable earnings power. Here it is the reverse: the market is not pricing decline, it is pricing roughly fair value on peak-cycle assets. At DKK 240 (about USD 35.3 ex-dividend) the stock trades at about 0.92x the USD 38.25 ex-dividend net asset value, and near the USD 40 at which Oaktree exited in October. The screener's 58% margin of safety and DKK 383 fair value are built on fiscal-2023 numbers and are wrong for today. Where we disagree with the market is narrow: the market appears to discount some normalization already (the stock is about 17% below its 52-week high of DKK 290.6 and fell from about DKK 250 in the past 50 sessions as the Hormuz reopening became visible), so a full fourth quarter of windfall earnings - already half booked at USD 78,419 per day - is being given little credit. That is worth roughly USD 4 per share of value accretion in the next few months. It is not a large enough gap to call the stock mispriced at today's price.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window is the next 3-9 months as the Gulf normalizes. If the Strait of Hormuz reopening leads to a fast unwinding of rerouting and ship-to-ship inefficiencies, spot product-tanker rates could fall sharply into the first half of 2027, Q1 2027 guidance (published with full-year results in early 2027) would print well below 2026, and the quarterly dividend would shrink mechanically with the 75% payout. Vessel values would follow rates down, cutting net asset value. There is no debt maturity wall or cash-burn hump - net debt is only about 16% of fleet value - and the newbuild program is funded, so this is a price and dividend risk, not a solvency risk. Undisclosed equity commitments to the LR2 joint venture are the one balance-sheet unknown.
picks.positioning_washout: The largest forced seller has already left: Oaktree sold its final 6.33m shares in an underwritten offering at about USD 40 (2026-10-06), and its board representative stepped down (2026-10-09). The remaining shareholder base is heavy in yield-focused holders attracted by a double-digit trailing yield. If quarterly dividends fall sharply in 2027 as rates normalize, those holders would sell - that is the realistic source of a sell-off, together with a sector-wide de-rating of tanker equities on peace or normalization headlines. Either could take the price into the low DKK 220s.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near DKK 226, which a sector-wide sell-off in tanker shares as the Gulf disruption fades could deliver. The thesis holds: TORM is earning record money, is lightly indebted (net debt USD 686m against USD 4.3bn of ships at 2026-09-30) and pays out 75% of its profit. But the right yardstick for a shipowner is net asset value, not a peak-year price-to-earnings, and at DKK 240 the shares already trade at about 0.92x a net asset value that is itself marked at peak ship prices. Our base fair value of DKK 272 (about USD 40) credits one more quarter of booked windfall earnings and a modest softening in vessel prices; that is only about 13% above today's price, short of the 20% discount this backdrop requires before we buy. At DKK 226 the discount clears that bar while still sitting well above our adverse case of DKK 180, the value if ship prices fall 30% and the market pays 0.85x for them. The past catalysts - the rate spike, two guidance upgrades and the exit of the former controlling holder - have already happened and are neither a plus nor a minus here. This is a cyclical asset with no lasting competitive moat, and its fortunes ride on the same oil-market disruption that drives every tanker stock, so it adds little independent return to the book; conviction is moderate.
picks.forcing_function: There is no event that forces a re-rating upward. The hard dates are the 2026-12-02 dividend payment and full-year 2026 results with 2027 guidance in early 2027; the latter is more likely to reset expectations down than up unless the Gulf disruption persists. A sector-wide de-rating as the Hormuz disruption fades is the most plausible route to the entry level we want.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# TORM plc (0RG4.L, London order-book line quoted in Danish kroner) - a deep dive on management and the setup

Debate date: 2026-11-16. Live price used: DKK 240.0 on the London line 0RG4.L (FMP quote, 2026-11-16). The same share trades at DKK 239.0 in Copenhagen (TRMD A) and USD 36.43 on Nasdaq (TRMD, still carrying the USD 1.35 dividend, which goes ex in New York on 2026-11-17). At USD/DKK 6.79 the London price equals about USD 35.3, i.e. already ex-dividend, consistent with the Copenhagen line.

Identity note: the peer-group file could not identify this ticker. It is TORM plc (ISIN GB00BZ3CNK81), a product tanker owner-operator with about 95 vessels on the water, listed in Copenhagen and New York. The screener metrics block is stale: its fiscal-year rows end in 2023 and its "latest quarter" is 2024-03-31. The scan's fair value of DKK 383 and its 58% margin of safety come from that 2023 earnings base and must not be used. This dossier relies on the five calls from 2025-11-06 to 2026-11-04, the Q3 2026 results release (2026-11-04), the guidance upgrade (2026-10-12) and the FMP balance sheet at 2026-09-30.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-11-06):** a "relatively stable market" story. Net profit USD 78m, dividend USD 0.62. The case rested on structural supply: refinery closures in Europe and the US West Coast lengthening voyages, and sanctions removing ships from the trading pool.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-26):** the supply story sharpened. Management stressed that 1 in 4 vessels in the combined Aframax/LR2 segment is under US, EU or UK sanctions, and that 2025 sanctions (more than 200 vessels) equalled almost three years of newbuild deliveries. Full-year 2025: TCE (time-charter-equivalent earnings, revenue net of voyage costs) USD 910m against guidance of USD 650-950m; net profit USD 286m; USD 212m returned.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-05-13):** the story turned on a geopolitical shock. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz "marked a further and unprecedented escalation in tanker rates". Net profit USD 122m; full-year TCE guidance raised to USD 1.15-1.45bn; Q2 bookings above USD 70,000 per day.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-08-26):** the peak quarter. EBITDA USD 416m, net profit USD 338m, Q2 earnings above USD 59,000 per day, interim dividend USD 2.40 (USD 246m). Management said 2026 would be the highest TCE year in TORM's history.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-11-04):** the story moved to "the OneTORM platform" (their integrated commercial, technical and operating model) and to reinvestment: 6 MR resales bought in Q2, 6 + 2 MR newbuildings, 8 LR2 newbuildings in a 50/50 joint venture after quarter-end, plus 2 more MR options. Net profit USD 199m, dividend USD 1.35. Management now frames the reopening of Hormuz as "the beginning of a new adjustment phase", not the end of the boom.

The arc runs from structural supply discipline, to a war-driven windfall, to heavy reinvestment justified by a "constructive view [that] does not rely on disruption". That last claim is the one to test.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Higher earnings translate directly into higher shareholder returns" | Dividends USD 0.62 (Q3-25), 0.70 (Q4-25), 2.40 (Q2-26), 1.35 (Q3-26); Q3-26 payout is 75% of net profit excluding one-offs (release 2026-11-04); USD 17.45 per share paid since 2023 | Matches. The payout policy is mechanical and has been kept. |
| 2025 TCE would land in USD 650-950m | Delivered USD 910m (Q4-25 call) | Delivered, upper half. |
| 2026 is the strongest year ever | 9-month EBITDA USD 891m (201 + 416 + 274); full-year EBITDA guidance raised to USD 1,300-1,500m (2026-10-12) then the low end lifted to 1,350-1,500m (2026-11-04) | Matches; Q4 coverage is 53% of days at USD 78,419/day. |
| Balance sheet stays conservative while investing | Net debt USD 686m at 2026-09-30 (debt 1,132m incl. 9m leases, cash 447m), against a broker fleet value of USD 4,333m - about 16% loan-to-value (debt over vessel value). CFO: loan-to-value "including all CapEx committed at mid-20[s]" | Matches, but the mid-20s figure depends on today's elevated vessel prices. |
| Net asset value (vessels at broker prices minus net debt) | USD 4,062m, or USD 39.60 per share, at 2026-09-30 | Value is mark-to-market at peak-cycle ship prices; the per-share NAV falls by USD 1.35 when this dividend leaves. |
| Commercial edge: MR fleet earned "more than $200 million of additional TCE" vs peers 2023-25 | Company-sourced, unaudited; roughly USD 65m a year on a USD 0.9-1.5bn TCE base | Plausible but self-reported; a modest edge, not a moat. |
| "Our constructive view does not rely on disruption" | Q3-25 (pre-war) net profit was USD 78m a quarter; Q3-26 is USD 199m. The step-up is mostly the disruption. | Richer than the numbers justify. Pre-war run-rate earnings were about one-third of today's. |

Dilution: about 20 million shares issued since 2023, mainly as vessel-purchase consideration; small RSU (restricted share unit) exercises continue at DKK 179.80 (2026-10-07, 2026-11-12). Share count now about 102.7m.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-rising, now consciously hedged.** Q3-25: "relatively stable market environment". Q1-26: "one of the strongest cross-segment market environments we've seen in several years". Q2-26: "highest annual TCE earnings in TORM's history". Q3-26 adds an explicit caveat - "shipping remains a highly cyclical and volatile industry. Market conditions can change quickly" - while arguing the reopening is "not the end of the story". The language is offensive (fleet growth, newbuilds) but carries the most cyclical caution of the five calls.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Guidance is a mechanical formula, explained by the CFO on the Q4-25 call: booked days at fixed rates plus open days at the forward curve, minus normal costs. It is revised upward as bookings fill - 2025 landed at USD 910m on a USD 650-950m range, and 2026 TCE guidance went USD 1.15-1.45bn (May) to higher (August) to USD 1.70-1.90bn (October) to USD 1.75-1.90bn (November). This is not sandbagging; it is a formula that follows the spot market. The stale screener field "beat 1/3 quarters" refers to 2023-24 and is not informative. **Reliability: High** (as a description of booked earnings; it says nothing about 2027).

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Why build/buy now, at peak prices?** (Evercore, Q3-26): management answered that vessel sales are opportunistic and "not a necessary tool" to fund the program.
- **Joint-venture equity cost for the 8 LR2s** (Clarksons, Q3-26): management declined to quantify, citing confidentiality. The size of the commitment is undisclosed - a real gap for a buyer.
- **Time charters to lock in rates** (Clarksons, Q3-26): management is not taking multi-year charters because the forward curve is not above its own normalized model - candid, but it also means 2027 earnings are almost entirely open to the spot market.
- **Clean-product exports from the Gulf** stand around 1m barrels a day versus 2.5-3m pre-war; management is "not confident" of a quick recovery while the conflict persists.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: newbuild and joint-venture commitments made at the top of the asset-price cycle, with the JV equity undisclosed (Q3-26).
- Red: earnings power roughly 2.5x the pre-war run-rate (Q3-25 USD 78m vs Q3-26 USD 199m); the base is a windfall.
- Red: the long-time controlling holder Oaktree sold its last 6.33m shares at about USD 40.05 (offering priced 2026-10-06, holding reported nil 2026-10-08) - the best-informed holder took the peak.
- Red: about 20m shares issued since 2023 (Q3-26 call).
- Green: low leverage - net debt USD 686m against USD 4.3bn of ships (2026-09-30).
- Green: a mechanical 75% payout that has been honored every quarter; the Oaktree overhang is now gone.
- Green: Q4 2026 already 53% booked at USD 78,419/day (as of 2026-10-28).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The new emphasis on "OneTORM" and "the value of each vessel throughout its life cycle" (Q3-26) is a pre-emptive defense of keeping old ships and buying new ones at high prices.
- "We have deliberately maintained more vessels on the water" contrasts with peers that sold older ships into the boom - TORM is choosing more earnings exposure over harvesting asset values.
- The board seat held by Oaktree's nominee ended 2026-10-09; governance is now a widely held Danish/US listed company with no anchor holder.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** The business is executing well inside a cyclical windfall; capital allocation (75% payout, low leverage) is disciplined, but the reinvestment is pro-cyclical.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** the stock trades at about 0.9x net asset value with peak-cycle earnings and peak-cycle vessel prices. The apparent price-to-earnings of around 4x is a peak artifact; the anchor is NAV, and NAV itself shrinks if ship prices normalize.

**Moat:** none in the economic sense. Product tankers are a price-taking commodity service; TORM's claimed commercial outperformance (about USD 65m a year) is a modest operating edge, not pricing power. Returns (book ROE about 30% on 2026 run-rate) are cyclical, not structural. **Secular threat:** manageable - long-run oil-product demand faces the energy transition, but an aging fleet and sanctions limit effective supply for years; it is not a terminal impairment within the holding horizon.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · no real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: Sallie Mae is the largest US private student lender and is gaining share at the moment its market is getting bigger. Federal PLUS reform, which caps federal graduate and parent loans from July 2026, is already showing in the numbers: third-quarter 2026 originations were a record $3.4 billion (up 15%), graduate originations rose 119% with FICO credit scores about 9 points above the book average, and October disbursements were up 35% month to date. Management estimates the reform could eventually add $4.5-5 billion a year, roughly 70% more than 2025 volume. Funding that growth no longer depends only on the bank balance sheet. A second partner, Sixth Street, committed on 2026-10-22 to buy at least $1.5 billion of new loans a year for three years, on top of the KKR arrangement from late 2025, and both pay recurring program-management and servicing fees (other income up $15 million year on year in Q3 2026). The third-quarter loss of $0.19 a share is largely accounting timing. CECL (the current expected credit loss standard) requires a lender to reserve for a loan's lifetime losses on the day it is made, so record originations brought $214 million of provisions in the quarter, while the planned whole-loan sale that would have booked gains was postponed. Underneath, credit outside one segment is stable: the reserve rate is 5.89%, down year on year, co-signers back about 95% of new loans, and borrowers leaving loan-modification programs are performing better than planned. The extra losses come from borrowers steered into default by debt-resolution firms, and management says those borrowers can pay, with early recoveries running at meaningfully higher rates. If 2027 earnings come in near the street's $3.00 a share (2028: $3.65), the stock at $16.55 trades at about 5.5 times next year's earnings and about 1.5 times book value of roughly $10.8 a share. For a franchise that earned more than 25% on equity in 2025 and has cut its share count 59% since 2020, that is cheap. Book value also understates the loans, which have been selling at mid- to high single-digit gains over a carrying value already net of a roughly 6% reserve. Conditions: fourth-quarter 2026 charge-offs land inside the $400-420 million full-year guide, 2027 guidance implies a clear rebound in earnings per share, and loan-sale premiums recover as rate volatility eases.
picks.bear_thesis: The 2026 reset is a credibility event and possibly the first chapter of a broader credit turn, not a one-off. In twelve months management went from 'not observed any material change in our borrowers' ability' (2025-10-23), to a $25 million debt-resolution hit 'concentrated, understood and manageable' (2026-07-23), to a $45 million hit, a net charge-off guide of $400-420 million against an original $345-385 million, and an earnings-per-share guide cut about 36% to $1.95-2.05 (2026-10-22). Loans 30 or more days delinquent were 4.2% against 4.0% a year earlier, and forbearance rose to 2.3% from 2.0%. The 2026 graduating class enters repayment this fall, with entry-level hiring under pressure from AI, and management admits it cannot see more than about twelve months ahead on credit. The hidden value in the loans, the main bull argument, just failed its test: the planned roughly $1 billion whole-loan sale was cancelled because higher long-term rates pushed premiums below the company's threshold. In the current backdrop of positive real rates and a steep yield curve, fixed-rate student loans are worth less to buyers, and that may last. Capital is thinning. Common equity is about $2.0 billion, the core capital ratio slipped to 11.8% at Q2 2026 from 12.4% at Q1, and the company spent heavily on buybacks at $22-26 a share this year with only $111 million of authorization left, so the buyback that supported the stock is close to exhausted just as growth needs capital. Expenses are running at $750-780 million a year to compete for graduate loans, and pricing pressure in that market is building. Three law firms opened shareholder investigations in late October, and insiders sold 68,000 shares with no purchases. The stock has fallen to a new 52-week low ($16.39 intraday on 2026-11-16) and keeps falling after a 2026-10-23 drop. If 2027 earnings land near $2.00 a share, which is plausible if charge-offs keep running above $420 million and sale gains stay small, 6 times earnings gives about $12, or about 1.1 times book. Confirmation would be: fourth-quarter charge-offs above guidance, a 30+ day delinquency rate above 4.5% in early 2027, 2027 guidance below about $2.25 a share, or another cancelled or sub-par loan sale.
picks.consensus_delta: The street is split (11 firms: 5 buy, 5 hold, 1 sell) and still anchored high. The consensus target is $25.67, and the four October targets averaged $24.50, 48% above today's price. 2027 consensus earnings per share are $3.00 and 2028 $3.65, which assumes 2026 was purely timing (CECL reserves on record growth plus a delayed sale) and that earnings bounce back about 50% next year. The market at $16.55 prices 2027 earnings nearer $2.00-2.25 at a distrusted multiple. Our base case of about $2.65 sits between the two. Where we disagree with the market: the franchise and growth are better than the share price implies, while the earnings path is worse than the street targets imply. The stock is cheap, but it is not yet safe.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window is the next three months. (1) The 2026 graduating class enters repayment between November 2026 and January 2027, when stress on young borrowers is seasonally highest, while entry-level hiring is soft. (2) Fourth-quarter numbers will carry more CECL reserves on elevated October disbursements (up 35%), and gains depend on closing the rest of the $600 million Sixth Street seed portfolio and the KKR flow sale of about $1.44 billion of loans held for sale. We do not name a price-wait level, because no identifiable forced seller is due at a specific level. The question is whether the thesis holds, not where a flush ends.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for proof: we buy once the fourth-quarter 2026 results, due around 2027-01-21, show full-year 2026 charge-offs at or below $420 million and 2027 earnings guidance of at least about $2.60 a share. The thesis is in doubt until that test. The business case is half proven. The growth half holds: record originations of $3.4 billion in the third quarter, graduate lending up 119%, and a second partner (Sixth Street) committing at least $1.5 billion a year all show that federal PLUS reform is handing Sallie Mae a bigger market. The earnings half has not held. On 2026-10-22 the company reported a $0.19 per share loss, raised its charge-off guidance for the second time, cancelled a loan sale because buyers' premiums fell with higher rates, and cut 2026 earnings guidance by about 36%, three months after calling the higher figure achievable. At $16.55 the stock prices much of that, at about 1.5 times book value and about 5.5 times the street's 2027 earnings. Our base fair value is $21 (8 times about $2.65 of 2027 earnings, cross-checked against adjusted book value), about 27% above today, against a downside case of about $12 if 2027 earnings settle near $2. That is roughly one-to-one with no structural floor, which is not enough to buy ahead of proof from a team whose forecasts just missed badly. The macro backdrop (positive real long rates, fearful credit) is a headwind for a lender whose hidden value depends on selling fixed-rate loans, though that is context, not the reason for waiting. Conviction is middling. The franchise, its narrow but real moat (scale, more than 2,100 school relationships, cheap deposit funding) and the share count cut by 59% since 2020 make this worth owning if credit stabilizes. A management team scored at 2 of 5 for credibility, deteriorating earnings delivery and a buyback nearly spent are why we wait for the January numbers instead of paying for the promise now.
picks.forcing_function: In order: (1) the CEO's fireside chat at TD Cowen on 2026-11-17, the first public comment since the reset, likely with an update on peak season and debt-resolution recoveries; (2) the 'insights … later this fall' on the size of the PLUS opportunity, promised on 2026-10-22; (3) the decisive one, the fourth-quarter 2026 results with full-year charge-offs and 2027 guidance, expected around 2027-01-21. A 2027 guide pointing to $2.60 a share or more with charge-offs inside $400-420 million would restore the earnings-power thesis and should send the multiple back toward 8 times. Further out, a resumed whole-loan sale at a normal premium, a new buyback authorization, or a third strategic partner for graduate loans (management's stated next priority, before the 2027 peak season) would each give the market a dated reason to re-rate.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Sallie Mae (SLM) — a deep dive on management and the setup
*Five earnings calls, October 2025 to October 2026, tested against the reported numbers. Prepared 2026-11-16, with the stock at $16.55 (Nasdaq, US dollars), a new 52-week low and down about 47% from its $31.06 high.*

**The takeaway.** Sallie Mae, the largest private student lender in the US, has executed the growth half of its story well: record originations and two new funding partners. It has missed on the earnings half. Over twelve months management kept saying that credit was "stable" and that its loans were worth more than the share price implied. Then on 2026-10-22 it reported a quarterly loss of $0.19 a share, raised its 2026 charge-off guidance for the second time, and cut 2026 earnings-per-share guidance by more than a third, to $1.95–$2.05 from $3.10–$3.20, three months after the finance chief described a "viable path" to the higher figure. The franchise holds up. Management's forecasting has not.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-23): credit is fine, buy the dip.** The message was "a successful quarter and peak season". Net charge-offs (loans written off as uncollectable, net of recoveries) were 1.95% of loans in repayment, and management said it had "not observed any material change in our borrowers' ability to meet their obligations". It bought back 5.6 million shares at $29.45 and promised a "first-of-its-kind" private-credit partnership.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-01-22): the new model.** The KKR partnership launched. Sallie Mae now sells newly originated loans to a partner for a fee instead of keeping them all on its own balance sheet. Management said federal PLUS reform (caps on federal graduate and parent loans) could add about $5 billion of yearly originations, roughly 70% growth over 2025 when fully phased in. It flagged that the new sale mechanics would distort reported credit ratios and added non-GAAP versions of them (figures that do not follow standard accounting rules). The market sold off on the softer earnings path. The CEO pointed to "high teens to low 20s" earnings growth in 2027.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-23): exploit the gap.** Earnings per share were $1.54. Management sold a $2 billion seasoned portfolio at "mid- to high single-digit" gains and launched a $200 million accelerated share repurchase (a buyback in which a bank delivers the shares up front). The stated reason was "the disconnect between the premium from our whole loan sales and our equity valuation". This was the high point of confidence.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-23): a new credit problem appears.** Earnings per share fell to $0.29. Management disclosed borrowers who "have both the willingness and capacity to repay" but were going straight to default after signing up with debt-resolution firms. It suspended many recovery efforts, estimated a $25 million hit, and said the hit would fit inside guidance.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-22): growth delivered, earnings pulled.** Originations reached a record $3.4 billion (up 15%), graduate originations rose 119%, and a second partner, Sixth Street, committed to buy at least $1.5 billion a year. Against that, the company lost money for the quarter, raised the debt-resolution hit to $45 million, lifted net charge-off guidance to $400–$420 million, and cancelled a planned whole-loan sale because higher long-term rates had pushed the price buyers offered below its threshold.

Over the year the story widened from "a high-return bank buying back stock" to "a lender plus a fee-earning loan manager, growing faster because of PLUS reform". The proof that the loans are worth more than book value, which a sale delivers, has stalled exactly when it was needed.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Credit is stable, losses in the "high 1s to low 2s" (Q1 2026) | 2025 net charge-offs were $346 million (2.15%). 2026 guidance went from $345–$385M, to the upper end (Q2), to $400–$420M (Q3), about 16% above the original midpoint. Loans 30+ days delinquent were 4.2% at Q3 2026, up from 4.0% a year earlier, and forbearance rose to 2.3% from 2.0% | Worse than the narrative. The rise is attributed to a "small segment", but the guidance moved twice |
| Loans are worth more than the stock implies; sale premiums of about 106–107 cents per dollar of loans | Q1 2026 sales booked $146M of gains on $3.3B plus $131M of reserve release. Gains fell to $3.7M in Q3 2026 against $136M a year earlier, after the planned sale was cancelled on price | The value is real but depends on rates. It cannot be counted at the Q1 premium |
| PLUS reform means 70% more originations over several years | Q3 2026 originations were up 15%, graduate originations up 119%, October disbursements up 35% month to date, full-year guidance of 12–14% growth held | Matches the narrative |
| Fee revenue from partnerships builds | Other income was $45–46M a quarter (up $15–16M year on year) | Matches, from a small base |
| 2026 earnings per share of $3.10–$3.20, with a "viable path" to the higher figure (Q2) | Now $1.95–$2.05. Year to date: $1.54 + $0.29 − $0.19 = $1.64 | A clear miss |
| Disciplined, value-creating buybacks | Shares are down about 59% since 2020 at an average of $17.19. 2026 buybacks so far averaged about $22–26 (Q3: 5.1M shares at $25.69), against a stock now at $16.55. About $111M of authorization was left at 2026-09-30, and common equity fell to about $2.0B (around $10.8 a share) | Good over the long run, poorly timed in 2026 |

A note on the screener figures. The "net margin 24%", "ROIC 8.7%", P/FCF 6.2x (price to free cash flow) and "net debt" numbers are industrial ratios that do not describe a bank. Free cash flow for a lender is mostly loan-sale timing, and its "debt" is funding, not leverage. This analysis does not rely on them.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY — Declining (from offensive to defensive)

- Q3 2025: "real momentum that will carry us through the rest of the year."
- Q4 2025: "high teens to low 20s" earnings growth in 2027.
- Q1 2026: "capable of performing in almost any environment."
- Q2 2026: "the current loss pressure is concentrated, understood and manageable."
- Q3 2026: "While we would prefer a different macroeconomic environment…" and "how our outlook has evolved".

Guidance has become less specific. The CEO now says he cannot see more than about twelve months ahead on credit, and 2027 talk has moved from a growth range to "we look forward to sharing our insights … later this fall."

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — Low

Origination guidance has been met every quarter (2025: $7.4B, up 6%, at the top of the revised range; 2026: 12–14% held). Earnings and charge-off guidance has not: the 2025 EPS guide was reset lower in October 2025 because of loan-sale timing, the 2026 charge-off guide was raised twice, and the 2026 EPS guide was cut about 36%. Our scan shows estimates beaten in only 3 of 7 quarters (43%). There is no pattern of setting a low bar. Instead, plans that depend on loan sales keep meeting a market that does not cooperate. Three law firms announced shareholder investigations between 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-30. These are advertisements, not lawsuits, but they show how sharp the reset felt.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Delinquency direction:** asked in every call (Orenbuch, Arfstrom). Each time the answer was that it was a seasonal peak, the loan-modification programs are working, or watch late-stage loans instead. The 30+ day rate is still above the year-earlier level.
- **Whether reported ratios still mean anything:** Shane (Q1 and Q3 2026) asked whether loan sales distort charge-off rates and the held-for-sale balance. Management acknowledges the distortion, which makes year-on-year credit comparisons hard for outsiders.
- **Gain-on-sale margins:** asked in Q4 2025 and Q3 2026, with no firm number given. The cancelled sale answers part of the question.
- **Grad loan mix and the net interest margin:** management will not commit until it has seen a full peak season. The long-run target of a "low to mid-5%" margin compares with 4.75–4.85% in Q2–Q3 2026.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: 2026 EPS guidance cut about 36% on 2026-10-22, three months after the "viable path" comment of 2026-07-23.
- Red: net charge-off guidance raised twice in 2026, and debt-resolution losses grew from $25M to $45M within one quarter.
- Red: the planned whole-loan sale was cancelled (Q3 2026) because rate volatility pushed premiums below management's threshold, the same premium management had cited to justify the buyback.
- Red: shares were bought at about $22–26 in 2026 and the stock is now $16.55. The buyback budget is nearly spent ($111M left) as capital ratios slip (CET1, the core bank-capital ratio, was 11.8% at Q2 2026 against 12.4% at Q1).
- Red: insiders made 3 open-market sales (68,000 shares) and no buys.
- Green: record originations of $3.4B in Q3 2026, graduate loans up 119% with FICO credit scores about 9 points above the book average, and 95% of new loans with a co-signer.
- Green: a second strategic partner (Sixth Street, at least $1.5B a year for three years, announced 2026-10-22) shows that outside buyers want the loans even after the cancelled sale.
- Green: the loan-modification programs are beating plan, with more than 75% of borrowers who left them still paying after 3 to 6 months (Q2 2026).
- Green: deposit duration was extended to 37 months from 23, leaving the company close to neutral to rate moves (Q3 2026).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "Misaligned third-party debt resolution practices" is a new phrase for a new kind of loss: borrowers who can pay but are being steered to default. Management's response, suspending outside recoveries and using AI to review calls, shows this is more than noise. "Adoption … has been slower than we initially expected" (Q3 2026) suggests it will spill into 2027.
- The language has moved from "loan sale premium versus equity value" (Q1) to "a more diversified and flexible funding model" (Q3). Management is quietly backing away from one-off portfolio sales as the source of value and leaning on recurring fees.
- Pete Graham is now Co-President as well as CFO, and Melissa Bronaugh has become Deputy CFO, which looks like succession planning. CEO Jon Witter speaks at the TD Cowen conference on 2026-11-17, the first look at management since the reset.
- Q3 2026 provisions (money set aside for expected losses) were $214M, mostly the upfront loss reserve that CECL accounting (the current expected credit loss standard) requires on the record originations. Part of the Q3 loss is that accounting timing, not losses that have already happened. This is the most important point for anyone who sees value here.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING** in earnings delivery and credibility, despite a stronger franchise and growing volumes.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** whether the 2026 credit and earnings reset is contained (one debt-resolution segment, plus upfront reserves on fast growth, plus one cancelled sale) or the start of a broader rise in losses among young borrowers. The next clean evidence is the Q4 2026 results and 2027 guidance in late January 2027.

**Moat:** narrow and regulatory/scale-based. Sallie Mae is the preferred lender at more than 2,100 schools, funds itself with cheap insured bank deposits, has decades of student-credit data, and has strong co-signer rates. Through-cycle returns on equity have been high (above 25% in 2025 on thin equity), but that partly reflects loan-sale gains. The moat is not widening: competition for graduate loans has added some marketing pressure. Trend: stable.

**Secular threat:** manageable. AI could reduce entry-level jobs for graduates, which is what lets borrowers repay, and federal policy could change again. The opposite force, PLUS reform, is enlarging the market. The cheapness looks like a fear discount on stable-to-growing earnings power plus a credibility discount the company earned. It does not look like a value trap on a shrinking base, but management must show that 2026 was a reset and not a trend.

Management credibility 2 of 5 · trajectory weakening · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: Rightmove is the UK's property-search habit. On 2026-11-06 it reported 90% of consumer time spent on UK property portals (Comscore), over 85% of traffic arriving direct or organically, and under 1% from AI chatbots - the AI-displacement fear that knocked the shares down in November 2025 and September 2026 has not shown up in any measurable number. That consumer dominance makes Rightmove a must-have cost for about 19,000 estate agents and housebuilders, which is why it can keep raising ARPA (average revenue per advertiser): Agency revenue rose 9% to GBP 164m in H1 2026 'predominantly ARPA led', and retention was the highest in over ten years (2026-07-31), still 92% at end-October. The economics are exceptional and improving: free cash flow margin about 56%, net margin 51%, ROIC (return on invested capital) about 236% in 2025 against about 217% in 2024, net cash about GBP 29m at mid-2026, free cash flow up 17.6% in 2025. Nearly every pound of profit is returned: over GBP 400m over the twelve months to July 2027, about 10% of the market value, so per-share growth runs well ahead of revenue - management now guides underlying EPS growth of at least 7% in 2026 and at least 10% in 2027 (2026-11-06). New Homes is the drag (revenue expected below 2025) and it is cyclical: when the housing cycle turns, as it has after past downturns, that segment recovers on top of the Agency engine. The new products (Online Agent Valuation, the fastest-growing product; Enhanced Leads up fourfold for rental partners; mortgage-in-principle submissions up over 50%) give a path back toward the at-least-10% revenue growth ambition for 2030. There is also a floor of strategic interest: REA Group offered up to 770p in September 2024 before walking away, the activist Sachem Head holds about 6%, and a 2026-10-08 blog report suggested renewed bidder interest. None of that is in our value, but it limits how far the shares can de-rate on a clean franchise. Conditions that must hold: time share stays near 9 in 10 minutes; AI-chatbot traffic stays marginal; Agency ARPA keeps rising at GBP 100-plus a year without hurting retention; the fees claim stays small relative to about GBP 250m of annual free cash flow.
picks.bear_thesis: The business is excellent; the price no longer pays you for the risks. At 558.8p the shares are up about 14% since 2026-10-12 and sit 88% of the way up their 52-week range, on an unconfirmed takeover rumour and activist buying rather than any upgrade to the operating outlook. That outlook has in fact been cut twice in 2026: revenue growth from 8-10% to 6-8% (2026-07-31) to 6-7% (2026-11-06), with 2027 guided 'similar', operating profit growth now 'at least 3%' for 2026 and 4-7% for 2027, and the operating margin floor down to 'at least 67%' from 70% in 2024. The EPS guidance rose only because buybacks are bigger and are now partly debt-funded - financial engineering, not better trading. The housing backdrop is getting worse, not better: five-year fixed mortgage rates rose to 5.5% from 5.0% at 30 June, buyer demand fell 10% and sales agreed fell 9% (2026-11-06), and New Homes developments on site are down 6% this year. Core membership is guided flat for 2027, so all growth must come from price increases on agents whose own commissions are under pressure - the retention dip from 93% to 92% is the first small sign of that strain. The structural risks are unresolved: AI-chatbot traffic is tiny but the disclosed ceiling moved from under 0.5% (July) to under 1% (November); AI-native rivals such as MyPorta (over 2,750 agents signed up) and Zoopla's repackaging aim at agents' cost base; and the GBP 1.5bn Newman collective claim on excessive fees is awaiting a certification ruling after the 2-3 November hearing - a certified claim would hang over pricing power, the very thing the thesis depends on. If the rumour fades and the sector de-rates again on AI fear, as it did in September 2026 when the shares traded below 450p, a 13-14 times free cash flow multiple on slower growth gives roughly 450-480p; in a genuine AI-share-loss scenario the multiple falls to about 11 times and the shares toward 360p. What would confirm the bear case: time share below 80% on Comscore, retention below 90%, ARPA guidance cut for Estate Agency (not just New Homes), or certification of the claim with a large damages estimate.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market has narrowed to almost nothing at this price. In September 2026 the market was pricing terminal AI displacement into a business whose own numbers showed none - that was the disagreement, and it has largely closed as the shares rose from below 450p to 558.8p. Today the street is split: named broker targets after the July cut cluster at 465-505p (Jefferies 465p, Goldman Sachs 505p, UBS 490p, Citi 486p, all Hold; JPMorgan underweight at 429p) with RBC at 675p, and Investing.com's average sits near 536p - below the share price. So the brokers are, if anything, more cautious than the tape, which is being carried by takeover hopes and activist buying. Our view is that the business is worth about 575p on its own: the street's Hold cluster underweights how much per-share growth the over-GBP 400m return delivers (EPS guided at least +10% in 2027), but the tape's rumour premium overweights a bid nobody has confirmed. We do not have an edge at 558.8p; we would at 479p.
picks.valley_of_death: No liquidation event, debt wall or forced selling threatens the business: net cash about GBP 29m at mid-2026, a new revolving facility used only to speed up buybacks, and about GBP 250m of annual free cash flow. The risks to the price over the next 3-9 months are: (1) the takeover rumour fading - with no bidder statement since 2026-10-08, part of the rise could unwind; (2) a certification ruling on the GBP 1.5bn Newman claim, due any time after the 2-3 November hearing, which would put a legal overhang on pricing power; (3) a weaker housing market - mortgage rates at 5.5%, buyer demand down 10%, sales agreed down 9% (2026-11-06) - feeding into agents' budgets and the next ARPA round; (4) any visible AI-traffic shift or a renewed sector sell-off on AI-agent fear like September 2026's; (5) FY2026 results in late February 2027, when the 2027 guidance (revenue similar to 2026, margin at least 67%) is restated.
picks.positioning_washout: There is no mechanical forced-seller setup: Rightmove is a FTSE 100 constituent with a steady dividend and no index deletion, lock-up or spin-off in view. The realistic route to our 479p level is a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off - UK online marketplaces re-rating down together on AI-agent fear, as Auto Trader and Rightmove did in the same sessions in September 2026 - or event-driven holders exiting if the takeover rumour fades. The shares traded below 479p as recently as 2026-10-09 (490.5p) and well below it in September, so the level is within normal trading range. The company's own buyback (a further GBP 80m before year-end) is a steady buyer that will cushion but not prevent such a move. The activist's roughly 6% stake is a holder, not a seller, while its debt-funded buyback push is being met.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near 479p, which a renewed sector-wide sell-off in UK online marketplaces, or the fading of the takeover rumour, could deliver. The thesis holds, and the 6 November trading update confirms it: Rightmove still takes 9 in 10 minutes of UK property-portal time, under 1% of its traffic comes from AI chatbots, agent retention is the second best in a decade, and revenue per agent is still rising. What it also shows is a slower company than two years ago - revenue growth guided at 6-7% this year and next, a lower profit margin floor, and earnings-per-share growth increasingly carried by buybacks, now partly funded with borrowed money. That is a fine business, but not one we want to pay full value for. The price has done the work our wait was meant to do in reverse: the shares rose from 492p on 12 October to 558.8p today, mostly on an unconfirmed takeover rumour and activist buying rather than company news. At 558.8p our unchanged fair value of about 575p is only about 3% above the price, far short of the 20% discount we require in today's backdrop. We keep our view of the business and our conviction (4 of 5) unchanged; our rating of the pure value case drops to 3 of 5 simply because the discount has almost gone. Near 479p the discount clears our bar again; the shares traded below that level a month ago. If a real offer emerges we would judge it on its terms - the board turned down up to 770p in 2024. The risks we are watching: the tribunal's certification ruling on the GBP 1.5bn fees claim (heard 2-3 November), any sign that AI assistants are taking traffic, retention slipping below 90%, and a housing market held back by 5.5% mortgage rates.
picks.forcing_function: For a value case on a clean franchise the forcing function is the capital return itself: over GBP 400m between 31 July 2026 and 31 July 2027 (about 10% of the market value), with a further GBP 80m of buybacks before year-end, retires shares every week and converts the steady free cash flow into per-share growth of at least 10% in 2027 as guided. Secondary: a confirmed approach from a strategic buyer (none confirmed; REA's 2024 proposals reached 770p), and the Competition Appeal Tribunal's certification decision, which is the dated binary on the legal overhang. FY2026 results in late February 2027 are the next scheduled check on the guidance.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Rightmove plc (RMV.L) - deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-09. Prices in pence (GBp) on the London listing. Live quote used: 558.8p (FMP, 2026-11-09; prior close 555.4p on 2026-11-06). Sources: five results calls (2024-07-26, 2025-02-28, 2025-07-25, 2026-02-27, 2026-07-31), the screener's fundamentals block, and the 2026-11-06 trading statement (four months to 31 October), read via the PR Newswire copy on finanznachrichten.de and OnlineMarketplaces' write-up.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The core story has not changed in two years: Rightmove is the UK's dominant property portal, a near-pure subscription business that sells listing packages to about 19,000 estate agents and housebuilders, and grows mostly by raising ARPA (average revenue per advertiser, per month) through package upgrades and add-on products.

What has changed is the emphasis.

- **H1 2024 (2024-07-26):** a steady-state compounder. Revenue +7%, ARPA "almost GBP 1,500", the talk was market conditions, Optimiser Edge take-up and a small minority stake in Coadjute. AI appeared only as a coding tool for engineers.
- **FY2024 (2025-02-28):** a formal "investment case" slide, 14% headcount growth and "24 AI-enabled product teams". The pitch shifted from "resilient toll-booth" to "platform with an expanding growth strategy". This came in the wake of REA Group's four rejected bids (705p-770p, ending 2024-09-30), and it reads partly as a defence of independence.
- **FY2025 (2026-02-27):** the AI build is now the centre of the story - "31 live strategic AI projects", "6,000 tech releases" - and management acknowledges a "competitive market" twice in the opening minutes. This followed the November 2025 investment plan that cut medium-term profit growth and knocked the shares down sharply.
- **H1 2026 (2026-07-31):** the language reaches "a leading agentic-powered property marketplace" (agentic = AI assistants that act on a user's behalf). Revenue guidance was cut from 8-10% to 6-8%, blamed on New Homes, while capital return was raised to over GBP 400m for the next twelve months.
- **Trading statement (2026-11-06):** revenue guidance narrowed again to 6-7% for 2026, with 2027 "similar"; profit growth trimmed to "at least 3%"; but underlying EPS (earnings per share) guidance raised to at least 7% for 2026 and at least 10% for 2027, helped by buybacks partly funded by a new revolving credit facility.

Net: the business story moved from "price-led compounder" to "AI-led platform", while the financial story moved the other way - slower revenue, a more leveraged buyback doing more of the per-share work.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Subscription model delivers in all market conditions" (2025-02-28) | Revenue 305m (2021) -> 425m (2025), a 8.5% three-year CAGR with no down year, through the worst transaction year in a decade (2023) | Matches |
| Growth is ARPA-led and discretionary | Agency revenue +9% to GBP 164m in H1 2026, "predominantly ARPA led"; FY2025 Agency +9% to GBP 305m | Matches |
| AI investment will accelerate growth | Revenue growth has slowed: 9% (2025) -> 7% (H1 2026) -> 6-7% guided for 2026 and similar for 2027, against a 2030 ambition of at least 10% a year | Story richer than numbers, so far |
| Profit margins stay elite | FCF margin 55.9%, net margin 51%, ROIC about 236% (2025, up from about 217% in 2024); 2027 operating margin guided at "at least 67%", down from 70% in 2024 | Matches on level, drifting on direction |
| EPS growth | Reported EPS 0.21 (2021) -> 0.28 (2025), a 7.5% five-year CAGR; FY2025 underlying EPS +11%; 2026 guided at least +7%, 2027 at least +10% | Matches, but an increasing share comes from fewer shares (weighted shares 790m in 2024 to 772m in 2025, about 726m voting shares by October 2026) |
| Consumer moat is intact against AI | Share of portal time 9 in 10 minutes on Comscore (June 2026; 90% again at the 2026-11-06 update), over 85% of traffic direct or organic; LLM (AI chatbot) referral traffic "less than 0.5%" in July, "under 1%" in November | Matches; note the November disclosure is a looser ceiling than July's |
| Retention | "Highest in over 10 years" (2026-07-31); 92% to end-October 2026 versus 93% a year earlier, "second highest in the last 10 years" (2026-11-06) | Matches; a one-point slip worth watching |

The screener's earnings-beat rate is 1 of 7 quarters. For a UK company that guides annually rather than quarterly, this is mostly an artefact of thin consensus data, not evidence of misses. The relevant record is the annual guidance record in section 4.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: **Stable**, with a defensive tilt on revenue and an offensive tilt on technology.

- 2024-07-26: relaxed and market-focused - "our platform and network effects remain unrivaled".
- 2025-02-28: promotional and confident - "confidence not just for 2025 but actually for quite a long way into the future".
- 2026-02-27: confident but concedes competition - "It is a competitive market out there, but our position is stable and it's strong."
- 2026-07-31: candid on New Homes - "in 2026 now, there is really not one" (green tailwind) - and still expansive on AI.
- 2026-11-06: operationally confident (four times the leads from Enhanced Leads, Comparison Assistant users sending over three times as many leads), while trimming revenue and profit guidance again.

Guidance has become more specific (separate ARPA, membership, growth-area and margin guides), which is a credibility positive even when the numbers are lower.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

- 2024 and 2025 were delivered: 2024 revenue +7% and 70% margin against guidance; 2025 revenue +9%, underlying EPS +11%.
- 2026 revenue guidance has been cut twice: 8-10% (November 2025 plan) -> 6-8% (2026-07-31) -> 6-7% (2026-11-06). Each cut was attributed to New Homes, where developments on site are 6% below end-2025 and the end market has, in management's words, no tailwind. Estate Agency ARPA expectations were left unchanged at the November update.
- 2026 profit growth guidance moved from 3-5% to "at least 3%", while EPS guidance moved up from at least 5% to at least 7%. The gap is financial engineering: more buyback, partly debt-funded.

Reliability: **Medium-High**. The core Agency business delivers what it guides. The repeated New Homes misses are cyclical and well flagged, not concealed. But the habit of offsetting revenue cuts with per-share support deserves scrutiny.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Agentic AI and timing** (Jefferies, 2026-07-31: "Are we talking weeks and months? Or ... months and years?"). The answer was "All of the above. It's happening." That is non-specific. Consumer monetisation: "our intention overall is to offer search experiences for free".
- **Competitive package changes at Zoopla** (2026-07-31): answered generically ("we always keep an eye on what's happening").
- **M&A and minority stakes** (Panmure, 2024-07-26 and 2026-07-31): consistently deflected - "no further comment really on sort of ownership".
- **Not asked on these calls but live:** the GBP 1.5bn Newman collective claim alleging excessive fees from April 2020 to April 2026. The Competition Appeal Tribunal heard the certification application on 2-3 November 2026 and has not ruled. Rightmove guided GBP 4-7m of 2026 exceptional costs for it in July, and the 2026-11-06 statement does not mention it.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- 🔴 Revenue guidance cut twice in 2026 (2026-07-31, 2026-11-06); 2027 revenue growth guided "similar" to 2026, well below the at-least-10% 2030 ambition.
- 🔴 Operating margin floor now "at least 67%" for 2027, against 70% in 2024: the AI investment is permanent cost, not a one-off.
- 🔴 Buybacks partly funded by a new revolving credit facility (2026-11-06), the move activist Sachem Head reportedly pushed for in late September 2026. Per-share growth is now partly leverage-driven.
- 🔴 The AI-chatbot traffic disclosure loosened from "less than 0.5%" (2026-07-31) to "under 1%" (2026-11-06). That is still tiny, but the ceiling doubled.
- 🔴 Mortgage rates rose to 5.5% from 5.0% at 30 June; buyer demand fell 10% and sales agreed fell 9% (2026-11-06).
- 🟢 Share of portal time at 90% on Comscore (2026-11-06), over 85% direct or organic traffic: the network effect shows no measurable erosion.
- 🟢 Agency retention 92%, second highest in ten years; Online Agent Valuation is the fastest-growing product; mortgage-in-principle submissions up over 50%.
- 🟢 ROIC rose to about 236% in 2025 from about 217% in 2024; FCF grew 17.6% in 2025.
- 🟢 Capital return of over GBP 400m reiterated (about GBP 125m returned since 31 July 2026, a further GBP 80m of buybacks before year-end).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary moved from "packages" to "products": the CFO said on 2026-07-31, "we can bring out products on their own and monetize them really, really well". This is a deliberate shift toward selling add-ons outside the package ladder, which is the main lever left if agent numbers stay flat (2027 core membership guided "broadly flat").
- The CFO change (Alison Dolan to Ruaridh Hook by February 2025) coincided with more granular guidance and the larger capital-return framing.
- Board refresh: Rosemary Leith joined on 2026-10-01 and David Thomas on 2026-11-06, "earlier than planned". With an activist on the register, this reads as governance tightening.
- Competition talk has become more explicit. "Competitive market" appears repeatedly from February 2026 onward, where earlier calls spoke of being "unrivaled".

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **STABLE.** The franchise metrics (time share, retention, ARPA, returns) are as strong as they have been in a decade. The financial trajectory has downshifted to roughly 6-7% revenue growth and 4-7% operating profit growth, with EPS growth of 7-10% lifted by debt-assisted buybacks.

The single most important thing to weigh: the price, not the business. At 558.8p the shares sit about 3% below this committee's 575p fair value, after a 14% rise since 2026-10-12. We found no new company-specific news behind most of that rise beyond an unconfirmed October takeover rumour and the activist stake. Paying up for a rumour on a business whose revenue growth is being guided down is the risk.

Moat: a **network** moat. Consumers go where the listings are, and agents must list where the consumers are; 9 in 10 minutes of portal time and vendors insisting that their agent is on Rightmove show this. Width is **WIDE** on the evidence: ROIC rising, FCF margin about 56%, no measurable share loss. Trend is **STABLE**: revenue growth is slowing for cyclical (New Homes) and investment reasons, not because of share loss.

Secular threat: **material, not terminal.** The force is AI displacement - search assistants or an AI-native portal (such as MyPorta, live with over 2,750 agents signed up but no published traffic) inserting themselves between home-movers and listings. Today's evidence (AI chatbot traffic under 1%) says the threat has not landed. The listing-supply network effect is hard to bypass because agents, not consumers, supply the inventory. The cheapness of late 2025 and September 2026 looked like a fear-print rather than a shrinking base; at today's price there is little cheapness left to judge.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a wide, durable moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.
picks.sop_fair_value: 575p per share (range 550-600p)
picks.sop_breakdown: Base case unchanged from 2026-10-12: 2027 free cash flow per share of about 36p (2026 free cash flow about GBP 250m growing 7-8% into 2027, on about 715-725m average shares after buybacks) times 16 = about 575p. The 2026-11-06 guidance (revenue 6-7% in 2026 and similar in 2027; EPS growth at least 7% and at least 10%) is consistent with that per-share figure: slightly lower revenue, offset by a faster share-count reduction. 16 times deliberately sits below the 18-20 times Rightmove commanded before the AI debate, to price a lasting AI and legal risk premium. Adjustments: about +4p net cash (GBP 29m at 2026-06-30), roughly offset by the new credit facility drawn for buybacks; about -8p probability-weighted cost of the competition claim. Growth areas (commercial property, mortgages, rental services, guided +20-30%) sit inside the cash flow. No takeover value included. Cross-checks: the screener's discounted-cash-flow value of 659.8p sits above; its no-growth earnings-power value sits far below, so fair value depends on Rightmove keeping its growth. Investing.com's consensus target average is about 536p (range 356-745p); MarketBeat cited about 595p in October; recent named targets cluster at 465-505p (Jefferies, Goldman Sachs, UBS, Citi, all Hold) with RBC at 675p (Buy) - our 575p sits inside that spread.
picks.sop_bull: About 700p per share. Rightmove is one business, so we value the whole company on free cash flow rather than by segments (no segment revenue block was supplied). The 18.5 times multiple is the middle of Rightmove's pre-AI-debate range and in line with the premium UK classifieds have historically held. Overlays: net cash about +4p (GBP 29m at 2026-06-30, falling as the credit facility is drawn); claim cost assumed small (GBP 4-7m exceptional cost guided for 2026). picks.sop_bear: About 360p per share. Parts: 2027 free cash flow of about GBP 230m (revenue growth 5%, margin pressure from AI spend and a weak housing market) on about 715m shares = about 32p per share, times 11 = about 355p - the multiple a market would pay if AI assistants were visibly taking home-mover traffic and the network effect were in question. Overlays: net cash about +4p less a probability-weighted cost of the Newman claim if certified (about -10p), plus a modest +10p for the cash-generative balance sheet still being returned. About 360p. Below this level the shares would be pricing terminal decline into a business whose returns on capital are still rising.

picks.macro_fit_note: Reflation quadrant (growth up, inflation sticky) and the discipline phase of the debt cycle (positive real long rates, cash flow rewarded, duration punished, expected horizon about 18 months): Rightmove is a cash-now business (free-cash-flow margin about 56%, about 16-18 times free cash flow), which suits this backdrop, but higher-for-longer rates pushed UK five-year fixed mortgages to 5.5% and cut buyer demand 10% (2026-11-06), weighing on transactions and New Homes - the two effects roughly cancel. picks.entry_plain: buy near 479 GBp, which a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off could deliver

picks.bull_thesis: Veidekke is a Norwegian-led contractor that did what it said it would. In 2020 it set a goal of a 5% pre-tax profit margin (profit before tax divided by revenue) and gave up growth to get there; it reached 5.0% over the twelve months to June 2026, with the second quarter of 2026 at 5.4% versus 4.7% a year earlier (release dated 2026-08-14). Earnings per share grew about 13% a year over five years (NOK 7.07 in 2021 to NOK 11.50 in 2025, trailing twelve months now NOK 12.50) while revenue grew under 4% a year, so the gains came from pricing and execution, not from taking risk. The order book is the strongest it has been: NOK 55.3B at 30 June 2026, up from NOK 49.2B, with about 55% converting to revenue within a year, helped by large public infrastructure such as the Oslofjord Link - work that is less sensitive to housing and interest rates. The balance sheet is a fortress: net interest-bearing assets of NOK 3.7B (about NOK 27 a share) and first-half operating cash flow of NOK 1.7B versus NOK 146M a year earlier. Returns are high (return on equity about 37%, return on invested capital about 20%) and the company historically pays out most of its profit. If margins hold at 5-5.5% on a growing backlog, earnings per share can reach NOK 14-15 within two years, and a 15 times multiple plus surplus cash supports about NOK 230. Conditions: margins hold through the next downturn in housing, the big infrastructure contracts are executed without the cost overruns that have historically plagued large fixed-price jobs, and Denmark and Sweden stop lagging.
picks.bear_thesis: The business is good but the share already prices it as permanently better. At NOK 222 (2026-11-10, a 52-week high, up from a NOK 159 low) Veidekke trades at about 18 times trailing earnings, or about 16 times after setting aside the surplus cash - a premium for a contractor, a business whose margins are thin (net margin 3.6% in 2025) and cyclical. The screener flags the margin at 1.27 standard deviations above its own history: this is what peak-cycle earnings look like, helped by full crews, a strong asphalt season and a lull in cost inflation. A single bad large contract can erase a year's margin gain, and the backlog now contains exactly the kind of very large infrastructure work (the Oslofjord Link) where contractors have historically lost money. The cash pile is partly customer prepayments that flow back out when volume slows, so treating all NOK 3.7B as surplus overstates value. The lost-time injury rate rose to 3.8 in Q2 2026 from 2.4 a year earlier, Danish construction revenue was flat, and the Norwegian housing market remains sensitive to interest rates. Our own earnings-power valuation is about 42% below the price. If the margin reverts to 4% and the market pays 12 times, value is about NOK 130 - roughly 40% below today. What confirms it: a third-quarter margin below last year's, order intake slowing, or a write-down on a large project.
picks.consensus_delta: On the deep-value question - is the market pricing terminal decline into a company with stable or growing earnings? - the answer is plainly no. The market is pricing the opposite: at NOK 222, a 52-week high, it pays about 18 times trailing earnings of NOK 12.50 for a contractor, implicitly treating the 5% margin as a new floor. Where we disagree with the market is only on durability: we think a 5% margin is closer to the top of a good cycle than a permanent level, because the screener shows it 1.27 standard deviations above its own history and because the gains now come from full crews and volume rather than repricing. No analyst price targets were available to test against (none in FMP; none cited).
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) is mostly about expectations, not solvency. With NOK 3.7B of net cash there is no debt wall and no liquidity risk. The risks are: the Q3 2026 report on 2026-11-12 must match a strong Q3 2025 (pre-tax profit about NOK 721M); the seasonal first quarter of 2027 will be weak as always; the Norwegian housing market remains rate-sensitive; and a cost overrun on any of the large infrastructure contracts would hit the margin story directly. picks.positioning_washout: Little forced-selling pressure is visible. The more likely seller is a sector-wide de-rating of Nordic contractors if housing or rates turn, which would be a buying opportunity rather than a thesis break. picks.moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. The thesis holds: Veidekke has delivered the 5% pre-tax margin it promised in 2020 (5.0% over the twelve months to June 2026), its order book is up about 12% to NOK 55.3B, and it sits on NOK 3.7B of net cash. picks.forcing_function: There is no event that forces a re-rating upward from here; the margin target - the re-rating driver - has already been met and priced. # Veidekke ASA (VEI.OL) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 2026-11-10. Prices in Norwegian kroner (NOK), Oslo listing. No earnings-call transcript was available from our data provider (FMP) for this listing, so this dossier leans on the company's own dated releases (Q2 2026 results, published 2026-08-14), the financial calendar on the investor-relations site, the FMP quarterly statements, and our screener's multi-year numbers. No quotes below are invented; every quote is from the 2026-08-14 release.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story over the last several years has been one of deliberate discipline over growth. In 2020 Veidekke set itself a public goal of a 5% pre-tax profit margin (profit before tax divided by revenue) and chose to take on fewer, better-priced contracts to get there. Revenue has grown only modestly since (NOK 37.6B in 2021 to NOK 43.1B in 2025, about 3.7% a year), while earnings per share rose much faster (NOK 7.07 to NOK 11.50, about 13% a year). That gap between slow sales growth and fast profit growth is the narrative made real: margin, not volume.

In 2026 the tone shifted from "we are getting there" to "we are there and still winning work". The Q2 2026 release (2026-08-14) calls it "a strong second quarter, with solid revenue growth, higher profits and improved profitability", and leans on a record-looking order book: NOK 55.3B at 30 June 2026, up from NOK 49.2B a year earlier, helped by large Norwegian infrastructure wins including the Oslofjord Link. The margin target has moved from a goal to a delivered fact (5.0% over the twelve months to June 2026).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim (source, date) | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Improved profitability" (Q2 2026 release, 2026-08-14) | Q2 pre-tax margin 5.4% vs 4.7% a year earlier; trailing-twelve-month margin 5.0%; FMP shows Q2 2026 pre-tax profit NOK 669M on NOK 12.3B revenue | Matches |
| "Our order intake is very high" (2026-08-14) | Q2 intake NOK 17.9B vs NOK 14.3B; backlog NOK 55.3B vs NOK 49.2B, about 55% converting within 12 months | Matches |
| Margin discipline over growth (strategy since 2020) | Revenue CAGR ~3.7%, EPS CAGR ~12.9% (5-year); ROE 37%, ROIC ~20% | Matches |
| Cash generation | First-half 2026 operating cash flow NOK 1.7B vs NOK 146M; net interest-bearing assets NOK 3.7B at 30 June 2026 vs NOK 1.2B a year earlier; trailing free cash flow NOK 4.44B | Matches, with a caveat: a contractor's cash pile is partly customer prepayments that unwind when volume slows, so not all of it is surplus |
| Seasonality | Q1 is structurally weak (Q1 2026 pre-tax profit NOK 27M; Q1 2025 a small loss), so one strong quarter must not be annualised | Context, not a flaw |

Data note: the screener's 100% gross margin is an artefact (Veidekke reports no cost-of-sales line in several FMP quarters); ignore it. The share counts in the FMP quarterly file also wobble (105M to 137M) - a data artefact; the market capitalisation of about NOK 30.0B at NOK 222 implies roughly 135M shares, which we use.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: Stable to Rising. The 2026-08-14 release is confident but not promotional - no formal guidance, just that the asphalt season "had a strong start" and that the project portfolio "continues to deliver good margins". There is no shift toward defensive cost or macro language. The one soft spot management itself flagged is Denmark, where construction revenue was flat while every other unit grew.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Veidekke gives targets, not quarterly guidance. The one target that matters - the 5% margin set in 2020 - was delivered on a trailing basis by mid-2026. The screener shows earnings beat estimates in 5 of the last 7 quarters (71%). Reliability: High.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without a transcript we cannot quote analyst questions. The obvious pressure points are: (a) whether 5%+ margins are a new floor or the top of a good cycle, given that Norwegian infrastructure spending and a strong asphalt season flatter the current numbers; (b) whether the cash pile will be returned (Veidekke historically pays out most of its earnings) or is needed as working capital; (c) the Danish business and the Swedish construction market; (d) safety - the lost-time injury rate rose to 3.8 in Q2 2026 from 2.4 a year earlier.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Green: trailing pre-tax margin reached the 5.0% target (12 months to June 2026).
- Green: order backlog up about 12% year on year to NOK 55.3B (30 June 2026), much of it public infrastructure.
- Green: net cash of NOK 3.7B (30 June 2026) and a Piotroski score of 8 of 9.
- Red: lost-time injury rate 3.8 in Q2 2026 vs 2.4 in Q2 2025 - a culture signal worth watching in a contractor.
- Red: the stock sits at its 52-week high (NOK 222 on 2026-11-10, range NOK 159-222), so the good news is in the price.
- Red: margin is 1.27 standard deviations above its own history - the classic peak-earnings warning for a cyclical contractor.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The language has moved from "turnaround" to "capacity utilisation" - management now credits volume and full crews, not repricing, for the profit gains. That is healthy but it also means the next leg of margin needs volume to hold. The Oslofjord Link win shows Veidekke is again willing to take very large infrastructure contracts, a category where contractors historically lose money; the discipline story will be tested inside that contract over several years.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: STRENGTHENING. The single most important thing to weigh: the business case is real and proven, but the share price at NOK 222 already pays about 18 times trailing earnings (about 16 times after setting aside the cash), which prices the 5% margin as permanent. The next dated test is the Q3 2026 report on 2026-11-12.

Moat: narrow. Veidekke's edge is local scale and execution reputation in Norwegian civil engineering plus owned asphalt and aggregates assets, which give some cost advantage. Returns are rising (ROIC ~20%) and margins expanding, so the moat is not eroding. No structural (non-cyclical) force threatens terminal value; the risks are cyclical (housing, interest rates, public budgets). The current price is not a fear-print; it is a fair-to-full price for a good contractor.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat none.

Base-case fair value about NOK 170 a share, against a price of NOK 222. This is close to the committee's prior NOK 160; the small rise reflects the higher trailing earnings and cash at 30 June 2026.
