# Yelp Inc. (YELP) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 2026-11-09 from five earnings calls (Q3 2025, 2025-11-06 through Q3 2026, 2026-11-05), the screener's financial record, the 2026-09-30 balance sheet (filed 2026-11-06) and FMP news. Prices in US dollars, NYSE listing; live price $19.58 on 2026-11-09.*

**The takeaway:** Yelp is still a highly cash-generative business that keeps beating its own forecasts, but the core advertising engine has now tipped from slow growth into shrinkage. Services advertising, the larger and healthier half, went from +7% a year ago to -2% in Q3 2026, and management guides to "increased pressure on advertising revenue across categories" in Q4. The growth story has moved to a small, fast-growing "Other revenue" line built on AI products. The question for a buyer is no longer whether the core is stable; it is whether the cash it throws off, and the new AI lines, outrun its decline.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-11-06):** a growth-and-buyback story. Services revenue rose 7% to a quarterly record $244M; restaurants, retail and other (RR&O) fell 2%. Management cut the full-year 2025 revenue range to $1.460-1.465B on "heightened macroeconomic uncertainties" but raised profit guidance. Capital allocation: cash, acquisition capacity, buybacks.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-13):** a five-year victory lap on "product-led growth and disciplined expense management", plus the Hatch acquisition (an AI lead-management tool for service professionals). The tone shifted from harvesting to investing: "We plan to increase our investments in 2026."
- **Q1 2026 (2026-05-08) and Q2 2026 (2026-08-06):** services advertising slowed to +1%, then flat ($241M); RR&O fell 11% and more; net income fell 27% and 28% year over year as investment rose. Other revenue nearly doubled. Buybacks were paused "as we work to pay down our revolving credit facility".
- **Q3 2026 (2026-11-05):** the language is now an "AI transformation". Net revenue fell 1% to $371M; services advertising fell 2% to $238M; RR&O advertising fell 13% to $99M; ad clicks fell 8%. Other revenue rose 82% to a record $34M, and management now sets a target of a $250M annual run rate for Other revenue by the end of 2028 (it is at $136M). Capital return is reframed as "more than 50% of free cash flow" through buybacks, resuming in 2027, alongside "strategic acquisitions through a combination of cash and financing".

The thesis has contracted: the core is now described as something to defend, and the growth narrative has moved to a line that is about 9% of revenue.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers say | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Disciplined, highly profitable business | Q3 2026 adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, excluding stock pay) $92M, a 25% margin, $17M above the top of guidance; trailing-twelve-month (TTM) free cash flow $262M on ~$1.46B revenue | Holds. Cash generation is real. |
| Services advertising is resilient | +7% (Q3 2025) -> +1% (Q1 2026) -> flat (Q2 2026) -> -2% (Q3 2026) | Does not hold. Four quarters of steady deceleration into decline. |
| AI products are building a new engine | Other revenue $34M in Q3 2026, +82%; Hatch run rate ~$37M, +55%; data licensing with OpenAI and Meta | Holds, but small: about 9% of revenue, and much of the growth is the acquired Hatch. |
| Buybacks shrink the share count | Diluted shares down 15% year over year; $200M spent in 2026 at prices well above today (Q3 average $26.14) | Holds mechanically, but the money was spent high and the program was paused low, with $75M still drawn on the revolver at 2026-09-30 (down from $100M at 2026-06-30). |
| Earnings growth | Q3 2026 net income $35M, -12%; diluted EPS $0.63 vs $0.61 (+3%) only because of the buyback | Per-share growth is now entirely from the smaller share count. |
| Full-year 2026 outlook | Now $1.455-1.460B revenue and $320-325M adjusted EBITDA; Q4 guide $347-352M, roughly 1-2% below a year earlier | Revenue range updated (the prior range could not be verified from licensed sources); adjusted EBITDA is down roughly 11% from 2025's $360-365M guide level. |

Balance sheet (2026-09-30): cash $120M, revolver $75M, leases $22M, a net cash position of about $23M. Goodwill and intangibles of $440M reflect the Hatch deal.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining on the core, rising on the new lines.** In Q3 2025 the CFO talked about "quarterly record" services revenue. By Q3 2026 the opening line about the core is defensive: "consumers and local businesses continue to face a challenging economic environment, contributing to increased pressure on advertising revenue." On RR&O, the COO was blunt (2026-11-05): "I wouldn't read into anything in terms of really sunny days ahead." Language on Yelp Host, Hatch and licensing is confident and specific (2.5 million annual calls, food ordering up 6x from June to October). Guidance on the core has become more cautious and less specific.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Management beat the top of its own revenue range in every quarter covered (Q3 2025 +$6M, Q1 2026 +$6M, Q2 2026 +$8M, Q3 2026 +$1M) and beat the top of its adjusted EBITDA range by $13-17M each time. The screener records 7 of 7 quarterly EPS beats. This is a sandbagging pattern, especially on costs, which makes the profit guide dependable. The warning is that the revenue beat shrank to $1M in Q3 2026: the cushion they build into revenue guidance is being consumed by the ad decline. **Reliability: High on profit, Medium on revenue direction.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- Why RR&O revenue fell 13% while paying RR&O locations rose 3% (2026-11-05). The answer: multi-location customers added locations without spending more per location - in plain terms, less revenue per advertiser.
- What it takes to stabilize advertising. Management answered about go-to-market for the new products and did not give a stabilization path for the core.
- The margin profile of Other revenue as it scales. The answer was qualitative; they are "certainly investing against growth opportunities" in the near term.
- No analyst got a direct answer on when buybacks resume beyond "2027, subject to market and economic conditions, as well as business requirements."

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: services advertising turned negative (-2%, Q3 2026), the first decline in the covered period.
- Red: ad clicks -8% and RR&O -13% (Q3 2026); Q4 guide flags "increased pressure... across categories".
- Red: buybacks of $200M executed at ~$26 average, then paused near $19 to pay down a revolver; capital return was pro-cyclical.
- Red: insider selling only - 35 open-market sales, no buys; the CFO sold 7,500 shares at $20.00 on 2026-10-15.
- Red: new language about acquisitions funded "through a combination of cash and financing" raises the risk of another goodwill-heavy deal.
- Green: profit beats every quarter; stock pay cut to 6% of revenue, a year ahead of plan.
- Green: Other revenue +82% to $34M, with licensing deals with OpenAI and Meta that monetize Yelp's review content inside AI assistants.
- Green: Request-a-Quote projects up about 10% (Q3 2026), with Yelp Assistant generating about 10% of them - consumer intent is still flowing through the platform.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The reporting vocabulary shifted from "Services revenue" (Q3 2025) to "Services ad revenue" (2026) as Hatch and other non-ad items were split out - the headline growth line is now Other revenue.
- "Paying advertising locations" is falling for services while multi-location RR&O accounts rise: the base is consolidating toward larger, more price-sensitive buyers.
- The cost per click rose 2% while clicks fell 8% (Q3 2026): Yelp can still lift price a little but volume is going the wrong way, which is the shape of a toll road with less traffic.
- Capital allocation priorities were reordered from "healthy cash balance, acquisitions, buybacks" (2025) to "invest in growth, acquisitions with financing, return more than 50% of free cash flow" (2026-11-05) - acquisitions moved up.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: turning.** Yelp is trying to rebuild growth around AI products while its core advertising business shrinks slowly. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing is the rate of decline in services advertising: at -2% a year the business is a cash machine worth far more than $19.58 a share (about $262M of free cash flow against a ~$1.06B market value); at -6% or worse, the cash flow falls fast enough that today's low multiple is fair.

**Moat:** a narrow but real network moat - two decades of local reviews (a content asset that AI companies now pay to license) and a two-sided base of ~509,000 paying advertising locations. Gross margin is steady at ~90%, but returns (ROIC about 9%) are modest and the moat is eroding: clicks, locations and services ad revenue are all falling. **Secular threat:** AI assistants and Google's AI answers can intercept local search intent before it reaches Yelp. This is material, not terminal: Yelp's content is being licensed into those assistants, and project requests are still growing. The cheapness is part fear and part a genuinely shrinking ad base - it is neither a clear mispricing nor a clear value trap until the decline rate settles.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.

picks.bull_thesis:
The bullish case is that a Multiconsult share is now a cheap ticket into a larger Nordic engineering group that the market still prices like two sub-scale firms, and that the savings and a recovering Norwegian business can lift it toward its larger peers' valuations.

Start with what you own. Since the 7 September 2026 merger agreement, approved by both sets of shareholders on 19 October 2026, each Multiconsult share converts into 0.9725 Rejlers class B shares, giving Multiconsult owners about 54% of Multiconsult Rejlers, a group of roughly 8,000 engineers listed in Stockholm and Oslo. At today's Rejlers price of SEK 151.00 and 0.955 kroner to the krona, those terms are worth about NOK 140, and Multiconsult trades at NOK 139.20 - a small discount rather than the 8% premium it carried in September.

Second, the Multiconsult half of the group is recovering. Second-quarter 2026 earnings per share were NOK 3.23 against NOK 1.45 a year earlier on revenue up 5.4%; trailing twelve-month earnings per share are back to NOK 10.11 from the NOK 9.22 trough, and trailing free cash flow has doubled to NOK 363 million. The business needs little capital, so recovered profit turns into cash.

Third, the savings. The companies stated SEK 100-120 million of annual cost savings. Capitalised at the group's own multiple of about 8 times operating cash profit, the full amount is worth roughly SEK 800-950 million of enterprise value, about 10% of the combined equity.

Fourth, the re-rating. The combined group trades at roughly 8 times trailing operating cash profit (EV/EBITDA, enterprise value divided by earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) against Norconsult near 9 times and Sweco near 11 times on our September check. Scale, a dual listing and index eligibility are the usual routes for a merged group to close part of that gap. If the group earns SEK 1.4 billion of operating cash profit after savings and the market pays 9.5 times, a Multiconsult share is worth about NOK 199.

What must hold: Multiconsult's margin recovery survives the seasonally weak second half; consultant attrition does not eat the savings; Nordic infrastructure, grid and energy spending keeps demand for engineering hours rising.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bearish case is that the merger has turned a cheap, high-return Norwegian business into a fixed slice of a lower-return Swedish one, and that what is left is a modest discount with real execution risk.

First, the ratio. On our 22 September 2026 check Multiconsult earned about 23% on equity against Rejlers' 8%, converted far more of its operating cash into free cash (Rejlers' capital spending absorbed about 78% of its operating cash flow), yet Rejlers traded at a slightly higher multiple of operating cash profit (8.4 times against 7.9 times). Multiconsult owners hand over 46% of the combined group to the weaker partner and pay for the privilege.

Second, the share no longer has its own price. It is 0.9725 Rejlers class B shares converted at the krona rate, so it falls with Rejlers, with the Swedish krona against the Norwegian krone, and with the Nordic consulting sector. None of those is under Multiconsult's control, and there is no cash element, no collar and no floor in the terms.

Third, the recovery is one quarter deep. The first quarter of 2026 (earnings per share NOK 3.99) was below the first quarter of 2025 (NOK 4.86); only the second quarter carried the half-year improvement. The company has beaten consensus in none of the last seven quarters, and reported operating margin of about 6% is well short of the 10% target.

Fourth, people businesses lose value in mergers. Savings in consultancy come from overlapping overhead and offices, and the engineers who walk take clients with them. If only SEK 45 million of net savings survive, the 2026 second half gives back the margin gain, and the sector multiple settles near 7 times, a Multiconsult share is worth about NOK 124.

Fifth, AI-assisted design tools can compress billable hours per project over the next decade, a material if not fatal pressure on an hourly-billing model. And the balance sheet carries NOK 1.41 billion of net debt including leases (about NOK 1.04 billion excluding them), so there is no cash cushion.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is now small. In September the market was paying 8% more for a Multiconsult share than the deal terms delivered; that disagreement has closed, and the share trades about 1% below terms. The remaining question is whether the combined group is worth more than the roughly 8 times operating cash profit the market pays for it. We think modestly yes - about NOK 152 per Multiconsult share - because the risk-adjusted savings and Multiconsult's second-half recovery are not in the trailing base. We do not think the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with recovering earnings power; it is pricing an ordinary, slightly cheap Nordic consultancy with merger execution risk, which is roughly right. The deep-value label in our screen came from 2025 trough figures and is stale.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) holds no liquidity crisis - leverage is about 1.5 to 2 times operating cash profit and inside the company's own target - but four things can push the price lower before the value case pays. First, the third-quarter 2026 report on 3 November and the fourth quarter fall in the seasonally weaker half; the 2025 third quarter earned only NOK 1.41 per share, and a repeat would show the recovery is one quarter deep. Second, the share now moves with Rejlers and the Swedish krona: a weak Rejlers report or a krona drop against the krone moves Multiconsult mechanically. Third, integration: management attention, consultant departures and one-off costs (about SEK 150 million in our estimate) land before savings do. Fourth, a Nordic consulting de-rating; the stock touched NOK 127.80 within the last year, so our NOK 126 level is reachable on a sector move alone.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure is limited but has one plausible source. The register is mainly Norwegian long-only institutions, domestic retail and the employee-linked Stiftelsen Multiconsult, a committed owner. At completion, Oslo-only mandates and Norwegian small-cap funds will hold a Swedish-domiciled company; the planned Oslo listing softens this, but index reweighting and mandate drift can produce selling that has nothing to do with value. A sector-wide de-rating of Nordic engineering consultancies is the more likely route to our level. Trading is thin (about 22,500 shares on 2 November 2026 against 27.6 million outstanding), so modest selling moves the price.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Wait for a better price: we buy near NOK 126, which a sector-wide sell-off of Nordic engineering consultancies could deliver.

The thesis holds. Multiconsult is a capital-light Norwegian engineering consultancy whose demand never left during the 2025 profit collapse and whose earnings are recovering: second-quarter 2026 earnings per share of NOK 3.23 against NOK 1.45, trailing free cash flow doubled to NOK 363 million. But a Multiconsult share is no longer priced on its own. Since shareholders approved the merger with Rejlers on 19 October 2026, each share is a claim on 0.9725 Rejlers class B shares, worth about NOK 140 today, and Multiconsult trades at NOK 139.20.

Our fair value is about NOK 152: the deal terms at today's prices, plus a risk-adjusted share of the stated savings, plus Multiconsult's recovery not yet in the trailing figures. That is about 9% above the price - a real but thin discount, short of the 20% we require before buying in the current reflationary backdrop. At NOK 126 the discount clears that bar; the level sits just above our adverse case of NOK 124 and just below the 52-week low of NOK 127.80, so it needs a sector or currency move rather than bad company news. The favourable case of NOK 199 requires the combined group to be re-rated toward its best-rated Nordic peers after completion.

Conviction stays at 3, unchanged from our last look: a good, recovering business inside a merger that pays the weaker partner too much, at a price that is fair rather than cheap. The 8% premium to the deal terms that stopped us in September is gone; what is missing now is the margin of safety. The third-quarter 2026 report due 3 November is the next check, and it was not available to us here.
picks.forcing_function: The shareholder vote, the nearest forcing event, has happened (19 October 2026). What remains: the third-quarter 2026 report on 3 November 2026, which tests whether the margin recovery held; completion of the merger, subject to closing conditions we could not date; and the first combined-group reports, where delivered savings and a combined set of financial targets give the market a reason to re-rate the group toward Norconsult and Sweco. None of these is a hard-dated payout; the re-rating is a judgement the market has to make after completion.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Multiconsult ASA (MULTI.OL) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-03. Prices in Norwegian kroner (NOK), Oslo listing.

**Source note.** No earnings-call transcript was bundled and none was retrievable this run (the paid FMP feed carries no transcript for this listing, and the web-search budget was exhausted). This review therefore rests on the hard numbers: FMP quarterly income statements through the second quarter of 2026, the screener's multi-year trajectory, Multiconsult's own investor-relations announcement list (read 2026-11-03) and Rejlers' investor page (read 2026-11-03). No management quote below is invented; where we describe management's position, we describe it from what they announced and what they did, not from words we have not seen. The third-quarter 2026 report is scheduled for release on 3 November 2026 at 08:30 CET (announced 27 October 2026); its figures were not available to us and are not used.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story changed category this autumn. Through mid-2026 Multiconsult was a stand-alone recovery story: a 118-year-old Norwegian engineering, design and architecture consultancy whose revenue kept growing (NOK 4.28 billion in 2021 to NOK 6.63 billion in 2025) while profit collapsed in 2025 (earnings per share down 39% to NOK 9.22) and then began to recover in 2026.

On 7 September 2026 the company announced a merger of equals with Rejlers AB, a Swedish engineering consultancy. Each Multiconsult share converts into 0.9725 Rejlers class B shares; Multiconsult holders end up with about 54% of a combined group to be called Multiconsult Rejlers, with roughly 8,000 staff and listings in both Stockholm and Oslo. Since then the narrative has been entirely about execution of the deal: an extraordinary general meeting (a shareholder meeting called outside the annual cycle) on 19 October 2026, at which both companies' owners approved the merger (Rejlers described "broad support" the same day); a chief financial officer for the combined group appointed on 8 October; and a proposed combined board on 12 October. Completion remains subject to "the other closing conditions", which the published pages do not date.

What this means for an investor: a Multiconsult share is now mostly a claim on a fixed number of Rejlers shares. The stand-alone recovery still matters, but only through its 54% share of the combined group.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim / narrative | What the numbers say | Read |
|---|---|---|
| 2026 is a recovery year | Second-quarter 2026 earnings per share NOK 3.23 vs NOK 1.45 a year earlier; first half NOK 7.22 vs NOK 6.31. Trailing twelve-month (TTM) earnings per share NOK 10.11 vs the NOK 9.22 full-year 2025 trough. | Corroborated, but the first quarter of 2026 (NOK 3.99) was below the first quarter of 2025 (NOK 4.86); the recovery is one strong quarter deep. |
| Demand held through the downturn | Revenue grew every year 2021-2025 (+10.8% three-year compound rate); 2025 +4.3%; second-quarter 2026 revenue NOK 1.75 billion, up 5.4%. | Corroborated. The 2025 problem was profitability, not demand. |
| Profit turns into cash | TTM free cash flow NOK 363 million vs NOK 173 million in full-year 2025; capital spending is light. | Corroborated on a TTM basis; 2025 free cash flow had fallen about 70%, so the cash conversion is recovering, not proven through a cycle. |
| Financial target of a 10% profitability margin | Second-quarter 2026 operating profit margin about 6.0% (NOK 106 million on NOK 1.75 billion); EBITDA (operating profit before depreciation and amortisation) margin about 9.8%. | The target is not being met on reported operating profit. |
| Leverage within the 1.0-2.0x target | Net debt NOK 1.41 billion including NOK 366 million of capitalised leases (about NOK 1.04 billion excluding leases) against TTM EBITDA of roughly NOK 690 million. | About 1.5x excluding leases, about 2.0x including them - within target, not net cash. |

Forensic caution: the reported cost-of-revenue line flips classification between quarters in the FMP data (gross profit of NOK 1,416 million in the second quarter of 2025 versus NOK 265 million in the second quarter of 2026 on similar revenue). Any valuation on enterprise value to gross profit (our methodology tag) would be anchored on noise, so we value on operating cash profit and earnings instead. The 85% "gross margin" in the screen is an artefact of this presentation, not a moat signal.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Without a transcript we cannot quote tone. What management did is itself informative: after a year of margin pressure it chose to merge with a peer of similar size and lower returns rather than run the recovery alone. Read plainly, that is a shift from an organic-recovery posture to a scale-and-synergy posture. The stated savings of SEK 100-120 million (as recorded in our prior review of the merger documents) are a cost-efficiency argument, not a growth argument. Trajectory of confidence: stable to defensive.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

The screen records zero beats in the last seven quarters against consensus, and the 2025 earnings collapse was not flagged far ahead. The 2026 half-year delivered a genuine improvement. Reliability: Medium-Low. Multiconsult does not give numeric quarterly guidance, so the beat record is the best available measure, and it is poor.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

From the record, not a transcript: (a) why merge at a ratio that hands 46% of the combined group to a partner with lower returns on equity (Rejlers roughly 8% against Multiconsult roughly 23%, per our 22 September 2026 check) and much weaker free-cash conversion; (b) how much of the stated savings survive consultant attrition, the main risk in any people business; (c) whether the 2026 margin recovery holds in the seasonally weak second half. We could not verify how management answered these.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: the exchange ratio values Rejlers at a richer multiple than Multiconsult, so Multiconsult owners are paying, not receiving, a premium for the 46% (September 2026 terms).
- Red: zero of the last seven quarters beat consensus; first quarter 2026 was down year on year.
- Red: unstable cost-of-revenue classification in the reported data.
- Green: second quarter 2026 earnings per share more than doubled; TTM free cash flow doubled.
- Green: shareholders of both companies approved the merger on 19 October 2026, removing the vote risk.
- Green: the share's 8% premium to the deal terms (22 September 2026) has disappeared; it now trades about 1% below them.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The new chief financial officer (Hans-Jorgen Wibstad, effective 1 November 2026) is appointed to Multiconsult first and earmarked for the combined group, a sign the Norwegian side keeps financial control. The chief executive will be Rejlers' Viktor Svensson with Multiconsult's Kristin O. Augestad as deputy, so operating leadership tilts Swedish. Multiconsult's own financial targets (10% margin, more than 50% payout, 8-10% growth including acquisitions) predate the merger and will be replaced by combined-group targets; until then they are not a promise anyone is held to.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: turning. The company has moved from a stand-alone recovery to a merger that, once completed, converts every Multiconsult share into 0.9725 Rejlers class B shares. The single most important thing to weigh: the price of a Multiconsult share is now set by the price of Rejlers class B times the ratio times the krona exchange rate (today about NOK 140), so any edge must come from the combined group being worth more than the market currently pays for it - that is, from savings delivered and a re-rating toward Nordic peers - not from Multiconsult's own discount, which the ratio has absorbed.

Moat: a narrow but real moat built on reputation, framework contracts and long client relationships with Norwegian public and energy clients (an intangible and switching-cost moat). Returns are respectable (return on equity about 29% on the screen's latest-year basis, return on invested capital about 14%) but not rising steadily; margins fell sharply in 2025 and partly recovered in 2026, so the moat is stable rather than widening. Secular threat: material, not terminal. Engineering design is sold by the hour, and AI-assisted design tools can compress billable hours per project; that would pressure revenue per engineer, though demand for infrastructure, energy and grid work is structurally rising. The cheapness is therefore not a value trap, but neither is it a deep discount.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

picks.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that a genuinely excellent business is being priced as an ordinary one for the length of a self-funded investment programme, and that the programme will eventually pay its owner.

The economics are not in dispute. Dunelm earns about 33% on invested capital, held a 52.5% gross margin in the year to June 2026 (up 10 basis points), spends only about 2.3% of sales on capital (GBP 43m on GBP 1,825m), and carries GBP 95m of debt excluding leases, 0.3 times EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation). Free cash flow on the company's definition rose from GBP 127m to GBP 155m and operating profit conversion to cash improved from 57% to 69% (2026-09-08 results).

It is still winning its market. Share of the GBP 25bn UK homewares and furniture market rose again to 7.9%; digitally enabled sales grew more than 9% and reached 42% of sales; the app produces about 40% higher basket values than web-only customers; customer satisfaction rose for a second year. Made-to-Measure window treatments, which arrive with a fitter and are hard for a marketplace to copy, grew double digits and kept doing so in the 2026-10-15 first-quarter update. That update also confirmed management's September warning was weather, not demand: the first six weeks were about -3%, the last seven about +4%, gross margin +10 basis points, full-year guidance unchanged.

The plan is the right one, badly received: about GBP 100m of cost removed by 2029, GBP 125m of extra capital to reopen the store pipeline (new stores pay back in under three years on the company's own evidence; only two opened last year against five to ten guided), and a target of mid-to-high single-digit sales growth. If the top line moves from about 3% toward 5-6% on a lighter cost base, 2029 earnings power is well above today's 76.8p. The chair and other directors bought in the market at roughly 732p-748p in the week after the September fall, and brokers dated in September 2026 (per the prior record: JPMorgan 1,050p, Deutsche Bank 1,000p, Shore Capital 1,000p, Canaccord 1,185p, Peel Hunt 1,225p; not re-verified this run) all sit above today's price.

Conditions: the cost programme reaches profit rather than being absorbed by wages; gross margin holds above about 52% through a promotional Christmas; store openings accelerate; the UK consumer does not weaken further.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bear case needs nothing to break. It needs only the next three years to look like the last four.

Revenue rose about 15.5% from GBP 1.58bn (FY22) to GBP 1.83bn (FY26) while diluted earnings per share fell from 84p to 76.8p and book value per share shrank about 4.2% a year. The FY26 cost bridge shows why: GBP 15m of productivity was swallowed by more than GBP 20m of inflation (GBP 23m in the results announcement) and about GBP 20m of volume-driven logistics and marketing that grows with digital sales; profit was held flat only with about GBP 10m of help, including GBP 3m of fire-insurance receipts, lower performance pay and GBP 1m of rates relief. Management does not disclose channel profitability.

The moat is narrower than the returns suggest: no switching costs, share gains slowing (about 50bp in 2023, 20bp in 2025, 10bp in 2026), and the FY26 margin gain was attributed to currency, partly offset by promotions; the second half ran near 51.7% against 53.4% in the first. In the last inflation wave gross margin fell from 49.6% to 45.3%.

The plan makes the owner wait: profit before tax guided broadly flat for FY27, GBP 125m of extra capital plus GBP 30-40m of one-off costs, and no special dividends before 2029, which cuts declared distributions from 70.5p to the 45.5p ordinary. If this third efficiency programme is absorbed like the first two, earnings stay near 77p, the market keeps paying 10-12 times, and the shares are worth roughly what they cost today with real downside if Christmas promotions erode the margin: the adverse case is about 577p.

What would confirm it: a weak 14 January 2027 Christmas update, gross margin below 52% at the 10 February 2027 interims, or the cost bridge again showing savings consumed by wage inflation after the April 2027 wage step.
picks.consensus_delta:
This is a deep-value framing question: is the market pricing terminal decline into stable earnings power? It is not. At 906.5p, about 11.8 times flat earnings and about 7 times EBITDA, the market is pricing Dunelm as a stable, ex-growth UK retailer - which is roughly what four years of flat earnings per share say it is. There is no terminal-decline discount left to arbitrage; the September sell-off to 734p-760p has fully reversed.

Where we still differ: the brokers dated in September 2026 (1,000p-1,225p in the prior record, not re-verified) assume the GBP 100m programme reaches profit from FY29. The company's own FY26 cost bridge - productivity fully consumed by inflation and digital variable costs, profit held flat only with about GBP 10m of help - argues that timing is optimistic, and this is at least the third efficiency programme. Where the market may be too cautious: the store pipeline and Made-to-Measure are genuine growth assets that a flat-earnings multiple gives little credit to. On balance the price sits at our base case, so the disagreement is not large enough to trade.
picks.valley_of_death: No solvency or liquidity event exists: net debt excluding leases is GBP 95m, 0.3 times EBITDA, and the 45.5p ordinary dividend is covered. The risky window (the months just ahead) is about earnings, not survival. November-December 2026 peak trading brings back the Black Friday choice management got wrong in FY26 Q2 (growth slowed to about 1.6% when it declined to discount): discount and the margin goes, hold and sales go. Free cash flow falls in FY27 as the GBP 125m extra capital and GBP 30-40m one-off spending begin, against an ordinary dividend that already absorbs most of it. The April 2027 wage step lands just as the cost programme must show up. The dated checks are 14 January 2027 (Christmas trading) and 10 February 2027 (interims, the first cost bridge under the new plan).
picks.positioning_washout: The forced-selling pressure, that is selling by holders who must sell regardless of value, was the income-fund exit after the 2026-09-08 removal of special dividends until 2029, cutting declared distributions from 70.5p to 45.5p. The price action says that wave has largely passed: the shares fell to 734p on 2026-09-09, directors bought at about 732p-748p, and the stock has since climbed back to 906.5p, above both the 50-day (about 828p) and 200-day (about 836p) averages. A renewed wash-out would need a new trigger, most plausibly a weak Christmas update. There is no index-deletion or lock-up overhang.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. The thesis holds - this is a high-return, lightly indebted, well-run UK homewares specialist - but at 906.5p the shares sit at our fair value of about 902p, so there is no margin of safety to buy.

Nothing dated has changed since the committee's 19 October answer: no announcement beyond routine notices, the final dividend went ex on 22 October, and the price has simply recovered the whole of the September fall. The forensic work stays clean (return on invested capital about 33%, gross margin 52.5%, net debt about 0.3 times EBITDA, management that warns early and names its own failures). The problem is the owner's arithmetic: revenue up about 15.5% since FY22 with earnings per share down from 84p to 76.8p, FY27 profit guided flat, and special dividends withdrawn until 2029 while GBP 100m of savings is reinvested.

The value case is real but the discount is gone. The value score stays high because the business qualifies and only the price does not; the price at which our base case would clear the 20% entry bar in this inflation-and-growth backdrop is about 752p, roughly where the September forced selling bottomed and directors bought. A return toward that level, for example on a weak 14 January Christmas update, is the setup this committee would re-examine. The spent strategy catalyst is neither a plus nor a minus here, and the macro backdrop (sticky inflation, a margin history that suffered in the last inflation wave) is context, not a reason.
picks.forcing_function: There is no hard event that forces a re-rating. The calendar items - the 14 January 2027 second-quarter update and the 10 February 2027 interim results - are reporting dates, not binding outcomes. What re-rates Dunelm is arithmetic: sales growth moving from about 3% toward the mid single digits while costs grow slower, so that flat earnings visibly end; on management's own guidance that cannot appear in FY27 profit, so the earliest evidence is the cost bridge at the February 2027 interims. Secondary signals: faster store openings in the interim capital-expenditure line, and any sign the special dividend returns before 2029.

# Dunelm Group (DNLM.L) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-16. Live price 906.5p (London listing, pence sterling, FMP quote). Sources: earnings-call transcripts dated 2024-09-11 (in practice the FY24 interim presentation), 2025-09-09, 2026-02-10 (FY26 interims) and 2026-09-08 (FY26 full-year results plus the new chief executive's strategy session); the screener's financial trajectory; the 2026-10-15 first-quarter trading update as reported in the press.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has moved from "a compounding product company that pays out its surplus" to "a business that must reinvest to grow again, and will pay its owners less while it does".

- **2024 (Nick Wilkinson era).** The pitch was steady compounding: "We're in growth, but our markets are not." First-half profit up 4.8% in line with sales, gross-margin discipline, a 35p special dividend "maintaining our track record in terms of cash generation and distribution". The language was confident and about balance - volume and margin together.
- **2025.** Same frame, weaker numbers. Market-share gains continued but slowed (about 20 basis points in the year), and the special dividend continued at 35p.
- **February 2026 interims.** The first visible strain. Management chose not to match "much deeper levels of discounting" over Black Friday, and second-quarter growth slowed to about 1.6%. A furniture forecasting failure hurt availability. A Bloomberg Intelligence analyst asked for channel profitability and was told it is not disclosed.
- **September 2026 (Clodagh Moriarty, new chief executive).** The pivot. "A solid year" with sales +3.1% to GBP 1,825m, gross margin 52.5% (+10 basis points), profit before tax flat at GBP 211m, and then a three-year plan: about GBP 100m of cost removed by the 2029 financial year and reinvested, GBP 125m of extra capital spending, GBP 30-40m of one-off costs, a return to "mid-to-high single-digit" sales growth, profit guided broadly flat for the 2027 financial year and no special dividends expected before 2029. The new voice is more self-critical ("we have to acknowledge that sometimes we are followers ... weren't on the app"; "We are not satisfied with the number of store openings").

What was dropped: the implicit promise that surplus cash would keep coming back as special dividends. What was added: stores as a growth engine again, Made-to-Measure window treatments as a named growth category, artificial-intelligence shopping (a launch partner for Google's conversational shopping in Europe).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers say | Read |
|---|---|---|
| "We yet again gained share to 7.9%" (2026-09-08) | Share gains of about 50bp (2023), 20bp (2025), 10bp (2026); the reported level has sat near 7.9% across consecutive disclosures | True but decelerating |
| Gross margin "strong ... consistency of our model" | 52.5% in FY26 (+10bp), helped by "a foreign exchange tailwind, partly offset by increased customer participation in promotional events". H1 FY26 was 53.4%, so H2 ran near 51.7% | Headline holds; quality weaker, currency-assisted |
| "Strong inroads covering the on-cost of inflation" | GBP 15m productivity vs more than GBP 20m inflation (skeptic check of the RNS: GBP 23m) plus about GBP 20m of volume-driven logistics and marketing; profit flat only with GBP 10m of "other items" (GBP 3m fire-insurance receipts, lower performance pay, GBP 1m rates relief) | The claim is generous; underlying profit fell |
| Earnings growth over time | Revenue GBP 1.58bn (FY22) to GBP 1.83bn (FY26), about +15.5%; diluted EPS 84p to 76.8p; net income GBP 171m to GBP 156m; book value per share shrinking about 4.2% a year | The key forensic fact: four years of growth with no owner earnings growth |
| "Strong cash generation" | Free cash flow GBP 155m (company definition) vs GBP 127m prior; operating profit conversion 57% to 69%; but dividends paid GBP 141m plus GBP 16m of buybacks for share schemes | True, but there was no headroom before the new capex |
| Balance sheet | Net debt excluding leases GBP 95m (RNS GBP 94.6m), 0.3x EBITDA, inside the 0.2-0.6x target; lease liabilities GBP 268.5m | Clean |
| "Q1 ... normalized" after hot weather (2026-09-08) | 2026-10-15 update: sales +1.1% to about GBP 433m, store like-for-like -0.8%; first six weeks about -3%, last seven about +4%; FY27 guidance unchanged | Borne out |

Data note: the screener's "TTM diluted EPS 1.54" is inconsistent with the 76.8p reported for the year to June 2026 and with flat guidance; it looks like an aggregation artefact and is not used.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable-to-declining on near-term confidence, rising on candour.** 2024: offensive and assured ("We feel we've struck the right balance"). February 2026: defensive, explaining a missed Black Friday and an availability problem. September 2026: more specific and more honest than before, but explicitly guiding to no profit growth next year and naming its own failures. The shift is from distribution language to investment language - from "track record in cash generation and distribution" to "bigger, better, and bolder".

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium-High.** The company delivered the FY26 cost plan it set at the interims ("We delivered to the cost plan that we set out"), warned the market about the weak start to FY27 before it reported, and the 2026-10-15 update matched that warning. Misses are operational rather than financial: two new stores against a guided five to ten, and the furniture forecasting failure. The screener shows one beat in the last three quarters, consistent with a company that guides soberly and does not over-deliver. No sandbagging pattern; no sign of aggressive accounting.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Channel profitability.** Asked directly at the February 2026 interims; not disclosed. Digital is the growth engine and also the source of the volume-driven cost; without the split, investors cannot tell whether mix shift is diluting margins.
- **Black Friday / promotions.** Raised after Q2 FY26 and flagged by management again in September 2026 as "considerations for us looking forward". Unresolved going into this Christmas.
- **Where the GBP 100m of savings goes.** The plan reinvests it; the market's question is when the owner sees any of it. Shares fell about 14% on the day (886.5p to 760p, 2026-09-07 to 09-08).
- **Store openings.** Repeated shortfall against guidance.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Red:
- Flat-to-falling earnings per share over four years despite share gains (FY22-FY26).
- Profit held flat in FY26 only with about GBP 10m of non-recurring or low-quality help (2026-09-08).
- Special dividends withdrawn until 2029; cash returned falls from 70.5p declared in FY26 to the 45.5p ordinary (2026-09-08).
- Gross-margin gain attributed to currency, which reverses (2026-09-08).
- About 8% of salaried support and distribution roles cut ahead of peak trading (per the strategy session coverage).
- Inflation sensitivity: gross margin fell from 49.6% (year to June 2019) to 45.3% (year to June 2023) in the last inflation wave.

Green:
- Return on invested capital about 33%, capital expenditure about 2.3% of sales, net debt 0.3x EBITDA (FY26).
- Digital participation up two points to 42%; the app produces about 40% higher basket values; Click and Collect growing quickly (2026-09-08).
- Made-to-Measure growing double digits, a service-attached category that marketplaces struggle to copy (2026-09-08, reiterated 2026-10-15).
- Directors bought in the open market at roughly 732p-748p in the week after the September fall.
- Customer satisfaction up for a second year from a top-quartile base.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The new chief executive's vocabulary is "customer obsession", "bigger, better, bolder" - growth language that replaces the outgoing team's "cash generation and distribution". Capital allocation has been re-ordered: reinvestment before special dividends.
- The chief financial officer now presents sales as overlapping "store-enabled" and "digitally enabled" figures, a new presentation that makes like-for-like store weakness (just under +1%) less prominent beside digital growth (above +9%).
- Management now says "sometimes we are followers" - an unusual admission that the plan is partly catch-up spending, not optional growth.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: turning.** The most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is an excellent, cash-generative, lightly indebted franchise whose owner earnings have not grown for four years, and management has now told you they will not grow in FY27 either while the surplus is redirected into stores, technology and cost removal. You are buying the probability that the third efficiency programme converts into owner earnings where the previous ones did not.

**Moat.** Scale-cost and brand in UK homewares: the largest specialist at about 7.9% of a GBP 25bn market, own-brand sourcing that supports a 52.5% gross margin, and a store estate that doubles as a fulfilment network. There are no switching costs. The returns are high and stable rather than rising, and share gains are slowing: a narrow but real moat, stable rather than widening.

**Secular threat.** Retail channel shift (online marketplaces and ultra-low-cost cross-border sellers) is real but currently being absorbed: Dunelm is growing digitally faster than the market and gaining share. The threat is manageable rather than terminal, so the cheapness is closer to a fear-print on UK discretionary retail and a re-set income story than a structurally shrinking base. The value-trap argument rests on earnings stagnation, not on a melting revenue base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

# CarGurus (CARG) - forensic dossier (debate run 2026-11-09)

Quarters read: Q3-2025 (2025-11-07), Q4-2025 (2026-02-19), Q1-2026 (2026-05-07), Q2-2026 (2026-08-06), Q3-2026 (2026-11-05). Price used: $34.55 (Nasdaq, USD, FMP quote 2026-11-09).

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
In late 2025 the story was "a two-sided marketplace with scale and data", with Marketplace revenue up about 14% in Q3-2025 and the CarOffer wholesale arm being wound down. Through 2026 the emphasis has moved from listings to software and data sold to dealers: PriceVantage (pricing, launched October 2025), VINMAX (merchandising boosts), Shopper Signals (lead scoring) and, in the week of the Q3-2026 call, StockVantage (which cars to buy at auction). Management frames these as roughly doubling its addressable market, from about $3.5B dealers spend on marketplaces to a further ~$4B spent on software and data (Q3-2025 call). The consumer side moved from "most visited site" to AI search (CG Discover, the "Guru" assistant) and an app inside the large chatbot platforms. The tone toward the macro shifted from "sheltered harbor" (Q3-2025) to an open admission in Q3-2026 that "dealer enthusiasm has not returned to 2025 levels" because of dealer margin pressure and stretched consumer affordability.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Double-digit growth continues | Q3-2026 revenue $258M, +12% year over year, top of guidance; full-year 2025 continuing revenue +14% | Matches |
| Profitable growth | Q3-2026 adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, excluding stock pay) $89.7M, a 35% margin; GAAP net income from continuing operations $52.8M, up only 2% | Partly - GAAP profit grew much slower than revenue as investment rose |
| Strong cash generation | Operating cash flow Q3-2026 $80.8M; trailing free cash flow about $325M (FMP) | Matches, but flattered: cash taxes paid were only about $9M over the last four quarters versus deferred tax charges of about $25M, and stock pay runs about $52M a year |
| Shareholder returns | Buybacks of $174M in Q1-2026, $28M in Q2, $23M in Q3; new $250M authorization on 2026-11-05 | Matches; share count falling |
| The reported revenue decline is not the core decaying | The 3-year revenue CAGR of -17% is the CarOffer wind-down (2022 revenue $1.66B included wholesale); continuing Marketplace grew every year | Matches |

The headline "11x free cash flow" overstates the true owner yield. After normal cash taxes and stock pay, owner earnings are roughly $200M a year, about $2.25 a share - nearer 15x the price.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Stable, slightly more defensive. Q3-2025: "we don't face a lot of pressure". Q4-2025: "2025 was a pivotal year". Q3-2026: dealer activity "moved in the right direction" but affordability "remains stretched" and "rising borrowing costs have added to that pressure". Language has moved from offense-only to offense plus "disciplined with our investments". A new CFO, Matthew Mandel, joined in late October 2026.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
High. The scan shows earnings beats in 7 of 7 quarters; Q3-2026 revenue landed at the high end of guidance and adjusted EBITDA near the high end; EPS $0.70 against a $0.66 consensus (Zacks, 2026-11-05). The Q3-2026 result included a $1.3M one-off real-estate tax true-up benefit, small. No sandbagging pattern beyond the usual conservative ranges.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- AI disintermediation (UBS, 2026-11-05): if a shopper finds a CarGurus listing through a chatbot and goes straight to the dealer, CarGurus gets no credit. Management's answer - car buying is a multi-week research process and shoppers still come back to the site - is plausible but unproven.
- Growth versus margin in 2026: asked repeatedly since Q3-2025; management prioritizes product investment and gives no margin floor.
- Dealer health: inventory up about 10% and dealer margins pressured; analysts keep probing churn risk.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
Red flag: GAAP net income grew only 2% in Q3-2026 while revenue grew 12% (Q3-2026).
Red flag: open-market insider activity is one buy against 33 sells over the scan window.
Red flag: cash taxes are running far below the book tax rate; free cash flow will compress when deferred taxes reverse.
Red flag: AI search can route shoppers around listing sites; management concedes attribution is "pretty indirect" in that case (Q3-2026).
Green flag: US net dealer additions of 251 in Q3-2026, the strongest quarter of 2026.
Green flag: US paying dealers buying at least one product beyond listings up about 16% year over year (Q3-2026).
Green flag: no borrowings; $165M cash against $182M of capitalized leases (2026-09-30).
Green flag: consistent buybacks shrinking the share count.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
"Marketplace" as a word is giving way to "platform", "workflow" and "intelligence" - a deliberate re-labeling toward software multiples. The CFO change is new; first-call commentary was limited to a factual answer on the tax true-up. Management now tracks "AI referral traffic and AI visibility" as a metric, which tells you the board is watching the chatbot channel closely.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: stable. The core marketplace keeps growing low double digits with a 35% adjusted margin and cash returned through buybacks. The single most important point: on normalized taxes and after stock pay the business earns about $2.25 a share, so at $34.55 the stock already trades around 15x owner earnings - fair, not cheap.

Moat: a network moat (the largest US shopper audience attracts the most dealers and vice versa), narrow rather than wide - returns on invested capital about 11%, and US competitors (Cars.com, Autotrader, Facebook Marketplace) keep dealer pricing power in check. Trend stable: share gains in traffic and dealers, gross margin 89%. Secular threat: material, not terminal - AI assistants could commoditize the discovery step, but dealers still pay for qualified leads and CarGurus is building into the dealer workflow. The cheapness relative to Auto Trader is mostly a fair reflection of a narrower moat and this AI risk, not a clear mispricing.

# Chewy (CHWY) - a deep dive on management and the setup

Debate date 2026-10-26. Live price $21.73 (NYSE, USD, FMP quote 2026-10-26). Transcripts covered: five calls, 2025-09-10 (Q2 fiscal 2025) through 2026-09-09 (Q2 fiscal 2026).

**Takeaway.** Chewy is a well-run, share-gaining online pet retailer whose story has stayed remarkably consistent for five quarters: recurring Autoship (automatic repeat ordering) revenue, steady customer additions, and margins that keep expanding. The numbers mostly corroborate the story on sales and cash flow. The softer spots are the gap between "adjusted" profit and reported (GAAP, generally accepted accounting principles) profit, a mid-year guidance reset in June 2026, debt-and-cash-funded buybacks plus two acquisitions, and one-sided insider selling.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **2025-09-10 (Q2 FY25):** the pitch was operating leverage - sponsored ads, health mix, a new automated fulfilment center, and roughly $125M of buybacks in the quarter. The finance chair was filled by an interim officer (Will Billings, chief accounting officer) while a permanent CFO (chief financial officer) search ran.
- **2025-12-10 (Q3 FY25):** adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, excluding stock pay and one-offs) margin 5.8%, up 100 basis points; free cash flow $175.8M in the quarter; "debt-free" with about $675M of cash. Tone: "running ahead of plan."
- **2026-03-25 (Q4 FY25):** a new CFO, Chris Deppe, an internal promotion. Management reframed the industry as "steady and resilient ... but without cyclical acceleration," explicitly not underwriting a rebound, and said growth would be "predominantly volume driven, with little or no contribution from pricing." The SmartPak (equine) purchase was described as a business that "requires a little bit of fixing."
- **2026-06-10 (Q1 FY26):** the first defensive note - the consumer "weakened in the latter parts of the quarter," fuel prices bit, and guidance was reset to "a more appropriately conservative view." The Modern Animal vet-clinic acquisition closed, taking the target to about 60 clinics by fiscal-2026 exit.
- **2026-09-09 (Q2 FY26):** stabilization, not recovery - "we did not see a meaningful recovery ... importantly, however, we did not see further deterioration." Sales were at the high end of guidance and guidance was raised modestly; AI cost savings were quantified (low tens of millions in fiscal 2026, about $50M annualized in fiscal 2027).

The core story never changed. What changed is the emphasis: from "acceleration" in 2025 to "share gains regardless of the market" in 2026, with vet care and AI added as new growth and margin legs.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Evidence in the financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Durable share-gaining growth | Revenue $8.97B (FY22) to $12.60B (FY26 fiscal year in the scan), 3-year growth ~7.6% a year; Q2 FY26 sales $3.33B, +7.3% (+5.7% organic) | Matches |
| Autoship makes revenue recurring | 84.4% (Q1 FY26) and 84.6% (Q2 FY26) of sales; Autoship sales +9.3% vs company +7.3% | Matches |
| Margins keep expanding | Gross margin ~29.8% and stable; adjusted EBITDA 7.5% (Q1 FY26), 6.8% (Q2 FY26); management admitted Q2 upside was "largely driven by timing and discrete benefits" | Matches on adjusted; GAAP is thinner |
| Profit growth | GAAP net income $393M (FY25) fell to $223M (FY26), EPS $0.91 to $0.52 (-43%); trailing EPS $0.66; net margin 1.8% | Diverges - the adjusted story is richer than reported profit |
| Strong free cash flow | Trailing free cash flow $568M (about 4.5% of sales), +24% year over year; capex ~1.3% of sales | Matches |
| Balanced capital allocation | Moved from "debt-free" with ~$675M cash (Dec 2025) to $592M of borrowings by 2026-08-02 (cash $612M, leases $527M), after buybacks and two acquisitions | Poorer than the story - the balance sheet weakened |
| Insiders are aligned | 0 open-market buys vs 26 sales (13.7M shares); the chief accounting officer sold 17,283 shares at $21.00 on 2026-10-15 | Neutral-to-negative signal |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: **Stable**, after a dip. Offensive in 2025 ("running ahead of plan," 2025-12-10). More measured in March 2026 ("not underwriting a meaningful rebound"). Defensive in June 2026 (guidance "reflects a more appropriately conservative view of the consumer environment"). Steady again in September 2026 ("the environment has broadly stabilized"). Guidance specificity has improved: AI savings were given a dollar figure, and the CFO publicly corrected a misread on third-quarter gross margin (it will step down from Q2 but still rise year over year).

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

The record is good. Earnings beat in 5 of the last 7 quarters (71%); Q3 FY25 adjusted EPS landed "near the high end"; Q2 FY26 sales landed at the high end of the range; Q1 FY26 EPS was $0.43 vs about $0.24 expected. The one blemish is the June 2026 reset, a macro-driven cut and not an execution miss, and the September raise partly reversed it (FY26 sales guidance $13.46-13.57B, adjusted EBITDA margin 6.7-6.8%). There is a mild pattern of conservative guidance followed by beats. Reliability: **High-to-Medium**.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Second-half gross margin** (Citi, 2026-09-09): how much sponsored-ads support is left. Management says it continues "albeit at a lower level than what you saw in 2025."
- **What the industry needs to grow again:** dog adoptions are tied to household formation and inflation-strained budgets. Management calls it "a short-term or transitory headwind," which is an assertion, not evidence.
- **Fuel costs:** the headwind was raised from low single digits to mid single digits after the Middle East conflict. It is being absorbed, but it shows the margin bridge has outside inputs.
- **Not addressed head-on:** the size of stock-based pay excluded from adjusted metrics, and why buybacks continued while the company took on debt.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- 🔴 GAAP EPS fell 43% (FY26 vs FY25) while adjusted metrics rose. The gap is stock pay, acquisition costs and integration.
- 🔴 Balance sheet: "debt-free" (2025-12-10) became $592M of borrowings (2026-08-02).
- 🔴 One-sided insider selling continues, including the chief accounting officer on 2026-10-15.
- 🔴 The June 2026 guidance reset shows the consumer is a real input, despite the "resilient category" framing.
- 🟢 Autoship rose to 84.6% of sales; active customers reached 21.7M (+3.8%) and net sales per active customer $602 (Q2 FY26).
- 🟢 Free cash flow grew 24%, and capex discipline (~1.3% of sales) has held.
- 🟢 The CFO seat is filled (March 2026) after an interim period.
- 🟢 Both acquisitions (SmartPak, Modern Animal) were "ahead of our expectations" in Q2 FY26.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The language shifted from "acceleration" to "outperform the broader pet category by roughly 2x to 3x." That frames success as relative share, not absolute growth, which is a quiet admission that the market is flat.
- AI moved from "capability development" to dollar targets. Management also said "we can't wait for inference cost to continue to come down," so AI cost is a variable for them too.
- Capital allocation is turning from organic-plus-buyback to acquisitive (vet clinics, equine). The new CFO, an internal FP&A (financial planning and analysis) leader, signals continuity, not a reset.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **STABLE**. The operating engine is intact and corroborated: recurring sales, customer additions, rising free cash flow. Reported earnings are thin and the balance sheet has taken on some debt. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing is that the stock's value rests on adjusted margins continuing toward the 10% long-term target. Reported net margin is under 2%, so every multiple applied to "earnings" is really a bet that the adjusted-to-reported gap closes.

**Moat:** a narrow but real moat. It combines switching costs (Autoship habits, pharmacy prescriptions, vet-clinic relationships) with scale-cost advantages in fulfilment. Return on invested capital is modest at 4.7% but rising off a loss-making base, and gross margin is stable at ~30%. That is a stable-to-widening profile, not an eroding one. **Secular threat:** manageable. Chewy benefits from the shift to online retail rather than suffering from it; the main structural risks are Amazon and mass retailers competing on price. The cheapness is a cyclical consumer-softness print on a growing base, not a value trap.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: VeriSign is a toll road on the internet's most valuable address space. It is the sole registry for .com and .net, earns about 88% gross margins, and turns 60-65% of revenue into free cash flow (cash from operations minus capital spending). The bull case is that 2026 is the start of a better growth phase, not a blip. The domain base reached 183 million names at 2026-09-30, up 6.1% from a year earlier, after a record 13.1 million new registrations in the third quarter (against 10.6 million a year before). Management raised its 2026 base-growth guide from 1.5%-3.5% in February to 6.5%-7% in October. Price comes on top of volume: the $0.71 .com rise to $10.97 took effect 2026-11-01. Management expects about half of it in 2027 revenue and most of the rest in 2028, because revenue is recognized over each registration's term. Unit growth of about 6% plus a price rise of about 7% phasing in means revenue can grow about 8% a year in 2027-28, against roughly 5% a year over 2021-25, with almost no extra cost. Two dated options sit on top. .web opens with a sunrise period in mid-December 2026 and general availability around April 2027, with premium-name pricing the .com contract does not allow. VeriSign Informed, a certificate-revocation checking service, gets pricing by year-end and availability in the first half of 2027. Capital returns are relentless: $1.14B returned in the last twelve months and $1.36B of buyback authorization left. On 2027 free cash flow of about $13.5 per share (about $1.17B on about 87M shares after buybacks) and a 28x multiple appropriate for a monopoly-like compounder growing earnings per share in low double digits, the stock is worth about $378, plus roughly $2 per share for .web: about $380. Conditions: this year's record new-registration cohort renews at or near the historical first-time rate (in the forties), registrars absorb the price rise without a jump in deletions, and the US Commerce Department and ICANN leave the pricing framework alone.
picks.bear_thesis: The bear case is not that the business breaks; it is that the price already assumes everything goes right. At $308.40 the stock trades at about 27 times trailing free cash flow ($1.02B, about $11.37 per share) and about 19 times EV/gross profit (enterprise value, market value plus net debt, divided by gross profit: about $28.97B against about $1.55B). It sits at the top of its 52-week range and about 13% above its 200-day average after rising from $208.86. Three things could compress that multiple. First, cash is not keeping up with revenue: third-quarter free cash flow fell to $261M from $303M a year earlier on higher cash taxes, and trailing free cash flow ($1.02B) is below FY2025 ($1.07B), even though revenue grew about 6%. Second, the record registration boom has not been tested by renewals. The third-quarter renewal rate already slipped to 74.3% from 75.4%, first-time renewers renew at about half the rate of mature names, and the CEO himself cited the 2016 China surge, when first-time renewal rates fell sharply over the following year or two. If the AI-driven cohort proves speculative, 2027 base growth could fall back toward 2%-3% just as investors capitalize the 2026 rate. Third, the balance sheet is being used: the company returned $1.14B in twelve months against $1.02B of free cash flow, cash fell from $618M to $476M, and net debt is about $1.31B, so buybacks cannot keep beating cash generation. Add 78 open-market insider sales against 2 small buys, a regulator that sets the .com price cap, and positive real long-term rates (the backdrop that punishes long-duration, high-multiple stocks). A de-rating to 18-19 times free cash flow on about $11.5-12 per share gives about $215, with no structural floor beneath it: the company has net debt, not net cash.
picks.consensus_delta: On the business we largely agree with the market; the only disagreement is on how much safety the price leaves. Analyst targets have been rising with the stock: Wedbush went from $324 (2026-07-24, stock $261.58) to $341 (2026-09-01) to $351 (2026-10-19), and the consensus is now $373.50 (range $367-$380, newest 2026-10-26 at $367 with the stock at $300.32). Those targets assume the 2026 registration boom carries into 2027 and the price rise flows through with no added churn, which together means about 8% revenue growth and a stable or higher multiple. Where we disagree: (1) the targets treat free cash flow as compounding with revenue, but trailing free cash flow ($1.02B) is below FY2025 ($1.07B) and the third quarter was down 14% on cash taxes; (2) the targets capitalize the record new-registration cohort as if it renews like the mature base, while the company's own data says first-time renewers renew in the forties versus the mid-eighties for mature names, and the renewal rate is already slipping (74.3% from 75.4%); (3) the targets do not price the backdrop: positive real long-term rates and a debt-cycle phase that punishes high-multiple, long-duration equities. The market is not pricing terminal decline into VeriSign; it is pricing near-perfection, which is the opposite of a deep-value setup. A deep-value entry needs a price that pays for the renewal-rate risk.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window, the months just ahead, is less a cash crunch (there is none: about $1B a year of free cash flow, no near-term financing need disclosed) than a narrative test. Three dated pressure points: (1) the fourth-quarter 2026 report in early February 2027, the first quarter after the price rise: seasonal holiday softness plus the first-renewal wave of the 2025-26 cohort could print a weaker base-growth number and a lower renewal rate, and with the stock at its 52-week high a soft number would be punished; (2) the 2027 guidance in the same report: if management guides base growth back toward low single digits, the market loses its main 2026 reason for a higher multiple; (3) .web sunrise (mid-December 2026) and general availability (around April 2027): uptake will be visible, and a tepid launch would cut the optional value analysts have begun to add. On the macro side, rising real yields are the shared factor that could de-rate all high-multiple quality stocks together; that is the sell-off we would buy into. Nothing here threatens solvency: net debt of about $1.31B is roughly 1.1 times annual operating income.
picks.positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling setup: no index deletion, no lock-up, no dividend cut (the $0.81 quarterly dividend was just declared, payable 2026-11-24). The holder base is quality and momentum money. After a run from $208.86 to $308.40, with the stock 95% of the way up its 52-week range and Zacks flagging it as a momentum stock (2026-10-22), the realistic washout is a style one: if the quality-growth factor de-rates on rising real yields, or momentum funds rotate, VeriSign can fall 15-20% with no change in the business. That sector-wide or style-wide sell-off is the seller we are waiting for, and it is what could bring the stock to our $255 level. # VeriSign (VRSN) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Covering five earnings calls, 2025-10-23 through 2026-10-22. Live price used: $308.40 (NASDAQ, US dollars, FMP quote 2026-11-02).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

VeriSign runs the registries (the master databases) for .com and .net under contracts with ICANN (the body that coordinates internet names) and the US Commerce Department. It cannot sell to the public; it sells each name wholesale to registrars such as GoDaddy, at a price the contract caps.

Across these five calls the story moved from "the domain base has stopped shrinking" to "the domain base is growing at the fastest rate in a decade."

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-23):** the tone was relief. The improved trends "that emerged at the end of 2024 continued through the first 3 quarters of 2025." Management first credited AI tools with "increases in registration and resolution activity." Much of the call was spent defending against worries (parked-domain advertising, the long legal fight over .web).
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-05):** 2025 closed with the base up about 4.5 million names to 173.5 million. The 2026 guide for base growth was a cautious 1.5% to 3.5%, with revenue guided to $1.715B-$1.735B.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-23):** management gave notice of a $0.71 rise in the annual .com wholesale price, from $10.26 to $10.97, effective 2026-11-01. Revenue guidance went up to $1.730B-$1.745B.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-23):** "the largest [new registrations] we have seen for any quarter in our history," and .web was delegated into the root zone with VeriSign as registry operator, ending a dispute that ran for years. Management said new products had not been "put on hold."
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-22):** base at 183 million names, up 6.1% from a year earlier; a record 13.1 million new registrations in the quarter; base-growth guidance raised again, to 6.5%-7%. Two new growth lines now have dates: .web (a 30-day sunrise period, the window when trademark holders register first, from mid-December 2026; general availability around April 2027) and VeriSign Informed, a certificate-revocation checking service announced 2026-10-05, with pricing promised by year-end and availability in the first half of 2027.

The arc is expansion. A one-product toll-road story has picked up two optional new products, but the economics are still almost entirely .com.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Demand for domain names is accelerating | Base +6.1% year on year to 183M (2026-10-22); new registrations 13.1M against 10.6M a year earlier | Corroborated |
| Revenue grows with base and price | FY revenue $1.33B (2021) to $1.66B (2025), about 5.2% a year over three years; Q3 2026 +5.7% | Corroborated, but growth stays mid-single-digit |
| Guidance is reliable and rising | Revenue guide raised from $1.715B-$1.735B (Feb) to $1.730B-$1.745B (Apr) to $1.755B-$1.760B (Oct) | Corroborated |
| Strong cash generation funds returns | FCF (free cash flow, cash from operations minus capital spending) was $1.07B in FY2025; trailing twelve months (TTM) to 2026-09-30 is $1.02B. Q3 2026 FCF was $261M against $303M a year earlier, which the CFO put down to "higher cash taxes and payments to employees and vendors" | Partly corroborated: FCF is falling while revenue rises |
| Shareholder returns | $1.14B returned in the last twelve months, more than the $1.02B of TTM FCF; cash fell from $618M (Q3 2025) to $476M (Q3 2026); net debt about $1.31B ($1.79B borrowings less $476M cash) | Returns now run ahead of cash generation |
| Earnings growth | Q3 2026 diluted EPS $2.35 ($2.41 before a $0.06 write-down on assets held for sale) against $2.27; TTM EPS $9.30; latest-quarter EPS up about 4% year on year | Slower than the full-year +10% |

The core claims hold up. The one softer number is cash: FCF is lower than a year ago while revenue is higher. Higher cash taxes explain it, not weaker demand. Even so, cash per share is not compounding as fast as the domain base right now, and buybacks are partly funded from the balance sheet.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY - Rising

- Q3 2025: careful and defensive ("the traditional use of domain names isn't going away").
- Q4 2025: measured; a wide, conservative base-growth guide.
- Q1 2026: confident enough to take a price rise.
- Q2 2026: "record metrics," .web resolved, products back on the agenda.
- Q3 2026: "the factors driving the solid domain name base trends ... further accelerated." The CEO also answered the renewal-rate question directly: first-time renewals run "in the forties," later renewals "in the mid eighties," and the new cohort falls into "the best renewing ... cohort, the online presence cohort."

Guidance has become narrower and more specific over the year, which is a sign of confidence.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY - High

Base-growth guidance went from 1.5%-3.5% (Feb 2026) to 6.5%-7% (Oct 2026), and revenue and operating-income guidance were raised at every call. Management under-promises at the start of each year. The screener's EPS "beat 3 of 7 quarters" is not a credibility problem: the misses are by a cent or so against consensus (Q3 2026 was $2.41 ex-charge against a $2.42 estimate), while VeriSign's own guidance has been beaten repeatedly. Reliability: High.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Renewal-rate dilution:** the Q3 2026 renewal rate is 74.3% against 75.4% a year ago, because the base now holds more first-time renewers. Analysts keep asking whether the AI-driven registration boom is low quality, like the China surge of 2016 that was followed by heavy deletions. Management says no and cites cohort analysis. The proof arrives through 2027 as this year's record cohort comes up for first renewal.
- **Price elasticity:** registrars have raised retail prices only "about 1% or less" since the April notice. The CEO said he "cannot speak for them." No early renewals ahead of the price rise were seen (Q3 2026).
- **New products:** asked how VeriSign Informed will be priced and what milestones to watch, the CEO pointed analysts to a microsite. Management will not commit to economics yet.
- **.web pricing:** management said it was "in the process of finalizing pricing." There is no revenue guide yet.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Green flags
- Record new registrations in Q2 and again in Q3 2026; base +6.1% year on year.
- The .com price rise ($10.26 to $10.97) took effect 2026-11-01. Management guides about 50% of it into 2027 revenue and most of the rest into 2028, because revenue is recognized over each registration's term.
- .web is resolved and dated; it is optional upside on top of the core.
- Gross margin is steady at about 88%; margins held through the 2021-22 inflation (gross margin 85.3% in 2019, 85.5% in 2021).

Red flags
- Q3 2026 FCF fell 14% year on year ($261M against $303M), and TTM FCF ($1.02B) is below FY2025 ($1.07B).
- Shareholder returns ($1.14B) exceed FCF; cash fell by $142M in a year; net debt is about $1.31B.
- Open-market insider activity: 2 buys (19 shares) against 78 sales (54,456 shares).
- Renewal rate is drifting lower (74.3%), and part of the new-registration boom has not yet faced a renewal.
- A $7.5M loss on assets held for sale in Q3 2026; small, but a sign of portfolio tidying.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "High assurance" has become the house phrase, used to tie .com, .web and VeriSign Informed into one platform story. Management is preparing investors for a multi-product company.
- AI has moved in the narrative from a threat (fewer clicks, parked-domain advertising) to a driver ("AI tools are making content and website creation faster and easier").
- Management explicitly intends to use premium-name pricing on .web, which the .com contract does not allow. The economics of .web could look different from .com.
- The CFO's FCF explanation (cash taxes) is credible, but no recovery path was offered.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: strengthening.** Unit demand is the best in a decade, a contracted price rise is now in effect, and two new products have launch dates. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the business case is excellent, but the price already reflects it.** At $308.40 the stock trades at about 27 times TTM FCF ($11.37 per share on about 89.7M shares), at the top of its 52-week range ($208.86-$312.78) and about 13% above its 200-day average. A franchise this good does not need a cheap entry, but it does need one that leaves room for the renewal-rate risk and the FCF softness.

**Moat:** a regulatory-license moat. VeriSign is the sole registry for .com and .net, and switching costs for registrants are very high. Width is wide: gross margin about 88% and steady, FCF margin about 60-65%, and ROIC far above any cost of capital (the reported 3,370% is distorted by negative book equity, but there is no doubt about the direction). Trend: stable, with the 2026 base re-acceleration a mild positive.

**Secular threat:** AI search and chat interfaces could, over a decade, reduce how much people rely on typing or clicking domain names. So far the evidence points the other way: AI is driving registrations. The more concrete structural risk is regulatory: the .com price cap and contract renewals are set by ICANN and the Commerce Department. Both risks are manageable, not terminal. This is not a value trap. It is a high-quality franchise at a full price.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a wide, durable moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.
