# Comcast (CMCSA) — a deep dive on management and the setup
*Debate run 2026-11-09. Transcripts: Q3 2025 (2025-10-30) through Q3 2026 (2026-10-22). Live price $24.51 (Nasdaq, USD, 2026-11-09).*

**The short version:** Comcast is a cash machine whose core business, home broadband, is slowly shrinking under attack from fixed wireless (home internet sold by mobile carriers) and fiber overbuilders. Management has been unusually candid about that, and it is spending heavily — price cuts, a five-year price guarantee, free mobile lines — to stop the bleeding. The content side (parks, studios, Peacock, Sky) is in better shape and is being split off into a separate public company by the middle of 2027. The numbers corroborate the candor but not yet the turnaround: free cash flow is real (about $17.1B over the trailing twelve months to 2026-09-30), but connectivity profit is still falling every quarter.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-30):** the story was "a deliberate investment phase." Mike Cavanagh said broadband would end up as a market of "2 multi-gig symmetrical providers," conceded "most of our footprint will eventually be overbuilt," and guided that the decline in Connectivity & Platforms EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — a cash-profit proxy) would "build slightly over the next several quarters." Leadership change: Steve Croney named head of connectivity.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-01-29):** the theme became execution of "the most significant go-to-market shift in our company's history" — four national speed tiers, a five-year price guarantee, a 12-month free mobile line. Management promised that "a meaningful portion" of free lines would convert to paid in the second half of 2026 and that connectivity profit would improve in the back half. The Versant cable-network spin was completed.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-23):** the high-water mark of the story — broadband net losses "improved by more than 100,000 year-over-year, the first year-over-year improvement since the fourth quarter of 2020," record wireless adds, record Olympic/Super Bowl advertising.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-23):** the narrative pivoted to structure. Three weeks earlier the company had announced the separation of NBCUniversal and Sky into a standalone company, targeted in "approximately 1 year," and the return of Michael Angelakis as the future Comcast chief executive. Peacock reached profitability.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-22):** tone turned defensive on connectivity. Management described fixed wireless as "aggressive," fiber pricing as having "pockets of irrational pricing," flagged an unusually large wave of two-year promotional roll-offs, and announced "the most significant operating and cost transformation in our company's history" with a roughly $1B fourth-quarter restructuring charge (reported 2026-10-22). Connectivity revenue fell about 2.6% and connectivity EBITDA about 4.4% year over year. Parks: Orlando softness guided to persist "at least next quarter and in the first half of next year."

The arc runs from "invest, then grow" to "split the company and cut costs." The growth promise for connectivity has been pushed out; the value-creation promise has shifted toward the separation.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Connectivity decline will "build slightly," then improve in the second half of 2026 (Q3 2025, Q4 2025 calls) | Connectivity EBITDA fell ~3.7% in Q3 2025, ~5.8% in Q2 2026, ~4.4% in Q3 2026 — it did build, and the Q3 2026 narrowing is the first sign of the promised improvement, but it is still falling | Partly delivered |
| Broadband losses turning (Q1 2026: first year-over-year improvement since Q4 2020) | The Q1 improvement did not become a trend; Q3 2026 was hurt by promotional roll-offs and aggressive competitor pricing | Not yet corroborated |
| Free lines will convert to paid in the second half of 2026 (Q4 2025) | Q2 2026: "positive early traction"; no conversion percentage has ever been disclosed | Unverified — a recurring non-number |
| Peacock will approach profitability (Q1 2026) | Peacock reached profitability in Q2 2026 and stayed profitable in Q3 2026 | Delivered |
| Cash generation is durable | Revenue flat for three years (3-year CAGR +0.6%; 2025 revenue $123.7B vs $123.7B in 2024); free cash flow $17.1B trailing twelve months, up ~25% in fiscal 2025 | Corroborated |
| Earnings growth | Fiscal 2025 EPS $5.39 (+30%) is flattered by one-offs and by the post-Versant comparison; trailing twelve-month diluted EPS is $3.16, and consensus forward EPS growth is only ~1% | The headline EPS growth overstates the earning power |

Net debt is about $79.8B (borrowings $87.4B less cash $7.6B at 2026-09-30, excluding leases), roughly 2.3-2.5 times EBITDA on our estimate — manageable, but it limits buybacks, which press coverage on 2026-11-08 described as on hold.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Declining on connectivity, rising on content.** Q3 2025: "intensely competitive environment, which we do not expect to change anytime soon" — candid but confident. Q1 2026: "early signs that the strategic pivot ... is underway" — the most offensive language of the run. Q3 2026: "near-term financial pressure," "pockets of irrational pricing," and a shift to cost and efficiency language ("structurally improve our cost base"). Guidance specificity has fallen: in Q4 2025 the chief financial officer said "I will stop short of giving a full EBITDA guide," and no connectivity framework has been offered since. On content, the tone is steadily more confident (Peacock profitable, The Odyssey, NBA ratings).

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Management gives directional rather than numerical guidance, which makes it hard to catch them out — and that is itself the point. Directional calls on the trough (the decline would "build") were accurate; calls on the recovery (broadband turning, back-half improvement) have been only partly delivered. Peacock guidance was met. The screener's 7-of-7 quarterly earnings-per-share beats reflects low consensus bars and cost control more than operating momentum. **Reliability: Medium.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- The free-line conversion rate: asked repeatedly (Q1 2026, Q2 2026), never quantified.
- Post-separation leverage, dividend policy and exchange ratio: asked in Q2 2026; answer was "nothing to add." The dividend split between the two companies is the largest unanswered question for the yield-holder base.
- Orlando parks softness and Epic Universe capacity: management now guides softness into the first half of 2027.
- Promotional roll-offs in the legacy base (Q3 2026): management admits it is "a pain point."

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Red flags**
- Q3 2026: a new round of the "most significant" transformation, with a ~$1B charge, one year after the last "most significant" go-to-market shift — the fixes keep getting bigger.
- Q3 2026: competitive language escalated ("irrational pricing"); peer Charter reported wider internet losses on 2026-11-06, so the pressure is industry-wide, not easing.
- Q2/Q3 2026: no capital-return framework for the two companies; buybacks reported paused.
- Insiders: 3 open-market sales (about 70,700 shares) and zero open-market buys.

**Green flags**
- Q2-Q3 2026: Peacock profitable two quarters running.
- Q3 2026: connectivity EBITDA decline narrowed to ~4.4% from ~5.8% in Q2.
- Business services generates "nearly $6 billion annually in EBITDA" with enterprise growth.
- Wireless: record line additions through 2026; over 10 million lines.
- The separation creates two cleaner stories and a potential sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately) unlock.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "Satellite is not yet a material factor" (Q3 2026) is the first time management has named satellite as a future competitor — a widening of the threat set.
- The language moved from "return to growth" to "position the business for return to growth over the long term" — a quiet extension of the timeline.
- Leadership churn: Croney (connectivity, 2026), Cavanagh co-CEO (2026), Angelakis returning as Comcast CEO (2027), a new NBCUniversal chief financial officer (Chris Halpin). The new voices emphasise cost and agility rather than growth.
- The proposed ITV acquisition for Sky signals the media company will be acquisitive, adding execution risk on the content side.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** The company is turning from a conglomerate defending cable into two separate companies, with an aggressive cost program on the connectivity side.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** the cash is real (about $4.80 of free cash flow per share against a $24.51 price), but the cash comes from a connectivity business whose profit is still falling about 4% a year. The investment works if that decline flattens; it is a slow value trap if it does not. The fourth-quarter 2026 results (late January 2027) are the next clean read.

**Moat:** scale-cost and network (a sunk, capital-efficient hybrid fiber-coax network) plus switching costs from bundling broadband with mobile. It is real but narrow, and the evidence says it is eroding: return on invested capital is only 6.8%, connectivity revenue and profit are falling, and management itself expects most of its footprint to be overbuilt. **Secular threat:** fixed-wireless and fiber overbuild (cord-cutting/broadband overbuild) is a material, not terminal, threat — the business still earns large cash margins and can defend share with price, and the content half is not exposed in the same way. The cheapness is partly a fear-print and partly a fair price for a shrinking core; at roughly 5 times free cash flow, the market is pricing more decline than the latest numbers show, but the burden of proof sits with management.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.

picks.bull_thesis: Boyd Gaming is a disciplined regional casino operator trading near 11 times underlying earnings (about $6.6 of trailing twelve-month EPS, excluding the 2025 FanDuel gain, at $72.21). Its property margins have held near 38-40% for years (Midwest and South adjusted margin 38% in Q3 2026, 'consistent with our third quarter margins over the last several years'), it kept its margins through the 2021-22 inflation, and the share count has fallen about 10% in a year (73.0M diluted shares in Q3 2026 vs 80.9M a year earlier). The core customer is healthy: excluding the Orleans and the Suncoast construction, Las Vegas Locals grew revenue and EBITDAR 3% in Q3 2026, backed by Southern Nevada wage growth near 6% and population growth twice the national rate. A visible pipeline adds earnings from 2027: the Norfolk, Virginia resort ('on time and on budget for a November 2027 opening'), the Suncoast and Orleans renovations finishing by early 2027, Par-A-Dice, and Sky River management fees that grew 13% in Q3 2026. If Las Vegas visitor traffic simply stops falling and Norfolk opens on time, a flat-to-growing EBITDAR base of roughly $1.33B with a shrinking share count supports a value in the low-to-mid $90s, and a re-rating toward peer multiples gives $110+. The conditions: margins hold, Norfolk opens on schedule, and the buyback is paced to free cash flow rather than debt.
picks.bear_thesis: The operating business is not growing. Reported Q3 2026 revenue ($990M) and adjusted EBITDAR ($319.6M) both fell about 1%, and the positive figures need management's adjustments for a closure, an asset sale, property taxes and tax pass-throughs. Las Vegas Locals EBITDAR fell 5% and Downtown 20% year on year, and the visitor softness management called near a turn in October 2025 ('much more positive than it was 3 months ago') has widened instead. Meanwhile buybacks run at $150M+ a quarter while trailing free cash flow was only $35M to 2026-06-30 (depressed by the roughly $360M FanDuel tax payment, but even normalized only about $250-300M a year after a $550-600M building program), so long-term debt has climbed from $2.27B in March to about $2.7B in September. That is a flat earnings base being levered up to shrink the share count, two years before the projects that are supposed to grow it open. Insiders sold 700,000 shares on the open market with no buys. The fiscal-2025 EPS of $22.56 and the screener's 487% margin of safety are artifacts of the one-off FanDuel gain. A consumer slowdown, more Las Vegas weakness, or a Norfolk delay would leave a regional casino at 6x EBITDAR worth the mid-$60s, with debt rising.
picks.consensus_delta: The street is not looking the wrong way. The consensus target is $87.70 (median $84, range $80-103), with five targets refreshed on 2026-10-23 after the print (Truist $95, Mizuho $103, Barclays $83, CBRE $85, Stifel $80). Analysts model a steady regional operator with modest growth (consensus forward EPS growth about 8%), which matches what management delivered. Where our view differs is on quality of the per-share growth, not on the level: the street credits the buyback without discounting that it is now partly funded with debt while EBITDAR is flat, and the post-print targets still assume the Las Vegas visitor softness turns, which management has predicted since October 2025 without it happening. The screener's headline margin of safety (487%) is not a disagreement with the market; it is the FanDuel one-off gain inflating 2025 earnings.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) holds no liquidity threat: total debt of about $2.7B against roughly $1.3B of annual EBITDAR is manageable, there is no near-term maturity wall in the materials, and the dividend is small. The risk is a slow grind: Q4 2026 and the first half of 2027 carry the Orleans room remodel (from early 2027) and the Suncoast room remodel (through Q1 2027), continued visitor softness in Las Vegas and Downtown, Hawaiian airfare pressure, and capital spending of roughly $140-155M a quarter for Norfolk ahead of any return. If buybacks keep running at $150M+ a quarter, leverage rises each quarter with no new earnings until November 2027. A consumer slowdown in a sticky-inflation backdrop would hit a flat base.
picks.positioning_washout: No forced-selling pressure is visible. Boyd has no index-deletion, lock-up or dividend-cut setup, and its holders are mostly long-only and value funds. Insider selling (23 open-market sales, about 700,000 shares, no buys) is a weak negative signal rather than a forced seller. Gaming stocks sold off broadly in Q3 2026 (a fund letter dated 2026-10-26 cites 'broad weakness in gaming stocks'), and the stock sits 12% below its 200-day average and about 25% up its 52-week range ($65-$91.41), so the sector selling has largely happened already.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. The thesis holds: Boyd Gaming is a steady, honestly run regional casino operator whose margins have stayed near 38% for years and whose share count has fallen about 10% in a year. Our base-case fair value is about $92 a share, a little above the street's $87.70, against a price of $72.21. We still pass, as this committee did on 2026-10-12, and the reason is the quality of the per-share growth, not the price. The third-quarter results on 2026-10-22 were the only new dated fact, and they confirmed the problem rather than fixing it: operating earnings were flat to down (adjusted EBITDAR $319.6M against $321.8M), Las Vegas Locals fell 5% and Downtown 20%, and the buyback is now partly paid for with new debt (total debt about $2.7B, up from $2.27B in March) while the projects that are meant to grow earnings open in late 2027 and 2028. Insiders have been selling, not buying. That is a flat business being levered up to shrink its share count, which is not the clean value case this book wants. What would change our answer: Las Vegas segment earnings growing again, or the buyback being paced to free cash flow with leverage stable, either of which we can check at the early-2027 results. Until then, Boyd is a fairly priced, decent business, not a buy.
picks.forcing_function: Nothing forces a re-rating in the next year. The buyback ($150M a quarter, $387M left at 2026-09-30) supports the share price but is already known. The real re-rating events are the Norfolk resort opening in November 2027 and a turn in Las Vegas visitor business, neither dated within our horizon in a way that would make it a catalyst. Next results are due in early February 2027 (about 103 days out).
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Boyd Gaming (NYSE: BYD) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Covers five earnings calls: Q3 2025 (2025-10-23), Q4 2025 (2026-02-05), Q1 2026 (2026-04-23), Q2 2026 (2026-07-23) and Q3 2026 (2026-10-22), checked against the screener's financials and the FMP quarterly statements through 2026-09-30. Note: this is Boyd Gaming, the US regional and Las Vegas locals casino operator, not the Chinese carmaker BYD Co.*

**Bottom line:** Boyd is a steady, honestly run regional casino operator whose earnings have gone flat. Property margins have held near 38-40% for years and management delivers what it says. But since the July 2025 FanDuel stake sale, almost all per-share progress has come from buybacks, and from 2026 those buybacks are being paid for partly with new debt while free cash flow is squeezed by a heavy building program. The story is credible. The growth is mostly scheduled for 2027-2028.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-23):** The FanDuel transaction dominated. Management had just received about $1.8 billion for its FanDuel stake, cut leverage (debt divided by annual operating earnings) to about 1.5x, and spoke openly about what to do with that balance-sheet room: "could be M&A, could be other things, could tick back up." Core-customer play was "strengthening"; destination (out-of-town visitor) business was soft, mainly at the Orleans.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-05):** A victory lap on 2025: record revenue, roughly $1.4 billion of EBITDAR (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and rent), more than $800 million returned to shareholders and an 11% cut in the share count. The 2026 pitch was a list of projects: Cadence Crossing (opened end of Q1 2026), the Suncoast modernization, the St. Charles convention center, the Sky River expansion, and a tax-bill tailwind for consumers.
- **Q1-Q2 2026:** The message moved from "growth" to "steady." Midwest and South kept delivering; Las Vegas Locals stayed weighed down by the Orleans and Suncoast construction.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-22):** The language now leans on adjustments. Reported revenue and EBITDAR both fell about 1%; management pointed to the Tunica closure (November 2025), the Shreveport sale (2026-08-01), higher Kansas Star property taxes and a lower tax pass-through to say that, adjusted, revenue grew 2% and EBITDAR 1%. Destination softness in Las Vegas is now described as "increased softness," not improving. The growth story has moved out to Norfolk (opening November 2027), Par-A-Dice (construction late 2027) and the Sky River hotel (2028; it was "mid-2027" on the Q3 2025 call).

The arc: from a cash windfall and an open question about how to use it, to a flat operating base where buybacks and future openings carry the per-share story.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Margins consistent" (every call) | Midwest and South adjusted margin 38% in Q3 2026, "consistent with our third quarter margins over the last several years"; company EBITDAR $319.6M vs $321.8M a year earlier on revenue of $990M vs $1,004M | Holds |
| Core customer strength | Las Vegas Locals ex-Orleans/Suncoast revenue and EBITDAR +3% in Q3 2026; Midwest and South EBITDAR $201.6M, flat year on year | Holds, but growth is low single digits |
| Las Vegas Locals recovery | Segment EBITDAR $87.4M in Q3 2026 vs $92.1M (-5%); Downtown $12.9M vs $16.1M (-20%) | Weaker than the story; destination softness widened |
| Capital investments paying off | Sky River fees drive Managed & Other EBITDAR to $29.8M vs $26.3M (+13%); Treasure Chest and St. Charles cited | Holds where the projects have opened |
| "Robust free cash flow" (Q4 2025) | TTM (trailing twelve months) free cash flow to 2026-06-30 only $35M. Q2 2026 operating cash flow was -$24M because of the roughly $360M tax bill on the FanDuel gain (accrued expenses fell from $602M to $342M); capital spending runs about $140-155M a quarter | Distorted by the one-off tax; normalized free cash flow after all building is roughly $250-300M a year, not "robust" against a $600M+ buyback pace |
| Buybacks reduce share count | Diluted shares 73.0M in Q3 2026 vs 80.9M in Q3 2025 (-10%); $164M repurchased in Q3 2026, $387M authorization left | Holds |
| Balance sheet conservatism | Long-term debt rose from $2.27B (2026-03-31) to $2.61B (2026-06-30) to about $2.7B total debt (2026-09-30); cash $297M. Net debt including leases about $3.0B | Leverage is drifting back up from 1.5x as buybacks outrun free cash flow |
| EPS +264% (fiscal 2025) | Fiscal 2025 EPS $22.56 includes the FanDuel gain (Q3 2025 EPS $17.81 alone). Underlying EPS is about $6.6 TTM (Q4 2025 $1.79, Q1 2026 $1.37, Q2 $1.75, Q3 $1.71 GAAP; Q3 adjusted $1.67 vs $1.72 a year earlier) | The headline growth is a one-off; underlying EPS is flat to slightly down |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable, drifting slightly defensive.** Q3 2025 was confident and forward-leaning ("customer trends ... have continued into October"). Q4 2025 was celebratory. By Q3 2026 the prepared remarks spend a full paragraph on adjustments before getting to growth, and the CFO declined to give sequential guidance on the fly: "I have tried to do it in past, and hopefully, I have learned to stop doing that." On M&A, management was disciplined rather than eager: "we are not gonna buy assets just because they are cheap." On online, it played down expectations for new licenses: "not anything that will be a tailwind for us." The tone is measured and candid, not promotional.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Boyd gives little formal guidance, which limits the test. Where it did guide, it delivered: the Online segment guide was raised to $60M of EBITDAR for 2025 and set at about $30M for 2026 after the FanDuel change; Cadence Crossing opened on schedule; Norfolk is "on time and on budget." The screener shows a beat in 6 of 7 recent quarters (86%), and Q3 2026 adjusted EPS of $1.67 beat the $1.65 consensus. One timeline slipped: the Sky River hotel phase moved from "mid-2027" (2025-10-23) to "2028" (2026-10-22), though that is a managed property and a fee stream, not Boyd's own capital. **Reliability: High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Leverage and capital use:** analysts asked repeatedly from Q3 2025 where leverage would settle after the windfall; management said leverage "could tick back up." It has: debt is rising while buybacks run near $150M+ a quarter.
- **Las Vegas destination softness:** raised every quarter since Q3 2025; management has called each bottom ("90-day booking pattern ... much more positive," 2025-10-23) and the softness has instead widened by Q3 2026.
- **Strip and mid-market M&A:** pressed in Q3 2026; management deflected with discipline language.
- **Online growth and new markets:** management answered that it is a small, well-run piece and will not "juice it."

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- 🔴 Las Vegas Locals EBITDAR -5% and Downtown -20% year on year in Q3 2026, after four quarters of being told destination business was close to turning.
- 🔴 Debt-funded buybacks: long-term debt up about $430M in the first nine months of 2026 while operating earnings were flat.
- 🔴 Insiders: 0 open-market buys against 23 sales (about 700,000 shares) in the screener's lookback.
- 🔴 Reported free cash flow is thin because the building program (Norfolk, Suncoast, Orleans, Par-A-Dice) is front-loaded; the payoff is 2027-2028.
- 🟢 Margins steady around 38% in Midwest and South for "the last several years."
- 🟢 Share count down about 10% in a year; dividend maintained at $0.20 a quarter (paid 2026-10-15).
- 🟢 Sky River management fees growing double digits; Online growing double digits on a clean comparison.
- 🟢 Kept its margins through the 2021-22 inflation (gross margin 47.8% in 2019 to 56.0% in 2022).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The shift to "adjusted for these items" framing in Q3 2026 is new; earlier calls led with reported growth.
- "Destination business" has gone from a temporary drag (2025) to a standing caveat attached to every Las Vegas comment.
- Management now says plainly that it does not "have to do anything" on M&A; the excess capital is going to buybacks by default.
- The Sky River hotel slipping from mid-2027 to 2028 is small but is the first timeline slip in the set.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** The operating base is flat; the per-share result depends on buybacks and on the 2027-2028 openings. The single most important thing to weigh: the buyback is now partly funded with debt while operating earnings are not growing, so the equity is getting more levered on a flat base until Norfolk opens in November 2027.

**Moat:** a narrow but real regulatory-license moat. State gaming licenses limit new competition in most of Boyd's regional markets, and its Las Vegas locals network has scale and loyalty-program advantages. Returns are respectable (ROIC, return on invested capital, about 12%) and property margins are stable, though the scan flags gross margin as contracting; the evidence supports a stable, not widening, moat.

**Secular threat:** manageable. Online casino and sports-betting apps could pull some play away from physical casinos, but Boyd participates through Boyd Interactive and its retained FanDuel market-access fees. No terminal-value threat is visible; the cheapness looks like flat earnings plus rising leverage, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

Earning roughly EUR 1bn of operating profit, this business alone justifies most of the share price at a contractor multiple. Second, APRR (the motorway network, about 52% economically owned) remains a legal monopoly with operating margins above 70% and roughly nine years to run. Even after the proposed levy - Morgan Stanley puts the hit at 9-12% of 2027 earnings for the exposed groups - its remaining cash flow is worth tens of euros per share. Third, there are real hidden assets: a stake in Getlink (the Channel Tunnel operator), airports, other concessions and treasury shares. France has no parliamentary majority; a budget forced through by special constitutional powers can be harsher than the draft, and the next government could revisit the concession contracts themselves. Operationally, light-vehicle traffic is falling on high oil prices tied to the Middle East conflict (2026-08-26) and road-building is down 5% on weaker local-authority spending. Earnings per share were flat in 2025 (+0.6%), free cash flow fell 12.2%, gross margin is contracting (12.9%), return on invested capital is a thin 6.3% and the Altman-Z solvency score is 1.0 because of EUR 10.8bn of net debt (including leases) at 2026-06-30. picks.moderator_conclusion: Buy now. picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Eiffage (FGR.PA) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-10-26. Live price EUR 99.70 on Euronext Paris (FMP quote, 2026-10-26; previous close EUR 97.42; 52-week range EUR 96.26-147.50). All figures in euros.

Short version: management has done what it said it would for three reporting periods running. Contracting (the "works" side: construction, infrastructure, energy systems) keeps growing its order book and margins hold. The concession side (mainly APRR, the motorway network Eiffage controls with about a 52% economic stake) is where the stress is, and that stress comes from outside the company: high oil prices cutting car traffic, and a French government that wants to more than double a special levy on motorway operators. The share price has fallen by about a third from its 52-week high. That fall is a verdict on French politics and on a concession that ends in the mid-2030s, not on the quality of management's execution.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **FY2024 results call (2025-02-27).** The story was scale and visibility. A record order book, up 11% year on year, strengthened by "the two major contracts of the EPR 2 [and] Line 15 East", about EUR 5 billion of new-nuclear work, more than EUR 1.1 billion of offshore-wind orders at Smulders, and a "total change of scale in Germany" through the Salvia and EQOS acquisitions. Management formalised a 45% dividend payout policy. The concession expiry question (what replaces APRR's profits once the concession ends) got a candid "it's still far too early to be able to say".
- **H1 2025 call (2025-08-29).** Same story, more Europe: revenue up 8.4%, growth in Europe outside France of 17.4%, order book up another 4%. A new theme arrived: the French "exceptional contribution" corporate surtax (EUR 135 million booked in the first half, about EUR 200 million for the year). Management called it "temporary" but conceded that "things are pretty unstable right now".
- **H1 2026 call (2026-08-26).** The framing moves to long-term structural demand: "sovereignty of energy, development of new mobilities, necessary adaptation to the climate change". The works side is still advancing (order book up again "on all of the branches lines of business"). For the first time the concessions are described as a drag: "performance is impacted by the decrease of the motorway traffic of the LVs [light vehicles] given the persistence of the oil price, which is high, direct consequence of the Middle East conflict." Road-building (Eiffage Route) is down 5% on weaker local-authority spending. Data centres are framed with deliberate restraint: one hyperscale project under way, perhaps three at most "on a frame of 6 to 12 months".

Net arc: the contracting growth story widened over the period (Germany, nuclear, grid, offshore wind, data-centre power), while the concession story narrowed from "cash machine" to "cash machine under political and traffic pressure".

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Evidence in the financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Very strong year... dynamic growth" (2025-02-27); revenue growth in 2025 and 2026 | Revenue EUR 19.2bn (2021) to 26.1bn (2025), +8.8% in 2025, 3-year compound growth 7.8% | Matches |
| Construction "back to growth" from 2025 (promised 2025-02-27) | H1 2025 construction +3.6% (2025-08-29); H1 2026 "construction line is back to growth" | Delivered |
| Earnings growth | Net income EUR 753m (2021) to 1.04bn (2024), then 1.02bn (2025): earnings per share +0.6% in 2025 | Poorer than the story. The French surtax (about EUR 200m) explains the 2025 stall; underlying growth continued |
| Margins "of good quality... no notion of impairment of the margin level" (2026-08-26) | Gross margin 12.9% and described as contracting; net margin 3.9%; margin 0.25 standard deviations below its historical peak | Broadly matches. The gross-margin drift is mostly mix (more acquired energy-services revenue), not price erosion, but it is a drift |
| Cash generation "extremely good" | Free-cash-flow margin 10.8%, price-to-free-cash-flow about 3.2x; free cash flow fell 12.2% in 2025 | Strong in level. Note that group free cash flow includes 100% of APRR, of which about 48% belongs to minority holders, and concession cash is a wasting asset that runs off at expiry |
| Balance sheet comfort ("cash available is significant", 2025-08-29) | Net debt EUR 10.80bn including leases (EUR 9.66bn excluding leases) at 2026-06-30, mostly concession debt; Altman-Z (a solvency score) 1.0 | Normal for a concession group, but leverage sits on the asset now under fiscal attack |
| Returns | Return on equity 14.6%; return on invested capital 6.3% | Modest. Capital-heavy concessions dilute the high-return contracting business |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: **Stable**, with the confidence shifting from the concessions to the works side.

- 2025-02-27: offensive. "Once again, a very strong year both in terms of earnings as well as order intake."
- 2025-08-29: offensive on operations, defensive on taxation. Results "went very well according to our expectations and confirms our outlook"; on French tax, "we do not have more visibility than you have".
- 2026-08-26: confident on works, matter-of-fact on concessions. Outlook for higher activity and results in 2026 confirmed; organic-growth guidance of 2-3% for energy systems reaffirmed ("the assumption of 2%, 3% organic growth is the right one"). On data centres, notably careful: "do not expect a tremendous jump overnight in activity."

Guidance has stayed qualitative (direction, not numbers) throughout, which is this company's long-standing style rather than a new retreat.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

- Promised a return to construction volume growth in 2025: delivered by H1 2025.
- 2025 outlook "confirmed" in August 2025: full-year revenue +8.8% delivered; net income flat only because of the surtax management had flagged in advance.
- 2026 outlook (growth in activity and results) confirmed on 2026-08-26; press coverage reports half-year profit up 11%.
- Earnings beat rate of 3 of the last 5 quarters (60%): neither sandbagging nor serial misses.

Reliability: **High** on what management controls; it does not and cannot guide French fiscal policy.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **The APRR expiry** (BNP Paribas, 2025-02-27): how will lost concession profit be replaced? The answer was a non-answer ("far too early"), and that remains the single largest unresolved question in the valuation.
- **French tax and the dividend** (Jefferies, 2025-02-27 and 2025-08-29): is the 45% payout a floor? Management: "it's not a floor". The surtax "will have an effect on dividends". Analysts were right to push: French fiscal risk has since escalated (see below).
- **Offshore wind** (Citigroup, 2025-08-29): no US exposure, but caution that European clients are stretched by their US problems.
- **Data-centre opportunity** (2026-08-26): analysts pushed on a large addressable market; management deliberately talked it down.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: Concession traffic falling (2026-08-26) because high oil prices, linked to the Middle East conflict, are cutting light-vehicle trips. Tolls are regulated, so lost volume is lost margin.
- Red: The French 2027 finance bill (article 22, filed at the National Assembly on 2026-10-01 after the government announced it on 2026-09-29) would raise the levy on long-distance transport infrastructure from a flat 4.6% to as much as 12.2% for the most profitable operators, and bars passing it through to tolls. Morgan Stanley estimates a 9-12% hit to 2027 earnings for the exposed groups. As of 2026-10-22 article 22 had not yet been debated.
- Red: The 2025 surtax already showed the state treats concession profits as a fiscal reserve; the dividend policy was explicitly "not a floor".
- Red: Eiffage Route down 5% (2026-08-26) on weaker local-authority orders.
- Green: Order book at a record and growing in every business line (2026-02 and 2026-08-26).
- Green: Long-dated, non-cyclical wins: about EUR 5bn of new-nuclear work (2025-02-27), a 12-year Arabelle Solutions nuclear components partnership, a 25-year Paris district-heating concession, a 5-year RTE grid-buildings contract, EUR 120m of high-voltage work for an AI campus (all 2026-08-26).
- Green: Disciplined mergers and acquisitions in markets it already knows (Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg through Baatz), no adventurism.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary moved from "record order book" to "sovereignty of energy" and "adaptation to the climate change": management is positioning the works business as a European-infrastructure franchise that stands on its own, as it should with APRR's end date approaching.
- The new head of concessions (Camille Bonenfant-Jeanneney, from January 2025, background in EU institutions, RATP and ENGIE) is a regulatory and stakeholder profile, not a traffic engineer: a hint that the next decade of concessions is a negotiation with the state.
- On treasury shares (5.8% of capital in early 2025): "we're not going to cancel". Buybacks are opportunistic and kept as a resource, not returned outright.
- Getlink stake: "prepared to strengthen, but we don't plan to take control". It is a financial option, not an empire-building signal.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **Stable.** The works franchise is strengthening and the concession franchise is being squeezed from outside; together they net to steady.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **how much of today's discount is a permanent transfer of APRR's cash flow to the French state.** If article 22 passes as drafted and traffic stays weak, the concession's remaining roughly nine years of cash flow shrink by a mid-single-digit euro amount per share in present value. If the levy is softened, much of the 2026 sell-off is overdone. The works business, which carries no such political exposure, is on its own worth a large part of the current share price.

Moat: the concessions hold a regulatory-license moat (a legal monopoly on the motorway network), wide while it lasts but finite (APRR and AREA expire in the mid-2030s) and now visibly subject to fiscal clawback. The works business has a scale-and-capability moat (few European contractors can deliver nuclear, high-voltage and hyperscale work), narrow but real, and widening in energy systems. Returns are modest (return on invested capital 6.3%) and stable rather than falling, so this is not an eroding moat in the sense of a melting franchise. On balance: narrow, stable.

Secular threat: none of the listed structural forces (artificial-intelligence displacement, energy transition and so on) threatens the terminal value; the energy transition is a tailwind for the works side. The real terminal question is the concession end date and the regulatory model that replaces it, a known, dated, political risk that is manageable rather than terminal. The cheapness therefore looks more like a fear print on French politics than a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

The Q3-2026 call turned defensive: 'intensifying competition and promotional activity, with the entry of new brands', still-restrictive credit, Seminovos margin down to 1.6% and expected to stay under pressure in rent-a-car, and a CFO statement that higher interest-rate expectations 'will require price adjustments going forward'. Each new Chinese entrant pressures new-car prices and therefore residual values, which is a slow-moving earnings leak. The equity is leveraged: net debt of BRL 33-36 billion exceeds the BRL 32 billion market value, Altman-Z is 1.2, Piotroski 4/9, and reported free cash flow over the last twelve months is about zero because fleet purchases ran ahead of sales. About BRL 8.3 billion of debt floats with the CDI rate, so a post-election Selic rise lands straight in the income statement. Tax reform adds a 2027-28 build-up of tax credits that may not come back as cash. If Brazilian rates rise and used-car prices fall together, the spread could slide back toward 4 points, earnings to about BRL 2.75 a share, and the leveraged equity would fall far more than the business.
picks.consensus_delta: The market is pricing Localiza as if Brazil's post-election rate and political risk will permanently push its returns back to the 2024 trough. The latest numbers say the opposite so far: the spread is 6.4 points and rising, profit is a record, and management is passing higher costs into prices (car-rental and fleet daily rates up 5-6% in Q3-2026). Where we disagree with the market is the size of the discount, not its direction: at about 7.5 times run-rate earnings the price already embeds a spread falling toward 4 points. Where the market may be right is residual values - a third depreciation step-up in a year would make the earnings base less reliable than the headline profit suggests.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window is the next 3-9 months. A Selic hike after the election would raise costs on about BRL 8.3 billion of floating-rate debt immediately; promotional pricing by new carmakers could push used-car prices down further (Seminovos margin already 1.6%), forcing another depreciation increase in Q4-2026 (results about February 2027); and car-rental price increases could meet softer demand. There is no maturity wall in the materials and liquidity is not the issue, but a leveraged equity can fall far more than earnings in that combination.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure appears largely done: the October 2026 sell-off, steepest after the 2026-10-25 runoff, looks like foreign and local investors cutting Brazil exposure across the board rather than holders forced out by a company event. There is no dividend cut, index deletion or lock-up here. The screener's smart-money score (9/100) shows institutions are underweight, which limits further mechanical selling.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Buy now. The thesis holds, and the Q3-2026 results on 2026-11-05 passed the test this committee set a week ago: record net income of BRL 1.125 billion (up 29%), a return spread of 6.4 points above the cost of debt, and lower net debt. At BRL 30.06 the shares trade at about 7.5 times run-rate earnings against our unchanged BRL 37 fair value, about 23% above today's price and above the 20% discount we require in the current macro backdrop. # Localiza&Co (RENT3.SA) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*As of 2026-11-10. Prices in Brazilian reais (BRL), Sao Paulo listing RENT3.SA. Last close BRL 30.06 (FMP quote, 2026-11-10), down about 45% from the 52-week high of BRL 54.87 and about 30% below its 200-day average.*

**The takeaway.** Over five calls (Q2-2025 to Q3-2026) management promised one thing - restore the return on invested capital (ROIC) above its cost of debt (the "ROIC spread") - and delivered it, with numbers that match. The Q3-2026 call on 2026-11-06 is the first one where the tone turns defensive: used-car prices fell sharply in the quarter, the used-car (Seminovos) margin compressed to 1.6%, and the CFO said higher interest-rate expectations "will require price adjustments" in car rental. The business is still printing record profit; the question has moved from "can they restore returns?" to "can they keep pricing ahead of faster depreciation and higher funding costs?"

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q2-2025 (2025-08-12) - repair mode.** The story was price recomposition (raising daily rates to cover higher depreciation and interest costs), cost cuts, exiting "severe use" truck contracts in fleet rental (31,000 cars in Dec-2024 to 23,000), and lifting Seminovos volumes. ROIC 13.7%, spread 4.1 points.
- **Q3-2025 (2025-11-14) - the IPI shock.** A cut in the federal tax on new entry-level cars (IPI, announced 2025-06-26) knocked down used-car values; Localiza took a BRL 929 million pre-tax one-off (impairment plus extra depreciation). Spread still rose to 5.3 points. Management first floated resuming growth "if interest rates decline."
- **Q4-2025 (2026-02-27) - target in sight.** Spread 5.5 points, adjusted net income BRL 3.4 billion for 2025, rental cash generation before interest about BRL 6.3 billion, "nearly doubling." New theme: Chinese and other new carmakers entering Brazil; Localiza signed a hybrid/electric purchase program. Guidance: 2026 is still a year of "accomplishing the mission of ROIC spread", growth resumes in 2027.
- **Q2-2026 (2026-08-07) - mission accomplished, with caveats.** Spread 6.1 points "within the company's target range", net income about BRL 1.0 billion (+30.6%), Seminovos at 92,000 cars a quarter. But depreciation assumptions were raised again "to reflect the dynamics of the automotive industry, characterized by the entry of new competitors."
- **Q3-2026 (2026-11-06) - record profit, defensive tone.** Net income BRL 1.125 billion (+29.1% on adjusted Q3-2025), spread 6.4 points for the first nine months, net debt down to BRL 33.1 billion. But the opening remarks are now about "intensifying competition and promotional activity", "still-restrictive credit", "higher depreciation, elevated interest rates and lower activity levels." Car-rental prices must rise again.

The growth story (resume expansion in 2027 once the spread is restored) has quietly moved back behind a pricing-defence story.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| ROIC spread restored to target | 4.1 pts (Q2-25) -> 5.3 (Q3-25) -> 5.5 (Q4-25) -> 6.1 (Q2-26) -> 6.4 (9M-26) | Matches |
| Profit growth | FMP quarterly net income: Q4-25 BRL 0.94bn, Q1-26 1.22bn, Q2-26 1.00bn; Q3-26 1.125bn reported. TTM diluted EPS 3.13 vs FY-2025 1.76 (which carried the IPI one-off and a deferred-tax write-off) | Matches; FY figures understate the run-rate |
| Strong cash generation, deleveraging | Net debt BRL 35.8bn incl. leases at 2026-06-30 -> BRL 33.1bn at Q3 (company definition). But TTM free cash flow is about BRL -43 million because fleet purchases ran ahead of sales (120,626 bought vs 92,043 sold in Q2-26) | Partly matches: operating cash is real, but reported FCF is consumed by fleet growth and renewal |
| Seminovos margin "low single digit, 1-3%" | 2.6% Q3-25 -> 1.6% Q3-26 (Brazil) | At the bottom of the range and falling |
| Depreciation "subtle upward trend, nothing major" (2025-08-12) | Raised again Q1-26 and Q2-26; Q3-26 marginal new-vs-sold price gap of 7-9%, implying BRL 8,500 to just over 10,000 per car | Diverges - the 2025 reassurance did not hold |
| Gross margin | Screener: 26.3%, contracting; quarterly gross margin about 26.8% in Q1-Q2-2026 | Pricing is keeping pace, not getting ahead |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rising through Q2-2026, **declining in Q3-2026**. Q4-2025: "this performance marked the company returned to its historical value creation spread range." Q2-2026: confident but hedged - the CFO on residual values: "I can argue both ways." Q3-2026: opens with the competitive and credit backdrop, and "in Rent a Car, the recent increases in interest rates expectation, combined with the higher depreciation will require price adjustments going forward." He still frames it well ("if we were a bank, we were increasing our bad debt provisions while increasing our ROEs"), and that framing is fair given the numbers.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Localiza gives no numeric guidance; it sets direction. On direction it delivered: spread restored (promised for 2026, reached in Q2-2026), severe-use fleet below 14,000 by Q2-2026 against a "fewer than 10,000" year-end goal, Seminovos at the ~90,000-a-quarter pace needed for a 15-month car cycle. Earnings beat 5 of the last 7 quarters (71%, screener); Q3-2026 net income of about BRL 1.03 a share beat the roughly BRL 0.98 consensus the committee noted on 2026-11-02. The miss is on residual values, where reassurances in 2025 had to be walked back three times. Reliability: **High** on operations, **Medium** on depreciation.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- Depreciation and residual values come up on every call (Morgan Stanley's Jens Spiess repeatedly; XP and UBS in Q3-2026). Management answers carefully but each quarter the number moves up.
- New Chinese entrants: management says the overlap is mainly small SUVs, not entry-level cars (2026-08-07); Q3-2026 concedes promotional pricing hit both new and used prices.
- Tax reform (CBS/IBS from 2027): a build-up of tax credits that may not be refunded in cash quickly, raising working capital in 2027-28 (Q3-2026).
- Rates: analysts asked in 2025 about passing lower rates to customers; in 2026 the direction reversed.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: Seminovos margin 1.6% (Q3-2026) and management says pressure "is supposed to persist" in rent-a-car.
- Red: depreciation estimates raised in each 2026 quarter; earnings quality rests on these estimates.
- Red: leverage - net debt (BRL 33-36bn) exceeds the equity value (about BRL 32bn); Altman-Z 1.2, Piotroski 4/9 (screener). About BRL 8.3bn of debt floats with the CDI rate.
- Red: reported free cash flow near zero over the last twelve months.
- Green: spread 6.4 points through 9M-2026; record car-rental utilization (82.4%) and fleet-rental margin 78.7% in Q3-2026.
- Green: about BRL 24.7bn of the BRL 33.1bn net debt is swapped to a fixed 12.6% plus spread, matched to fleet-rental contract terms.
- Green: operating fleet age down to 7.8 months (Q3-2026), lowering maintenance costs.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The CEO, Bruno Lasansky, led the 2025-08 and 2026-02 calls but not the Q2-2026 or Q3-2026 calls; the CFO fronted them. No change of role is stated, but the defensive messaging has come from the finance seat.
- "Restore the ROIC spread" (2025) has become "maintain adequate returns" (Q3-2026) - a shift from offence to defence.
- Nora Lanari (Q3-2026): price pressure "creates opportunities for Localiza ... we are becoming even more relevant to some OEMs" - the scale-buyer advantage being re-sold as the moat.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: stable.** Returns are at target and capital allocation has been disciplined (truck exits, fleet rejuvenation, Voll stake sold at about 5 times cost in January 2026), but the Q3-2026 call shows the pricing-versus-depreciation race tightening rather than easing. The single most important thing for sizing: this is a leveraged equity - the enterprise is roughly half debt - so a modest change in rental earnings or in the multiple the market pays moves the share price a lot in both directions.

**Moat.** Scale-cost: Brazil's largest car buyer (about 90,000 cars a quarter) gets better purchase terms from carmakers and runs the largest used-car retail channel, which together keep its cost of a rented car-day below rivals. Returns are high and rising (ROIC spread 4.1 to 6.4 points over five quarters), so the moat is narrow but real and not eroding on the evidence. **Secular threat:** new-entrant price competition and electrification hurt used-car values, but that is a cyclical and pricing problem the company is passing on, not a shrinking base; ride-hailing and autonomous driving are distant in Brazil. Manageable. The cheapness looks like a fear-print on Brazil rates and politics (October 2026 sell-off after the 2026-10-25 runoff) rather than a value trap.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

# Odfjell SE (ODF.OL) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-16. No earnings-call transcript was available from our data provider (FMP) for this Oslo listing, so this note is built from the company's third-quarter 2026 results release (published 2026-11-04, webcast 2026-11-05) as summarised on the Inderes release service and Baird Maritime, from FMP's quarterly statements (reported in US dollars), and from this committee's own prior coverage (2026-10-19 and 2026-10-26). Quotes are limited to what those sources carry; nothing is invented.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Odfjell is one of the two global leaders in deep-sea stainless-steel chemical tankers (Stolt-Nielsen is the other) and owns stakes in four tank terminals at shipping hubs. Over the past year the story has moved from "repaired balance sheet, strong rates" to "solid execution in a softening, disrupted market".

- 2Q26 (reported 2026-08-20): the best quarter in two years, net income about USD 51-54M on record revenue, and a USD 0.52 per share dividend for the first half, paid 2026-09-03. Management already guided the third quarter lower in that release.
- 3Q26 (reported 2026-11-04): net result USD 40M (adjusted USD 43M) against USD 54M (adjusted USD 56M) in 2Q26; time-charter earnings (revenue after voyage costs) USD 192M versus USD 195M; earnings per ship-day USD 27,892 versus USD 29,486. Volumes carried were the highest since 2022 (3.6M tonnes). The CEO framed it as "solid performance in a volatile market" and guided again: the underlying net result in 4Q26 is expected to be "somewhat lower than in the third quarter".

The thread that runs through both releases: the fleet is full and well-run, but per-day rates are easing, chemical volumes are still below pre-conflict levels, and vegetable-oil and biofuel cargoes are filling the gap.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Solid performance" in 3Q26 | Net income USD 40.4M, EPS USD 0.51, revenue USD 328.5M (FMP, quarter to 2026-09-30); TTM EPS USD 2.04 | Matches - down from 2Q but well above 1Q26 (USD 0.40) |
| Q3 would be softer (guided 2026-08-20) | Adjusted net down from USD 56M to USD 43M; TCE/day down 5% | Delivered as guided |
| Terminals are a steady second leg | Terminal contribution USD 2.2M in 3Q vs USD 1.8M in 2Q | True but small - about 5% of group profit |
| Balance sheet repaired | Equity USD 1,043.5M at 2026-09-30 (USD 13.18 a share); total debt USD 1,145M incl. USD 386M of leases; cash USD 166M; net debt USD 979M incl. leases, about USD 593M excl. leases | Holds, but lease liabilities jumped USD 112M in the quarter as two long-term chartered newbuilds arrived |
| Fleet renewal is self-funded | Sale of two 15-year-old coated tankers after quarter end, expected gain about USD 9.6M; two more stainless supersegregators committed on long-term contracts | Consistent - recycling old tonnage into new, partly via charters (which raise lease debt) |

The step-up in lease liabilities is the one forensic point to watch: "net debt" rose from USD 909M to USD 979M in a quarter of positive free cash flow, purely because chartered-in ships go on the balance sheet. It is a real, fixed obligation, not an accounting quirk.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Stable. The tone is measured and specific in both releases: management names the direction of the next quarter each time ("somewhat lower") and names the risks ("vessel deliveries and potentially diminishing inventories" for the coming quarters, per Baird Maritime's summary of 3Q26). No shift to defensive cost language; the emphasis stays on fleet renewal and contract cover.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

High. The 2Q26 release guided 3Q26 lower and 3Q26 came in lower but solid. Guidance is directional rather than numeric, which limits how precisely it can be scored, but the direction has been right two quarters running. The screener's beat rate (4 of 7 quarters) says consensus is roughly centred, with no pattern of sandbagging.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without a transcript we cannot quote the questions. The obvious pressure points, from the releases: (1) how far rates fall as newbuild deliveries arrive in 2027; (2) whether the dividend, now paid on a half-yearly basis from results, follows earnings down; (3) how much more chartered-in tonnage (and lease debt) the renewal programme adds.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: two consecutive quarters of guided-down earnings (2Q26 release, 3Q26 release); per-day earnings down about 5% quarter on quarter; lease liabilities up USD 112M in 3Q26; chemical volumes still below pre-conflict levels; management itself flags newbuild deliveries as a risk.
- Green: record volumes since 2022 in 3Q26; terminals' contribution rising; old ships sold at a gain (about USD 9.6M, after 2026-09-30); 2Q26 dividend of USD 0.52 a share paid 2026-09-03; equity per share up slightly to USD 13.18.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The cargo mix is shifting toward vegetable oils and biofuels to compensate for weaker core chemical volumes - useful, but those trades are more contestable by coated product tankers, which are the swing capacity that can erode Odfjell's niche. Fleet growth is coming increasingly through long-term charters rather than ownership, which keeps capital spending light but raises fixed lease commitments.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: stable. Odfjell is executing well into a cyclical downshift it has twice warned about; nothing in the numbers says the business is broken, and nothing says the cycle has turned up. The single most important thing for sizing: at roughly 1.0 times book value (about NOK 127 a share at USD/NOK 9.64) and about 6 times trailing earnings, the market is already pricing mid-cycle, so the payoff depends on how far 2027 rates fall when newbuilds land.

Moat: narrow but real. Stainless-steel parcel tankers with many segregated tanks are a scale-and-know-how niche (two global leaders, long contract relationships), plus terminal assets. Returns are cyclical (ROE 17%, ROIC about 12% on the scan) rather than structurally falling - the 2025 dip and 2026 recovery track freight rates, not lost position. Secular threat: manageable - the energy transition shifts cargo mix (more biofuels, fewer petrochemicals over time) but chemicals and vegetable oils still need parcel tankers. The cheapness is an honest cycle discount, not a value trap and not a fear-print.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

# SAX.DE - Stroer SE & Co. KGaA - Interrogator dossier (2026-11-10)

Live quote: FMP, EUR 39.24 on XETRA, 2026-11-10. The Q3 2026 statement has not been published yet; it was expected around 12 Nov 2026 and no coverage of it exists.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
In March 2026 the story became "from OOH to AI platform business". The FY2025 dividend was cut to EUR 1.85 and paired with a buyback of up to EUR 50m running to November 2026. The H1 2026 story was "OOH and DOOH keep driving growth": organic growth rose from 1.1% in Q1 to 4.2% in Q2, while the data and e-commerce arms (Statista, AsamBeauty) were downplayed. Behind all of this runs the take-private narrative. I Squared approached in 2025 and withdrew in Jan 2026. I Squared and Blackstone weighed about EUR 45 in May 2026, then Blackstone left. In Jul 2026 I Squared and InfraVia reportedly reached an understanding with the founder pool (43.96%). None of it has been confirmed, and none has turned into a formal offer as of 2026-11-10.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
- H1 2026 group revenue was about EUR 1.037bn, +6% reported and +2.7% organic. Adjusted EBITDA was EUR 273m (+3%) and adjusted net income EUR 56m (+7%). OOH segment revenue grew about 8% organic and segment EBITDA about 10% to roughly EUR 224m. These claims are corroborated.
- Screen P/FCF of 6.9x (TTM FCF EUR 318m) is pre-lease. Lease payments to cities and transit authorities of roughly EUR 210m a year bring true equity FCF to about EUR 110-120m, a cash yield of roughly 5% on a EUR 2.19bn market cap.
- Lease-inclusive net debt was EUR 1.81bn at 30 Jun 2026. Altman-Z is 1.1. Recent dividends and buybacks were partly debt-funded. Management targets leverage of about 2.35x by year-end.
- EPS is flat to down: 2.25 for FY25 and 2.20 TTM, with the latest quarter -6% YoY. That contrasts with the +17% forward consensus.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Management confirmed 2026 guidance at both Q1 and H1: low-to-mid single-digit organic growth with adjusted EBITDA broadly stable. Tone improved from defensive (the 2025 German OOH slump) to modestly confident on DOOH. Management keeps a strict no-comment on M&A. A CFO search was described as advanced in August.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
The record is mixed. In Q3 2025, organic sales fell 2% and EBITDA 6%, slightly below consensus. H1 2026 beat operating expectations. Only 3 of the last 7 quarters beat (43%). The modest guide is credible; the forward EPS consensus is not.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
Analysts press on the takeover status (always unanswered), the strategic future of Statista and AsamBeauty, the leverage path, DOOH pricing against classic OOH (classic fell 1.3% in Q2 2025), and the CFO vacancy. Bernstein rates the stock Market-Perform with a EUR 36 target (13 Aug 2026), below the current price.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
Red: lease-heavy debt with Altman-Z 1.1; the dividend was cut in 2026; shareholder returns are partly debt-funded; the data arms are shrinking and t-online is exposed to AI answer engines; insider buy ratio is 0; the stock trades above the only dated broker target.
Green: OOH concessions have a narrow but real moat; DOOH is growing double-digit; there is credible sponsor appetite (I Squared won oOh!media in Aug 2026); treasury shares were retired (Aug 2026).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
The price runs from EUR 36.93 (12 Oct) to 39.24 (10 Nov) with no company-specific news, and sits 77% up the 52-week range. Speculation on the Q3 print or the takeover is being re-priced in. UBS disclosed a 3.19% voting stake on 29 Sep 2026, which is likely event-driven or financing-related positioning, not a fundamental holder.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
A decent OOH concession franchise priced near fair value once leases are counted (SoP base about EUR 40). The headline cheapness is lease accounting. The take-private remains soft and unconfirmed. Capital allocation (debt-funded payouts, conglomerate sprawl) is the weakest link. Wait for a meaningfully lower price; do not pay for the rumoured EUR 44-45 bid.

# Currys plc (CURY.L) - a deep dive on management and the setup
As of 16 November 2026. Price used: 147.9p (London listing, pence sterling; live quote 16 November 2026).

Source note: no earnings-call transcript for Currys is available in our licensed data feed, and none was bundled. This dossier is built from the company's dated regulatory announcements (the full-year results of 2 July 2026, the trading update of 10 September 2026, and the filings since), secondary summaries of those releases, and the screener's financial history. Quotations from calls are not reproduced because we could not source them verbatim; where we describe management's message, we describe what the published releases say.

## 1. Narrative arc
The story has moved in three steps over roughly three years. In 2023 it was survival: revenue fell from about £10.1 billion (year to April 2022) to £9.5 billion, the company booked a £481 million net loss (largely a Nordic goodwill write-down), and the agenda was cost cuts, pension de-risking and debt reduction. In 2024 it was defence and repair: two takeover approaches (from Elliott and from JD.com) were rejected as undervaluing the company, the Greek business was sold, and the balance sheet moved to net cash. From 2025 to now it is a measured recovery: revenue grew about 6% to £9.25 billion in the year to April 2026, adjusted pre-tax profit rose 18% to £191 million, and capital returns resumed (a £50 million buyback launched on 2 July 2026, with purchases continuing into November 2026). The newest chapter is a change of voice: Alex Baldock handed over to Fredrik Tonnesen, formerly head of the Nordic business, on 3 August 2026.

What has been quietly de-emphasised: the earlier talk of the instalment-credit and services businesses as the main margin driver is now presented as part of a broader "solutions" mix, and there is still no disclosed bad-debt figure on the credit book.

## 2. Claims versus financials
| Claim (from releases) | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Recovery is real and broad-based | Revenue +6.3% to £9.25bn (year to April 2026); group like-for-like (same-store) sales +7% in the 17 weeks to late August 2026, with the UK and Ireland +6% and the Nordics +9% | Matches |
| Profit is growing faster than sales | Adjusted pre-tax profit +18% to £191m; reported net income £165m against £108m a year earlier | Matches, from a low base |
| The business is cash-generative | Trailing free cash flow of £622m in the screener counts about £195m of annual shop rent as financing; the company's own after-rent free cash flow is about £157m | Richer story than the true after-rent cash |
| Margins are improving | Gross margin was about 17.6% to 18.3% depending on definition, down roughly one point in a growth year; extra revenue of about £548m added only about £11m of gross profit | Diverges: volume was partly bought with price |
| Strong balance sheet | Net cash of £176m at April 2026 excluding leases; including about £749m of capitalised leases, net debt is about £776m; year-end cash is guided to "well in excess of £100 million" | Matches only on the ex-lease definition |

The screener's 6 times price-to-free-cash-flow and its discounted-cash-flow value of about 312p both lean on the pre-rent cash figure. On a rent-consistent basis the stock is about 11 times adjusted earnings.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory
Stable. The 10 September 2026 update, the first under the new chief executive, held guidance (about £199 million of adjusted pre-tax profit for the year to April 2027) rather than raising it, despite 7% like-for-like growth. That is a cautious, credible tone: management did not chase the stronger sales line, which some commentators attributed partly to one-off World Cup and summer-heat demand. The language remains about cost discipline, cash return and steady execution, not new growth bets.

## 4. Guidance credibility
Medium to high. The prior-year guide for about £180 million or more of adjusted profit was delivered at £191 million. The screener shows earnings beats on only two of the last four quarters (50%), but Currys reports half-yearly and the beat rate is computed on sparse, interpolated estimates, so we give it little weight. No sandbagging pattern is evident beyond ordinary conservatism.

## 5. Analyst pressure points
- Gross margin: why a point of margin was lost in a year of growth, and whether price competition with Amazon and AO World is permanent.
- The instalment-credit book: growth without a disclosed bad-debt or impairment figure.
- Cash: why year-end net cash is guided down from £176 million to "well in excess of £100 million" while a £50 million buyback runs.
- Cost inflation: the UK Budget of 29 October 2026 left employer National Insurance unchanged but lifted the National Living Wage 3.9% to £13.21 an hour from April 2027 and, per the British Retail Consortium, adds about £250 million to the retail sector's business-rates bill from April 2027.

## 6. Red flags and green flags
- Red: gross margin down about a point in the year to April 2026 while sales grew.
- Red: the group finance chief, Bruce Marsh, sold 500,000 shares at about 146.3p on 14 October 2026 (disclosed 16 October 2026), stated as being to fund a property development. Small against his position and explained, but a sale by the finance chief at today's price is not an endorsement that the shares are cheap.
- Red: tangible book value is slightly negative (about £2.29 billion of the £2.41 billion of equity is goodwill), so there is no asset floor.
- Red: a non-executive director, Magdalena Gerger, will leave the board on 19 January 2027 for other commitments (announced 27 October 2026). Routine, but it removes a remuneration and nominations committee member.
- Green: like-for-like growth in both regions, profit up 18%, a buyback in progress, and a Budget on 29 October 2026 that did not add a fresh employer National Insurance increase.
- Green: Piotroski score of 7 out of 9 (a nine-point accounting-quality checklist).

## 7. Hidden signals
The leadership change promoted the Nordic head, the region with the better recent margin story, which suggests the board is backing operational discipline over a strategic pivot. The steady drip of share-buyback filings through October and November 2026 confirms capital is being returned as promised. The gap between basic shares (about 1,017 million implied by the 16 November 2026 market value) and diluted shares (about 1,107 million) is unusually wide and has grown every year; share-based pay is a real cost to holders.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict
Trajectory: stable. The recovery is real and cash-backed, management is credible and is returning cash, but the economics are thin (return on invested capital roughly 2% on the screener's definition and about 7% on an adjusted basis, an operating margin under 3%).

The single most important thing for the director: the cheapness on the screen is mostly an accounting effect of leases. Once rent is charged, fair value is close to today's price, so the case is a sound business at roughly fair value, not a deep discount.

Moat: a narrow, scale-and-cost moat (the UK's largest specialist electricals retailer, with buying scale, a services and repair arm, and a store network that supports delivery and installation). Returns are low but not falling; margins are stable-to-slightly-down. The secular threat is the shift to online pure-plays and marketplaces (Amazon, AO World) and direct-to-consumer brands, which is material but manageable: Currys already does a large share of sales online and has held market share. The cheapness is mostly a fair price for thin economics, not a value trap and not a mispricing.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

The governance clean-up is done. Management is credible on cash and cost, and less so on growth.

The macro backdrop rewards cash-now businesses like this one, but that is context, not a reason to buy.

picks.forcing_function: What would force the market to re-rate: the ongoing buyback and progressive dividend shrink the share count steadily, and a footwear-cycle turn led by Nike would be the real catalyst. picks.interrogator_dossier:
# JD Sports Fashion (JD.L) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 2026-11-09. Sources: half-year results calls of 2023-09-21, 2024-10-02, 2025-09-24 and 2026-09-23, plus the screener's fiscal-year financials. Prices are in pence on the London listing (JD.L); the live quote used is 96.28p (FMP, 2026-11-09).*

**Bottom line:** JD is a highly cash-generative retailer whose earnings have been sliding for three years while its balance sheet has been getting steadily stronger. Management is credible on cash and costs and less credible on the top line: each year the story of a "structural growth market" has been replaced by a little more "controlling the controllables". The cash is real; the growth is not, for now.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **September 2023 (H1 FY24):** a governance and expansion story. The chairman talks about a new CFO, CTO and legal counsel, disposing of the fashion brands, buying out minorities in Iberia, Germany and Central Europe, and the pending Courir acquisition in France. Growth is the theme.
- **October 2024 (H1 FY25):** still a growth story — revenue "breaking the £5 billion milestone", JD-brand organic growth of 9%, double-digit organic growth in North America and Europe, and the Hibbett acquisition just closed. Nike's "stumble" is acknowledged as a headwind but framed as diversifiable ("if Nike is a little bit off form, we have New Balance and Adidas").
- **September 2025 (H1 FY26):** the tone shifts to discipline. Priority three of the April 2025 strategy update is "cash generation and shareholder return". Like-for-like sales fall 2.5% and growth comes from acquisitions (Hibbett, Courir) and new space.
- **September 2026 (H1 FY27):** fully defensive. "Our response to a maturing market and challenging trading conditions is to control the controllables." Organic sales fall 0.7%, like-for-like sales (sales at stores open in both years) fall 2.8%, and the store count is 106 lower. The proud line is now cash: net cash before leases of £168m, up almost £300m year on year, and "cash is king and cash is real."

The growth drivers introduced in 2023-24 (US expansion through acquisitions, the "structural growth market") have quietly given way to store productivity, apparel mix and buybacks. The phrase "maturing market" appears for the first time in 2026.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Highly cash-generative business" (every call) | FCF margin 7.9%, FCF up 40% in the latest year; net cash before leases swung from £125m net debt to £168m net cash (Aug 2025 to Aug 2026) after returning £260m | Matches |
| Market-share gains in North America and Europe (2025) | Revenue grew from £10.5bn (FY24) to £12.7bn (FY26), but mostly acquired (Hibbett, Courir); like-for-like negative in 2025 and 2026 | Richer than the numbers |
| Gross margin "maintained through trading discipline" | Gross margin steady around 47-48% for years; the 2026 call admits a 50bp underlying hit from price investment, offset by supplier marketing money | Broadly matches |
| Operating discipline protecting profit | Net income fell from £539m (FY24) to £490m (FY25) to £436m (FY26); H1 FY27 operating profit fell 19.5% and margin 120bp | Diverges — costs are controlled, but margins are not |
| Buybacks create value per share | Adjusted EPS fell 13.7% in H1 FY27 against a steeper fall in pre-tax profit; the share count is shrinking | Matches |

The headline earnings trajectory (EPS 0.10 in FY24 to 0.085 in FY26, down 10% in the latest year) is poorer than a "resilient" narrative implies. The cash trajectory is better than the earnings trajectory, which is the core of the bull case.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining on growth, stable on cash.**
- 2023: expansive ("the pace at JD is quite extraordinary").
- 2024: confident but with caveats (the "legendary UK summer", Nike's stumble).
- 2025: defensive ("a tough couple of years", national insurance rises, governance clean-up).
- 2026: defensive and specific — guidance is given as a fixed range (£700m-£800m pre-tax profit before adjusting items, £460m-£520m free cash flow after leases) and language centres on cost, capital and cash. The CEO concedes "heat created by the market leader... is not today the case", a direct admission that the Nike product cycle still drives the business.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Management held its full-year guidance range at the 2024 half year and kept the FY27 range "unchanged from the Q2 trading statement" in September 2026. That FY27 range sits well below the prior year's profit, so the expectation was reset during 2026 rather than met. The screener shows earnings beats in only 3 of the last 7 quarters (43%). There is no clear sandbagging pattern: guidance is reset downward when trading turns, then held. **Reliability: Medium.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **The footwear cycle and Nike:** analysts asked in 2025 and again in 2026 what it takes for footwear to return to growth. The answer was qualitative (end promotions, wait for new franchises such as the Adidas Samba, On, Salomon). There is no dated recovery marker.
- **Inventory:** management says it is "comfortable" while noting the industry may be too heavy, which is why the market stays promotional.
- **Mexico franchise and US womenswear (2026):** management frames franchising as capital-light growth. It is real but small.
- **Dividend cover:** the CFO signals a progressive dividend toward a yield "around 2-plus percent". The interim dividend was raised 21% to 0.40p.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: like-for-like sales negative in both H1 FY26 (-2.5%) and H1 FY27 (-2.8%).
- Red: three years of falling net income despite revenue up about 20%, so acquisitions have bought revenue but not profit.
- Red: heavy dependence on Nike, about half of revenue by Barclays' estimate, where brand heat is still weak (CEO, 2026-09-23).
- Red: North America operating margin down 220bp in H1 FY27, with the standalone Finish Line business being wound down.
- Green: net cash before leases up almost £300m year on year to £168m (Aug 2026), even after £260m of shareholder returns.
- Green: online sales up 5.2%, apparel up 4% to 36% of the mix, and like-for-like operating costs flat (H1 FY27).
- Green: adjusting items have shrunk to mainly the amortisation of acquired intangibles, so statutory and adjusted profit are converging. This marks the governance clean-up as done.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "Fewer, bigger, better stores" has replaced store-count growth as the space story. It signals saturation in mature markets.
- Capital-allocation language has moved from acquisitions (2023-24) to buybacks and dividends (2025-26). This is a classic sign that management sees fewer high-return reinvestment options.
- The CFO now quotes free cash flow after leases as a headline metric, a more conservative and more honest measure than in 2023.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Earnings are drifting lower, but cash generation, the balance sheet and governance are all improving, and capital returns are rising.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** the stock has already re-rated from about 64p to 96p over the past year and now trades near the top of its 52-week range. At roughly 9 times this year's guided earnings and a free-cash-flow yield of about 10%, it is cheap in absolute terms. Most of the discount to peers is explained by negative like-for-like sales and the Nike dependence, and the recovery in the Nike product cycle has no date.

**Moat:** a narrow scale and brand moat. JD is the preferred wholesale partner of Nike and Adidas for premium allocations, with a multi-brand, multi-country store estate that brands need for reach. The width is modest: return on invested capital is 8%, gross margin is steady around 47-48%, and operating margin is under pressure. Gross margin is not eroding, so the moat is stable rather than shrinking. **Secular threat:** manageable. Brand direct-to-consumer selling (the retail channel shift) was the structural fear, but Nike's partial return to wholesale has eased it. The cheapness reflects a cyclical earnings trough plus supplier concentration, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.
