picks.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that the market is pricing INPEX as a pure bet on the oil price when the company's own recent history shows a much higher floor under its earnings, and that you are paid well in cash while you wait for that to be recognised.

Start with the fact that settles the argument about downside. In full-year 2025, with Brent crude averaging just $67.80 and the yen at about 149.5 to the dollar, INPEX earned 394 billion yen, or 330.56 yen per share. That is the scenario the market is now reflexively selling - oil returning to the $65 to $70 area - and in that scenario the company still earns roughly 8.9 times today's share price of 3,502 yen. The current year is better than that: first-half 2026 profit was a record 263.1 billion yen (2026-08-07) and the full-year forecast was raised from an opening 330 billion yen (2026-02-12) to 510 billion yen, with analysts now at about 552 billion. So the real question is not whether earnings fall from a war-inflated peak - they will - but whether they fall below a level that still makes 3,502 yen cheap. On the company's own disclosed sensitivity of roughly 6.5 billion yen of net profit per dollar of Brent (2026-02-12: about 30 billion yen direct plus about 20 billion through the liquefied natural gas price lag), a move from today's $92 to a mid-cycle $80 costs about 78 billion yen, leaving roughly 430 billion yen - and the Abu Dhabi volume recovery as the Strait of Hormuz normalises adds back some of what 2026 lost to a 30% sales-volume constraint.

Second, the asset mix is better than the oil-beta label implies. Roughly 70% of net profit comes from Ichthys, the Australian liquefied natural gas plant INPEX operates, and management confirmed on 2026-08-07 that its selling price follows oil with a four-to-six-month lag. That lag is why the current year is largely locked in, and it makes Ichthys behave more like contracted infrastructure than spot commodity exposure. Its operating record is genuinely good: 12 cargoes a month for three consecutive months, a company record (2025-08-08). The company added to that interest on 2026-09-25. Behind Ichthys sits a domestic Japanese gas pipeline and terminal network with utility-like characteristics, and a Middle East concession position that kept producing through a closed chokepoint.

Third, the capital return is real, formalised and mechanically accretive. The 2026-10-21 Investor Day committed to a progressive dividend from a 90-yen-per-share floor, total shareholder returns of at least 50%, and net debt to equity held between 0.3 and 0.5 times. For the current year that is 112 yen of dividend (3.2% at today's price) plus about 140 billion yen of buybacks (3.4% of the market value), for about 6.6% of cash returned. Critically, those buybacks are being executed at about 0.80 times book value - the share count has already gone from 1,460 million in 2020 to roughly 1,162 million today, a 20% reduction - so every repurchase adds to book value per share rather than diluting it. At 0.80 times a book value of about 4,391 yen per share, and with net debt at only 0.22 times equity against a 0.3 to 0.5 target, there is both the discount and the capacity for this to continue.

Fourth, the valuation gap against live peers is wide. On the multiples we pulled on 2026-11-10, INPEX trades at 9.5 times trailing earnings and 0.80 times book, against Woodside at 13.2 times and 1.12 times, ConocoPhillips at 14.1 times and 2.44 times, and EQT at 11.2 times and 1.23 times. Woodside is the closest comparison - Australian liquefied natural gas, and a near-identical 4.3% return on invested capital against INPEX's 4.9% - which makes the gap hard to justify purely on quality.

Fifth, management is candid in a way that is itself worth something. They pre-disclosed a production problem before it hit the numbers (the Ichthys booster-compressor commissioning, 2026-02-12), they volunteered the Australian policy risk to their most important asset unprompted (2026-08-07), and they beat their own 2025 forecast. They also reason in real rather than nominal terms about shareholder cash (2026-02-12), which matters when inflation is running hot.

What must hold: Brent averaging $75 or better over the next 18 months; Ichthys running without a serious interruption; the Australian domestic-gas reservation proposal either not landing or landing in a diluted form; the buyback continuing; and the Abadi build decision around mid-2027 arriving at a capital number the market can live with. If those hold, a move to roughly 4,250 yen - about 11.5 times mid-cycle earnings and 0.97 times current book value - is simply the removal of an unusually wide discount, not a re-rating that requires anyone's imagination.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that INPEX is a low-return business whose record year is a war premium, whose cheapness is overstated by two accounting artifacts, and which is about to commit its largest-ever block of capital at a return below its cost of capital.

The first and most important point is that the headline cheapness is partly an illusion. The screen shows price to free cash flow of 5.9 times and a free-cash-flow margin of 34.4%. Both are mis-mapped. The data provider files almost all of INPEX's development spending under investing activities rather than capital expenditure: full-year 2025 shows 694 billion yen of operating cash flow against reported capital expenditure of just 3 billion yen, which is what manufactures the ratio, while investing outflows that year were 667 billion. Real free cash flow after all development spend was about 27 billion yen in 2025, and the 2026 guidance of roughly 1,000 billion yen of operating cash flow against an 859 billion yen investment outflow implies about 141 billion. Against that, the dividend and buyback together are about 270 billion yen. The capital return exceeds free cash flow and is being part-funded from the balance sheet - net debt rose from 1,076 billion yen at the end of 2025 to 1,102 billion at 2026-06-30. This is not a cash-flow compounder; it is a balance sheet being spent down at a controlled rate.

The second artifact is the enterprise value to earnings-before-interest-tax-depreciation-and-amortisation multiple of 3.4 times, which makes INPEX look 40% cheaper than Woodside at 5.6 times. That gap largely vanishes after tax. INPEX paid about 744 billion yen of tax on roughly 1,173 billion of pre-tax profit in 2025 - an effective rate near 63%, reflecting Abu Dhabi and Australian resource taxation. That is why a 56.2% gross margin becomes a 19.6% net margin, and it means host governments, not shareholders, capture most of the upside in a good price year. On post-tax earnings the discount to global peers is nearer 25% to 30%, which is a reasonable price for a Japanese listing where the government holds a blocking stake, the company cannot be acquired, and nobody can force a re-rating.

Third, the returns do not justify the growth plan. Return on invested capital was 4.9% on 4,262 billion yen of capital; return on equity was 8.3%. Into that record, the company intends to take a final investment decision on Abadi, a multi-billion-dollar Indonesian gas development, around mid-2027 (2026-10-21), with production only in the early 2030s and payback running into the 2040s. A business earning under 5% on capital making its largest-ever commitment is the textbook route by which a cheap resource company stays cheap. Note also what management emphasises: the 770 billion yen cash reserve being accumulated to fund it (2026-08-07). They are managing the financing, not defending the return - and no analyst on these calls asked what return they expect.

Fourth, the concentration risk is severe and the host government is hostile at the margin. Roughly 70% of net profit comes from one plant in Australia, where the chief executive himself described, unprompted, a live proposal to reserve 20% of liquefied natural gas exports for the domestic market - which on his own account would mean "the gas price domestically will go down for plummet" - alongside discussions about higher taxes on foreign operators and an admission of "business environment deterioration" (2026-08-07). That is an undated policy risk sitting on the asset that is the entire thesis.

Fifth, the earnings base is a peak and the peak is reversing in front of us. The 2026 forecast went from 330 billion yen on 2026-02-12 to 510 billion on 2026-08-07, a 55% upgrade driven by price, not execution, during a period when the Strait of Hormuz was closed. Brent has since fallen from $115.81 on 2026-10-26 to $92.34 on 2026-11-10. On the company's own sensitivity of roughly 6.5 billion yen per dollar, that 23-dollar move is worth about 150 billion yen of annualised profit - and because the Ichthys price follows oil with a four-to-six-month lag, it lands in 2027, not now. Consensus of 472 billion yen for 2027 was set at much higher oil and looks stale; the downgrades have not happened yet. Meanwhile the underlying trend is not growth: revenue fell 11.2% year on year with a three-year compound decline of 4.7%, and earnings per share fell 4.2%, against a narrative of "steady growth" that is only true of production volumes and operating cash flow.

Sixth, and this is the regime point: everything that could re-rate this stock resolves on a single shared macro factor. The current regime read (2026-11-02) names energy and the Strait of Hormuz as a breached shared resolution driver and a two-sided diplomatic binary, with one bank calling $105 Brent into December and another $70 on a deal. INPEX offers no resolution-driver independence whatsoever. If the de-escalation continues, there is no company-specific mechanism to arrest the slide.

What would confirm the bear: Brent settling below $70 and staying there; the 2027 guidance in February 2027 coming in near or below 400 billion yen; the Australian reservation policy being legislated; or an Abadi decision at a capital number above expectations. In that world, roughly 310 billion yen of profit on de-rated multiples takes the shares to about 2,700 yen, around 0.67 times a shrunken book value - a level the market already touched this year, at 2,951 yen, when Brent traded at $60.
picks.consensus_delta:
We disagree with the market on two things.

The first is the shape of the downside. The market is treating INPEX as a pure instrument on the oil price - the shares gave back 13.5% in nine sessions as Brent fell 20%, with no company news - which implies that a return to $65 or $70 oil guts the earnings. The company's own recent history says otherwise, and this is the most useful fact in the file: in full-year 2025, with Brent averaging just $67.80 and the yen at about 149.5, INPEX earned 394 billion yen, or 330.56 yen per share. That is 8.9 times today's price of 3,502 yen and 0.80 times book value, while the company pays a 3.2% dividend with a 90-yen floor and retires 3.4% of its own shares a year below book. The bear scenario has already been run as a live experiment, and the answer was a perfectly respectable year. Note this also corrects our own prior work: the last look assumed $65 to $70 oil implied a roughly 30% fall, and the evidence does not support that.

The second is where the cheapness is, and here we disagree with the bulls. The 3.4-times cash-earnings multiple that makes INPEX look 40% cheaper than Woodside is not a free lunch - a 63% effective tax rate consumes most of it, and on post-tax earnings the gap narrows to roughly 25% to 30%, which is a fair price for a government-blocked Japanese listing earning 4.9% on invested capital. Likewise the 5.9-times free-cash-flow headline is an accounting artifact of mis-mapped development spend; real free cash flow is roughly 141 billion yen this year, not 690. The genuine edge is narrower and more boring than the screen suggests: a 0.80-times book-value discount on a candidly run, asset-backed business that is shrinking its share count against it.
picks.valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next two to six months, and three things land inside it.

Third-quarter results on 2026-11-12 are the first numbers since oil broke, with consensus at 130.43 yen of quarterly earnings per share. Because Ichthys pricing lags oil by four to six months, these should still be strong - which is itself a risk, since a strong print into a falling commodity invites the market to look straight through it.

February 2027 is the real pressure point. That is when the 2027 guidance arrives, and it is where the 20% oil decline actually shows up. Consensus of 472 billion yen for 2027 was set at much higher oil; on management's own sensitivity of roughly 6.5 billion yen per dollar of Brent, the move from $115.81 on 2026-10-26 to $92.34 on 2026-11-10 is worth about 150 billion yen of annualised profit. The analyst downgrades have not happened yet, and they will cluster.

Third, the work-up to the Abadi decision around mid-2027. The risk here runs the wrong way round from how it is usually framed: a large capital number attached to a business earning 4.9% on capital is more likely to de-rate the shares than to lift them.

Beyond those dates, the undated hazard is Australia. The proposal to reserve 20% of liquefied natural gas exports for the domestic market would, on the chief executive's own account (2026-08-07), collapse the domestic gas price - and it sits on the asset generating about 70% of profit.
picks.positioning_washout:
Yes, and it is the sector-wide kind rather than forced selling by holders who must sell regardless of value. A wash-out is a sharp sell-off by forced or non-fundamental sellers; what happened here is its close cousin - a factor de-rating, where an entire sector or style is sold on a macro variable rather than on anything the company did.

Energy as a factor broke hard. Brent fell from $115.81 on 2026-10-26 to $92.34 on 2026-11-10, about 20% in nine trading sessions, with an 8.7% single-day drop on 2026-11-04 and a further leg on 2026-11-09 after the Wall Street Journal reported the US president playing down new strikes on Iran. INPEX followed: 4,049 yen on 2026-10-26 to a 3,413-yen close on 2026-11-06, then 3,502 yen on 2026-11-10 - down 13.5% - taking out the 3,540-yen level we named last time. There was no company news in the window; the only releases were a buyback progress notice (2026-11-09) and two forest-carbon items. The shares now sit about 10% below their 200-day average and roughly 23% up a 52-week range that runs from 2,951 to 4,955 yen.

The constructive detail is who is on the other side. The company's own monthly treasury-stock notices (2026-09-07, 2026-10-07, 2026-11-09) confirm the roughly 140-billion-yen buyback is still executing through the decline, at about 0.80 times book value.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Buy now. The sector-wide energy sell-off we said would deliver our price arrived, the thesis holds, and at 3,502 yen the shares clear our bar with a little room to spare.

On 2026-10-26 this committee said it would buy INPEX near 3,540 yen and named the seller: a sector-wide sell-off in energy once Strait of Hormuz risk receded and oil fell. That is precisely what happened. Brent crude fell from $115.81 on 2026-10-26 to $92.34 on 2026-11-10, about 20% in nine trading sessions, with the Wall Street Journal reporting on 2026-11-09 that prices were staying below $100 as the US president played down new strikes on Iran. INPEX fell 13.5% alongside it, closing at 3,413 yen on 2026-11-06. There was no company news in that window - only a buyback progress notice and two forest-carbon items. The market answered the wait we set, so we resolve it rather than extend it.

The business case is intact and, if anything, better understood than last time. First-half 2026 profit was a record 263.1 billion yen with the Strait of Hormuz closed and Abu Dhabi volumes down 30% - the diversification claim tested in the worst available conditions and verified. The 2026-10-21 Investor Day committed to a progressive dividend from a 90-yen floor, total returns of at least 50%, and net debt to equity of 0.3 to 0.5 times, against 0.22 today. On 2026-09-25 the company added to its stake in Ichthys, the plant it operates and the source of about 70% of profit.

Our fair value stays at 4,250 yen, about 11.5 times mid-cycle earnings and 0.97 times a book value of 4,391 yen per share - a multiple below every live global peer we checked on 2026-11-10 and roughly level with Japan Petroleum Exploration. We are holding conviction at 3, and the reasons are specific. This business earns 4.9% on invested capital and is heading toward its largest-ever capital commitment, a decision on the Abadi gas development around mid-2027 - a big number attached to low returns is more likely to de-rate the shares than to lift them. # Forensic dossier — INPEX Corporation (1605.T), Tokyo listing, Japanese yen

Prepared 2026-11-10. Transcripts reviewed: 2025-08-08 (first half 2025), 2026-02-12 (full year 2025 and the first 2026 outlook), 2026-08-07 (first half 2026). Supplemented by INPEX's own news releases through 2026-11-09 and the company's Investor Day of 2026-10-21. Price used throughout: 3,502 yen (the 2026-11-10 Tokyo quote; the day's range was 3,478 to 3,525).

## 1. Narrative arc

Across these three calls the story travels from "our big plant runs reliably" to "our portfolio is war-proof," and the supporting numbers largely keep up.

On 2025-08-08 the message was operational. First-half profit was 223.5 billion yen, about 10 billion better than a year earlier, and the single fact the chief executive led with was that the Ichthys liquefied natural gas plant in Australia had shipped "12 cargo per month for three consecutive months this year... the first time that we have been able to ship at that rate on record." The full-year forecast was lifted to 370 billion yen. United States tariff risk was dismissed in one line — "we currently do not operate in the United States, and we don't export to the US, either." Abadi, the big Indonesian gas project, was introduced as newly entering front-end engineering design (the detailed design stage that precedes a build decision).

On 2026-02-12 the tone turned technical and, to management's credit, pre-emptively bad. Full-year 2025 profit landed at 394 billion yen, comfortably through the 370 billion they had guided. The opening 2026 forecast, however, was only 330 billion yen — a deliberately cautious oil deck. The company also volunteered a production problem before it showed up in results: a booster compressor module at Ichthys needed commissioning through 2026, so cargo shipments would run at "about 10 cargo per month" rather than 12, described as "a one-off factor." Most usefully for an outside analyst, the finance director quantified the oil sensitivity: of roughly 52 billion yen of guidance swing attributable to the oil deck, "about JPY 30 billion on the oil price" came directly and "about a JPY 20 billion of impact" came through the liquefied natural gas price lag, which he put at four months. The dividend rationale also changed character here, discussed below.

On 2026-08-07 the frame changed again, this time because the world did. The Strait of Hormuz — the shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf — had closed. Abu Dhabi sales volumes were down "by around 30%." And yet first-half profit was the highest on record at 263.1 billion yen and the full-year forecast was raised from 330 billion to 510 billion yen. The chief executive called it "the victory of our portfolio." A new strategic thesis arrived with it: the energy system is shifting from efficiency toward security and resilience, and "security doesn't come for free... over the medium to long term, overall energy cost could potentially increase." Shareholder returns were set at 112 yen per share of dividend (12 yen higher than the prior year) plus about 140 billion yen of buybacks, for a total payout near 53%. The guidance assumed the Strait would "normalize around October."

The Investor Day of 2026-10-21 then formalized the framework: production of 630,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2026 rising above 800,000 once Abadi starts in the early 2030s, operating cash flow growing from about 1 trillion yen to 1.5 trillion by 2035, a progressive dividend with a 90-yen-per-share floor, total shareholder returns of at least 50%, net debt to equity held between 0.3 and 0.5 times, and an Abadi build decision "around mid-2027."

What was quietly dropped or softened: the 2026-08-07 slide showed production of 730,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day while the October Investor Day headlined 630,000 for 2026. The two figures sit on different bases (gross versus the company's net entitlement), but a reader comparing the two presentations would notice the headline shrank. And the Ichthys Train 3 expansion plus the Beetaloo shale gas resource have stayed at the "we are studying that" stage across all three calls — on 2026-08-07, visibility was still "really up to the result of Abadi exploration and the activities that we will undertake." That is a growth driver that has been described for years without ever being dated.

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Last 10 years, INPEX has continued to achieve a steady growth" (2026-08-07) | Revenue fell 11.2% year on year with a three-year compound decline of 4.7%; earnings per share fell 4.2% year on year with a three-year compound decline of 3.2%. Operating cash flow and production volumes did grow. | Half true, and the half that is true is not the half that matters to a shareholder. Growth is real in cash flow and barrels; per-share earnings have gone sideways to down. |
| "Highest profit on record" first half 2026 (2026-08-07) | First-half 2026 net profit 263.1 billion yen against 223.5 billion a year earlier. Second-quarter earnings per share 132.33 yen against 81.13 yen, up 63%. | Verified. |
| "The victory of our portfolio" — Abu Dhabi down 30%, profit still at a record | Confirmed: profit rose while the Middle East was constrained. Ichthys and higher oil prices carried it. | Verified, and genuinely impressive. |
| Shareholder returns of about 53% of profit, funded comfortably | 112 yen of dividend plus roughly 140 billion yen of buybacks is about 270 billion yen against guided operating cash flow of about 1,000 billion and a guided investment outflow of 859 billion. Net debt rose from 1,076 billion yen at the end of 2025 to 1,102 billion at 2026-06-30. | True but incomplete. Returns currently exceed free cash flow and are being part-funded from the balance sheet. There is capacity (net debt is 0.22 times equity against a 0.3 to 0.5 target) — but this is debt-assisted, not self-funded. |
| The screen's headline: price to free cash flow of 5.9 times, free cash flow margin 34.4% | The data provider maps almost all of INPEX's development spending to investing activities rather than to capital expenditure. Full-year 2025 shows operating cash flow of 694 billion yen against reported capital expenditure of just 3 billion — which is what produces the flattering ratio — while investing outflows were 667 billion. True free cash flow after all development spend was roughly 27 billion yen in 2025, and is guided to roughly 141 billion in 2026. | This is the single most important finding in the file. INPEX is not a 5.9-times free-cash-flow machine. Anyone sizing a position on that number is sizing on a mis-mapped accounting line. |
| Strong margins | Gross margin 56.2%, but pre-tax profit of about 1,173 billion yen in 2025 carried 744 billion of tax — an effective rate near 63%, reflecting Abu Dhabi and Australian resource taxation. Net margin is 19.6%. | Verified and structural. It is why a 56% gross margin becomes a 20% net margin, and why the cheap-looking enterprise value to earnings-before-interest-tax-depreciation-and-amortisation multiple of 3.4 times overstates the bargain. |
| Growth investment will create value | Return on equity 8.3%, return on invested capital 4.9% on 4,262 billion yen of invested capital. An Abadi build decision worth many billions of dollars arrives around mid-2027. | The central unresolved question. A business earning under 5% on capital is about to make its largest-ever capital commitment. |

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

Stable, with a rising operational confidence and an unusually high level of candour throughout.

2025-08-08 — confident and specific, anchored on a verifiable operational record ("12 cargo per month for three consecutive months... the first time... on record").

2026-02-12 — technically confident, strategically cautious. The opening 2026 forecast of 330 billion yen was conservative by design, and management handed analysts the sensitivity arithmetic rather than hiding behind it ("about JPY 30 billion on the oil price... about a JPY 20 billion" from the price lag).

2026-08-07 — the most confident of the three, and the most candid. Asked about Australian political risk, the chief executive did not deflect: "we do have concern, and that is honestly what we feel," then described flying to Canberra, then argued against the host government's own reasoning — "they're just discouraging the investor mindset... that kind of business environment deterioration is something that we honestly have in Australia." Management that volunteers a structural risk to the asset generating roughly 70% of its profit is management telling you something true.

The language mix is healthy: offensive and specific when discussing projects, defensive only about variables genuinely outside management's control (oil, the exchange rate, host-government policy). There is no drift into cost-cutting euphemism.

## 4. Guidance credibility

High on the annual framework, medium on any single quarter.

The pattern is consistent: set a conservative oil deck, then raise. For 2025, 370 billion yen was guided on 2025-08-08 and 394 billion was delivered. For 2026, 330 billion was the opening figure on 2026-02-12, lifted to 510 billion on 2026-08-07, and the analyst consensus now sits at about 552 billion with ten analysts covering. That is a 55% upgrade inside six months.

This cuts both ways, and the direction matters right now. The upgrade was overwhelmingly a price event, not an execution event, so it is reversible at the same speed. Management said as much when pressed on whether they could hold the payout commitment: about 70% of profit is Ichthys, and "that LNG price is 5 or 6 months behind" the oil market, which gives near-term visibility — and equally guarantees that a sharp fall in oil shows up with a four-to-six-month delay rather than never.

The screener's quarterly beat rate of 3 out of 7 (43%) looks inconsistent with the annual record, and the reconciliation is straightforward: the conservatism sits in the annual oil assumption, while quarterly outcomes are set by the oil price and the exchange rate inside the quarter, which nobody forecasts well. Score: high reliability on the annual framework, medium on the quarter.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Pressed and answered well: the durability of the 510 billion yen forecast and the 53% payout given oil volatility (2026-08-07). The answer was mechanical and useful — the Ichthys price lag of five to six months means the current year is largely locked, with the caveat that "if the Strait of Hormuz... will be delayed, then there will be a negative impact."

Pressed and genuinely unresolved: Australian country risk. The proposal to reserve 20% of liquefied natural gas exports for the domestic market would, on the chief executive's own account, create a domestic glut where "the gas price domestically will go down for plummet." Analysts pushed; management agreed it was a real concern; nothing is settled. This is the live structural risk to 70% of profit.

Deflected: Ichthys Train 3 and Beetaloo volume visibility, across all three calls.

Honest but ad hoc: on 2026-02-12 an analyst challenged how the dividend number was reached — "it's not really a clear number... maybe it's kind of a halfway." The answer confirmed the suspicion. It was arrived at by discussion inside a total-payout envelope rather than by formula, with an interesting twist: management explicitly reasoned in real terms, noting that "with the inflationary environment, there will be a decline in real" value of a fixed nominal yield. The 90-yen progressive floor announced on 2026-10-21 is the fix for the ad-hoc process.

What nobody pressed hard: the expected return on the Abadi capital. Analysts asked about timing, financing and the 770 billion yen cash reserve being accumulated for it. They did not ask what rate of return a business earning 4.9% on capital expects to earn on its largest-ever project. That is the gap in the coverage.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 Return on invested capital of 4.9% (full year 2025), with a multi-billion-dollar build decision due around mid-2027. Low returns plus big capital commitments is the classic way a cheap resource company stays cheap.

🔴 Shareholder returns exceed free cash flow and are part-funded by rising net debt (1,076 billion yen at end-2025 to 1,102 billion at 2026-06-30).

🔴 Roughly 70% of net profit comes from one asset in one jurisdiction that is actively debating diverting a fifth of export volumes to its domestic market (2026-08-07), alongside talk of higher taxes on foreign operators.

🔴 An effective tax rate near 63% means host governments, not shareholders, capture most of the upside in a good price year.

🔴 The 5.9-times free-cash-flow headline is an accounting artifact, as is the 34.4% free-cash-flow margin. Real free cash flow is roughly 27 billion yen (2025) to 141 billion (2026 guided).

🔴 Revenue down 11.2% and earnings per share down 4.2% year on year, against a narrative of "steady growth."

🟢 A record first-half profit achieved with the Strait of Hormuz closed and Abu Dhabi volumes down 30% — portfolio diversification that was claimed and then demonstrated.

🟢 Bad news is pre-disclosed. The booster compressor production hit was flagged on 2026-02-12, before it appeared in results.

🟢 Risks are volunteered, in blunt language, about the most important asset (2026-08-07).

🟢 The share count has fallen from 1,460 million (2020) to roughly 1,162 million today — a 20% reduction, executed persistently below book value, which quietly adds to book value per share.

🟢 The capital-return framework was formalized on 2026-10-21: a 90-yen progressive dividend floor, total returns of at least 50%, net debt to equity of 0.3 to 0.5 times.

🟢 On 2026-09-25 the company acquired an additional interest in Ichthys — adding to the asset it operates and understands best, rather than buying a story.

🟢 The downside is empirically known, not modelled. In full-year 2025, with Brent crude averaging just $67.80 and the yen at about 149.5 to the dollar, INPEX still earned 394 billion yen, or 330.56 yen per share.

## 7. Hidden signals

Three shifts are worth noting.

First, the dividend reasoning moved from convention to real returns. On 2026-02-12 management set the payout by arguing that a nominal yield which was adequate under deflation is inadequate under inflation. A management team thinking in real terms about shareholder cash is a better steward in the current environment than one anchored to a 30% payout tradition.

Second, the strategic vocabulary moved from efficiency to security, and management presented it as analysis rather than as a pitch — including the uncomfortable half: "security doesn't come for free," new pipelines raise costs, and "users they want energy with high security, but they want the price to remain at the current level." That is a producer-friendly worldview argued honestly.

Third, the Abadi framing changed from a growth project to a financing exercise. The emphasis on accumulating a 770 billion yen reserve, on net debt to equity staying within 0.3 to 0.5 times, and on matching "sound financial management comparable to the Ichthys development period" tells you management knows the capital number, not the gas, is what investors fear.

One more, in what was not said. The chief executive's 2025-08-08 line that INPEX does not operate in or export to the United States was framed as a tariff shield. Read the other way, it is an admission that the company has no position in the lowest-cost gas basin in the world — which is part of why its return on capital sits where it does.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

Classification: STABLE.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: INPEX is not the cash-flow machine the screen shows. Once the development spending that the data provider files under investing activities rather than capital expenditure is counted, free cash flow is roughly 27 billion yen (2025) rising to about 141 billion (2026 guided) — and the dividend plus buyback together, at about 270 billion yen, exceed it. A decision on a multi-billion-dollar Abadi development arrives around mid-2027 from a business earning 4.9% on invested capital. Size this as a cheap, candidly managed, asset-backed cyclical that is returning capital out of a strong balance sheet. Do not size it as a compounder.

Economic moat: regulatory-license and scale-cost in type, narrow in width. The evidence supports narrow rather than wide and does not support erosion: return on invested capital was 4.9% in 2025 against 5.0% in 2024 — low and flat, not falling away — and the gross margin's slide from 59.6% to 56.2% tracks the oil price rather than any structural loss of position. The genuine advantages are real but modest: a long-life Ichthys offtake arrangement priced off oil with a four-to-six-month lag, which behaves more like contracted infrastructure than spot commodity exposure, and a domestic Japanese gas pipeline and terminal network with utility-like characteristics. Against that, a 63% effective tax rate means most of the licence rent accrues to host governments.

Secular threat: material, not terminal. Gas is the transition fuel and Japan's pivot toward energy security helps rather than hurts, as management argued on 2026-08-07. But the entire asset base is hydrocarbon, reserve life is roughly 16 years at current output, and Abadi's payback period extends into the 2040s and beyond, which is exactly the window where terminal demand becomes contestable.

The conclusion that follows: the cheapness here is mostly a fear-print on a cyclical, compounded by a persistent governance and tax discount — not a structurally shrinking base. It is a discount worth owning, with a real structural tail that argues against ever sizing it as a core holding.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

Cross-checks: about 0.67 times a book value per share that would itself shrink to roughly 4,050 yen on currency translation, which is where Japan Petroleum Exploration trades today (0.65 times book); and just below the 2,951-yen low the shares actually printed earlier this year when Brent traded at $60. The fall case sits at 2,700 yen and the base case at 4,250 yen, so the two sit a broadly similar distance from today's 3,502 yen - this is not a lopsided bet. What makes it worth owning anyway is that you are paid about 6.6% in cash while the argument resolves: a 112-yen dividend (3.2%) with a 90-yen floor committed on 2026-10-21, plus roughly 140 billion yen of buyback (3.4% of the market value) being executed at 0.80 times book value, which adds to book value per share rather than merely supporting the price. There is no structural floor underneath - net debt of 1,102 billion yen rules out a net-cash floor, there are no deal terms and no tender, and a dividend yield is not a floor - so the downside is a valuation judgement, not a contractual one. The honest summary: a cheap, asset-backed, candidly run cyclical bought on a sector sell-off, where the return comes from the discount closing slowly and the cash arriving reliably, not from a sharp re-rating.

picks.peer_comps_note:
Cheap against peers, and we checked the multiples live on 2026-11-10 rather than from memory - the peer file carried no override anchors, and stale pre-shock multiples would have inflated the apparent discount. On trailing earnings and book value: INPEX 9.5 times and 0.80 times; Japan Petroleum Exploration 9.4 times and 0.65 times; EQT 11.2 times and 1.23 times; Woodside Energy 13.2 times and 1.12 times; ConocoPhillips 14.1 times and 2.44 times. On enterprise value to cash earnings: INPEX 3.4 times against Woodside 5.6 times, ConocoPhillips 5.8 times, EQT 5.5 times and Japan Petroleum Exploration 3.7 times.

Woodside is the fair comparison - Australian liquefied natural gas and a near-identical return on invested capital of 4.3% against INPEX's 4.9% - which makes a 40% gap on cash earnings look like a genuine anomaly. But two corrections are needed before crediting it as edge.

First, the peer file's supporting evidence cites INPEX's "5.9x P/FCF" as proof of cheapness. That figure is an accounting artifact, not economics: the data provider maps nearly all of INPEX's development spend to investing activities rather than capital expenditure, showing 694 billion yen of operating cash flow against 3 billion of capital expenditure in 2025 while investing outflows were 667 billion. Real free cash flow was about 27 billion yen in 2025 and roughly 141 billion guided for 2026. That leg of the peer case should be discarded.

Second, most of the cash-earnings gap is tax, not mispricing. INPEX's effective rate is about 63% against materially lower rates at the Anglo peers, so on post-tax earnings the discount narrows to roughly 25% to 30% - which is a defensible price for a Japanese listing with a government blocking stake, no takeover possibility, and 4.9% returns on capital. The residual gap we do credit is the book-value discount: 0.80 times against Woodside's 1.12, on a company buying back 3.4% of itself a year below book.

One shared-factor caveat we apply ourselves, since the peer file does not flag it: INPEX and Woodside both just de-rated on the same unresolved driver, the oil price and the Strait of Hormuz, so part of the gap is sector beta that moves on a factor neither company controls, not single-name alpha.
picks.thesis_evidence:
The business case is corroborated by the latest dated numbers, and the fall that brought the shares to our price was a sector-wide sell-off, not company news.

On the business: first-half 2026 net profit was a record 263.1 billion yen and the full-year forecast was raised to 510 billion (2026-08-07), achieved with the Strait of Hormuz closed and Abu Dhabi sales volumes down about 30% - which is the portfolio-diversification claim tested and verified. Second-quarter earnings per share were 132.33 yen against 81.13 a year earlier. On 2026-09-25 INPEX bought an additional interest in Ichthys, the asset it operates. The 2026-10-21 Investor Day reaffirmed the framework: 630,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2026 rising above 800,000 after Abadi, operating cash flow growing toward 1.5 trillion yen by 2035, a progressive dividend from a 90-yen floor, total returns of at least 50%, and net debt to equity of 0.3 to 0.5 times (currently 0.22). The monthly treasury-stock notice of 2026-11-09 confirms the roughly 140-billion-yen buyback is still running into the weakness.

On the fall: this was a sector-wide and style-wide energy sell-off, not forced selling by holders who must sell regardless of value, and not an information event about INPEX. Brent crude fell from $115.81 on 2026-10-26 to $92.34 on 2026-11-10, about 20%, with daily legs of 8.7% on 2026-11-04 and a further drop on 2026-11-09 after the Wall Street Journal reported the US president playing down new strikes on Iran. INPEX fell from 4,049 yen on 2026-10-26 to a 3,413-yen close on 2026-11-06 and 3,502 yen on 2026-11-10, taking out the 3,540-yen level we named. The only INPEX releases in that window were the buyback progress notice (2026-11-09) and two forest-carbon credit items (2026-11-02 and 2026-11-05). The shares now sit about 10% below their 200-day average.

The one load-bearing claim we would want to watch rather than call in doubt: 2027 earnings. Management confirmed on 2026-08-07 that Ichthys pricing follows oil with a four-to-six-month lag, so the 20% oil decline lands in 2027, not in the current year, and the consensus 472 billion yen for 2027 was set at much higher oil. Our 4,250-yen fair value is built on mid-cycle profit of about 430 billion yen, not on consensus, so a downgrade to that level does not impair the thesis - it is already assumed.
picks.macro_fit_note:
The backdrop is mixed rather than helpful. The macro read puts the economy in a reflation quadrant - growth up with hot, sticky inflation, on real output of about 3.4% annualised and consumer prices running near 3.7% at a six-month annualised rate - and the debt cycle in a discipline phase, where positive real long-term rates are being imposed and holding, so "duration punished, cash flow rewarded", with an expected horizon of about 18 months. On the surface an energy producer paying out 6.6% in cash is exactly the cash-now asset that backdrop rewards. Two things pull it back to neutral. First, INPEX's cash-now profile is weaker than the screen implies: the 5.9-times free-cash-flow headline is a mapping artifact, real free cash flow is roughly 141 billion yen against a guided 859-billion-yen investment outflow for 2026, and a large part of that spend is long-dated Abadi development, which is precisely the duration this phase punishes. Second, the commodity itself is deflating inside a reflationary quadrant - Brent is down about 20% since 2026-10-26 - so the inflation tailwind is not reaching this company's realisations.

On inflation pass-through, the record for this name is mixed: its gross margin fell about 2.7 percentage points through the 2021-22 inflation, from 57.0% to 54.3%. The transcript explains why, and it is structural rather than a management failing - INPEX has no pricing power of its own. On 2026-08-07 management stated that roughly 70% of net profit comes from Ichthys and that "LNG price is 5 or 6 months behind" the oil market, so its selling price is indexed to a commodity with a lag rather than set by the company; on the cost side the chief executive said energy security "doesn't come for free" and that "over the medium to long term, overall energy cost could potentially increase." An indexed selling price is a partial inflation hedge, but a rising cost base with no pricing authority is not. This is context only and moves nothing in the decision above.

Equinor pays USD 9.3B of Norwegian tax in Q4 2026 and expects H1 2027 tax to be higher still, so reported cash flow and the net debt ratio deteriorate just as prices fall. The 2027 buyback becomes quarterly and price-linked from February 2027 and would shrink toward USD 2B a year. None of this threatens solvency (cash USD 24B, Altman Z about 3.0, Piotroski 8 of 9); it threatens the share price.
picks.positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling pressure tied to the company itself: the dividend is growing, not being cut, and the Norwegian state holds about two-thirds of the shares as a permanent owner. The path to our NOK 290 level is a sector-wide sell-off in oil and gas producers as momentum and commodity-linked money exits the energy trade on a Hormuz settlement and a normalising crude price. The shares traded at NOK 226-300 for much of the past year at USD 60-75 Brent, so the level is reachable on the factor alone.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near NOK 290, which a sector-wide sell-off in oil and gas producers as crude normalises could deliver. Nothing dated since our 2026-10-26 look changes that answer. The thesis holds: the Q3 2026 results on 2026-10-28 confirmed a well-run, near-net-cash producer, with production guidance raised to about 4%, a higher dividend and a credible 2027 capital-return framework. But at NOK 427.90 (2026-11-02, Oslo listing) the shares still sit about 22% above our NOK 350 fair value by the parts, because the market is paying for Brent above USD 100 that is already slipping (down about 8% today on a Hormuz reopening plan). Norway's 78% petroleum tax means most of the windfall goes to the state, and fiscal 2025 shows what normal prices earn. At NOK 290 the shares would sit about 21% below fair value, enough to clear our 20% entry bar in today's reflation backdrop, with a downside case near NOK 230 if Brent returns to the low 60s. Conviction stays low (2): this is a good business at the wrong price, and its share price hinges on one shared macro driver, oil and the Hormuz binary, that the rest of the book is already exposed to. The value case alone is weak at this price for the same reason; it would strengthen materially near our level.
picks.forcing_function: No company event forces a re-rating up from here. The scheduled dates are Q4 2026 results and the first quarterly buyback tranche for 2027 in early February 2027, and the Q3 dividend ex-date of 2027-02-15. picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Equinor ASA (EQNR.OL) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 2026-11-02. Quarters covered: Q2 2025 (call 2025-07-23), Q3 2025 (2025-10-29), Q4/FY 2025 (2026-02-04), Q2 2026 (2026-07-22), Q3 2026 (2026-10-28). Prices in Norwegian kroner (NOK) on the Oslo listing; Equinor reports in US dollars.*

**Bottom line:** Equinor is a disciplined, well-run producer whose management has delivered what it promised on production, costs and capital returns for five straight quarters. The numbers that look terrible in the annual history (earnings per share down 32% in fiscal 2025, a 3-year EPS decline of about 40% a year) are the tail of the 2022 gas-price windfall unwinding, not a broken business; the trailing-twelve-month (TTM) figures to 2026-09-30 have already swung back up (TTM EPS 4.81, TTM free cash flow about USD 11.2B) because Brent crude ran from about USD 72 in June to USD 113-117 in late October. The credibility question is therefore not management; it is the commodity price the market is capitalising.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Mid-2025 (Q2 2025):** the story was "control what we can control" in a weak price tape — flat costs, firm capital spending, Johan Castberg (a large new Barents Sea oil field) reaching 220,000 barrels a day in under three months, and a USD 955M write-down on US offshore wind (Empire Wind and the South Brooklyn terminal) after US policy turned against the industry.
- **Late 2025 to early 2026:** portfolio pruning (Peregrino in Brazil sold for USD 3.5B; Nigeria, Azerbaijan, Argentina exits), the growth story shifted to US onshore gas and Brazil (Bacalhau), and renewables were quietly shrunk to a smaller, project-financed book.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-28):** the tone is now a windfall quarter — adjusted operating income of USD 12.35B before tax, "almost twice the level from the same quarter last year", production guidance raised from about 3% to about 4% growth, record refining at Mongstad, and a new capital-return framework for 2027 (dividend growth above 5% a year plus USD 2-4B of buybacks at USD 60-80 oil). New growth avenues appear: a stake in the Lackawanna gas power plant in Pennsylvania (selling power to the data-centre build-out), Namibia entry, Bay du Nord in Canada with Shell as partner.
- **What was dropped:** the old "renewables as a growth pillar" language. What was added: gas-to-power in the US and a cautious, non-linear stance on buybacks above USD 80 oil.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| ~4% production growth in 2025, ~4% again 2026 | Q3 2026: "year to date ... almost 5%", guidance raised to ~4% | Matches |
| Flat / falling unit costs | Q3 2026: 10% underlying cost cut "somewhat behind" on FX and energy costs | Mostly matches, slipping at the margin |
| Strong balance sheet | Cash USD 24B; net debt ratio 3.8% at Q3 2026; recomputed net debt USD 5.67B incl. leases (ex-lease about 1.4B) | Matches — but management itself warns the year-end ratio is "somewhat above 10%" once the six-month Norwegian tax lag is adjusted for |
| Capital distribution of ~USD 9B in 2025, buybacks raised to USD 3B in 2026 | Dividends 0.37 then 0.39 per share per quarter; four buyback tranches | Matches |
| Earnings power | Fiscal 2025 EPS 2.0 (down 32%), net margin 4.8%, FCF margin 5.6%; TTM EPS 4.81 | The recovery is price-driven, not structural |
| Offshore wind "double-digit equity returns" | USD 955M impairment Q2 2025; Empire Wind first power slipped to H1 2027 | Weaker than claimed |

The scan's "Graham" and "Buffett" fair values (NOK 103) are artefacts of the depressed fiscal-2025 earnings; the cash-flow models sit near the price (DCF +11%, owner earnings +6%). EPS beat rate is only 2 of 7 quarters (29%), but that reflects commodity noise around consensus more than over-promising.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable.** Q2 2025 was defensive ("we continue to focus on what we are able to control"). Q3 2026 is confident but deliberately restrained: "while commodity prices are cyclical, it is important to focus on what we can control", and on buybacks above the band, "you should not expect a linear relationship ... we want to avoid being too cyclical". The CFO is using the windfall to build the balance sheet rather than to promise more — a sober signal.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** Production guidance has been met or raised every year in the window; the capital-spending guide (about USD 13B organic for 2026) is held; distributions were delivered exactly as set out at the February capital markets update. The one repeated miss is offshore wind timing and value (Empire Wind impairment, first power pushed into 2027).

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Buybacks above USD 80 oil** (BNP, Barclays, Q3 2026): management refused to give a formula — upside to distributions in a spike is discretionary, not contractual.
- **Johan Sverdrup decline** (ABG, 2025): the giant field "will come off plateau"; no date given.
- **US gas-to-power strategy** (ABG, Q3 2026): an analyst said he "struggles to give investors a good answer" on why Equinor should own Pennsylvania power plants — a capital-allocation question that remains open.
- **Safety** (Barclays, Q3 2026): incident frequency has ticked up this year.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: six-month Norwegian tax lag means Q4 2026 and H1 2027 carry heavy tax cash outflows (USD 9.3B expected in Q4 2026 alone) — the headline balance sheet flatters.
- Red: board member Hilde Møllerstad sold 1,662 shares at NOK 442.50 on 2026-10-28 (small, but a sale at the top).
- Red: offshore wind write-downs (Q2 2025) and a 2027 slip at Empire Wind (Q3 2026).
- Red: diversification into US power (Lackawanna) at a cyclical high.
- Green: production delivery and the fast Castberg and Bacalhau ramp-ups.
- Green: dividend growth above 5% a year formally committed (Q3 2026).
- Green: exploration collaboration with Aker BP and Vår Energi (2026-10-26) supports the Norwegian shelf to 2035.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The language shifted from "renewables" to "power" and "the intersection between the gas markets and the power markets" — Equinor is repositioning from transition spending toward monetising its gas. The new quarterly buyback framing (no annual number) makes distributions explicitly price-linked; in a falling oil tape the buyback will shrink mechanically toward USD 2B a year.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: stable.** The business is executing well; the single most important thing to weigh is that the share price (NOK 427.90 on 2026-11-02, after hitting NOK 454.60) capitalises an oil price that already fell about 8% in a day on a Hormuz reopening plan. On mid-cycle prices (Brent about USD 75, European gas about USD 10/MMBtu) our fair value is near NOK 350.

**Moat:** narrow — a regulatory-licence and scale-cost position on the Norwegian shelf (low break-even, pipeline access to European gas buyers), with ROIC around 10.7% that is cyclical rather than structurally eroding. **Secular threat:** manageable — the energy transition caps long-term terminal growth, but long-term gas contracts with the UK and Germany and production held to 2035 make the shrinkage slow; cheapness here would be cyclical, not a value trap. The current price is not cheap.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: SoftwareOne is a repaired business still priced as a broken one, and since August each repair claim has been checked by a later dated number. It resells software licences and cloud capacity - mostly Microsoft, increasingly Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google - to about 70,000 customers and wraps advice and managed services around them. It merged with Crayon on 1 July 2025. The evidence: like-for-like growth (the merged firm compared with what the two firms did separately a year earlier) went from 1.4% in 2025 to 11.6% in the first half of 2026 and 10.3% over the first nine months; the adjusted EBITDA margin (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, before one-off costs) rose from 20.9% in 2025 to 23.7% over nine months, and management raised full-year guidance to above 24% on 2026-11-11. All CHF 100m of merger savings were delivered by mid-2026, six months early, with a further CHF 5-10m due by year-end; integration costs were guided down to CHF 75-85m from CHF 80-100m. North America, down 12.6% in 2025, has grown three quarters running. The direct business returned to growth (+2.9% in Q3 2026) as promised on 2026-08-26, and the margin guide was raised after Microsoft's October partner-margin cut took effect, which supports management's 'no material impact' claim. Cash is real on the company's basis: about CHF 200m of free cash flow over the twelve months to June 2026 (operating cash flow CHF 271.6m less CHF 71.9m of capital spending), a 69% conversion of reported EBITDA. At CHF 8.78 the equity is worth about CHF 1.89bn; adding net debt of CHF 408-483m gives an enterprise value of about CHF 2.3-2.4bn, roughly 6 times 2026 adjusted EBITDA of about CHF 400m and under 10 times trailing free cash flow. Listed reseller peers traded at 9-14 times EBITDA in our September 2026 live pull. Two further supports: Microsoft's push to move large customers from enterprise agreements to its cloud-subscription programme, which management says could bring 2-3 times 2026's conversion volumes in 2027-28 (2026-11-11), and AI-vendor diversification (OpenAI select partner, October 2026; Anthropic select partner tier, 2026-11-09). Conditions that must hold: the margin stays at or above 24% through 2027, cash conversion stays near 60% as capital spending rises, and Microsoft does not cut partner economics materially again.
picks.bear_thesis: The discount is real, but part of it is the price of three risks that have not gone away. First, Microsoft dependence. The direct business - about 40% of revenue and the largest profit pool, at a roughly 51% line-level margin - grows 2-3% and its economics are set by Microsoft's incentive programme, which Microsoft re-cuts every fiscal year. The October 2026 cut looks absorbed for now; the 2027 framework rewards fast-growing partners, and a firm growing direct at 2% is not obviously one of them. Second, the growth engine is slowing. Like-for-like growth fell from 11.6% in the first half to 7.4% in Q3 2026 as the early-renewal boost (about 4 points, per management on 2026-08-26) unwound. The channel arm, sold in August as 'a very scalable business model' after +35.6%, grew only 7.3% in Q3 on CHF 34.6m of revenue, and management did not explain why. The part of the business that deserved a premium multiple is smaller than our first model assumed and is decelerating. Third, cash. Capital spending roughly doubles to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28 for AI and automation, to be funded 'from the release of net working capital'. In a business carrying about CHF 4.5bn of pass-through receivables against a similar amount of payables, that is partly a decision about when suppliers get paid, not new cash. Free cash flow of about CHF 200m could fall toward CHF 120-150m in the investment years. Net debt rose from CHF 369m at December 2025 to CHF 408m at June 2026 on a floating-rate CHF 550m term loan and CHF 200m of revolver drawings, in a credit market whose risk spreads are wide. Underneath, the services arm (about half of revenue at an 8.5% margin) sells skilled labour, and AI tools are compressing the price of that labour. It is growing 11% today, so this is a material long-run threat rather than a present one. What would confirm the bear case: full-year 2026 results (around end-March 2027) showing free cash flow below CHF 150m, a 2026 margin below 24%, or direct falling again in 2027 as Microsoft's new framework lands.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market: the shares trade as if the post-merger recovery were unproven and the cash were mostly accounting. Both claims are weaker than the price implies. Since August the company has published three sets of checkable numbers, and each confirmed the recovery: growth, margin, savings, North America, the direct business returning to growth, and margin guidance raised after Microsoft's October cut took effect. The market has not paid for the November confirmation: the shares were CHF 8.72 the day before this review and CHF 8.78 today, below the CHF 9.11 fifty-day average. No dated analyst price targets were found for this listing in FMP; this committee's earlier review recorded consensus 2027 earnings per share of about CHF 0.85 and EBITDA estimates of about CHF 289m - a 16.6% margin against a company guiding above 24%. If those EBITDA figures are still in the models, the street is either using stale pre-merger assumptions or refusing to capitalise the adjusted measure. We sit in between: we do not capitalise adjusted EBITDA at peer multiples, because after interest, tax and doubled capital spending only about 40% of it reaches shareholders. But even on that cash anchor, about CHF 165m of normalised free cash flow at a 6.35% yield, the equity is worth about CHF 12 a share - about 37% above today's price. Where the market may be right: the channel slowdown in Q3 and the unproven 'cash-neutral' funding of the 2027-28 investment programme.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) runs to the full-year 2026 results, due around the end of March 2027. Q4 2026 is the largest quarter and faces a tough comparison (Q4 2025 grew 11%), while the early-renewal boost from Microsoft's July price rise has already unwound; reported growth could print at the low end of the mid-to-high single-digit guide. Microsoft's 2027 incentive framework (its fiscal year starts in July) rewards fast-growing partners; a direct business growing 2-3% could lose more margin than the October cut cost. Cash is the pinch point rather than profit: capital spending steps up to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28, and if the promised working-capital release does not materialise, free cash flow falls and net debt (CHF 408m at June 2026, floating rate) stops declining while credit markets remain stressed. There is no liquidation event or near maturity wall in the materials: the bridge loan was repaid in January 2026, and gross debt is a CHF 550m term loan plus CHF 200m of revolver drawings at about 1.1 times leverage.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure in this name has largely run its course. The July 2025 merger issued about 65m shares to Crayon holders - largely Norwegian institutions and index funds who owned a Norwegian small-cap and inherited a Swiss mid-cap. The lock-up (the window insiders are barred from selling) lapsed long ago, and the slide to CHF 5.83 in early 2026 is consistent with that supply being absorbed. The dividend per share was roughly halved after the merger (about 15 centimes for the first half of 2026 against about 30 a year earlier), which pushed out income-focused holders; that repricing is behind the stock. What remains is momentum and factor flow: the shares have fallen from CHF 9.595 on 2026-10-26 to CHF 8.78 on normal volume (about 503,000 shares today) with no company news. That is why we no longer wait for CHF 8.00: the named source of forced selling has already sold, and the recent drift is not a seller we can predict.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Buy now. The thesis holds, and the 2026-11-11 third-quarter update answered the two questions our price-wait was protecting against. Microsoft's 5% cut to partner margins on its core office products took effect on 1 October; six weeks later management raised full-year margin guidance to above 24%, not down. The direct business, which fell 1.8% in the second quarter, grew 2.9% in the third, as promised in August. Meanwhile the price fell from CHF 9.595 to CHF 8.78 with no company-specific news. Our CHF 8.00 buying level assumed forced selling by holders who must sell regardless of value - the inherited Crayon shareholder base - and our own analysis already judged that selling largely done. On the cash anchor, the base-case fair value of CHF 12.02 sits about 37% above today's price, comfortably clear of the 20% discount we require in the current growth-up, inflation-sticky backdrop. The adverse case of CHF 7.60 is about 13% below. The new revenue split published on 11 November cut our adverse case from CHF 7.85, because the channel arm is smaller and slower than we had inferred. Conviction stays at 4 rather than 5 for three reasons. Durability depends on Microsoft, which re-cuts partner economics every year. Channel growth slowed from 35.6% to 7.3% in a single quarter, unexplained. And the 2027-28 doubling of capital spending has to be funded by a working-capital release that has not yet been shown. Debt markets are under strain, and SoftwareOne's debt is floating-rate, so the macro backdrop is a mild headwind. That is context, not a reason to wait. What would change our mind: full-year 2026 free cash flow below about CHF 150m, a 2026 margin below 24%, or a 2027 Microsoft framework that pushes direct back into decline.
picks.forcing_function: There is no hard-dated event that forces a re-rating. The merger-savings catalyst already happened (2026-08-26). What remains is a series of dated checkpoints: the full-year 2026 results around the end of March 2027 (the first full year with the Microsoft cut in force; full-year free cash flow and the 2027 guide); the first details of Microsoft's 2027 partner incentive framework, normally published ahead of its July fiscal year; the first-half 2027 results around late August 2027, the first look at the capital-spending step-up and whether it is cash-neutral. A residual, unhandicapped possibility: a business with about CHF 400m of adjusted EBITDA and a market value under CHF 2bn could attract a strategic or private-equity bid. We assign it no value.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# SoftwareOne Holding (SWON.SW) - a deep dive on management and the setup

Prepared 2026-11-16. Sources: the full-year 2025 results call (2026-03-31), the first-half 2026 results call (2026-08-26), the third-quarter 2026 trading update (released 2026-11-11), the screener's financial block and a live SIX quote of CHF 8.78 (2026-11-16). All figures are in Swiss francs (CHF) on the Zurich listing.

SoftwareOne resells software licences and cloud capacity - mostly Microsoft, increasingly Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google and others - to about 70,000 corporate and public-sector customers, and wraps advice and managed services around those sales. It merged with Crayon, a Norwegian competitor, on 1 July 2025, which raised the share count from roughly 152 million to roughly 215 million.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **March 2026 (full-year 2025): "we returned to growth".** The story was repair. Like-for-like growth (the merged company compared with what the two firms did separately a year earlier) was only 1.4% for 2025, but Q4 2025 reached 11%. Management leaned on three promises: North America (down 12.6% in 2025) would return to growth in 2026, Microsoft's enterprise-agreement incentive cuts were behind them ("we do not see any headwinds effect"), and synergies would reach CHF 80-100 million. Google Cloud global distribution (won February 2026) was introduced as the new growth lever for the channel arm (sales through 12,000 resellers).
- **August 2026 (first half 2026): "integration is now substantially completed".** The story moved from repair to delivery: 11.6% like-for-like growth, a 24.9% adjusted EBITDA margin (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, before one-off costs), CHF 100 million of run-rate synergies six months early, North America up 8.6%. A 2030 target of a 28%-plus margin appeared, with capital spending stepping up to about 8% of revenue in 2027-28 for AI and automation, "funded from the release of net working capital".
- **November 2026 (Q3 trading update): "solid", not "exceptional".** Growth slowed to 7.4% at constant currency, as flagged in August (about 4 points of first-half growth came from customers renewing early ahead of Microsoft's July price rise). The margin guide was raised from above 23% to above 24%. The language is noticeably calmer, and the channel arm, the star of the first half (+35.6%), grew only 7.3% in the quarter. A new theme appeared: Microsoft enterprise-agreement-to-cloud-subscription conversion volumes in 2027-28 "could be 2-3 times higher than in 2026".

The arc is consistent: each call narrows the claims to things that can be checked, and the next one checks them.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim (date) | What happened | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| North America returns to growth in 2026 (2026-03-31) | +8.6% in H1 2026, +5.5% in Q3, +7.6% over nine months (2026-11-11) | Delivered |
| Synergies CHF 80-100m (2026-03-31) | CHF 100m run-rate by H1 2026, a further CHF 5-10m by year-end; CHF 85m realised through the income statement since 2025 | Over-delivered |
| Adjustments below CHF 30m and narrowing (2026-03-31) | Adjustments fell from CHF 33m to CHF 18.4m (H1 2026); 9M reported EBITDA CHF 250.9m vs adjusted CHF 283.3m, a CHF 32m gap, mostly integration costs | Delivered |
| Integration costs CHF 80-100m (original) | Guided down to CHF 75-85m; CHF 56.3m spent by Q3 | Delivered |
| Direct business returns to growth in H2 2026 (2026-08-26) | Q3 direct +2.9% after Q2's -1.8% | Delivered, modestly |
| Microsoft's 5% partner-margin cut from October 2026 is "absolutely no material impact" (2026-08-26) | The cut took effect 1 October; six weeks later the margin guide was raised, not cut. Q3 adjusted margin 21.1%, up 2.1 points | Consistent so far; only the full year proves it |
| Cash conversion above 60% (repeated) | 69% over the twelve months to June 2026 (operating cash flow CHF 271.6m less CHF 71.9m capital spending, about CHF 200m) | Delivered on the company's basis |
| Channel is a "very scalable business model" (2026-08-26) | +35.6% in H1, then +7.3% in Q3 (CHF 34.6m); nine months +25.5%, CHF 111.4m | The first real wobble |

Where the screener's numbers diverge: the scan shows a net margin of 0.1%, return on equity of 1.8%, an Altman Z-score (a bankruptcy-risk score) of 0.5 and trailing free cash flow of CHF 585m. Most of this is noise. The 2025 net income of CHF 0.9m was struck after merger costs and purchase-price amortisation; H1 2026 alone earned CHF 54.3m. The Z-score is distorted by CHF 4.5bn of pass-through receivables against CHF 4.5bn of pass-through payables. The CHF 585m free cash flow is wrong: it captures year-end supplier-payment timing; the company figure is about CHF 200m. The live balance-sheet correction (net debt CHF 483m gross of other financial assets, CHF 408m as the company reports it, 30 June 2026) is right, and the scan's "net cash" never existed.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY - Rising, then steadying

- March 2026: cautiously confident, defensive on North America ("2025 was a disappointing year in North America").
- August 2026: the most assertive call - "I'm proud of our performance", "exceptional" growth in channel, "absolutely no material impact" from Microsoft.
- November 2026: "solid third quarter". The guidance raise is margin only; revenue growth guidance stays mid-to-high single digit. Confidence is now expressed through numbers rather than adjectives, which is healthier.

Specificity has risen across the three releases: synergy counts, integration-cost ranges and a cash-conversion target are all checkable.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY - High

Every dated operational commitment made in March 2026 was met or beaten by November. The screen's earnings-beat rate of 2 of 7 quarters reflects statutory earnings that were swamped by merger accounting, not missed operating guidance. One caution: a firm that guided a 23-25% range, then "above 23%", then "above 24%" may be managing expectations low (sandbagging), which helps credibility but means some of each beat was banked in advance.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Sustainability of first-half growth** (Kepler, 2026-08-26): management conceded about 4 points came from early renewals. Q3's 7.4% confirmed the slowdown.
- **Microsoft incentives** (UBS, both calls): asked twice; answered firmly. This is the single largest dependency and the one analysts keep returning to.
- **Capital spending** (Berenberg/Deutsche Bank): the 2027-28 step-up to about 8% of revenue is to be "cash neutral" through working-capital release. That is unproven and in a pass-through business is partly a choice about supplier timing.
- **Tax** (Zürcher Kantonalbank): a 42% statutory rate in H1 against a 20% cash rate; 30% guided for 2026.
- Not asked, and not answered: what drove the channel slowdown in Q3, and how much of the lower Q3 margin (21.1%) is seasonal mix.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- 🟢 Synergies over-delivered and early (2026-08-26), and integration costs guided down.
- 🟢 Adjusted-versus-reported gap narrowed as promised (CHF 33m to CHF 18.4m, H1 2026).
- 🟢 Margin guidance raised after the Microsoft margin cut took effect (2026-11-11).
- 🟢 North America and the direct business returned to growth as promised (H1 and Q3 2026).
- 🔴 Channel growth fell from 35.6% (H1) to 7.3% (Q3 2026) - the part of the business the bull case values at a premium.
- 🔴 Net debt rose from CHF 369m (December 2025) to CHF 408m (June 2026) despite the cash generation; the dividend per share was roughly halved after the merger.
- 🔴 Capital spending roughly doubles in 2027-28; free cash flow will fall unless working capital is released.
- 🔴 The H1 transcript contains a garbled sentence on adjustments ("CHF 60.9 million of the total of CHF 18.4 million"); we rely on the CHF 18.4m total, which reconciles with the reported-to-adjusted gap.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The leadership shrank from co-chief operating officers (Raphael Erb and Melissa Mulholland, March 2026) to a single chief executive (Erb, August 2026); Mulholland has left. The new executive board adds regional heads and a channel/vendor leader. The voice is now more operational and less evangelical.
- "Conversion volumes in 2027 and 2028 could be 2-3 times higher than in 2026" (2026-11-11) quietly re-frames Microsoft's push of large customers from enterprise agreements to its cloud-subscription programme as a multi-year tailwind rather than a one-off - a claim worth testing in March 2027.
- AI vendor diversification is being built: OpenAI select partner (October 2026), Anthropic select partner tier (2026-11-09). Small today, but it reduces single-vendor dependence.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: strengthening.** The merger has been integrated on time and under budget, and the margin has risen about 4 points in a year.

The single most important thing to weigh: **how much of the adjusted profit reaches shareholders as cash once capital spending doubles in 2027-28.** At CHF 8.78 the company is valued at about CHF 1.89bn of equity plus CHF 0.4-0.5bn of net debt, roughly 6 times 2026 adjusted EBITDA of about CHF 400m and under 10 times trailing free cash flow of about CHF 200m. If cash conversion holds near 60% through the investment phase, that is cheap; if conversion falls toward 35-40%, it is roughly fair.

**Moat:** narrow - switching costs and scale in licence management (70,000 customers, Gartner and IDC leader in software asset management), and vendor authorisations (first global Google Cloud distributor). Returns are rising off a low base (ROIC about 11%) and margins are widening, so the trend is stable-to-improving, not eroding. **Secular threat: material, not terminal.** Two forces: Microsoft can and does re-cut partner economics at will, and AI-driven productivity deflates the price of the labour in the services arm (about half of revenue, 8.5% margin). Neither shrinks the base today: services grew 11.2% in Q3. The cheapness reads as a post-merger, leverage-and-noise discount rather than a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

Channel, about CHF 89m at 11 times: CHF 980m (a premium to the group for growth, trimmed from our earlier 12 times because Q3 growth slowed to 7.3%). picks.bull_thesis: New Corteva is the world's number four or five crop-protection maker and was spun off from its seed business (now Vylor) on 2026-10-01. It trades at about $9.08, an equity value of about $6.1B on 667.3M shares, and roughly 7x this year's guided trough EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization) of $1.10-1.125B once net debt, pension and minority interests are added. The core of the business is working. New-product volumes rose 20% in Q3 2026 at stable prices, Arylex and Pyraxalt (about $650M of combined sales) are each growing more than 20%, North America volume rose 19% and EMEA organic sales rose 14% (Q3 2026 call, 2026-11-12). About two-thirds of the portfolio is patented or otherwise differentiated, earning 10-15% higher margins, and management says nothing major loses patent protection before the end of 2028. The damage is concentrated in one place: Latin America organic sales fell 31%, which management attributes to Brazilian distributors working down inventory (its own product, sold in during 2025) while farmer applications held up. If that is a one-season destock, 2027 EBITDA should recover toward the roughly $1.3B base set out at the 2026-09-15 Investor Day, helped by more than $200M of net cost improvements planned for 2027-29 and a new CEO who says everything is on the table, including country and product exits. At 8-9.5x a recovered $1.25-1.45B, the shares are worth $12-17. The balance sheet is investment-grade-minded: net debt after the spin is roughly $0.7-1.0B, and the pension was largely funded during 2026 (the liability fell from $2.21B to $0.66B).
picks.bear_thesis: The guidance cut came only eight weeks after Investor Day, and management admitted that 'too much of the product we sold into the Brazil channel last year didn't go to ground.' Some 2025 sales, part of the base the 2029 targets build from, were pulled forward. The implied Q4 2026 EBITDA margin of about 7-9%, on high-single-digit price declines with flat volume, shows price erosion as well as a timing problem. Brazilian generic pricing from Chinese suppliers has been called temporary on every call since Q4 2025 and has not turned. Management said 'we've continued to see negative developments since then', so Q4 could miss again and the first 2027 guide could start near $1.0-1.1B. Cash is opaque: nine-month operating cash flow from continuing operations was -$1.24B, and the CFO deflected a direct question about roughly $800M of unexplained cash movement in Q3. Legacy DuPont-era PFAS ('forever chemical') liabilities stay with New Corteva through EIDP. They are shared and capped under the 2021 agreement with Chemours and DuPont, but they are a real tail, and state attorneys general tried to block the spin over them (2026-09-14). FMC, the closest US crop-protection peer, is down to about $5 with a market value of $0.65B after its own Brazil-driven miss, which shows how far this sector can de-rate. Returns on the remaining asset base are thin, with heavy goodwill. At 6.5x a stuck $1.0B EBITDA, less about $2.4B of debt, pension, minority-interest and legacy claims, the equity is worth about $6.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market. Street targets have collapsed from a one-year average of about $66.50 (combined company) to three targets in the last month averaging $13.33, with the newest at $13 and $11 (2026-11-13 and 2026-11-16). The market is now pricing New Corteva as though the Brazil damage is permanent and the business looks like FMC. Our view is narrower. The franchise outside Latin America is growing (new products +20%, North America volume +19%), and the balance sheet bears no resemblance to FMC's. But the street's 'temporary' framing of Brazil has been wrong on every call since Q4 2025, and management's own 2026-07-31 claim that the channel was 'not oversupplied' was contradicted three months later. We do not yet have the evidence to say the street is looking the wrong way. The disagreement is that the stock is cheap if, and only if, 2027 restarts from at least $1.2B of EBITDA.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead). Q4 2026 is guided to an EBITDA margin of about 7-9%, and management flagged continued deterioration in Brazil after the quarter ended, so another reset at the February print is possible. Brazilian farmers face high interest rates and El Nino weather, and Corteva's own barter and credit exposure in that market (near $1B of barter revenue disclosed in early 2026) carries collection risk. picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure. There was a mechanical seller at the spin: Corteva left the S&P 500 for the S&P MidCap 400 on 2026-10-01, which forced large-cap index funds out and brought mid-cap funds in. That rebalancing is complete. The 24% drop after 2026-11-11 was company news, not forced selling. Former holders of the combined company who wanted seed exposure may keep drifting out of the smaller crop-protection stub, and plaintiff-firm activity adds headline pressure, but neither is a level we can name with confidence.
