picks.interrogator_dossier:
# China Hongqiao Group (1378.HK) - Forensic Dossier

*Refreshed 26 October 2026 (continuing coverage from the 22 September 2026 dossier). Price used throughout: HK$19.50, the Hong Kong close on 26 October 2026 (previous close HK$19.02 on 23 October). Reporting currency is the Chinese yuan (RMB); per-share values are converted at roughly 1 RMB = 1.17 Hong Kong dollars.*

**Starting point: there are still no earnings calls to interrogate.** China Hongqiao reports twice a year and holds no English-language earnings call that our data vendor carries. Our paid data connector was not responding today and our web-search allowance was exhausted, so this refresh rests on the dated filings already verified on 22 September 2026, plus the live price tape fetched today. No new company filing, results release or management statement was found in the five weeks since. This dossier therefore tests the company's disclosed numbers and dated corporate actions, not a management script.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The five-year story is about the cost base, not growth.

- **2021-2022, the squeeze.** Revenue rose from RMB 114.5bn to RMB 131.7bn while net profit fell from RMB 16.1bn to RMB 8.7bn; gross margin dropped to 13.8% in 2022 as energy and alumina (the refined ore that is smelted into metal) costs spiked.
- **2023, the trough and the relocation.** Net profit RMB 11.5bn while a large block of smelting capacity moved from coal-fired Shandong to hydro-powered Yunnan.
- **2024-2025, the payoff.** Net profit RMB 22.4bn, then RMB 22.6bn; gross margin 26.8%, then 25.1%.
- **First half of 2026, the record.** Revenue RMB 87.5bn (up 8.0%), attributable net profit RMB 17.2bn (up 39.2%), pre-announced on 11 July 2026 and delivered exactly on 21 August 2026.

The narrative shift that matters: across ten months the group raised a lot of capital - a US$1.5bn Hong Kong placement (18 November 2025), an RMB 10.2bn convertible bond, which is a bond that can turn into shares (8 May 2026), and an RMB 12bn private placement at its listed A-share unit (31 July 2026) earmarked for wind, solar and downstream processing - and a subsidiary bought a related-party new-energy business for RMB 240m (11 September 2026). The pitch is moving from "lowest-cost smelter" towards "integrated aluminium and renewables group".

Since 22 September the only new information is the price: the shares slid from HK$21.36 (13 October) to HK$18.02 (22 October) before bouncing to HK$19.50 today. A headline on 24 October pointed to strong results at a listed subsidiary; we could not verify its figures and do not use them.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim in the screener inputs | What the filings show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Trailing diluted earnings per share RMB 5.44 | The vendor treats half-year reports as quarters: 1.39 + 1.31 + 1.07 + 1.67 = 5.44 is two full years. True trailing figure is about RMB 2.74 diluted (HK$3.2), so about 6 times earnings at HK$19.50. | Fails - data artifact |
| Trailing free cash flow RMB 59.4bn (this bundle) | Same half-year summing problem; the best sourced annual figure is RMB 27.8bn for 2025. The 5.5 times price-to-cash-flow screen figure is too flattering by roughly half. | Fails - data artifact |
| Latest-quarter earnings up 72% | Correct comparison is first half 2026 versus first half 2025: earnings per share up about 32%, net profit up 39.2%. | Overstated |
| Model discounts (cash-flow model +52%, Graham +83%) | Fed by the doubled earnings and cash-flow inputs. | Fails - inherits the artifact |
| Margins expanding | Gross margin 13.8% (2022) to 25.1% (2025) to about 28% trailing; first-half 2026 gross margin 30.9%. | Holds |
| Net debt about RMB 0.4bn | Holds only if RMB 8.9bn of short-term investments are counted as cash. On cash and equivalents alone (RMB 48.9bn) against borrowings and leases (RMB 58.2bn), net debt is RMB 9.3bn. Either way a sharp improvement from RMB 27.8bn a year earlier. We use the stricter RMB 9.3bn. | Holds, definition-dependent |
| Insider buy ratio zero | The company repurchased RMB 5.1bn of shares in 2025 but issued RMB 10.5bn of new stock the same year. | Net issuer |

The headline finding is unchanged: the deep-value flag rests on a trailing earnings figure double the real one. The balance-sheet improvement is real.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Stable. With no calls, tone is read through disclosure. The 11 July 2026 profit alert was specific (an expected rise of about 39%) and was matched exactly on 21 August. Dividend policy speaks confidence: the 2025 final dividend of HK$1.65 was up 62% and paid 12 June 2026 at about a 53% payout. The language around new capital has moved from defending the core (cost, relocation) to expanding into renewables and downstream - offensive, not defensive.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Medium-to-high on what is guided, which is little. The company gives profit alerts, not forward guidance, and the 2026 alert was precise. The screener's "beat 5 of 7 quarters" is built on the same mislabelled half-year periods and should not be read as a quarterly track record. Score: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- Capital raising while the core business throws off cash: why issue shares, a convertible and a subsidiary placement in a record year?
- Related-party transactions with the founding family's wider group (the September 2026 Weiqiao Xinchuang purchase is small but sets a pattern).
- Carbon cost on the remaining coal-fired Shandong capacity now that aluminium sits inside China's national carbon market (from September 2026): no disclosed cost per tonne yet.
- Sell-side targets: on 22 September the published consensus was about HK$36, roughly 85% above today's price, and we found no evidence it has been cut. A consensus that has not followed a 53% fall from the HK$41.36 high is a pressure point in itself.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: net issuance of shares in 2025 despite buybacks; the RMB 10.2bn convertible (8 May 2026) adds about 390m potential shares and caps any rally near HK$28-29 where it converts.
- Red: rising related-party and diversification activity (31 July and 11 September 2026).
- Red: the screener's core valuation inputs are double-counted.
- Red: margins were squeezed in the last inflation shock (gross margin 19.6% in 2019 to 13.8% in 2022).
- Green: record first half 2026, delivered exactly as pre-announced (21 August 2026).
- Green: net debt down by RMB 18-27bn in twelve months; short-term borrowings down from RMB 49.7bn to RMB 16.0bn.
- Green: the 45Mt national smelting cap makes an existing licence scarce.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The recent price action is sector-wide, not company-specific. Over 13-15 October 2026 Hongqiao fell 8.7% (HK$21.36 to HK$19.51) while Aluminum Corporation of China fell 7.6% (HK$7.77 to HK$7.18) on the same days, and both bottomed on 22 October and bounced on 23 October. Aluminium futures still trade near US$3,120 per tonne (COMEX, 26 October), elevated against the long-run average. The selling looks like a de-rating of Chinese aluminium as a group, not news about Hongqiao.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: pivoting - from a pure low-cost smelter to a group spending its windfall on renewables and downstream processing, partly funded with new shares.

The single most important thing to weigh: the earnings you are paying about 6 times for are at a cyclical high, and the screener's cheaper-looking numbers are a data error. At HK$19.50 the shares sit at our base-case fair value, not below it.

Moat: narrow and stable. It is a scale-cost advantage (captive bauxite and alumina, hydropower in Yunnan) plus a scarce regulatory licence, in an undifferentiated commodity sold at a world price. Return on invested capital of 9.8% on the last full year is respectable, not wide-moat territory, and the recent margin gain is cycle-driven.

Secular threat: manageable. Aluminium demand benefits from electrification, but the remaining coal-fired capacity now carries a rising carbon cost. The relocation to hydropower has already de-risked most of it. The cheapness is neither a clear mispricing nor a value trap: a good cyclical business priced about where it should be on peak earnings.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Develia S.A. (DVL.WA): a deep dive on management and the setup (2026-10-26)

**Source note.** FMP has no earnings-call transcript for this Warsaw listing, and this run's web-search budget was used up, so this dossier rests on three things: FMP's quarterly statements (through 2026-06-30), Develia's investor-relations page, and dated headlines on Bankier.pl. No management quotes appear below because none were sourced. All figures are in Polish zloty (PLN). The live price is PLN 8.27 (FMP quote, 2026-10-26, Warsaw Stock Exchange).

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
Develia, the former LC Corp, is one of Poland's largest listed homebuilders. It sells apartments off-plan in Warsaw, Kraków, Wrocław, Gdańsk and Katowice, and it books revenue only when it hands a finished unit to the buyer. Over 2021-2025 the story was simple volume growth. Revenue rose from about PLN 0.91B to PLN 2.08B, and net income rose from PLN 154M to PLN 443M. Part of that came from the purchase of Nexity's Polish business. Steadily larger dividends followed: PLN 0.45 (2022), 0.40 (2023), 0.50 (2024), 0.58 (2025) and 0.73 per share, which was paid on 2026-09-30.

The 2026 story is a handover year. By 2026-09-30 the company had handed over 3,406 units in nine months, against 1,963 a year earlier (Bankier, 2026-10-08). Presales (signed off-plan contracts that become revenue later) were 2,706, against 2,500. The board targets 3,750-3,950 handovers for 2026 (Bankier, 2026-06-15, board member Karol Dziecioł). The same report flagged cost pressure from oil-based materials, the first defensive note in the dated record.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim / storyline | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| A record handover year | 9M handovers 3,406 vs 1,963; H1 2026 revenue PLN 1.89B vs PLN 0.75B | Matches |
| Profit growth | Q2 2026 net income PLN 142M vs PLN 108M (Bankier 2026-09-11, in line with consensus); TTM EPS 1.27 | Matches |
| Margins holding | Gross margin 31% in Q1, 24% in Q2, 39% in Q3 2025, 31% in Q4 2025 | Lumpy; Q2 2026 is the weakest print, an early sign of the cost squeeze or of mix |
| Demand intact | Q3 2026 presales about 954 (by subtraction) vs about 801 in Q3 2025 | Matches, about +19% |
| Continued land buying | Kraków land for about 97 units (2026-10-16); Warsaw JV land, PLN 121.3M net, about 539 units, sales from Q1 2027 (2026-10-13) | Restocking continues; supports 2027-28 volume |
| Generous payouts | PLN 0.73 per share dividend (about PLN 340M) paid 2026-09-30 | Paid; cash at 2026-06-30 (PLN 942M) was before the payout |

The forensic gap: 2026 earnings are front-loaded. Hitting the handover target needs only about 350-550 more units in Q4 2026, against 834 in Q3. So the second half will earn less than the first, and the trailing EPS of 1.27 overstates run-rate earnings power. My estimate for full-year 2026 EPS is about 1.10-1.20.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Stable. The handover target is specific and on track. The June remark on oil-linked costs is the only shift toward defensive language. Without transcripts, finer tone shifts cannot be assessed.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Medium-High. The 2026 handover target looks achievable (91% of the low end was reached by September). The Q2 profit landed in line with consensus. Dividends have risen four years in a row. There is no evidence of misses, but the record is short and not transcript-verified.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
Coverage is thin: two hold-equivalent ratings and one buy over 12 months (Bankier). Trigon DM cut its rating to hold on 2026-04-20 but raised its target to PLN 11.5 from 10. The likely pressure points are the margin path under cost inflation, whether 2027 handovers can follow a record 2026, and Polish mortgage affordability.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red: gross margin fell to 24% in Q2 2026, from 31% in Q1.
- Red: management flagged oil-linked cost pressure (2026-06-15).
- Red: the stock is in the lower quarter of its 52-week range (PLN 7.65-11.20) and about 17% below its 200-day average, despite in-line results. Part of the fall is the PLN 0.73 dividend going ex in late September.
- Red: inflation history shows this business is exposed. Gross margin fell from 39.1% (2019) to 30.8% (2021).
- Green: presales up about 8% over nine months and about 19% in Q3; land restocking in Warsaw and Kraków.
- Green: TTM free cash flow of about PLN 347M (roughly 11x price to free cash flow) and an 8.8% trailing dividend yield.
- Green: modest leverage. Net debt including leases is about PLN 147M at 2026-06-30, or roughly PLN 490M (about PLN 1.06 per share) after the September dividend.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
In October 2026 managers subscribed for series L incentive shares and traded shares (ESPI filings, 2026-10-12). The direction and size were not verified, so this is neutral. The internal merger of LC Corp entities (plan dated 2026-08-31) is housekeeping.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: stable. Develia is a well-run, cash-returning cyclical developer earning about 18% on equity, with roughly 10% return on invested capital. Its 2026 earnings are a handover peak. The single most important thing to weigh is the multiple on normalized earnings (about PLN 1.0-1.15 per share), not on the TTM 1.27. On that basis the stock trades at about 7-8x earnings, cheap but not dramatically so for a Polish developer.

Moat: narrow. Scale in land banks and brand in five big-city markets help, and returns are steady rather than falling. Homebuilding has low barriers, though, and margins swing with build costs. No structural force threatens terminal value. Poland's housing shortage is a support, and the risks are cyclical (rates, affordability, costs), not secular. The cheapness reflects a cyclical, front-loaded earnings year, not a shrinking base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.
picks.sop_breakdown: Base case: normalized EPS of about PLN 1.05 (2026E about 1.15 on front-loaded handovers; 2027E about 1.00-1.10 from the 2026 presales book) x 9x = about PLN 9.5. That is roughly 2.3x post-dividend book of PLN 4.15 at an 18% return on equity. The paid dividend is excluded. Net debt definition: borrowings plus leases minus cash, about PLN 490M after the September payout, which is embedded in earnings and book.
picks.sop_bull: Whole-company basis (no segment block; a residential developer is one business). Normalized EPS PLN 1.20 (2026-27 handovers near 3,800 a year, gross margin about 30%) x 10x = PLN 12.0 per share. Net debt of about PLN 1.06 per share (including leases, after the September dividend) is already inside an earnings-based multiple, so no overlay is added. The 2026 dividend has been paid and is not counted again. Cross-check: about 2.9x the post-dividend book of about PLN 4.15.

Trough EPS PLN 0.80 (handovers fall back toward 3,000 and gross margin compresses to about 25% under cost inflation) x 7x = PLN 5.6 per share, about 1.35x post-dividend book of PLN 4.15. Net debt (about PLN 490M including leases, after the PLN 340M dividend paid 2026-09-30) is already reflected in equity and earnings. There is no net-cash or deal overlay.

picks.catalyst_status_plain: already happened
picks.peer_comps_note: Peers: the listed Polish residential developers (Dom Development, Atal, Murapol, Archicom, Lokum, Ronson, Marvipol). The peer file gives no live anchor multiple, so none is quoted from memory. Its verdict is in line: modestly cheap on book and earnings, but the gap is explained by higher leverage and a land-heavy balance sheet. That is consistent with an in-line, not deeply discounted, position within a sector that moves together on Polish rates and mortgage affordability.
picks.thesis_evidence: The thesis holds. Nine-month 2026 presales of 2,706 (+8%) and handovers of 3,406 (+74%) were reported on 2026-10-08. Q2 2026 net profit was PLN 142M (+31%, in line), reported 2026-09-11. The 2026 handover target of 3,750-3,950 (2026-06-15) is 86-91% achieved, and land restocking continued on 2026-10-13 and 2026-10-16. The share price fall below the 200-day average reflects the dividend going ex (about PLN 0.73, late September 2026) and a sector-wide de-rating of Polish developers, not company-specific bad news.
picks.macro_fit_note: Reflation (growth up, CPI +3.7% y/y) with a debt cycle where positive real rates are being imposed: duration is punished and cash flow rewarded. Develia pays back in cash now (about 11x free cash flow, 8.8% yield), which suits that backdrop. But its margins were squeezed by the 2021-22 inflation (gross margin 39% to 31%), and firm real rates strain mortgage affordability, so the two effects roughly offset. Pass-through: no evidence that price increases are sticking. Management flagged oil-linked cost pressure on 2026-06-15, and Q2 2026 gross margin fell to 24% from 31%.
picks.entry_plain: buy near 7.9 PLN, which a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off could deliver

picks.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Genus is a royalty-led genetics franchise that has just proved it can compound profit through a downturn, and that two options, China and the gene-edited pig, are worth far more than the market is paying for them.

The proof is in the fiscal 2026 numbers reported on 10 September 2026: adjusted profit before tax (the company's preferred profit measure, excluding one-off items) up 35% to 100.2 million pounds, adjusted earnings per share up 35% to 110.3 pence, free cash flow of 62 million pounds at 94% cash conversion, borrowings net of cash down to 0.4 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, return on adjusted invested capital up to 18.4% from 15.0%, a 10% dividend increase and the first share buyback in the company's history, 60 million pounds or roughly 4% of the shares, running through fiscal 2027. The porcine business (PIC) earns a 30.9% divisional margin, supplies roughly half of the United States market and 19 of the 20 largest producers, and is paid royalties per pig produced, so its genetic lead compounds each generation and cannot be bought off a shelf.

The options. The China pig business, now a 49% joint venture with a state-backed partner, grew royalty revenue 52% and market share from 3.4% to 5.4% in a year of falling Chinese pork prices, with a stated ambition of double-digit share. The gene-edited pig that resists porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, the most expensive disease in pork production, has cleared the United States, Canada, Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Uruguay, Peru and the Dominican Republic; first commercial negotiations in Peru are on terms management says match the prices shown at its 2022 capital markets day, and the Chinese disease-challenge studies are complete with a submission being assembled. The cattle business (ABS) has moved from losses toward a 7.5% margin with a double-digit ambition.

In the favourable case the market pays a premium franchise multiple for the porcine core, a growth multiple for China, credits the cattle margin plan and gives real value to the gene-edited pig, which together reach about 3,200 pence. Conditions: the North American disease season passes in the second half of fiscal 2027 as guided, a first gene-edited-pig contract is signed with disclosed terms, and China keeps taking share.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that this is a good business at a full price, which reached a deep-value screen only because of an accounting gain, entering a half-year management has already said will be weaker.

The statutory fiscal 2026 accounts show 285 million pounds of net income and 425 pence of earnings per share, inflated by a 204 million pound non-cash gain on deconsolidating China and a 12.8 million pound favourable swing on the accounting rule that marks live animals to fair value. The screener's 14,773-pence fair value and 5% margin of safety rest on that artefact and should be ignored. Management's own normalisation bridge on 10 September 2026 walks adjusted profit before tax from 100.2 million pounds down to 90.3 million, implying normalised earnings near 99 pence per share. At 2,410 pence the shares trade at about 24 times that, a full multiple for a business whose reported revenue has not grown for four years (658 million pounds in fiscal 2026 against 690 million in fiscal 2023).

Guidance for fiscal 2027 is only moderate growth, explicitly in line with consensus, and second-half weighted: the interim results due around February 2027 will show lower profit than a year earlier, because the comparison contains a 5.6 million pound partner milestone and a fully consolidated China. On top come a severe North American disease season cutting piglets born and therefore royalties, lower Brazilian breeding-stock sales, depressed dairy prices hurting sexed-semen volumes, and higher development spending. Free cash flow is guided lower because China's cash now arrives only as joint-venture dividends.

The gene-edited pig has slipped repeatedly (fiscal 2024, then fiscal 2025, then calendar 2025 for the United States), and no contract, volume or revenue is disclosed; Mexico, Japan and China carry no timeline. Strip it out, use conservative multiples on a flat-volume porcine core and today's cattle profit, and the parts are worth about 1,600 pence, a third below today's price. Confirmation would be a weak February 2027 interim with the disease headwind extending, or a further regulatory delay.
picks.consensus_delta: There is no disagreement with the market on the coming year to exploit: management guided fiscal 2027 adjusted profit before tax moderately higher in constant currency and said explicitly on 10 September 2026 that this is in line with consensus. Where we do disagree is on the denominator. Screens built on the statutory accounts see 425 pence of earnings, a 43% net margin and a fair value of 14,773 pence; all of it comes from a 204 million pound non-cash gain on deconsolidating China. The real earnings base is about 99 pence normalised. At 2,410 pence the shares price that correctly at about 24 times. The second point of disagreement, the durability of per-pig royalties through a disease season and a pork-price downturn, was a reason to like the shares at 2,142 pence; after a 12% rise with no new information the market has largely closed that gap.
picks.valley_of_death: No solvency risk: net borrowings are about 0.4 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation and the dividend is covered about four times. The risky window is the share price into the interim results due around February 2027, which management has guided will show lower profit than a year earlier (the comparison contains a 5.6 million pound partner milestone and a fully consolidated China), alongside a severe North American disease season cutting piglets born, lower Brazilian breeding-stock sales, depressed dairy prices hurting sexed-semen volumes and higher development and commercialisation spending. Free cash flow is guided lower as China's cash now arrives only as joint-venture dividends. A further delay on the gene-edited pig would add to the pressure.
picks.positioning_washout: Little forced-selling pressure is in prospect. There has been no dividend cut to drive out income holders, no index event or lock-up, and the company itself is a daily buyer through fiscal 2027 under its 60 million pound buyback, about 4% of the shares, which cushions any sell-off. The realistic route to our entry level is a wider de-rating of UK mid-cap and agricultural-input shares, or the market reacting to the headline profit fall in the February 2027 interim, rather than holders who must sell regardless of value.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Wait for a better price: we buy near 1,950 pence, which a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off in UK mid-caps and agricultural-input shares could deliver.

Nothing about the business has changed since our last look, and we keep the same answer. Genus remains a quietly excellent company: over three years management turned a cyclical, China-exposed livestock-genetics group into a higher-margin royalty business with a strong balance sheet, lifting group adjusted operating margin from 11.7% to 17.6% and return on adjusted invested capital to 18.4%, generating 62 million pounds of free cash flow, forming a growing China joint venture and launching the first buyback in its history. The thesis holds.

What has changed is the price, and it has moved against us. The shares are 2,410 pence on 9 November 2026, up about 12% from 2,142 pence on 22 September 2026, with no new company announcement in between. Our base-case fair value is about 2,400 pence after correcting the porcine profit we had overstated and the central costs we had overstated, so the shares now sit roughly at fair value: about 24 times normalised earnings of 99 pence, a full price for a business whose revenue has not grown in four years and whose next half-year will report lower profit by management's own guidance. The screener's 14,773-pence fair value is an artefact of a one-off accounting gain and should be ignored.

The gene-edited pig is a soft catalyst with no fixed date and no contractual payout; by this book's rules it is neither a plus nor a penalty, and we judge only the residual value case, which at today's price is nil. At 1,950 pence, near the low of the past twelve months (1,943 pence), the shares would be about 20 times normalised earnings with roughly 23% upside to fair value against about 18% downside to our adverse case of 1,600 pence. That level clears the 20% entry discount the current reflation backdrop requires. Two developments could justify paying more: a signed gene-edited-pig contract with disclosed terms, or an interim in February 2027 that confirms the North American disease headwind is passing with the full-year outlook intact. Note that the buyback is a daily buyer, so a clean move to our level may not come.

The moat is narrow and widening: the pig business is close to wide, with rising returns and margins, while the cattle business holds the group rating back. No secular force threatens the terminal value; the pressures are cyclical.
picks.forcing_function: There is no hard date that forces a re-rating. In order of importance: the mid-November 2026 annual-meeting trading update (customary, not yet published), which will say whether the first-half headwinds are tracking as guided; the fiscal 2027 interim results around February 2027; a first signed gene-edited-pig commercial contract with disclosed terms, which has no date; the Chinese regulatory submission for the gene-edited pig, also undated; and completion of the buyback in the second half of fiscal 2027.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier — Genus plc (GNS.L), London Stock Exchange

Prepared 9 November 2026 (continuing coverage; the forensic findings below were first set out on
22 September 2026 and re-checked today against the same transcript set). Sources: Genus earnings
presentations from September 2023 through September 2026 (the latest is the fiscal 2026 preliminary
results call of 10 September 2026), together with the audited trajectory from our own screener and
the company's reported statements.

Price used throughout this update: 2,410 pence per share (London listing, quoted in pence), the live
quote on 9 November 2026. Market value roughly £1.56 billion on about 64.5 million shares, a share
count already down from 66.1 million as the £60 million buyback announced on 10 September 2026
retires stock. The shares have risen about 12% from 2,142 pence on 22 September 2026, with no new
company announcement in between that we could find; the next scheduled update is the annual-meeting
trading statement, which Genus has historically issued in mid-November (19 November in 2025).

One correction carried forward from our own review: the porcine segment profit used in the
valuation is £89.2 million once the £5.6 million partner milestone and £4.7 million of one-off
production benefits (both disclosed as sitting inside the porcine division) are removed, not the
£99 million first written. Group central costs implied by the disclosed segment arithmetic are about
£18.2 million a year (130.8 porcine plus 22.9 cattle minus 135.5 group operating profit).

---

## 1. Narrative arc

**Where the story started (February 2024).** Genus was a company in trouble and saying so. The
opening headline was a 31% fall in adjusted profit before tax (the profit measure the company uses
to strip out one-off items) to £29.2 million on revenue down 5%. China was the villain in both
divisions. The chief executive listed four strategic priorities and the tone throughout was
defensive: cost savings, a research review that killed projects, a "value acceleration programme"
in the cattle business that was, at that moment, mostly a euphemism for £10 million of annualised
cuts. The gene-edited pig — a pig bred to resist porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, the
single most expensive disease in pork production — had just slipped from fiscal 2024 to fiscal 2025
approval, and management spent an uncomfortable stretch of the call explaining a data-hygiene
validation requirement the regulator "had not previously communicated."

**Where it is now (September 2026).** The same chief executive opened with "excellent results" and
had the numbers to support it: adjusted profit before tax up 35% to £100.2 million, free cash flow
of £62 million, borrowings net of cash down to 0.4 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation
and amortisation from 1.5 times, a 10% dividend increase and the company's first-ever share buyback
at £60 million. The pig-genetics joint venture in China was formed and the gene-edited pig had
cleared the United States regulator and four more Latin American and North American jurisdictions,
with the first commercial sales now being negotiated in Peru.

**What was quietly dropped, and what was added.** Two things disappeared from the script. First, the
new-royalty-customer count in China, which was the headline proof point in 2024 and 2025 ("13 new
royalty customers... this doubles PIC China's royalty customer base"), was explicitly retired in
September 2026: "we have previously communicated the number of new customers... reflecting on that,
[we] feel that the appropriate metrics are more market share, and royalty revenue growth." That is a
defensible change — and the replacement metrics are better and were disclosed — but it is still a
goalpost being moved, and the reader should know it happened. Second, the four strategic priorities
became three, with research spending folded into the other three rather than standing alone.

What was added is more important: a new metric called adjusted royalty revenue, which adds the
company's 49% share of joint-venture royalties to its own. It reached £197 million in fiscal 2026,
on a four-year compound growth rate of about 6%. This was introduced precisely because the China
joint venture removed a growing business from the consolidated accounts, and it is the single most
useful number the company now publishes.

**The through-line.** Across three years the story has moved from "we are defending a cyclical
business against China" to "we have converted the porcine business into a royalty annuity, fixed
the cattle business's cost base, monetised China at a good price, and now have surplus capital." The
narrative did not get louder; the numbers caught up with it.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Where | The actual numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "The royalty model is resilient through the pig cycle" | Repeated every call since Feb-2024 | Pork producers had their worst losses since 2008-10 in FY24, yet pig-division royalty revenue and profit still grew. In FY26, with Chinese pork prices falling all year, China royalty revenue grew 52% | Holds up. This is the strongest verified claim in the file |
| Value acceleration in cattle will deliver £20m of cumulative annualised benefit | Sep-2024 | Phases one and two delivered about £21m; phase three added £7m in-year and exited at a £9m annualised run rate. Cattle margin went from under 5% to 6.3% to 7.5% | Delivered, and slightly beaten |
| "Adjusted profit before tax and earnings per share both increased by 35%" | Sep-2026 | Correct as stated — but this is the point where the reader must be careful (see below) | True, and incomplete without the normalisation |
| Revenue growth | All calls | FY22 £593m, FY23 £690m, FY24 £669m, FY25 £673m, FY26 £658m. Revenue has gone nowhere for four years | The profit growth is entirely margin and mix, not volume-driven top-line. Management has never claimed otherwise, to their credit |
| "Return on invested capital improved materially" | Sep-2026 | Return on adjusted invested capital 18.4%, against a restated 15.0% the prior year, where the restatement removed biological-asset fair-value uplifts in joint ventures | Verified, and the restatement made the comparison harder on themselves, not easier |

**The single most important forensic point in this file.** Our screener shows fiscal 2026 net income
of £285 million, earnings per share of £4.25 (425 pence), a net profit margin of 43.4% and a
"Buffett fair value" of roughly 14,773 pence. Every one of those figures is an artefact. The
statutory accounts contain a £204 million non-cash gain on deconsolidating the China pig business
when it became a joint venture, plus a £12.8 million favourable swing on the accounting standard
that marks live animals to fair value. Strip those out and the company earned adjusted earnings per
share of 110.3 pence. Anyone valuing this share off the reported 425 pence — or off a 6% margin of
safety derived from a 14,773-pence fair value — is valuing a one-off accounting entry. That number
should be discarded entirely.

**The second most important point, and this one is to management's credit.** On the September 2026
call the chief financial officer walked the market through a normalisation bridge that most
management teams would have buried in an appendix. Reported adjusted profit before tax of £100.2
million becomes: minus £12.2 million (removing the China business's actual contribution), plus £7.5
million (adding back a full year at the ongoing 49% share), minus £5.6 million (a milestone payment
from the Chinese partner), plus £5.1 million (joint-venture proceeds and hedging), which gives a
pro-forma £95.0 million; then minus £4.7 million of one-off production benefits — £2.8 million of
favourable input costs and a £1.9 million farm sale — for a normalised base of **£90.3 million**.
Against a comparable £72.8 million the prior year, that is 24% growth rather than 35%.

This is unusually honest disclosure. It is also a downgrade: the true earnings power of this company
entering fiscal 2027 is roughly 10% below what the headline implies. Normalised earnings per share
is closer to 99 pence than 110 pence.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Rising, decisively — from a low base.**

- *February 2024 (defensive).* "It's a difficult environment for our customers who are suffering
  their worst losses since the financial crisis." Guidance was cut to "at least £58 million." The
  gene-edited pig timeline slipped and the explanation was technical and apologetic.
- *September 2024 (stabilising).* "We achieved considerable progress in structurally strengthening
  Genus, despite the challenging trading conditions." The word "despite" is doing heavy lifting.
- *February 2025 (offensive).* "PIC is stronger than ever. ABS has turned the corner... The high
  investment period is behind us and we've now passed the peak of exceptional cash outflows." That
  is the sentence where the tone flipped, and it was made by the then chief financial officer, not
  the chief executive — a finance person putting her name to a cash-flow inflection is a harder
  commitment than a chief executive's optimism.
- *September 2026 (confident but calibrated).* "Excellent results," followed immediately by a
  self-imposed downgrade of the earnings base and an outlook that concedes "cyclical weakness in a
  number of agricultural markets." When an analyst gently pushed — noting the market was "quite
  quick to pick up on the more negative aspects" of the outlook — the new chief financial officer
  did not reach for reassurance. He itemised the headwinds: North American disease pressure in the
  first half, Brazilian breeding-stock sales falling from an exceptional base, depressed dairy
  prices hurting sexed-semen volumes, higher product-development and gene-edited-pig spending.

Specificity has increased in both directions over the period, which is the pattern you want. In
2024 the company gave vague reassurance about China; in 2026 it gave market share (3.4% rising to
5.4%), royalty growth (52%) and joint-venture entity profit (£15.2 million) and then told you which
parts of the prior year would not repeat.

**One change of voice to note.** The chief financial officer changed between February 2025 (Alison
Henriksen) and September 2026 (Andy Russell). The normalisation bridge and the buyback discipline
both arrived with the new incumbent. When asked why the buyback was only £60 million — "a
relatively modest number in the grand scheme of things" — the answer was a straight capital-
allocation argument: net joint-venture proceeds were about £81 million, leverage should end fiscal
2027 near the bottom of the one-to-two-times target range, and the balance sheet should stay ready
for acquisitions. That is a better answer than a bigger buyback would have been.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: High, with one clearly identified exception.**

Trading guidance has been met or beaten every time it has been testable in this file:

- February 2024 guided fiscal 2024 adjusted profit before tax to "at least £58 million." The
  September 2024 call reported £59.8 million. Delivered, modestly beaten.
- September 2024 guided "solid profit growth from PIC and a return to profit growth for ABS" for
  fiscal 2025. The February 2025 interim delivered pig-division profit up 16% in constant currency
  and cattle-division profit up. Delivered.
- The cattle turnaround programme was quantified in advance (£20 million cumulative annualised over
  two years) and came in at about £21 million, with a third phase added on top. Delivered.
- Currency headwinds were pre-announced with numbers (roughly £6 million in February 2024, £8-9
  million in September 2024) rather than used later as an excuse. That is a small tell, and a good
  one.

**The exception is regulatory timing on the gene-edited pig, and it is a repeated miss.** In
February 2024 approval was expected in fiscal 2025, having just slipped from fiscal 2024. In
September 2024 it was calendar 2025. In February 2025 it was still calendar 2025. The approval did
eventually come, but commercialisation has landed years later than the original plan and is only now
beginning, in Peru rather than the United States. Management has been consistently candid that the
timing is not in their control — "in almost any country, it's been very difficult to predict the
timing... even [in the United States] it took probably years longer than we had expected" — but a
director must treat every future regulatory date from this company as indicative, not contractual.

The screener records a beat rate of one out of one quarters. That sample is too small to mean
anything; the four-call qualitative record above is the better evidence, and it is good.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**What analysts keep pushing on:**

1. *The quality of Brazilian and Chinese joint-venture profit.* Peel Hunt's first question in
   September 2026 went straight at it: both markets are facing weak pig prices after an exceptional
   year. Management conceded directly — "we are probably going to see lower growth in Brazil in
   fiscal 2027" — which is the honest answer but confirms that £19.1 million of the group's profit
   share came from a Brazilian business that had a 56% profit year on strong breeding-stock sales.
   Breeding-stock sales are the cyclical, low-quality part of this company's revenue mix.
2. *North American disease.* Pressed on what the bad porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome
   season means for fiscal 2027 royalties, the answer was specific and unflattering: fewer piglets
   born means fewer royalties, the effect bit in the second half of fiscal 2026, and recovery is
   only expected "in the second half of fiscal 2027." There is an irony here worth stating plainly —
   the disease the company's flagship product is designed to prevent is currently reducing its
   royalty income.
3. *Gene-edited pig timing in Mexico, Japan and China.* Asked every single call. Never answered with
   a date, and management explicitly refuses to give one. The September 2026 update on China was
   genuinely new and substantive — local disease-challenge studies completed successfully across
   multiple generations of pigs, dossier being assembled for submission, then an expert scientific
   panel, then a recommendation to the Ministry of Agriculture — but that is still three unbounded
   steps away from revenue.
4. *The path to a double-digit cattle margin.* Asked repeatedly. The answer is always "over the
   medium term... the next few years," never a year. Cattle margin is 7.5% today.

**What analysts are not pressing on, and should be.** Nobody asked what the 49% China joint venture
does to group earnings quality — specifically, that a fast-growing business is now equity-accounted
rather than consolidated, so its revenue and cash flow no longer appear in the group's own numbers
and its cash reaches Genus only as dividends. The chief financial officer himself flagged that
fiscal 2027 free cash flow will be lower than fiscal 2026 "principally due to the China joint
venture formation," but no analyst followed up on the magnitude.

**One topic where the earlier warning turned into the bad news.** In February 2025 an analyst asked
whether high beef prices were a downside risk to sexed-semen volumes. Management was relaxed. In
September 2026 the fiscal 2027 outlook names exactly that dynamic — "whilst beef prices remain high,
[that] dynamic has an impact on our Sexcel volumes [and] then impacts our margins" — as a first-half
headwind. The analyst was right and got there eighteen months early.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Reported earnings are unusable without adjustment.** A £204 million non-cash gain and a £12.8
million biological-asset swing make the statutory figures meaningless for valuation, and they are
what automated screens pick up.

🔴 **Revenue has not grown in four years** (£690 million in fiscal 2023 to £658 million in fiscal
2026, part of which is the China deconsolidation). All profit growth has come from margin, mix and
cost. That engine has finite runway.

🔴 **The fiscal 2027 earnings base is about 10% below the headline** (£90.3 million normalised
versus £100.2 million reported), and growth from there is only "moderate" and "in line with
consensus" — meaning there is no disclosed expectations gap to exploit.

🔴 **The first half of fiscal 2027 will report lower profit year on year**, by management's own
phasing guidance, because the comparative half contained a £5.6 million milestone and a fully
consolidated China business. Any investor buying before February 2027 should expect to read a
down-half.

🔴 **Regulatory timing on the gene-edited pig has slipped repeatedly** across three years, and
Mexico, Japan and China remain open-ended.

🔴 **A cattle-industry competitor merger is pending.** Management confirmed that two rivals — named
on the call as ST Genetics and Select Sires — have been trying to merge for about three years and
that there are "rumours out there that they might be able to navigate that." A completed merger
would create a larger competitor in the one business where Genus is already sub-scale on margin.

🟢 **The normalisation bridge is exemplary disclosure.** Management voluntarily reduced its own
headline by 10% and told the market to use the lower number.

🟢 **Return on invested capital is rising, not falling** — 18.4% against a restated 15.0% — and the
restatement was self-penalising. Rising returns on rising capital is the signature of a widening
competitive position, not an eroding one.

🟢 **The cash-flow inflection promised in February 2025 arrived.** Free cash flow went from £40.9
million to £62 million with 94% cash conversion, borrowings net of cash fell to £71.8 million and
leverage to 0.4 times.

🟢 **The China joint venture was struck at a good price and the business kept growing afterwards.**
Net proceeds of roughly £81 million, and the entity then grew royalty revenue 52%, volumes 71% and
profit 81%, lifting market share from 3.4% to 5.4% in the world's largest pork market — during a
year of falling Chinese pork prices.

🟢 **Capital discipline over gesture.** The first buyback in the company's history was sized at £60
million against £81 million of proceeds, explicitly to preserve acquisition capacity, and the
dividend payout ratio is a conservative 32% of adjusted earnings.

🟢 **The gene-edited pig cleared the United States regulator** and now has approvals or favourable
determinations in Colombia, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, the United States, Argentina, Canada,
Uruguay and Peru, with first commercial negotiations under way on terms management says are in line
with the prices set out at the 2022 capital markets day.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The metric substitution in China.** Retiring the customer-count disclosure in favour of market
share and royalty growth is, on the evidence, an upgrade — but note the reasoning given: "winning a
customer could mean you win 2% of their market share or it could mean you win 100%." That is an
admission that the impressive 2024-25 customer-win numbers were less meaningful than they sounded at
the time. Anyone who bought the story on customer count in 2024 was buying a softer number than they
realised.

**"Early innings" is the tell on China's real size.** Describing large Chinese customers, the chief
executive said "we only have 1 of their farms and they might have 100 farms." Read together with 5.4%
market share and an ambition to reach "double digits... certainly not in fiscal 2027, but in future
years," this is a genuine multi-year compounding opportunity — and simultaneously an admission that
almost none of it is in the next two years' numbers.

**The partner's real contribution is political, not commercial.** Asked twice what the state-backed
Chinese partner brings, the answer was candid: no change in management, no new customers yet, but
"what they really bring to the table is connectivity with the government... we do see benefit in
that relationship in terms of navigating the [gene-edited pig] regulatory process." The joint
venture is, in part, a regulatory-access vehicle. That is a sensible reason to have done it and a
poor reason to model near-term synergies.

**Capital allocation language hardened.** In 2024 the company talked about investment and cost
savings. In September 2026 it published a four-tier framework — organic investment first, a
progressive dividend second, disciplined acquisitions third, and returning surplus capital last —
and then acted on all four tiers in the same year. The phrase "we are monitoring the market, but we
will remain disciplined" on acquisitions, from a company sitting at 0.4 times leverage against a
one-to-two-times target, is the sentence that most deserves watching. There is roughly £100 million
of unused balance-sheet capacity here and a management team that has just proved it can sell an
asset well. The risk is that it proves less good at buying one.

**Two outside hires into the cattle business.** Commercial and operational excellence leaders were
recruited "from outside of our industry." Combined with the programme being declared complete in
the first half of fiscal 2027 and folded into business-as-usual, this reads as management accepting
that the easy cost savings are done and the remaining margin expansion has to come from selling
more, which is harder.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

Over three years this management team took a cyclical, capital-hungry, China-exposed animal-genetics
business and converted it into a higher-margin royalty business with a strong balance sheet, while
most of its end markets ran against it. Group adjusted operating margin went from 11.7% to 17.6%.
Return on invested capital went from 15.0% to 18.4%. Free cash flow went from negligible to £62
million. Borrowings net of cash fell from 1.5 times earnings to 0.4 times. They did it on flat
revenue, which is the hardest way to do it, and they told the market plainly which parts of the
result will not repeat.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position: the entry
multiple is being set against an earnings base that management has just marked down by 10%, in a
year they have told you will get worse before it gets better.** At 2,142 pence the shares are about
19 times reported adjusted earnings of 110.3 pence, but roughly 22 times the normalised 99 pence
that is the honest starting point for fiscal 2027 — and the first half of that year will print lower
than the prior year. The business quality is not the question here. The question is entirely the
price and the timing, and the next scheduled piece of news is a weak one.

**Economic moat: narrow, and widening.** The moat type is a combination of switching costs and
intangible genetic assets. In pigs it is close to wide: roughly 50% share of the United States
market, business with 19 of the 20 largest producers, royalty contracts that align the company's
economics to customer productivity, and a closed nucleus breeding programme whose genetic advantage
compounds every generation and cannot be replicated by a competitor buying equipment. The evidence
that this moat is widening rather than eroding is unambiguous: returns on capital and margins are
both rising, and the company gained share in China during a downturn precisely because its genetics
pay for themselves when producers are losing money. The reason the overall rating is narrow rather
than wide is the cattle business, which is roughly half of group revenue, earns only a 7.5% margin,
faces at least three credible competitors, and has a pending competitor merger that could make its
position harder.

**Secular threat: manageable.** There is no structural force melting this company's terminal value.
Global demand for animal protein is growing, and improved genetics is one of the few levers that
raises output while lowering the environmental cost per kilogram — a point the United Nations food
agency has endorsed and the company has documented with certified life-cycle assessments. The
pressures in the file — Chinese pork prices, depressed milk prices, high beef prices suppressing
sexed-semen demand, a bad disease season in North America — are cyclical, not secular. The cheapness
in the shares is therefore a de-rating of a growing business, not a low multiple on a shrinking
base. That said, the optical cheapness is smaller than the screener suggests once the one-off
accounting gain is removed.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend widening · structural threat manageable.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Colruyt Group (COLR.BR, Euronext Brussels, EUR) - deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-09. Live price EUR 36.64 (FMP quote, Euronext Brussels; 52-week range EUR 29.80 to 39.86; market value about EUR 4.37B on about 119.3M shares).

**Source limits, stated up front.** FMP holds no earnings-call transcripts for this listing, and Colruyt does not publish a conventional quarterly call (it reports twice a year, with an analyst meeting the day after). This run's web-search budget was exhausted before any third-party coverage could be pulled, so no management quotes are used below. The evidence is: the FMP half-yearly income statements (through the half to 2026-03-31), the screener's fundamentals block, Colruyt's own investor-relations financial calendar and press-release page (both read 2026-11-09), and the dated facts our committee recorded on 2026-10-05. No analyst price targets could be found or verified; none are used.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Over the last three years the story has moved from "Belgium's price leader, plus a portfolio of energy and other side businesses" to "a simplified, Belgium-focused grocer defending its share." The side assets were steadily sold (the large one-off profit is visible in the year to March 2024, when net income jumped to EUR 1.05B on EPS of EUR 8.33, against EUR 201M the year before), and the French retail business was exited (losses from discontinued operations of EUR 11-22M per half in the last two halves show the tail of that exit). What is left is a low-margin grocer on about EUR 10.6B of revenue.

The most recent turn came on 2026-09-30 (as recorded by this committee on 2026-10-05): at the annual meeting Colruyt said operating profit for the year to March 2027 will decline slightly, reversing the at-least-flat outlook given in June 2026, and that its combined Belgian market share had slipped again, to 28.3%. The narrative has therefore contracted from "stabilise and grow" to "defend."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim / theme | What the numbers show | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Price leadership protects volume | Revenue fell 3.6% in the year to March 2026 (EUR 10.96B to 10.57B); the latest half (to 2026-03-31) was EUR 5.28B vs 5.54B a year earlier, down about 4.7% | Diverges: the price promise is not holding share |
| Earnings stable after the portfolio clean-up | Operating profit (EBIT, earnings before interest and tax) by half, from FMP: EUR 244.9M (H1 to 2024-09), 220.6M (H2 to 2025-03), 221.8M (H1 to 2025-09), 158.3M (H2 to 2026-03). Full-year roughly EUR 380M vs about 465M two years earlier | Diverges: a step down, and the 2026-09-30 warning says it keeps falling |
| Margin discipline | Group EBIT margin about 3.6% on the last full year; the screener flags gross margin as contracting and 0.71 standard deviations below its historic peak | Thin and slipping |
| Cash returns to shareholders | Share count down from about 126.8M (H1 to 2023-09) to about 119.7M (H2 to 2026-03), roughly 5.6% retired; a EUR 0.966 dividend went ex on 2026-10-02 | Matches: buybacks are real and continuing |
| Balance sheet strength | Net debt about EUR 167M excluding leases (borrowings EUR 861M less cash EUR 694M at 2026-03-31); Altman-Z 3.2 | Matches: solvency is not the issue |

One data warning: the screener's trailing-twelve-month EPS of EUR 5.22 does not reconcile with the two reported halves (EUR 1.24 + 1.28 = 2.52). It most likely carries a disposal gain or a double-count; we use the reported EUR 2.53 full-year figure.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Declining. In June 2026 the company guided operating profit at least flat; by 2026-09-30, three months later, it guided a slight decline and disclosed another share loss. That is a shift from offensive language (growth, store renovations, e-commerce automation) to defensive language (protecting the price image, cost control). The press releases between 2026-10-01 and 2026-11-09 are all operational (store reopenings in Mons, Evere and Dilbeek; new Okay and Spar stores; more than 100 picking robots at the Collect&Go centre) and contain no financial update.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Medium-low. The June 2026 outlook lasted one quarter before it was cut. The screener shows results beating in only 3 of the last 6 periods (50%) and EPS down 7.3% in the latest year. There is no sandbagging pattern; if anything, guidance has been too generous.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without transcripts we cannot quote analysts. The recurring questions any grocery analyst puts to Colruyt are visible in the numbers: (1) where the market-share loss stops (it has slipped repeatedly to 28.3%); (2) how much margin must be given back to defend the "lowest price" promise against hard discounters and against Albert Heijn's expansion in Belgium; (3) whether the buyback continues once profits fall. The next chance to test these is the half-year release on 2026-12-15, with the analyst meeting on 2026-12-16 (Colruyt financial calendar, read 2026-11-09).

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: guidance reversed within one quarter (June to 2026-09-30).
- Red: market share down again, to 28.3% (2026-09-30).
- Red: revenue down about 4.7% year on year in the half to 2026-03-31, with EBIT for that half down to EUR 158M from 221M a year earlier.
- Red: margins were badly squeezed in the 2021-22 inflation (operating margin down about 4.2 points from the pre-inflation base), so a sticky-inflation backdrop is unkind.
- Green: low net debt (about EUR 167M ex-leases) and a large owned store estate.
- Green: steady share retirement (about 5.6% of shares in three years) and a reliable dividend.
- Green: real operational investment (store renovations, automation of online order picking).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The company is still spending on renovations and automation while profit falls, which signals that management is choosing to defend share with capital and price rather than harvest margin. That is strategically sensible for a price leader but means near-term earnings carry the cost. The 2026-10-08 extraordinary meeting approved the routine employee capital increase, which slightly offsets the buyback.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: deteriorating. The single most important thing to weigh: the stock has risen about 10% since our last look (EUR 33.24 in early October to EUR 36.64 today) with no new company information, while the only dated fact on the table, the 2026-09-30 profit warning, points the other way. The price now sits above a reasonable fair value for a shrinking-share grocer.

Moat: scale-cost (a price-leadership grocer with dense Belgian logistics and an owned estate). It is real but narrowing: market share and operating margin are both falling, so the moat reads as eroding rather than wide. Secular threat: the pressure is competitive (hard discounters and a strong Dutch entrant), not a structural decline of grocery itself, so the terminal value is not under threat; it is a cyclical-to-competitive squeeze. The current price is not a fear print; if anything the market is looking through the warning.

# Central Japan Railway (JR Central, 9022.T) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 16 November 2026. Prices in Japanese yen on the Tokyo listing (9022.T). Live quote used: 4,552 yen (FMP, 16 November 2026 close, up 1.8% on the day; 52-week range 3,202-4,830 yen).*

**Source note.** No earnings-call transcript was bundled and the licensed data connector has none for this listing. JR Central's own investor-meeting handouts for the half-year (presented 29 October 2026) are published as encrypted PDFs that could not be read. This dossier therefore rests on: the quarterly statements in the licensed FMP feed (through 30 September 2026); the half-year results and revised full-year forecast released 28 October 2026 as reported by Kabutan (28 October 2026) and Honichi (9 November 2026); the analyst-target aggregate on kabuyoho.jp (as of 27 October 2026); and this committee's own prior reviews (31 August and 26 October 2026). No management quotations are offered because none could be read first-hand; the "tone" sections are inferred from what management did (forecast and dividend changes), not from what it said.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has three chapters. First, recovery (fiscal years to March 2023 and 2024): the Tokaido Shinkansen - the high-speed line between Tokyo, Nagoya and Osaka, the densest intercity rail corridor in the developed world - came back from the pandemic, and net income went from a 52 billion yen loss to 219 billion yen and then 384 billion yen. Second, a peak (the year to March 2026): the Osaka Expo (April-October 2025) and strong inbound tourism pushed revenue to about 2,006 billion yen and net income to a record 553 billion yen, about 571 yen per share. Third, normalisation under a construction burden (now): management guided in April 2026 to a 15% fall in operating profit for the year to March 2027, blaming the end of the Expo, rising wages, repair and electricity costs, while the Chuo Shinkansen - the magnetic-levitation line from Tokyo to Nagoya, cost roughly 10 trillion yen, earliest opening 2036 - moves into heavier construction after Shizuoka Prefecture lifted its block on 18 July 2026.

What changed since our last look is that the "normalisation" turned out milder than management guided. On 28 October 2026 the company raised its full-year forecast and its dividend.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim / guidance | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| April 2026: operating profit 702 bn yen for the year to March 2027 (-15%) | First half (April-September 2026) operating profit 447.2 bn yen (-1.5% year on year), revenue 1,013 bn yen (+3.1%). Forecast raised 28 Oct 2026 to 757 bn yen operating profit, revenue 2,049 bn yen | Original guide was conservative; corrected upward |
| April 2026: net income 447 bn yen, EPS about 471 yen | Raised 28 Oct 2026 to net income 487 bn yen, EPS 513 yen (+9.0%) | Matches this committee's own "normalised" EPS of about 515 yen set in August |
| Cost pressure from wages, repairs and power | Quarterly cost of revenue up from 222 bn (Jul-Sep 2025) to 239 bn yen (Jul-Sep 2026) on revenue up only 3%; operating profit for the quarter 228.0 bn vs 232.8 bn yen | Real and persistent; margins are being squeezed |
| Dividend policy steady at 32 yen | Raised to 34 yen for the year (interim 17 yen) on 28 Oct 2026 | Small but a positive signal; still a yield of about 0.75% |
| Balance sheet able to fund the maglev | Borrowings on the narrow (FMP total-debt) basis 4,279 bn yen and cash plus short-term investments 1,028 bn yen at 30 Sep 2026; long-term investment portfolio (the maglev construction fund) up to 2,639 bn yen from 2,545 bn in June | Funded, but the cash is ring-fenced for construction |
| Share count falling | Weighted shares 982 mn (Jun 2025 quarter) to 949 mn (Sep 2026 quarter), about -3.3% | Buybacks in the year to March 2026 were real; the pace has since slowed |

A definitional warning the director must know: the licensed feed classified about 486 bn yen of long-term liabilities as debt at 30 June 2026 (total 4,807 bn yen) but as "other liabilities" at 31 March and 30 September 2026 (4,308 and 4,279 bn yen). This committee's prior reviews used the wider 4,807 bn figure. For consistency and prudence this review treats that 486 bn yen as debt-like, giving net debt of about 3,737 bn yen at 30 September 2026; on the narrow basis it is 3,250 bn yen. The gap is worth roughly 510 yen per share, so the definition matters.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Stable to slightly rising. Management guided low in April 2026 and has now raised once, in October, while keeping its second-half assumptions cautious: the raised full-year operating profit of 757 bn yen implies only about 310 bn yen for October-March, against about 376 bn yen in the same half a year earlier (when the Expo was running). That is either prudence or a genuine expectation of cost-led margin pressure; the first-half beat argues for prudence. The language reported in the press around the results was about inbound, domestic tourism and business travel supporting revenue, and wages and power costs weighing on profit - the same defensive cost framing as in April.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

High. The company routinely guides conservatively and raises at the half-year (it did so in October 2025 as well, lifting revenue guidance from 1,865 to 1,937 bn yen). The screener records beats in six of the last seven quarters (86%). The pattern is sandbagging, not over-promising. Reliability: High.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without a readable transcript, the recurring questions are inferred from the record: (a) the total cost and schedule of the Chuo Shinkansen, for which the company still publishes no target return on capital; (b) how much cash goes back to shareholders while the line is built - the buyback authorisation fell from 110 bn yen in the year to March 2026 to a 20 bn yen cap in April 2026, and nothing larger was announced on 28 October 2026 as far as could be verified; (c) whether the self-imposed ceiling of about 5 trillion yen on long-term debt will bind; (d) whether wages and electricity costs can be passed on through fares.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: operating profit fell in both quarters of the half (-0.9% in April-June, about -2% in July-September 2026) despite record revenue - costs are rising faster than fares.
- Red: shareholder cash return remains thin (dividend 34 yen, about 0.75% yield; buyback cap 20 bn yen) while the maglev absorbs capital for a decade.
- Red: the 2021-22 inflation crushed margins (gross margin from 48% to 17% in the year to March 2022, though that was mostly a pandemic volume collapse); the cost base is genuinely inflation-exposed.
- Green: forecast and dividend raised on 28 October 2026 (net income +8.9%, EPS 513 yen, dividend 32 to 34 yen).
- Green: interest cover remains strong (quarterly operating profit about 228 bn yen against interest expense of about 20 bn yen).
- Green: net debt fell on both bases between June and September 2026.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The dividend raise, though small, is the first increase above 32 yen in this cycle and came in the same release as the forecast raise - a signal that management sees the post-Expo base as durable. The growth in the long-term investment portfolio (2,383 bn yen at December 2025 to 2,639 bn yen at September 2026) continues: cash is being parked for the maglev rather than returned. The "other" segment (mainly rail-car manufacturing) grew external revenue 22% in the half, a minor but rising contributor.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: stable. The single most important thing to weigh: JR Central's earnings power is a durable monopoly, but for the next decade much of its cash is committed to the maglev, so the shareholder's return depends on the multiple the market will pay for earnings that are not distributed. At about 8.9 times the raised earnings guide and about 0.81 times book value, that multiple is low; the question is only whether today's price leaves enough room.

Moat: regulatory-licence and scale - the Tokaido Shinkansen is a legal and geographic monopoly with no realistic substitute on most of its routes (air competes only at the ends). The return evidence is steady rather than rising: return on equity around 11% on trailing figures, operating margins compressed by costs but still the highest among the JR operators. Width: wide; trend: stable. Secular threats are manageable: remote work trimmed business travel after the pandemic but ridership has since recovered to records; the maglev will partly cannibalise the Tokaido line, but it is JR Central's own asset. The cheapness reflects capital absorption and thin payout, not a shrinking base - it is not a value trap, but it is not a deep discount at today's price either.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a wide, durable moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: JD Sports is a cash machine priced like a shrinking business. Management guided on 2026-09-23 to £460m-£520m of free cash flow after leases for the year to January 2027. Net cash before leases improved by almost £300m year on year to £168m at 1 August 2026, after £260m was returned through buybacks and dividends. The interim dividend rose 21% and the buyback is shrinking the share count, which is why adjusted earnings per share fell less than pre-tax profit in the first half (down 13.7%). The governance clean-up is finished: adjusting items are now mostly amortisation of acquired intangibles, and statutory pre-tax profit rose 75%. The mix is improving: apparel is 36% of sales and growing 4%, online grew 5.2% to 20% of sales, and like-for-like operating costs were flat. The upside case is a turn in the footwear product cycle, with the CEO citing new heat in the Adidas Samba, On and Salomon and a recovering Nike. Like-for-like sales fell 2.5% in H1 FY26 and 2.8% in H1 FY27, and H1 FY27 operating margin fell 120bp to 5%. North America, the largest region, saw margin fall 220bp. Revenue growth since 2024 was bought through Hibbett and Courir, not earned organically. The CEO concedes the market leader (Nike, roughly half of JD's revenue by Barclays' estimate) is not creating heat, and the industry is over-inventoried and promotional, with youth unemployment and cost-of-living pressure rising. Return on invested capital of 8% is modest, and the earnings-beat rate is 3 of 7 quarters. Most importantly, the stock has already re-rated from a 64p low to 96p, near its 100.1p 52-week high, with no new company fact behind the move. If the Christmas peak disappoints and pre-tax profit slips toward £650m, earnings fall to about 9.5p, and at 6.5 times plus modest net cash the shares are worth about 68p.
picks.consensus_delta: The market is no longer pricing terminal decline. The shares have risen from a 63.98p 52-week low to 96.28p, near the 100.1p high, and sit 17% above their 200-day average. The deep-value case was strongest a year ago; it is now largely in the price. Where we might disagree with consensus is that the cash generation is under-appreciated: management guides £460m-£520m after-lease free cash flow while the peer data and the screener use pre-lease cash figures that overstate the cheapness (a 4.9x price-to-free-cash-flow ratio). picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) is the Q3 trading statement, typically late November, and the Black Friday to Christmas peak, which carries the bulk of annual profit. The CEO said on 2026-09-23 that youth unemployment and cost-of-living pressure both increased, and the footwear market remains highly promotional with too much stock in the industry. A weak peak could push profit to the bottom of the £700m-£800m range or below it, and a stock that has re-rated 50% off its low has little cushion. There is no debt wall: net cash before leases was positive at the seasonal low point. Lease liabilities are large but long-dated.
picks.positioning_washout: There is little sign of forced selling. JD is a FTSE 100 constituent with no index deletion risk at this market value, no lock-up and no dividend cut. Holders are not yield-driven, since the dividend yield is only about 1.3%. The Pentland founding family holds a large stake, which is a stable anchor rather than an overhang. After a strong October run, the more likely pressure is momentum holders taking profit if the Q3 update disappoints. That is ordinary selling, not forced selling.

Pass for now.

Nothing dated about the company has changed since this committee last looked on 12 October 2026, so the committee's answer stands. The governance clean-up is done. Management is credible on cash and cost, and less so on growth.

Why we pass: profit has fallen three years running, like-for-like sales are negative, and about half the business still depends on Nike's product cycle, which the CEO admits is not creating heat. Our base-case fair value is about 95p, close to today's price, with a plausible downside to about 68p and an upside to about 130p only if the footwear cycle turns. That is no margin of safety. What would change our mind is a dated fact: a Q3 or Christmas trading update showing like-for-like sales back in growth with margins holding. Separately, a fall in the share price would reopen the discount, and we would re-examine the name on either.
picks.forcing_function: What would force the market to re-rate: the ongoing buyback and progressive dividend shrink the share count steadily, and a footwear-cycle turn led by Nike would be the real catalyst. Neither has a hard date. The nearest dated read is the Q3 trading statement expected in late November 2026 (not yet announced), then the full-year results in spring 2027.
