picks.bull_thesis:
Inchcape is an automotive distributor, which is a better business than a car dealer. A car manufacturer hires it to run the whole operation in a country the manufacturer does not want to run itself: importing, pricing, marketing, managing the dealer network and supplying parts, across about 40 markets. That is why a company with a 3% net margin earned a 29% return on capital employed (operating profit divided by the capital tied up in the business) in 2025 and converted 104% of adjusted profit after tax into 315m pounds of free cash flow (results of 2026-03-03).

The market is pricing the whole group off its worst region. The published regional figures show where the damage is. In the first half of 2026 the Americas earned 115m pounds at a 6.5% margin (up 60 basis points) and Europe and Africa earned 94m pounds at 5.1% (up 20 basis points); together that is 84% of group operating profit, and both posted record profits in 2025. Asia-Pacific, chiefly Australia, earned only 39m pounds at 3.5%, after electric-vehicle share jumped from about 8% to about 25% in six months. Even after the 2026-10-22 update (Asia-Pacific volumes down 37%), group volumes grew 3% in the quarter, year-to-date organic volume growth of 7% sits at the top of the 3-5% guide, management reiterated more than 100% cash conversion, and the earnings-per-share (EPS) growth target is still about 10%.

The price does most of the work. At 643.5 pence the shares trade at about 7.2 times 2026 adjusted earnings (roughly 89 pence if the about-10% growth guide holds on 2025's 80.8 pence). The company is returning roughly 13% of its 2.14bn pound market value a year, through a 5% dividend yield (32.3 pence) and a 250m pound buyback that retires more shares per pound at this price. The growing regions are riding the wave of Chinese manufacturers, about 25% of group volumes and up roughly 40% in the first half of 2026, and keep adding bolt-on deals: Iceland in 2025, Silver Star in Bulgaria from 2026-07-01, and Volvo and Jaguar Land Rover in Peru and Costa Rica, announced 2026-10-01 and completing in Q1 2027. If Asia-Pacific merely stops falling as Subaru's electric models and the new Chinese brands (Deepal, Foton) build up, earnings per share resume growth on a shrinking share count. A director bought shares at about 645 pence on 2026-10-27.
picks.bear_thesis:
Inchcape does not own its customers. It rents access to them under per-market contracts that manufacturers can take back. Its own chief executive drew the boundary on 2026-07-28: distribution belongs in small, medium and complicated markets, while manufacturers should run the big markets themselves. BYD is already taking medium and large European markets in-house (2026-03-03), and the contract book churns: close to 60 wins in four years with a record number of exits, including 13 in Asia-Pacific and 2 in the Americas in the first half of 2026.

The earnings base is drifting down. Group adjusted operating profit fell from 584m pounds in 2024 to 563m in 2025, and Asia-Pacific fell from about 235m to 182m to a 78m pound annualised rate in the first half of 2026, before Q3 volumes fell another 37% (Australia about 50% in a flat market). The 2026 margin guide was cut to about 5.5% from about 6%, and the EPS growth commitment was trimmed to about 10% (2026-10-22). Statutory profit before tax fell 33% in the first half of 2026 (124m against 186m pounds), as interest on roughly 2bn pounds of vehicle inventory rises. The adjusted figure fell only 10% at constant currency. The Americas, now the largest profit pool, is at a cyclical high: management said Colombia and Peru growing at over 40% is not sustainable.

Two tail risks sit under that. The first is an unquantified indemnity on UK motor-finance commissions, retained from the old UK retail sale and now live under the regulator's redress scheme from 2026-03-31. The second is a rising-rate backdrop that makes inventory funding dearer. A cheap multiple on falling earnings can stay cheap for a long time.
picks.consensus_delta:
The market has moved from doubting the 2026 earnings shape to pricing a cut, and the 2026-10-22 guidance trim made the cut official (margin about 5.5% from about 6%, EPS growth about 10% from more than 10%). At 643.5 pence the shares trade at about 7.2 times 2026 adjusted earnings, a multiple that assumes Asia-Pacific stays broken and the weakness spreads.

Our disagreement is narrow and specific. We now take the published regional numbers at face value: Asia-Pacific is only about 70m pounds of our 490m pound base, and we value it at 5 times. What we do not accept is that the Americas and Europe and Africa, 84% of first-half profit with widening margins, deserve the group's 7 times multiple. The independent second opinion's 782 pence base is a different opinion, not a verified correction. Its specific number fixes cut our regional profit but also removed a central-cost line that does not exist and updated the share count, and on net they leave the value near 930 pence.
picks.valley_of_death:
Over the next six months there are clear ways this gets worse before it gets better.

First, estimate cuts. Asia-Pacific volumes fell 37% in Q3, against roughly 26% expected, so further cuts and a lower multiple are possible. The adverse case of 505 pence is about 22% below today's price.

Second, interest costs. Rates are rising in this backdrop, and the first half already lost 10% of adjusted profit before tax (33% of statutory) to finance costs and other items on inventory funding.

Third, the UK motor-finance indemnity, which management will revisit with the full-year results around early March 2027 and which we carry only as an estimated 40m pound provision in the base case.

Fourth, the Americas peak. Colombia and Peru face tough comparisons in 2027.

None of this threatens solvency: leverage is 0.5 times against a 1 times ceiling, and the buyback keeps running.
picks.positioning_washout:
There is no sign of a wash-out (a sharp sell-off by forced or non-fundamental sellers). The fall from 739.5 pence (2026-10-02) to about 626 pence on 2026-10-22, and the 630-650 pence range since, came from company news and broker downgrades on the Asia-Pacific outlook, not from index or forced selling.

The shares sit about 19% below their 200-day average (790.6 pence) and near the bottom of the 52-week range (604.5 to 895 pence). The company itself is the marginal buyer, retiring stock through the buyback at a lower price. A director bought at about 645 pence on 2026-10-27, and the 5% dividend yield gives holders a reason to wait.
picks.forcing_function:
Two dated events could force a re-rating.
- The investor webinar on 2026-11-19: management promised to show how its distribution contracts have performed over time, which is the evidence that would answer the contract-churn bear case.
- The full-year results, expected around early March 2027: these settle whether the second half of 2026 held up outside Asia-Pacific, show the first Asia-Pacific numbers after the cost cuts, and quantify the motor-finance indemnity.
Underneath both, the buyback keeps shrinking the share count. The Peru and Costa Rica deal, completing in Q1 2027, adds to the Americas base.

# Inchcape plc (INCH.L): a deep dive on management and the setup

Prices are in pence on the London listing. The live quote used is 643.5 pence (FMP, 2026-11-16). Source material: the transcripts of the Q3 2025 trading update (2025-10-23), the full-year 2025 results (2026-03-03) and the half-year 2026 results (2026-07-28); the published regional figures for full-year 2025 and the first half of 2026; and the Q3 2026 trading update of 2026-10-22, from secondary coverage.

## 1. Narrative arc

Across the three calls the story narrowed from "a diversified distributor growing everywhere except a soft Asian premium segment" to "two strong regions carrying one broken one".

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-23):** the tone was confident. Organic revenue grew 8%, volumes grew 13% against a market up 5%, and management promised a stronger second half. Asia was "a difficult environment", and management framed the problem as weak premium demand and production timing at Japanese manufacturers.
- **Full year 2025 (2026-03-03):** the Americas and Europe and Africa posted "record PBT performances" (PBT is profit before tax), and adjusted operating profit fell slightly to 563m pounds. The regional split was Americas 230m, Europe and Africa 151m and Asia-Pacific 182m, with Asia-Pacific down from about 235m in 2024. Two new themes arrived: BYD "in-sourcing distribution in medium to large-scale markets in Europe", and a cost programme focused on Asia-Pacific.
- **Half year 2026 (2026-07-28):** Asia-Pacific became the story. Australia "fast forwarded 3 years in 6 months" on electric-vehicle adoption, and regional profit fell to 39m pounds on a 3.5% margin, against 115m in the Americas (6.5% margin) and 94m in Europe and Africa (5.1%). Management raised the buyback to 250m pounds and kept the target of more than 10% earnings-per-share growth.
- **Q3 2026 update (2026-10-22):** that target was trimmed to about 10%, the full-year margin guide was cut to about 5.5% from about 6%, and Asia-Pacific volumes fell 37%, with Australia down about 50% in a flat market.

The growth drivers stayed the same throughout: contract wins, Chinese manufacturers in Latin America and Europe, bolt-on deals (Iceland in 2025, Silver Star in Bulgaria on 2026-07-01, Peru and Costa Rica announced 2026-10-01) and buybacks. What quietly dropped out was any confidence on Asia-Pacific margins. In March 2026 the chief financial officer said cost work would "underpin margins as we have seen previously". By July the region's margin was down 320 basis points.

## 2. Claims vs financials

| Claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| "Highly cash-generative, capital-light" | 2025 free cash flow 315m pounds, 104% conversion of adjusted profit after tax, 29% return on capital employed (operating profit divided by the capital tied up in the business) | Corroborated over a full year. The first half of 2026 converted only 65% (84m pounds), which is seasonal. The Q3 update reiterated more than 100% for the full year. |
| ">10% EPS growth" | Adjusted EPS (earnings per share) 80.8p in 2025, up 13%, mostly from buybacks. Flat at 35.5p in the first half of 2026. Trimmed to about 10% on 2026-10-22. | Delivered in 2025 through the share count, not through profit (adjusted operating profit fell 1% at constant currency). The 2026 promise is now weaker. |
| "Resilient margins of around 6%" | 6.2% in 2025 (6.0% excluding disposal gains), 5.3% in the first half of 2026, about 5.5% guided for 2026 | Missed in 2026. |
| "Asia-Pacific will rescale in H2" (Q3 2025 and March 2026) | Asia-Pacific profit 182m pounds in 2025, down about 23%. 39m in the first half of 2026. Volumes down 37% in Q3 2026. | Contradicted twice. |
| "Americas and Europe and Africa at records" | Americas 230m pounds (up 11%) and Europe and Africa 151m (up 6%) in 2025. Both margins expanded in the first half of 2026. | Corroborated. |
| Screener: net margin 3%, statutory EPS down 29% | Statutory PBT in the first half of 2026 was 124m pounds against 186m (down 33%). Adjusted PBT 188m, down 10% at constant currency, on higher finance costs. | The statutory line is much weaker than the adjusted line. Finance costs on roughly 2bn pounds of vehicle inventory are a real, recurring drag. |

The regional figures matter for valuation. The regions sum exactly to the group (563m pounds in 2025, 248m in the first half of 2026), so there is no separate central-cost line to subtract.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

The trajectory is declining, but management stays specific. In October 2025 the language was offensive: "super excited about expanding the scale", with Q3 results "supportive" of a stronger second half. By March 2026 the language was defensive: a "cost reduction program", "making sure margins stick". In July 2026 the chief executive was candid ("fast forwarded 3 years in 6 months"), and he conceded that big markets "should run them themselves". Guidance stayed numerical throughout, which is a credit to management.

## 4. Guidance credibility

- The 2025 "year of growth" guide was delivered on earnings per share and not on operating profit.
- The 2026 guide of a 6% margin and more than 10% EPS growth was cut in October 2026.
- The 3-5% volume guide was met at the top end (7% year to date).
- Asia-Pacific recovery calls were missed twice.
- The screener shows a 0-of-1 earnings beat rate.

Reliability is medium. Management is honest about the shape of results but has been too optimistic about the weak region.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

- **Contract churn.** Analysts asked in July 2026 about exiting contracts won only recently. Management answered "close to 60 contract wins" in four years "with a higher number of exits", including 13 exits in Asia-Pacific and 2 in the Americas in the first half. The promised Investor Day evidence is now the 2026-11-19 webinar.
- **UK motor-finance indemnity.** Analysts asked about this in October 2025. It remains "unquantified", and the regulator's redress scheme took effect 2026-03-31.
- **Whether the shift in Australia is structural.** Management answered "Yes, I do."
- **Peak growth in Colombia and Peru.** Management said those markets were growing "like topsy" and conceded the pace is "not sustainable".

## 6. Red flags and green flags

- Red flag: the Asia-Pacific margin fell 320 basis points in the first half of 2026, and regional volumes fell 37% in Q3 2026.
- Red flag: management drew its own boundary (2026-07-28) that big markets go direct, and BYD is in-sourcing in Europe (2026-03-03).
- Red flag: statutory PBT fell 33% in the first half of 2026, and finance costs are rising.
- Red flag: the motor-finance indemnity is unquantified.
- Red flag: the Americas peak is acknowledged.
- Green flag: margins expanded in the Americas and in Europe and Africa (2026-07-28).
- Green flag: 2025 cash conversion was 104%, and the full-year target was reiterated on 2026-10-22.
- Green flag: leverage is 0.5 times EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation). The buyback was raised to 250m pounds, about 12% of the current market value.
- Green flag: a non-executive director bought 5,000 shares at about 645 pence on 2026-10-27, which is small but at today's price.
- Green flag: about 25% of volumes are now with Chinese manufacturers, and those volumes grew around 40% in the first half of 2026.

## 7. Hidden signals

- **Exits.** "Portfolio management" has become the euphemism for exits. The frank admission of more exits than in the past is new.
- **Who manufacturers need.** Management now describes Inchcape's role in terms of which manufacturers need it ("small to medium-sized and more complicated markets"), not in terms of global scale.
- **Leadership.** There was an executive leadership reshuffle in which the former Americas chief now leads the commercial function.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

The trajectory is stable. Capital allocation is disciplined: 40% of earnings is paid out as dividends, and the rest goes to buybacks and value-disciplined bolt-ons. The group earnings base, however, is drifting down because of Asia-Pacific.

**The single most important point for the director:** about three-quarters of the profit, from the Americas and Europe and Africa, is healthy. The open question is whether Asia-Pacific settles at about 40-80m pounds a year or keeps shrinking, and whether manufacturer in-sourcing spreads beyond BYD.

**Moat.** The moat comes from scale and cost, plus switching costs in the operating know-how manufacturers buy in small, complex markets. It is narrow. Returns on capital are high (29%), but contracts are revocable and churn is rising. The trend is eroding at the edges (Asia-Pacific exits, BYD in-sourcing, the chief executive's own boundary), while it is widening with the Chinese manufacturers entering Latin America and Europe.

**Secular threat.** Manufacturers going direct is a real but manageable channel-shift threat. In the small markets where Inchcape operates, manufacturers lack the scale to do it themselves. The cheapness is mostly a fear-print on Asia-Pacific and not a terminal shrinking of the whole base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

The load-bearing claims are corroborated by the latest dated numbers.

picks.bull_thesis: Centrica is Britain's largest household energy supplier, trading in London at 156.20 pence on 16 November 2026, about 12% below its 200-day average and in the lower quarter of its 52-week range (144p to 220p), with net cash (about 709 million pounds adjusted, 30 June 2026). The bull case is that the market still prices Centrica as the fading 2023 gas-trading windfall and has not re-priced the contracted infrastructure being built in its place. The anchor is the 9 July 2026 Sizewell B agreement: a 20-year regulated contract at 70.50 pounds per megawatt-hour in 2025 money, rising with inflation and extending the plant to 2055, for a small capital share funded from the nuclear partnership's own cash. That turns a merchant cash stream with a hard stop into a long inflation-linked annuity, which is worth more while inflation runs above 3%. The older nuclear fleet was extended to 2030 (22 July 2026), and the company has bought the flexible assets a renewables-heavy grid lacks: the Severn gas plant, half of the Grain LNG terminal, batteries and solar. Earnings beat estimates in 6 of the last 7 quarters, and gross margin is 38.7% and rising. Jefferies (3 November 2026, buy, 200p) argues that retail and infrastructure make up about 85% of expected 2027 core profit, that this 'visible' part grows about 17% a year from 7.8p a share in 2026 to 14.7p in 2030, and that the shares trade on about 11 times 2027 earnings against about 17 times for peers. For the bull case to work, free cash flow must turn positive into 2027, the buyback must restart at the February 2027 results, and Rough must get a support regime or a clean closure.
picks.bear_thesis: The bear case is not that Centrica is a bad company; it is that the balance-sheet strength the value argument rests on is being spent, and the earnings the low multiple is built on are not backed by cash. The company's own interim release (23 July 2026) shows a 570 million pound free cash outflow in the first half of 2026 and adjusted net cash down to 709 million pounds, from 1.5 billion at the end of 2025 and about 2.5 billion a year earlier, while the interim dividend was raised to 2.0 pence (paid 22 September 2026) and large nuclear equity commitments remain to be funded. The screener's 328 million pounds of trailing free cash flow, and the 24 times price-to-free-cash-flow multiple built on it, do not reconcile with that statement. The buyback was paused on 19 February 2026 and management ruled out a near-term restart in July. Retail is guided to the lower end of its 500 to 800 million pound core-profit range, the 2027 trading outlook was lowered to about 250 million pounds, and household bad debt runs above the regulator's allowance (above 4% of revenue against 3.8%, per Jefferies, 3 November 2026). Revenue is down 2.1% last year and 6.4% a year over three years, and latest-quarter earnings per share fell 52% year on year. In the last inflation shock gross margin collapsed from 35.7% (2019) to 9.6% (2021). What would confirm the bear case: net cash below about 400 million pounds at the February 2027 results with the buyback still dormant.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is narrow and runs opposite to the sell side. Post-interim targets (late July 2026, about 200p to 215p) and Jefferies' 200p (3 November 2026) imply roughly 28% to 38% upside from 156.20 pence. Jefferies' case rests on 'visible' retail and infrastructure earnings growing about 17% a year to 2030 and on Centrica trading at about 11 times 2027 earnings against about 17 times for peers. What those targets do not address is cash: the company reported a 570 million pound free cash outflow in the first half of 2026 and net cash fell to 709 million pounds, with nuclear equity still to fund and the buyback off. A 200p target needs either a dated cash-flow turn nobody has given or a regulated-network multiple for a business that is not yet a regulated network. Under the deep-value lens, the question is whether the street is pricing terminal decline into stable earnings power. It is not: the market is pricing a smaller, more capital-hungry business roughly correctly, and the recent rise to about 156p has already closed most of the gap to our fair value.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window, the months just ahead, is shaped by cash. Over the next three to nine months Centrica must fund phased Sizewell C equity, the cash costs of the 1,300-job restructuring before its savings land, and household bad debt running above the regulator's allowance, while earnings are guided to be weighted to the first half. There is no liquidation event or debt wall: the company is solvent with net cash. The likely bad outcome is slow rather than sudden: net cash below about 400 million pounds at the February 2027 full-year results with the buyback still paused. A Rough closure decision without a support regime would bring clean-up costs forward.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure is limited. The base is income-oriented and index-heavy (a FTSE 100 member with low beta), the dividend was raised rather than cut and paid on 22 September 2026, so there is no mechanical trigger for yield funds to sell. The slide from about 220p to a 144p low was orderly, and the shares have since recovered to about 156p. There has been no wash-out (a sharp sell-off by forced or non-fundamental sellers) to buy into, and with the buyback paused the marginal buyer of 2024 and 2025 is absent.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. This is the same committee continuing coverage, and nothing dated in the business has changed since our last look on 19 October 2026: no trading update, no buyback restart and no Rough decision were announced. What changed is the price, up from about 149 pence to 156.20 pence today, helped by a broker upgrade (Jefferies, buy, 200p, 3 November 2026), and that narrows the gap to our 160 pence fair value to about 2%. Centrica is a competently run, solvent company swapping a volatile trading windfall for contracted infrastructure cash flow, and the 9 July 2026 Sizewell B contract is a genuinely good piece of work. But valued by its parts the business is worth about 160 pence in the base case, against 206 pence if everything goes right and 105 pence if the current cash trend simply continues. Our reason to pass is not the price alone: the company's own interim release shows a 570 million pound free cash outflow in the first half of 2026, net cash has fallen to about 709 million pounds while a rising dividend and new nuclear equity are funded from it, the buyback is paused, and returns are falling from their peak, so the moat is eroding. A low multiple on a shrinking, more capital-hungry base is not a value position. The thesis holds in that nothing has disproven the pivot; what would change our answer is dated evidence of cash cover: positive free cash flow and a buyback restart at the February 2027 full-year results, or a Rough support decision. The macro backdrop, which rewards cash flow now, is a headwind but did not move this answer.
picks.forcing_function: There is no firmly dated event that forces a re-rating. The real decision point is the full-year results in February 2027, where the company either restarts the buyback and shows free cash flow covering the dividend and capital spending, or does not. A government storage support regime for Rough has no published date and depends on a third party. Under the deep-value lens, a buyback reauthorisation or an asset sale (Spirit Energy, or a stake in the nuclear portfolio) would be the re-rating events; none is announced as of 16 November 2026.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Centrica plc (CNA.L) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 16 November 2026. Price used: 156.20 pence (London listing, GBp; live quote from the paid data feed, FMP, 16 November 2026: previous close 160.65p, day range 156.20p to 159.85p, 52-week range 144p to 220.30p, 50-day average 150.3p, 200-day average 176.9p). Shares in issue are about 4,530 million (market value of about 7.07 billion pounds divided by the price). No earnings-call transcript was bundled and the paid feed has no transcripts or news for this London listing, so this deep dive is built from the screener fundamentals, the company's dated disclosures (2025 full-year results of 19 February 2026, interim results of 23 July 2026), and a fresh web search for anything new since this committee's last full look on 19 October 2026. That search found no new company announcement dated after 19 October 2026: no trading update, no buyback restart, and no decision on Rough. The one dated item is a broker view, not a company fact: Jefferies upgraded the shares to buy with a 200p target on 3 November 2026. No management quotes are reproduced, because we did not have a transcript in hand, and we will not invent them.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has moved in three stages over roughly two years.

- 2023 to 2024: the windfall. Centrica earned net income of 3.93 billion pounds in 2023 on 26.5 billion pounds of revenue, an exceptional year driven by gas trading and upstream profits during the European energy crisis. Management used it to rebuild the balance sheet (net cash of about 2.7 billion pounds at the end of 2024) and to run a large share buyback.
- 2025: the normalisation. Revenue fell to 19.5 billion pounds and the company reported a statutory loss of 72 million pounds for 2025 (results of 19 February 2026). On that day the buyback was paused to fund investment, and guidance for the trading arm (Centrica Energy, the optimisation business) was cut to about 250 million pounds of core profit (EBITDA, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) for 2026.
- 2026: the pivot to contracted infrastructure. The narrative is "swap volatile trading profit for long-dated, inflation-linked cash flow": a 20-year regulated contract for Sizewell B (9 July 2026, 70.50 pounds per megawatt-hour in 2025 money, inflation-linked, plant life extended to 2055), the older nuclear fleet extended to 2030 (22 July 2026), the Severn gas plant (May 2026), half of the Grain LNG import terminal, and equity committed to the new Sizewell C station. A 1,300-job cost programme accompanies it (23 July 2026).

What was dropped: the buyback as the central per-share lever. What was introduced: regulated and contracted assets as the valuation anchor. What remains unresolved: Rough, the offshore gas storage field, whose future depends on a government decision on storage support with no published date. Nothing in this arc has moved since 19 October 2026.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (dated) | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Earnings are normalising, not collapsing (19 Feb 2026) | Net income 586m (2021), -782m (2022), 3.93bn (2023), 1.33bn (2024), -72m (2025). Trailing diluted earnings 0.11 pounds a share to 30 June 2026; latest-quarter earnings per share down 52% year on year. | Partly true. The base is falling. |
| Full-year 2026 expectations "largely unchanged", earnings weighted to the first half (23 Jul 2026) | Retail guided to the lower end of its 500 to 800 million pound EBITDA range; trading arm about 250m for 2026, and a 2027 trading outlook of about 250m against a market expectation nearer 320m. | Guidance held, but at the low end, and the trading outlook was lowered. |
| Capital discipline while investing | Interim release (23 Jul 2026): free cash outflow of 570 million pounds in the half; closing adjusted net cash 709 million pounds, down from 1.5 billion at end-2025 and about 2.5 billion a year earlier. Balance-sheet recomputation at 30 Jun 2026: cash 3.47bn against 2.74bn of debt including 206m of leases, net cash 730m. | Diverges. Cash is being consumed, not generated. |
| Dividend progression is affordable | Interim dividend raised to 2.0 pence, paid 22 Sep 2026, out of the cash balance rather than free cash flow. | Story richer than cash flow. |
| Balance sheet strength | Net cash, solvent. The screener now shows Altman-Z (a solvency score) of 3.1 and Piotroski (a nine-point accounting-health score) of 6/9, down from the 5.0 and 7/9 our last look used. | True on solvency, but the cushion is thinning. |

A data conflict the director must know about: the screener records trailing free cash flow of 328 million pounds and a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of about 24 times. The company's own interim release shows a 570 million pound free cash outflow in the first half of 2026. The screener figure does not reconcile with the published cash flow and should not be used to support value.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Trajectory: declining on the near term, rising on the long-term asset story. Without a transcript we judge tone from the shape of the disclosures. February 2026 was defensive (buyback paused, trading guidance cut). July 2026 was offensive in capital allocation (nuclear, LNG, generation) but cautious on cash, with management ruling out a near-term buyback in favour of investment. That is a team confident about 2035 and visibly less specific about cash in 2026 and 2027. Nothing new has been said since.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

The screener shows earnings beats in 6 of the last 7 quarters (86%), but the trading guidance that was beaten had itself been cut. No dated guidance on free cash flow or on a buyback restart has been given, which is the guidance that matters for value. Reliability: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- When the buyback returns, and what net cash level management will defend. Not answered with a date.
- Rough: whether the government grants a support regime, and what closure would cost. Third-party dependent, undated.
- The phasing of Sizewell C equity calls against a thinning cash balance.
- Household bad debt above the regulator's allowance: Jefferies (3 November 2026) put residential bad debt above 4% of revenue at the half year against Ofgem's 3.8% allowance, and expects it below the allowance only from 2028.
- Sell-side targets sit well above the price: post-interim targets of about 200p to 215p (late July 2026), and Jefferies at 200p (3 November 2026), resting on "visible" retail and infrastructure earnings of 7.8p a share in 2026 growing to 14.7p by 2030. That growth path is an analyst forecast, not company guidance, and it does not address the cash outflow.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Red flags
- 🔴 Free cash outflow of 570 million pounds in H1 2026 (interim release, 23 July 2026) while the dividend was raised.
- 🔴 Adjusted net cash down from about 2.5 billion pounds (mid-2025) to 709 million (30 June 2026).
- 🔴 Buyback paused since 19 February 2026, with management ruling out a near-term restart on 23 July 2026.
- 🔴 Revenue down 2.1% last year and 6.4% a year over three years; net margin about -0.4% for 2025.
- 🔴 In the last inflation shock gross margin fell from 35.7% (2019) to 9.6% (2021): this business did not pass costs through.

Green flags
- 🟢 Sizewell B contract (9 July 2026): thirty years of inflation-linked revenue for a small, self-funded capital share.
- 🟢 Older nuclear fleet extended to 2030 (22 July 2026).
- 🟢 Solvent with net cash; return on invested capital of about 39% on the screener (flattered by the trading arm and a small capital base).
- 🟢 Gross margin 38.7% and expanding in the latest year.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The vocabulary has shifted from "returns to shareholders" to "investment" and "contracted". That is a genuine strategic pivot, but it moves the company from a cash-return story to a capital-intensive one exactly when long-dated borrowing costs are high and the market pays for cash now. The household supply arm is showing stress through bad debt above the regulator's allowance. The shares rose from about 149p (19 October) to 160.65p (13 November) and 156.20p today without any company announcement, which looks like a sector move and broker support (Jefferies, 3 November) rather than news.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: turning. Centrica is pivoting from a merchant trading and retail business to a part-contracted infrastructure owner. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: the company is funding a rising dividend and new nuclear equity out of a shrinking cash balance rather than out of free cash flow, and the next hard evidence on whether that turns is the full-year results in February 2027.

Moat. The retail book (British Gas) has scale and brand but sits under the regulator's price cap and competes on switching; the trading arm earns volatility, not a moat. Returns are high but falling from the 2023 peak, and the screener's free cash flow has fallen by about 28% a year over three years. That is an eroding moat, with the contracted nuclear stake the one widening piece. Secular threat: the energy transition is material rather than terminal. It shrinks gas supply, upstream gas and gas storage over time, but Centrica is reinvesting into assets a renewables-heavy grid needs (nuclear, flexible generation, batteries). The cheapness is mostly the market correctly pricing a smaller, more capital-hungry business, not a fear-driven mispricing.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a moat that is being eroded · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.

picks.bull_thesis:
Jet2 is the best-run leisure travel business in the United Kingdom, trading at roughly seven times its earnings and about six times its free cash flow. The bull case is that the market is pricing a cyclical squeeze as if it were permanent.

The evidence: revenue reached a record 7.48 billion pounds in the year to March 2026 (up 4.3%), passengers passed 20 million, and free cash flow was 495 million pounds - 2.6 billion pounds since the pandemic (FY26 results call, 8 July 2026). Management has a high-credibility record: it flagged its own small miss on flight-only pricing early (November 2025) and landed full-year operating profit inside its 435-440 million pound guide. The September 2026 trading statement showed booked passengers up 8.8% on capacity up 7.6%, with Gatwick ahead of plan.

Three drivers can lift profit from here. First, the newer bases (Bournemouth, Luton and from March 2026 Gatwick) carry start-up costs today and should mature into profit; Gatwick is guided to break even by the year to March 2029. Second, the A321neo fleet (232 seats against 189, lower cost per seat, about 22% of the summer 2026 fleet) lowers unit costs as it grows. Third, the buyback shrinks the share count: about 22 million shares were bought back in the year to March 2026 and a further 250 million pounds runs to 31 May 2027, roughly 9% of today's market value of about 2.7 billion pounds.

Consensus, as cited in the committee's prior record, expects earnings per share to recover toward 188p for the year to March 2028 and 243p for the year to March 2029. On those numbers the stock trades at about eight and six times earnings respectively, with a balance sheet that carries roughly break-even own net debt and an undrawn 500 million pound credit line. If flight-only pricing stabilises and Gatwick scales, a multiple of nine to ten times recovery earnings gives 1,700-2,150p.

Conditions: flight-only yields stop falling, hotel cost inflation moderates toward package price growth, and no large demand shock (conflict, recession) hits the 2027 summer booking season.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that Jet2's profit has stopped growing even as it adds capacity, and that the cheap multiple reflects a narrowing moat in a crowded market rather than a mispricing.

The evidence: net income fell from 447 million pounds (FY25) to 410 million pounds (FY26) while seat capacity grew about 8%. Flight-only ticket yield fell 7% in both the November 2025 and July 2026 calls; management calls this 'investing in price' and 'investing in load factor', which is another way of saying it cannot hold fares. Hotel costs, 45% of the cost base, rose about 6.5% while package prices rose 3%, of which about one point was customers trading up. Return on capital employed slipped from a 17% three-year average to 14.4%, and our scan's return on invested capital of 6.4% is near the cost of capital. Free cash flow fell about 25% year on year as bookings moved closer to departure.

The headline net cash of about 2.0 billion pounds is mostly customer deposits; the CFO himself put own cash at about 1.2 billion pounds, roughly equal to the 1.28 billion pounds of debt including leases. In a shock those deposits become a refund liability, not a cushion, and the new 2 times leverage target signals more borrowing to fund the Airbus order book. Consensus earnings for the year to March 2027 of about 136p (cited in the prior record) imply the stock is not cheap on this year's numbers at about 11 times.

What would confirm the bear case: the 18 November 2026 interim results showing summer 2026 profit flat or down despite higher passenger numbers, winter flight-only yields still falling, or capacity guidance for summer 2027 that again outruns the market. The business is also exposed to inflation: its gross margin fell from 13.8% to a loss through the 2021-22 period (largely pandemic-driven), and it has shown only partial pass-through of hotel cost increases.
picks.consensus_delta: The street is not pricing terminal decline; it is pricing a profit plateau. Seven brokers average a target of about 1,617p (MarketBeat aggregator, 3 November 2026), only about 6% above today's price, with five buys and two holds. Our base case of 1,720p sits a little above that, so the disagreement with the market is modest. Where we differ is on composition: the street leans on the headline 2.0 billion pounds of net cash, which we largely exclude because most of it is customer deposits, and on the recovery in earnings per share to about 188p by the year to March 2028, which we accept only in the base case. The street may also be too relaxed about flight-only yield, which has fallen 7% in two reporting periods running. We do not see a large expectations gap at 1,525p.
picks.valley_of_death: No liquidation risk, debt wall or forced dilution: own cash roughly matches debt, the 500 million pound facility is undrawn to October 2030, and the fleet is financed through long-dated asset-backed borrowing. The risk over the next three to nine months is earnings disappointment. The 18 November 2026 interim results could show summer 2026 profit flat despite more passengers, and the winter booking season (typically sold from January) has been late and price-led in each of the last two years. Hotel cost inflation, sustainable aviation fuel mandates (32 million pounds of extra premium in FY26) and employment-tax rises all pressure margins. A demand shock - renewed Middle East conflict hitting eastern Mediterranean bookings, as in spring 2026, or a UK consumer slowdown - would compress the customer-deposit float and free cash flow quickly. Any of these could take the shares back toward the 1,250p entry level.
picks.positioning_washout: There is no forced-seller setup specific to Jet2: no index deletion, no lock-up, no dividend cut to drive out yield holders, and the company itself is a steady buyer through the 250 million pound buyback. The path to 1,250p is a sector-wide sell-off: European leisure and airline shares de-rate together on fuel spikes, geopolitical shocks or UK consumer weakness, as they did in March 2026 when Jet2 set a 12-month low near 980p. That is why the wait is tied to a sector or style sell-off rather than to mechanical selling.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Wait for a better price: we buy near 1,250p, which a sector-wide sell-off of UK consumer and airline shares could deliver.

The thesis holds. Jet2 is a well-run, cash-generative leisure travel business with credible management, a strong own-cash position and an aggressive buyback. Nothing dated has changed since the committee's last look on 19 October 2026; the price has moved only from 1,510p to 1,525p.

The issue remains the price, not the business. Our fair value is about 1,720p, only about 13% above today's 1,525p, which does not clear the 20% bar we require in a growth-with-sticky-inflation backdrop, while the adverse case of about 1,200p is about 21% below. At 1,250p the trade becomes attractive: about 38% upside to fair value against little downside to the adverse case. The shares were near 980p as recently as March 2026, so a sector-wide sell-off of that kind is not far-fetched.

We hold the value case at a middle rating. The moat is real but narrow and being tested: profit fell in FY26 while capacity grew about 8%, flight-only fares have been cut 7% two periods running, and return on capital has slipped from 17% to 14.4%. Until pricing stabilises, the low multiple partly reflects a business that is buying growth with price, which limits how much we will pay.

The interim results on 18 November 2026 are the next dated test. A clear profit increase with stable winter yields would strengthen the case; a profit fall with more price-cutting would argue for a lower fair value.
picks.forcing_function: No single event forces a re-rating. The nearest dated checkpoint is the interim results on 18 November 2026, which will show whether summer 2026 converted higher bookings into profit and give the first read on winter pricing. Beyond that, the forcing mechanism is slow: the buyback steadily retiring stock to May 2027, Gatwick progressing toward break-even by the year to March 2029, and the summer 2027 capacity and yield guidance, typically given in the new year. A re-rating needs evidence that flight-only pricing has stopped falling.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Jet2 plc (JET2.L) - a deep dive on management and the setup

Debate date: 16 November 2026. Live price 1,525p (FMP quote, London listing, pence). Transcripts read: interim results call of 19 November 2025 (half year to 30 September 2025) and full-year results call of 8 July 2026 (year to 31 March 2026). The next dated release is the interim results for the half year to 30 September 2026, scheduled for 18 November 2026 (FMP earnings calendar), two days after this debate.

The short version: management is credible and conservative, the balance sheet is strong, and the cash returns are real. But the last eighteen months show a business that is growing passengers by giving away price, with profit flat to slightly down while capacity grows about 8% a year. That is a narrow moat that is being tested, not a widening one.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

In November 2025 the story was "record numbers" and expansion: passengers up 6%, the new bases at Bournemouth and Luton, and the launch of London Gatwick, described as "a once-in-a-generation opportunity to accelerate our growth" (H1 FY26 call). The Gatwick base was explicitly not expected to make money until the year to March 2029.

By July 2026 the emphasis had shifted from growth to resilience. The words used most were "resilient", "robust" and "controlled": operating profit "remained resilient even after absorbing Gatwick startup investment costs and wider industry cost pressures" (FY26 call). The growth story is still there (over 20 million passengers, up 5%), but the profit story has become one of absorbing costs. Capital returns moved to the centre: 363 million pounds returned in the year, "more than ever before", and a further 250 million pound buyback to run to 31 May 2027.

A new strand appeared in July 2026: a medium-term leverage target of 2 times net debt to EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) on an own-cash basis. That is a quiet signal that management intends to use more of the balance sheet over time, mainly to finance the Airbus fleet.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record revenue" (FY26) | Revenue 7.48 billion pounds, up 4.3%; three-year growth about 14% a year, flattered by the post-pandemic rebound from 1.23 billion in 2022 | True, but growth has slowed sharply |
| Operating profit "resilient" | Net income fell from 447 million pounds (FY25) to 410 million (FY26); FY26 operating profit guided at 435-440 million against 446.5 million the year before (29 April 2026 trading update) | Profit fell while capacity grew about 8%. "Resilient" is generous |
| Package price "resilient, up 3%" | About 1 point of the 3% came from customers trading up to four- and five-star hotels; hotel costs, 45% of the cost base, rose about 6.5% | Partial pass-through only; the cost of the holiday rose faster than its price |
| Flight-only demand strong (+15% passengers) | Flight-only ticket yield down 7% in both calls | Volume bought with price |
| "Over 2 billion pounds of net cash" | True on the headline basis, but most of it is customer deposits. The CFO himself split out "1.2 billion pounds of our own cash, excluding customer advances"; against about 1.28 billion pounds of debt including leases, own cash is roughly break-even | The headline overstates distributable cash |
| Free cash flow 495 million pounds; 2.6 billion since the pandemic | Consistent with the trailing figures; free cash flow fell about 25% year on year as customers booked later | True, but declining and timing-sensitive |
| Earnings per share "stable" | Earnings per share roughly 208-211p in both FY25 and FY26 - stable only because about 22 million shares were bought back | Per-share stability is buyback-supported |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Trajectory: stable, with a defensive tilt.

- November 2025: confident, expansionary - "Further growth in the first half across all our key metrics." The CFO was candid about uncertainty: "there's a lot of moving parts ... I'm not being evasive, but there are."
- July 2026: still upbeat ("I hope you're as excited about the future as we are"), but the vocabulary moved to cost absorption, "investing in price" and capital returns. On the Middle East conflict, management described later bookings and a bounce-back in eastern Mediterranean destinations rather than a lasting hit.

There is no sign of panic and no sign of rising ambition either. The language is that of a well-run operator in a tougher market.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Reliability: high.

- The November 2025 guide for flight-only pricing was "mid-single digits down"; the CFO volunteered that the outcome was "slightly worse" at minus 7%. Flagging a small miss early is a good sign.
- FY26 operating profit landed inside the 435-440 million pound range guided in April 2026.
- The beat rate in our data is 50% (one of two quarters), and FMP shows the November 2025 half-year earnings per share at 300p against a 281p estimate.
- The July 2026 capital spending cut of about 350 million pounds for the following year was explained as Airbus delivery timing, "timing only, it doesn't undermine any of our growth plans". That is plausible given industry-wide Airbus delays, but it also flatters near-term free cash flow.

No sandbagging pattern, and no pattern of over-promising.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- Capacity versus price: analysts asked in both calls whether growing capacity 8-9% when competitors grow less would force further fare cuts. Management answered with flexibility ("we can make adjustments") rather than with yield guidance. This is the central unresolved question.
- Cost per seat: management repeatedly declined to give unit-cost guidance before Eurocontrol fees and slot declarations were known.
- Booking curve: later bookings came up in both calls; management treats them as a timing effect, but they reduce visibility and the customer-deposit float.
- AI distribution (July 2026): asked whether large language models would change how holidays are booked, management said "We've not seen a big impact from LLMs at the moment" and that direct bookings are steady at just under 80% for holidays. Honest, but untested.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Red flags:
- Profit falling while capacity grows about 8% a year (April 2026 trading update; FY26 results, July 2026).
- Flight-only yield down 7% two reporting periods running (November 2025, July 2026).
- Return on capital employed down from 17% (three-year average quoted in November 2025) to 14.4% in FY26.
- Hotel cost inflation (about 6.5%) running ahead of package price (3%, of which 1 point is mix).
- Gatwick start-up costs, with profitability not expected until the year to March 2029.

Green flags:
- Strong own-cash position, an undrawn 500 million pound revolving credit facility extended to October 2030.
- Shareholder returns at record levels, with the share count falling: about 22 million shares bought back in FY26 and a further 250 million pounds under way to May 2027.
- Fleet renewal to the A321neo (232 seats against 189, lower seat cost; about 22% of the summer 2026 fleet).
- Industry-leading customer service and low cancellation rates, which support the package-holiday brand.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "Investing in price" and "investing in load factor" have become standing phrases. When a company describes price cuts as investments, it is telling you that it does not have the pricing power to hold fares.
- The new 2 times leverage target signals a shift from a cash-rich to a more geared capital structure as the Airbus order book is financed.
- The CFO's own-cash framing (1.2 billion pounds excluding customer advances) is a welcome bit of honesty that the headline net-cash figure hides.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: stable. Capital allocation is disciplined (buybacks at single-digit earnings multiples, fleet renewal, no acquisitions), and management is credible.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: Jet2's profit has stopped growing even as capacity grows. The investment case depends on Gatwick and the newer bases maturing into profit and on flight-only pricing stabilising. The interim results on 18 November 2026 are the next test of whether summer 2026 converted bookings into profit.

Moat: scale-cost plus brand (the integrated package-holiday model, about 80% direct distribution, customer-service reputation). It is real but narrow, and the evidence - return on capital falling from 17% to 14.4%, yields given away to fill seats - says it is being tested rather than widening. Our scan's return on invested capital of 6.4% sits near the cost of capital. Secular threat: manageable. AI-led travel search could change distribution over time, but management reports no impact so far and the direct-booking share is steady. The cheapness looks like a cyclical fear-print on a competitive, cost-inflated leisure market, not a structurally shrinking base - but the moat needs proof that pricing can hold.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Corteva (CTVA) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*Debate date 2026-11-16. Live price $9.075 (NYSE, USD; FMP quote 2026-11-16, down about 4% on the day and about 24% since the 2026-11-11 results).*

**Read this first.** The Corteva that trades under CTVA today is not the company in most of the screener's numbers. On 2026-10-01 Corteva spun off its seed business as Vylor (VYLR, one Vylor share per Corteva share). What is left is a pure crop-protection company (herbicides, insecticides, fungicides and biologicals) with about $7.6B of 2025 pro forma sales and about $1.27B of 2025 adjusted pro forma operating EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization; 8-K pro forma filing). The screener's fiscal-year figures (revenue $17.4B, EPS $1.60, P/FCF 2.3x, DCF fair value $39, the $30.73 consensus target) describe the combined company before the spin, and none of them can be used to value the stock at $9. The same is true of the "live corrections" balance sheet (debt $7.45B, cash $3.93B at 2026-09-30): that is the consolidated pre-spin balance sheet. New Corteva's own carve-out balance sheet at 2026-09-30 (8-K) shows cash of $1.72B (plus $0.42B restricted), short-term borrowings of $0.84B, long-term debt of $2.37B and a pension and retiree-benefit liability of $0.66B. On 2026-10-01 Vylor paid New Corteva $761M, which went straight to repaying a $600M revolver and $161M of commercial paper, so net debt after the spin is roughly $0.7-1.0B before the seasonal cash swing. The share count at the spin was 667.3M.

## 1. Narrative arc

- **Q3 2025 (2025-11-05) to Q2 2026 (2026-07-31): the combined company was on a roll.** The October 2025 split announcement was framed as "not that we believe things aren't going well today. They are." Guidance went up twice: 2025 EBITDA to $3.8-3.9B, then 2026 to $4.1-4.3B on 2026-07-31. Crop protection was described as delivering "top and bottom line growth... in what I'd still describe as less than ideal market conditions" (Q4 2025).
- **Brazil was a known, recurring soft spot.** Every call from Q4 2025 onward mentions "competitive pricing dynamics" in Latin America from Chinese generics. On 2026-07-31 Chuck Magro said high-single-digit price declines in Brazil were "not the new normal" and the channel was "healthy... we would not say it is oversupplied."
- **Q3 2026 (2026-11-12): first call as a stand-alone crop-protection company, under a new CEO (Luke Kissam) and a new CFO (Jeff Rudolph).** The tone changed completely. Latin America organic sales fell 31% in the quarter. Management said conditions "deteriorated sharply in the final weeks of the third quarter" and "we've continued to see negative developments since then." Full-year 2026 adjusted pro forma EBITDA guidance is now $1.100-1.125B, against the roughly $1.3B framed at the 2026-09-15 Investor Day, a cut of about 14% only eight weeks later.

## 2. Claims vs financials (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| "Differentiated" products drive the business (about two-thirds of the portfolio, 10-15% higher margins) | New-product volume +20% in Q3 2026 at stable price; Arylex and Pyraxalt each growing more than 20%, about $650M combined | **Holds.** This is the real asset. |
| The Brazil channel was healthy and not oversupplied (2026-07-31) | Q3 2026: "too much of the product we sold into the Brazil channel last year didn't go to ground" | **Contradicted.** Some 2025 sales were effectively pulled forward into the channel. Management owned this, which is the most important forensic finding here. |
| Investor Day 2026 EBITDA of about $1.3B; 2029 target $1.45-1.65B | Guidance cut to $1.10-1.125B on 2026-11-11; nine-month EBITDA $943M (flat), Q3 $222M (-17%), implied Q4 margin of about 7-9% | **Contradicted for 2026.** The 2029 bridge now starts from a lower base. |
| Cash on track for about $1.5B at year-end | Nine-month operating cash flow from continuing operations was -$1.24B (including large pension top-ups: the liability fell from $2.21B to $0.66B); the CFO deflected a direct question about roughly $800M of unexplained cash movement in Q3 | **Unverified.** A cash bridge is owed. |
| Little near-term patent exposure | "Nothing major that comes off... by the end of '28"; acetochlor (North America) and older Brazil molecules are already in their generic phase | **Plausible**, and consistent with pricing pressure being concentrated in named molecules. |

The scan's annual figures (EPS +23%, FCF +82%, gross margin 47%) belong to the combined seed-plus-crop-protection company. They do not describe this business. Seed carried the higher margins and the cash.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory - Declining

Through H1 2026 the tone was confident ("the company is slightly ahead", 2026-07-31). In Q3 2026 it turned defensive and cost-led: "Everything is on the table... if you're not making it and you're not selling it, we're looking to see what we need to do to reduce our cost." The new CEO said Brazil is "a top priority for me" but gave no quantified recovery path. The prepared remarks lean on "the demand is there; what has changed is when people buy", which is a destocking framing rather than a demand-loss framing. That may well be correct, but nobody has proved it yet.

## 4. Guidance credibility - Medium for the old team, Low so far for the new one

The combined company raised and beat guidance through 2025 and H1 2026 (the screener records 5 of 7 quarters beaten). The stand-alone company's first guidance, given at the 2026-09-15 Investor Day, was cut within eight weeks. That guidance was also set when, by management's own account, Brazil channel inventory was already too high, which suggests the problem was underestimated rather than hidden. Two securities-fraud "investigations" by plaintiff firms (2026-11-12 and 2026-11-13) followed the roughly 24% one-day drop. These are routine after a large drop and are not evidence in themselves.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

- **Cash** (KeyBanc, Q3 2026): where did about $800M go between pro forma Q2 and Q3? The answer was to refer to the filings.
- **Q4 implied margin** (KeyBanc): sales down only low-to-mid single digits but EBITDA margin around 7-9%. The answer was that pricing is down high single digits with flat volume, which signals that price, not just destocking, is the problem in Q4.
- **Brazil pricing** (Mizuho, every quarter): the "not the new normal" answer from 2026-07-31 did not hold up.
- **Patent cliffs** (JPMorgan): answered credibly.

## 6. Red and green flags

- Red (Q3 2026): channel overstock from 2025 sales admitted, and guidance cut eight weeks after Investor Day.
- Red (Q3 2026): Latin America organic sales -31%, and "negative developments since then" means Q4 risk remains open.
- Red (Q3 2026): the cash bridge was unexplained, and nine-month operating cash flow was -$1.24B.
- Red (2026-09-14): state attorneys general tried to block the separation over legacy PFAS ("forever chemical") liabilities. Those liabilities sit with New Corteva through EIDP, inside the 2021 cost-sharing agreement with Chemours and DuPont (Corteva's share is 29% above the first $300M, within a $2B combined DuPont-Corteva cap).
- Green (Q3 2026): new products +20% in volume at stable prices, North America volume +19%, EMEA organic +14%.
- Green (Q3 2026): productivity is ahead of plan, R&D spending went up while SG&A came down, and nothing major comes off patent before the end of 2028.
- Green (2026-10-23): first stand-alone dividend of $0.05 a quarter, a modest about 2% yield.

## 7. Hidden signals

- The vocabulary has shifted from "growth platforms" to "transformation office", "exit countries/products" and "sell straight through distribution". The new CEO is preparing a restructuring ($130-140M of 2026 restructuring charges for the manufacturing network).
- "We own that" on the Brazil inventory: candid, and it moves the blame to the 2025 commercial decisions of the prior regime.
- Robert King, the crop-protection head for four years, left with the Q2 2026 call. Every key voice is now new.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: deteriorating near term.** The single most important thing for the director: at about $9 the stock trades on roughly 7x 2026 trough EBITDA (enterprise value of about $8.0B including net debt, pension and minority interests), so the price already assumes a lot. The open question is whether the Brazil damage is a one-season channel destock, which would get EBITDA back toward $1.25-1.3B in 2027, or a structural reset of Latin American pricing from Chinese generics, which would leave EBITDA stuck near $1.0-1.1B. The Q4 2026 print and the first 2027 guide (expected early February 2027) settle it.

**Moat:** narrow but real. It rests on intangible and regulatory assets (patented actives and registrations; about two-thirds of the portfolio is differentiated, with a 12-active pipeline). Off-patent molecules erode on a schedule, and returns are thin: the combined company's ROIC was about 5% with heavy goodwill. The moat is stable, not widening. Generics replace actives as they age, and the pipeline replaces them in turn.

**Secular threat:** manageable. Chinese generic oversupply and the shift to biologicals are cyclical-to-structural pressures that the pipeline has historically offset. No terminal threat applies. The cheapness looks more like fear than a melting base, but the forensic flags above have to clear first.

The arithmetic decides the timing. picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Kunlun Energy Company Limited (0135.HK) — a deep dive on management and the setup

**Date of this review:** 9 November 2026 (continuing coverage; the committee last ruled on 2 November 2026, on a full debate dated 22 September 2026).
**Price used throughout:** HK$7.57 (live quote from the paid market-data service, 9 November 2026). Market value about HK$65.3 billion.
**Currency:** Kunlun reports in Chinese yuan and trades in Hong Kong dollars. At today's rate of 1 yuan = 1.1747 Hong Kong dollars, every accounting figure below has been converted before being compared with the share price.

**Limitation stated up front:** Kunlun holds no earnings call that any accessible source carries, and the paid market-data service has no transcript or company-specific news for this listing (both checked 9 November 2026). The web-search budget for this run was exhausted before any additional search could be made, so this review relies on the licensed financial statements, the live quote and peer quotes, and the verified findings of the 22 September review and its independent check. No management quote is invented to fill the gap. Kunlun reports half-yearly; no new financial period has been published since the half year to 30 June 2026.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Kunlun is the natural-gas arm of PetroChina, which owns about 54% of it. It sells gas through city pipelines and to industrial users, runs liquefied-natural-gas (LNG) receiving terminals and processing plants, and holds a small oil and gas production arm abroad. The story the company tells is consistent and unexciting: steady volume growth as China switches from coal to gas, conservative finance, and a rising dividend. What has quietly changed over three years is profitability. Revenue kept rising (188.96 billion yuan in 2025, up about 1%), but operating profit fell from 13.55 billion yuan in 2023 to 9.71 billion in 2025, a drop of about 28%. The narrative has shifted from growth to resilience — volumes and the balance sheet — because the margin story stopped working.

Since the last look on 2 November 2026 nothing new has been published: no results, no trading update, no capital-return announcement.

## 2. Claims versus the financials

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Volumes are still growing | Gas sales volume 30,156 million cubic metres in the first half of 2026, up 3.65% (company results, 25-26 August 2026) | Holds |
| The balance sheet is exceptionally strong | Cash and short-term investments 48.06 billion yuan against total debt 21.30 billion at 30 June 2026: net cash 26.76 billion; Moody's raised the issuer to A1 on 11 August 2026 | Holds |
| Earnings are improving | Attributable profit rose 3.1% in the first half to 3.26 billion yuan, but profit before tax was flat (6.69 billion versus 6.74 billion) and the gain came from minority shareholders taking a smaller share of a smaller result; earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation fell about 7-10% year on year depending on the data source | Richer than the numbers |
| Shareholder returns are rising | Interim dividend 0.1916 yuan, about 18% above the prior interim; forward run-rate about HK$0.389 a share, a 5.1% yield at HK$7.57 | Holds, from a low base |

Two corrections from the independent check of 22 September remain in force: the dividend yield is about 5.1%, not 5.3%, and the 5.07 billion yuan cash-flow figure is a half-year number, not a full year. The screener's own fair value and margin of safety compare a yuan model output with a Hong Kong dollar price and should be ignored; its return-on-equity and return-on-capital figures are roughly double the true values of about 7.9% and 5.8%.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

No call exists to read tone from. Judged by actions: stable and defensive. Payout rising, no buyback, no special distribution, cash still accumulating. Trajectory: stable in posture, declining in profitability.

## 4. Guidance credibility

Kunlun does not publish numeric earnings guidance. The screener records 0 of 2 recent periods beating estimates, and earnings per share fell 13% in 2025. Volume targets have broadly been met. Reliability: medium — conservative on balance sheet, unreliable as a signal of margin direction.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

The questions analysts cannot get answered are the same as in September: when, if ever, the 26.76 billion yuan net cash pile is returned to shareholders; how far the regulated spread between imported gas cost and the residential selling price can fall; and whether the parent will let Kunlun distribute more than about half its earnings. The published consensus price target of about HK$8.47 from seven analysts (as gathered on 22 September) sits close to this committee's base case, so the street already sees roughly what we see.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

- Red: operating profit down 28% from 2023 to 2025 on rising revenue (annual reports).
- Red: the first-half 2026 earnings rise was a minority-share effect, not operational (results, August 2026).
- Red: cash earning about 1.4% a year while a 54% state owner decides its use.
- Green: net cash of 26.76 billion yuan, about 48% of market value (30 June 2026).
- Green: Moody's A1 upgrade on 11 August 2026.
- Green: interim dividend up about 18% (August 2026); the dividend goes to holders on 26 November 2026.

## 7. Hidden signals

The share price has gone nowhere for seven weeks: HK$7.55 on 22 September, HK$7.575 on 2 November, HK$7.57 today, with the 50-day average at HK$7.56. Peers have kept falling — China Gas Holdings is at HK$5.05 near its year low of HK$4.81, China Resources Gas at HK$16.57 and ENN Energy at HK$49.08, both below their 200-day averages. Kunlun's stillness while its group de-rates is the cash pile and the parent's ownership acting as ballast, not a re-rating.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict for the director

Trajectory: deteriorating. Profitability has fallen for two years, and returns on capital sit below the cost of capital. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: the discount is in the cash and the assets, not in the earnings or the dividend, and the cash has a 54% gatekeeper with no stated intention of releasing it.

Moat: a regulatory-licence and scale moat in pipeline gas distribution — real, but its returns are falling, so it is eroding rather than wide. Secular threat: manageable. Gas is the transition fuel in China, displacing coal; electrification is a decades-long threat to residential and industrial gas demand, not a near-term terminal one. The cheapness is neither a pure fear-print nor a value trap: it is a fair price for a low-return franchise with an idle cash pile, and becomes attractive only at a lower price or a capital-return decision.

# HBR.L - Harbour Energy plc - Forensic dossier (2026-11-10)

Price used: 268.2 pence (London listing, FMP quote 2026-11-10). Sources: half-year 2026 results call (2026-08-06), full-year 2025 call (2026-03-05), earlier calls (2025-03-06, 2025-08-07), and the trading and operations update of 2026-11-05.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
Harbour has told the same story for two years: buy scale and diversify away from the UK North Sea, then run the portfolio for cash. The Wintershall Dea deal (2024) gave it Norway, Germany, Argentina and Mexico; LLOG (US Gulf, from February 2026) and Waldorf (UK, from July 2026) added more; Indonesia and Vietnam were sold. The story has moved from "integration" (2025) to "cash returns and deleveraging" (2026). Management says the portfolio is now weighted toward lower-cost, lower-tax basins - Norway alone was 177,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day (boe/d) of the 501,000 boe/d nine-month average, more than the UK's 142,000.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
- Production: claimed record output above 500,000 boe/d at the half year; the 2026-11-05 update confirms 501,000 boe/d for nine months, and guidance was raised to 500,000-505,000 (from 490,000-500,000). Claim matches the numbers.
- Free cash flow (cash left after capex and tax): outlook went $1.8B (2026-08-06) to about $2.6B (2026-11-05). The CFO said on 2026-08-06 that about $0.5B of the earlier raise came from oil and gas prices; the November raise is again mostly prices (pre-hedge realised oil $92 a barrel, European gas $17.1/mscf year to date), partly offset by a working-capital build and hedging losses. So most of the upside is the commodity tape, not the business.
- Accounting profit is weak: net loss of $186M in 2025 and a trailing loss per share of about $0.08, because UK Energy Profits Levy (a windfall tax running to 2030) and heavy depreciation from the acquisitions eat reported earnings. Cash is the better lens here, and cash is strong (trailing free cash flow $3.24B to 2026-06-30, which includes working-capital timing).
- Balance sheet: net debt fell to $5.1B at end-September from $5.4B at 30 June (excluding about $0.86B of leases); leverage 0.6x, Moody's Baa2 stable, the $1.0B LLOG bridge loan fully repaid, the $3.0B credit facility extended to 2031. The scan's Altman-Z of 0.9 (a bankruptcy-risk score) reflects big decommissioning provisions and acquisition goodwill, not a funding problem.
- Unit operating cost drifted up: $13.9/boe in Q3 versus $12.8 a year earlier; full-year guidance about $14.5/boe held.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Calm and repetitive in a good way. Linda Cook and Alexander Krane avoid production promises beyond the year and frame returns as "minimum dividend plus top-ups". Confidence has risen across 2026 as guidance was raised twice; there is no defensive language. The one guarded area is long-dated growth (Zama in Mexico, first oil "towards the end of 2029"; Kan; Southern Energy LNG in Argentina around year-end 2027).

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Good. In 2026 production guidance was raised twice and free cash flow guidance raised twice; capex guidance ($2.2-2.4B) unchanged; cost guidance held. The beats are partly price-driven, but the operational parts (production, project timing - Skarv satellites started a year early in August 2026) were delivered.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- How much of the cash flow raise is price versus performance (asked 2026-08-06; the answer conceded most was price).
- Dividend versus buyback: management prefers buybacks, partly to absorb share blocks sold by the former owner BASF (stake down from about 47% to about 16%, including a directed buyback in September).
- Zama timing and the next wave of project approvals.
- Unanswered in the material read: post-2026 production profile and the size of the after-tax decommissioning bill.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
Red: reported losses despite record output; UK windfall tax to 2030; rising unit costs; a natural-decline asset base that needs constant reinvestment or deals; free cash flow heavily geared to a Hormuz-driven oil and European gas premium that can unwind; large decommissioning liabilities; hedging that gives away some upside.
Green: net debt falling fast ($1.0B repaid since LLOG); investment-grade rating; buybacks of $550M year to date, more than 9% of the share count; BASF overhang mostly cleared; diversified across Norway, UK, Argentina, US Gulf, Mexico.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
- Q4 2026 tax payments of about $1.8B are flagged, so year-end net debt will not fall as fast as the headline free cash flow suggests.
- The company is buying back stock instead of raising the dividend - a sign management thinks the shares are cheap, and also a way to keep the payout flexible if prices fall.
- Hurricane Isaias and maintenance hit October output (511,000 boe/d still high) - US Gulf adds hurricane risk the old UK book did not have.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
A competent, disciplined operator using a commodity windfall to cut debt and shrink the share count. The equity is cheap on cash flow, but it is a leveraged claim on oil and European gas prices with a declining asset base and a hostile UK tax regime - not a compounder. Value is real at the right price; the price paid matters more than the narrative.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving.
