# Polaris Media ASA (POL.OL) - deep dive on management and the setup

Prepared 2026-11-16. Live price used: NOK 60.00 (Oslo listing, FMP quote, 2026-11-16).

Source note: no earnings-call transcript exists in FMP for this Oslo listing, and none could be found on the web. This dossier is built from the company's own quarterly press releases (Q4 2025 published 2026-02-12, Q2 2026 published 2026-08-14), third-party summaries of the Q3 2026 report (published 2026-11-05), the dividend notice for fiscal 2025, and FMP's quarterly statements through 2026-09-30. Quotes are from the press releases, not from a call. Where a figure comes from an AI-generated summary rather than the filing itself, it is flagged.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Polaris Media is a Norwegian and Swedish regional newspaper group (Adresseavisen, the Polaris Media Nord-Vestlandet / Sor / Nord-Norge titles, and Stampen Media in western Sweden, now 100% owned). Over the past two years the story has moved through three chapters:

- 2024-2025, "cash out the stake": the share price story was dominated by the group's holding in Schibsted's marketplace business (now Vend Marketplaces). Sales of those shares funded a NOK 1.0 billion dividend proposed in Q3 2024, a record payout in 2025 (about NOK 1.1 billion in total, including an extra NOK 20.40 per share), repayment of all bank debt and the buy-out of the rest of Stampen.
- 2025, "fix Sweden": Q3 2025 carried NOK 27 million of Swedish restructuring charges (68 positions cut, targeting about SEK 88 million of annual savings) and the exit from Swedish parcel distribution, completed 31 May 2026.
- 2026, "earnings growth from digital subscriptions": the last Vend shares were sold in June 2026 for NOK 759 million net, and management's message shifted fully to the operating business: "Veksten i digitale brukerinntekter er fortsatt den viktigste driveren for inntektsvekst" (digital user revenue growth remains the most important revenue driver, Q2 2026 release). A CEO succession was announced in September 2026: Oyulf Hjertenes takes over in Q1 2027.

The holding-company angle is now gone. What remains is a plain regional publisher with a cash pile.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Digital user revenue is the growth engine | Q2 2026: digital user revenues +16%, digital subscriptions 492,500 (+8%), 77% of the base. Q3 2026: adjusted digital revenue NOK 413m, +10% (summary). | Matches |
| Cost cuts lift earnings | Q2 2026 operating costs -3%, Sweden -9% in local currency. Q3 2026 operating costs NOK 752m vs NOK 803m. Adjusted EBITDA year to date NOK 276m, +32%, margin 10.3%. | Matches |
| Group revenue is growing | Revenue has been flat for five years (NOK 3.47bn in 2021, NOK 3.43bn in 2025). Q2 2026 revenue -2% (NOK 902m); Q3 2026 broadly flat. Print advertising and print subscriptions are still shrinking. | Story richer than numbers: this is a margin story, not a growth story |
| Strong balance sheet | 2026-09-30: cash and short-term bond funds NOK 840m, bank debt about NOK 2m, lease liabilities NOK 530m. Net cash before leases about NOK 838m (about NOK 17 per share); after leases about NOK 309m. | Matches, with a caveat: about NOK 720m of current liabilities is mostly prepaid subscriptions, so part of the cash is customers' money that recurs rather than spare capital |
| Earnings quality | Reported EPS has swung wildly: NOK 13.84 in 2024 (gains on the marketplace shares), NOK 0.15 in 2025, trailing twelve months (TTM) NOK 1.37 to Q3 2026. The operating line is cleaner: TTM EBIT about NOK 104m on FMP's data, Q3 2026 EBIT NOK 58-65m. | The trailing EPS is real but small; the 2024 figure was a one-off |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rising. Q4 2025 was headlined "Sterk resultatforbedring" (strong earnings improvement); Q2 2026 "Sterk resultatvekst" (strong earnings growth) with growth in both countries; Q3 2026 delivered the highest adjusted EBITDA margin for a third quarter since 2021 (summary). The language is consistently defensive on revenue ("the advertising market remains challenging", "tight cost focus") and confident on margins. Outlook for 2027 (Q3 2026, summary): user revenue growth in both countries, advertising marginally up in Norway and slightly down in Sweden.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

The company gives no numeric guidance, so there is little to test. The qualitative calls (Swedish savings, digital growth, cost discipline) have been delivered across the last four quarters: adjusted EBITDA +54% in Q4 2025, +112% in Q1 2026, +23% in Q2 2026 and +22% in Q3 2026. The screener shows 4 of 7 quarters beaten (57%), which mostly reflects the noisy reported EPS. Reliability: Medium-High.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

No call transcript is available, so this section rests on the releases. The open questions any analyst would push on: (a) what the board does with roughly NOK 840m of liquid assets now that the Vend stake is gone (extra dividend, buy-backs or acquisitions; the September 2026 buy-out of the minority in Polaris Media Sor shows acquisitions are on the table); (b) how long print decline keeps offsetting digital growth at the revenue line; (c) what the new CEO changes from Q1 2027. No sell-side price target for this listing could be found on FMP or the web.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Green:
- Adjusted EBITDA up 32% year to date to September 2026 on flat revenue: the cost base is genuinely lower (Q3 2026).
- Digital subscriptions growing 8% with digital now 77% of the base (Q2 2026).
- Debt-free apart from leases; ordinary dividend raised to NOK 3.30 for fiscal 2025 (paid 20 May 2026) from NOK 2.00.
- Margins held through the 2021-22 inflation (gross margin 80.4% in 2019 to 83.9% in 2022).

Red:
- Revenue has not grown in five years; group margin is only about 10% even after the cuts.
- The cash return on the operating business is thin: return on invested capital about 1.5% on the screener's numbers (distorted by goodwill and by the cash pile, but not by much).
- The large one-off gains are finished; there is no second marketplace stake to sell.
- CEO transition in Q1 2027 adds execution uncertainty.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- Vocabulary moved from "financial flexibility" (2024-25, when the Vend shares were the story) to "resultatvekst i mediehusene" (earnings growth in the media houses) in 2026: management now wants to be judged on operations.
- The proceeds of the last Vend sale were parked "in low-risk bond funds and bank deposits" (Q2 2026) rather than paid straight out, which suggests the board is keeping the option to buy more local titles, as it did with Polaris Media Sor in September 2026.
- Insider buying is nil on the screener (buy ratio 0.00).

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: strengthening at the margin line, flat at the revenue line. The single most important thing to weigh: the stock at NOK 60 already prices the recovery. Market value is about NOK 2.94bn; take out about NOK 838m of net cash and NOK 288m of associate holdings and add back the NOK 530m lease liability, and the operating business is valued at roughly 6.4 times TTM adjusted EBITDA of about NOK 377m (an IFRS-16 figure, meaning before lease costs) - a normal multiple for a regional publisher, not a discount.

Moat: intangible brand plus local-scale. These are local news monopolies in Trondheim, the Norwegian west and north coast and Gothenburg, with loyal paying subscribers - a narrow but real moat. Margins are rising, not falling, so the moat is stable rather than eroding. The secular threat is material but not terminal: print revenue keeps shrinking and search/AI tools compete for readers' attention and for advertising, but paying digital subscribers for local news have proven sticky. The cheapness the screener flags (DCF and Graham fair values far below the price) is an artefact of the depressed reported earnings; on a cleaned-up basis the stock is roughly fairly priced, neither a fear-print nor a value trap.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

CECONOMY runs MediaMarkt and Saturn, Europe's largest consumer-electronics chain (about 1,000 stores, 11 countries, roughly EUR 24 billion of sales). picks.thesis_evidence: The operating thesis holds: preliminary fiscal 2025/26 adjusted operating profit of about EUR 515 million (October 2026) beat the EUR 500 million target; the June 2026 quarter grew sales 9.8% (reported August 2026); EU approval of the JD.com purchase came on 3 November 2026 with closing expected by 12 November 2026. The investment case for a minority holder is a separate matter: the payout depends on JD.com's undated delisting offer, which the price already discounts.

CECONOMY earns cash now rather than on a long-dated story, but its margins dipped in the 2021-22 inflation (gross margin down 2.1 points) and the price is set by the deal, not the macro. No pass-through evidence in the transcript.
picks.entry_plain: no entry - pass for now

picks.bull_thesis: Chery has become one of the world's most successful car exporters, and the profit numbers now show it. Third-quarter 2026 revenue was RMB 97.9B (renminbi), up 34% year on year, with attributable profit of RMB 5.40B, up 16%, and operating profit of RMB 5.99B, its best quarter. Gross margin (sales minus the direct cost of building the cars, as a share of sales) rose from 13.0% in the first half of 2025 to 16.3% in Q3 2026 because overseas cars earn more than cars sold in China. Group exports reached 1.75M cars in the first ten months of 2026, up 65%, already more than all of 2025, and October exports alone rose about 59%. New-energy cars (battery-electric and plug-in hybrid) were 41% of first-half revenue, up from 26%, so the business is not stuck on the petrol side of the electric shift. Borrowings fell from RMB 15.9B to about RMB 9B in 2026. At HK$22.46 the shares cost about 6 times this year's expected profit (GF Securities forecasts RMB 19.0B for 2026 and RMB 21.8B for 2027, note dated 2026-11-04) and sit near the 52-week low of HK$21.74, after the end of the 12-month IPO lock-up (the window pre-listing holders were barred from selling) around 2026-09-25 added supply. If exports keep growing and margins hold near 16%, a re-rating toward 8 times profit, still below most listed Chinese carmakers, gives a value in the high HK$30s, which is where the covering brokers sit (CICC HK$40 on 2026-04-29, CITIC Securities HK$46 on 2026-05-12, GF Securities HK$32.06 in November 2026). Conditions: export growth stays above 30%, gross margin stays above 15%, and no major destination market (Russia, the Middle East, Latin America, Europe) shuts the door.
picks.bear_thesis: The cheapness is partly an illusion and partly a fair price for real risks. First, the much-quoted net cash of about RMB 110B (cash and short-term investments of RMB 122.9B less RMB 13.0B of debt and leases at 2026-09-30) is not spare money: the company owes suppliers RMB 158.8B in trade and bills payable, and liabilities are about 79% of assets. That cash is supplier credit, and it would shrink if volumes fell or if Beijing enforced its 2025 push for carmakers to pay suppliers within 60 days. Second, earnings quality is mixed: about RMB 7.4B of the last four quarters' RMB 18.5B net profit came from outside the core business (currency gains, interest, joint ventures), and the first-half 2026 profit fell 11.7% when currency gains shrank. Third, the home market is collapsing for Chery: October 2026 domestic sales were roughly 95,000 against about 155,000 a year earlier, down close to 40%, so the whole growth case now rests on exports, which are exposed to tariffs, local-content rules, Russia's rising import fees and currency swings - the risks GF Securities itself lists first. Fourth, the end of the IPO lock-up around 2026-09-25 created a supply of shares that may still be coming to market, and the stock keeps making new lows. If exports stall and margins return to the 13-14% of 2025, profit could fall back toward RMB 14B, and at a distressed 5.5 times that is about HK$15.6 a share. The cash-flow record is also thin: free cash flow (cash from operations minus capital spending) fell from RMB 41.9B in 2024, flattered by a jump in payables, to RMB 12.9B in 2025, and our data feed has no 2026 cash-flow figures to check.
picks.consensus_delta: The market is pricing Chery as if its cash were spare and its earnings at risk of collapse - the shares are worth about the same as the headline net cash. We disagree on both halves. The cash is mostly supplier credit and deserves little standalone value, so the stock is not the near-free option some screens suggest (our screen's 369% margin of safety and RMB 78.7B net-debt figure are both overstated). But the earnings are better than the price implies: core operating profit is at a record (RMB 5.99B in Q3 2026) and gross margin is rising on exports. Brokers still sit at HK$32-46 (GF Securities HK$32.06, CICC HK$40, CITIC Securities HK$46); we think the lower end is the right anchor, because those higher targets were set in April-May 2026 before the domestic slump deepened.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) holds three threats. First, more share supply: pre-listing holders became free to sell around 2026-09-25, and the stock has kept making new lows, so selling may continue into early 2027. Second, the domestic market: Chinese car demand is weak and Chery's home sales fell close to 40% in October 2026, so a price war at home could eat into the margin gains won abroad. Third, trade policy and currency: any new tariff or local-content rule in a big export market, or a stronger renminbi, would hit the only growth engine. There is no debt wall - borrowings are only about RMB 9B - and no forced liquidation risk, but a working-capital squeeze (paying suppliers faster) could drain cash quickly.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure comes from the IPO lock-up ending around 2026-09-25 (secondary source; the size of the unlock is not verified). Cornerstone investors took about US$587M of the US$1.2B IPO. Because most pre-listing shares are unlisted domestic shares, how much can actually be sold in Hong Kong depends on conversion approvals, which we could not confirm. There is no dividend-cut or index-deletion pressure. The shares at HK$22.46 are below the HK$30.75 IPO price, so IPO buyers are under water, which can add selling on rallies.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Buy now. Chery is cheap on its earnings, about 6 times this year's expected profit at HK$22.46, while its core profit and margins are at records on the back of fast export growth (Q3 2026 operating profit RMB 5.99B, gross margin 16.3%). The thesis holds. Our fair value is HK$29.0, about 29% above the price, which clears the 20% discount we require in today's macro backdrop. We deliberately do not count the headline RMB 110B net cash as spare money, since it is funded by supplier credit, and that is why our fair value sits well below the screen's figures and the broker targets. Conviction is moderate, not high: profit leans on non-operating income, the home market is falling sharply, exports carry trade-policy risk, and share supply from the lock-up expiry may keep pressure on the price for a few months. Size it as a moderate position and re-check after the full-year results in March 2027.
picks.forcing_function: No single dated event forces a re-rating. The most likely drivers are, in order: (1) full-year 2026 results around late March 2027, which should show profit near RMB 19B and could carry a larger dividend; (2) monthly export figures that keep printing growth above 30%; (3) the end of lock-up selling. A share buyback or a higher payout policy would be the clearest trigger, but none has been announced.

# Chery Automobile (9973.HK) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-16. Live price HK$22.46 (Hong Kong listing, FMP quote). Company reports in renminbi (RMB); HK$1 = RMB 0.8478 today.

**Source caveat.** No earnings-call transcript exists in our data feed for this ticker, and none was found on the open web. This dossier therefore tests management's published statements (the interim report of 2026-08-20 and the third-quarter release reported late October 2026, as summarised by CnEVPost and a GF Securities note dated 2026-11-04) and the monthly sales releases against the reported financials (FMP quarterly statements to 2026-09-30). No quotes below are from a call; quoted phrases come from the published reports.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Chery listed in Hong Kong on 2025-09-25 (a US$1.2B IPO, the largest carmaker IPO of 2025) on a two-part story: "new energy and globalization". Fourteen months later the second half of that story has taken over completely. In the first half of 2026 overseas revenue was RMB 98.97B, up 51% and about 69% of the total, while revenue from petrol-engine cars fell about 25%. By October 2026 the wider Chery Group exported 200,618 cars in the month, up about 59%, roughly 68% of everything it sold. Domestic sales in the same month were roughly 95,000 against about 155,000 a year earlier, a fall of close to 40%.

So the business has turned from a Chinese carmaker that also exports into an exporter that also sells in China. The battery-electric and hybrid half of the story is real (new-energy revenue of RMB 59.3B in the first half, up 64%, 41% of revenue), but much of that growth is also sold abroad.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim (date) | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Overseas expansion lifts margins (interim report, 2026-08-20) | Gross margin 13.0% (H1 2025) -> 16.1% (H1 2026) -> 16.3% (Q3 2026). FY2025 annual gross margin was 13.8%. | Matches |
| Profit dip in H1 2026 was "mainly due to factors outside core operations" | H1 attributable profit RMB 8.57B, down 11.7%, while other income and gains fell 27% to RMB 6.03B (mostly lower foreign-exchange gains). Gross profit rose 25%. | Matches - but it also shows how much of past profit was non-operating |
| Growth recovers in the second half | Q3 2026 revenue RMB 97.9B (+34% year on year), attributable profit RMB 5.40B (+16%), operating profit RMB 5.99B, the best quarter on record. | Matches |
| Strong balance sheet, net cash | Cash plus short-term investments RMB 122.9B against borrowings and leases of RMB 13.0B at 2026-09-30, so net cash of about RMB 110B. But trade and bills payable alone are RMB 158.8B, and liabilities are 79% of assets. Receivables, inventory and prepayments total about RMB 117B against roughly RMB 226B of operating liabilities. | Partly - the cash is mostly supplier credit, not spare money |
| Free cash flow | FY2024 free cash flow (cash from operations minus capital spending) RMB 41.9B, inflated by a RMB 25.5B rise in payables; FY2025 RMB 12.9B. Our feed shows zero for the last four quarters, which is a missing-data gap, not a real zero. | Unverified for 2026 |

The pattern is the usual one for Chinese carmakers: the headline cash pile is funded by paying suppliers slowly. That float is stable while volumes grow, but it would shrink if volumes fell or if Beijing's 2025 push for carmakers to pay suppliers within 60 days is enforced harder.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Stable to rising. The interim report talks of the company continuing to "advance its global expansion" and that it "will expand its product lineup, strengthen brand positioning and increase investment" - offensive language, backed by research spending up 28% in the first half and up again in Q3 (RMB 4.37B). There is no defensive turn toward cost-cutting. Note that we cannot judge how management answers hard questions, because no call transcript is available.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Chery gives no formal profit guidance. The group set a 2025 export target and beat it, and in 2026 group exports to October (1.75M, up 65%) already exceeded the whole of 2025. Delivery on volume ambitions is good. Profit delivery is lumpier: earnings per share fell in H1 2026 on lower currency gains before recovering in Q3. Reliability: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without a transcript we infer them from broker notes and the numbers: (1) the domestic collapse - October domestic volume down close to 40% - and whether price cuts at home will follow; (2) the share of profit coming from currency gains, interest and joint ventures; (3) trade-policy risk on the export engine (tariffs, local-content rules, Russia's rising recycling fees, currency swings), which GF Securities lists first among its risks; (4) the payables float and supplier-payment rules.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: domestic sales down roughly 40% year on year in October 2026 (group data, 2026-11-01).
- Red: non-operating income was about RMB 7.4B of the last four quarters' RMB 18.5B net profit (Q4 2025 to Q3 2026), and the currency-gain part of that will not repeat.
- Red: liabilities at about 79% of assets; the net cash rests on RMB 159B of payables.
- Red: the 12-month IPO lock-up for pre-listing holders ended about 2026-09-25 (secondary source, not checked against the prospectus). The shares have since fallen to a 52-week low (HK$21.74).
- Green: gross margin up three points in a year on export mix, now 16.3% (Q3 2026).
- Green: Q3 2026 operating profit RMB 5.99B, up about 38% year on year; borrowings cut from RMB 15.9B to about RMB 9B during 2026.
- Green: exports up about 59% in October 2026, new-energy sales over 100,000 a month for seven months running.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The reporting emphasis has shifted from "five brands" and domestic share to overseas plants (three of twelve major bases are now abroad) and new-energy revenue mix. Petrol-car revenue is shrinking fast at home and being replaced abroad, which makes Chery a bet that emerging markets keep buying Chinese cars for longer than China itself does. Joint-venture income fell 38% in the first half, a quiet sign that the legacy partnerships matter less.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: turning, from a domestic carmaker to an export-led one. The single most important thing to weigh: the stock looks like it trades at about the value of its cash (market value about RMB 110B against net cash of about RMB 110B), but that cash is supplier credit. Value it on earnings, not on the cash pile. On earnings it costs about 6 times this year's expected profit, which is cheap but not free for a business whose profit depends on export trade policy.

Moat: narrow, from scale and cost. Chery is one of the lowest-cost car producers in the world, and returns are rising (gross margin up, return on equity high on a thin equity base, return on invested capital about 9%). It has no pricing power at home. Secular threat: manageable. The shift to electric cars is the force that could hurt a petrol-heavy maker, but Chery's new-energy share is rising fast (41% of revenue), so the cheapness looks more like fear of the Chinese car sector, export tariffs and share overhang than a shrinking business.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

Q3 2026 (quarter ended 2026-09-30): revenue RMB 97.9B up 34%, operating profit RMB 5.99B, attributable profit RMB 5.40B up 16%, gross margin 16.3% against 13.0% in H1 2025. Inflation resilience cannot be measured from its accounts (listed too recently), and there is no pass-through evidence in the transcript because none was available.
picks.entry_plain: buy at today's price

picks.bull_thesis: Teladoc is a solvent, cash-generative virtual-care platform priced as if its decline will continue, and the latest quarter (reported 2026-10-28) suggests both halves are stabilizing. Integrated Care, the employer and health-plan business that serves over 100 million covered members, grew 2025 segment revenue 3.3% to $1.58 billion with adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, excluding stock pay and one-offs) of $239 million at a 15% margin, and in Q3 2026 its revenue landed near the top of guidance with margin above it. Chronic-care enrollment has turned back up on multi-condition bundles, and Teladoc 1, a whole-person care model for cardiometabolic populations launching broadly in January 2027, gives the segment its first genuinely new product in years. In BetterHelp, the consumer therapy business, the move to insurance is working faster than planned: insurance revenue went from $13 million in all of 2025 to $32 million in Q3 2026 alone, weekly covered sessions reached about 27,000 (an annualized run rate over $140 million versus a 2026 exit target of $125 million set in April), and Q3 cash-pay revenue came in better than feared. Consolidated adjusted EBITDA rose about 14% year over year in Q3 to $79 million, GAAP earnings guidance was raised, and the company holds $850 million of cash against a net debt of $185 million (0.5x trailing adjusted EBITDA). If BetterHelp revenue bottoms in 2027 as insurance offsets cash-pay, consolidated revenue stops shrinking, free cash flow can move from about $150 million toward $200 million, and the convertible notes due June 2027 are retired largely from cash, leaving a debt-light company. On that path, a mid-teens multiple of free cash flow, or 8.5x Integrated Care EBITDA plus a modest value for an insured BetterHelp, supports roughly $13 a share. Conditions: Integrated Care organic growth turns positive; BetterHelp total revenue declines shrink each quarter through 2027; the June 2027 maturity is handled without a dilutive equity raise.
picks.bear_thesis: The screener makes Teladoc look far cheaper than it is. Its 5.4x price to free cash flow rests on a data-feed figure of $233 million for the trailing year that ignores roughly $30-42 million a quarter of capitalized software; on the company's own definition free cash flow was $85.4 million for the first nine months of 2026 (down from $113.5 million a year earlier) and is guided to $135-165 million for the year, and stock pay of roughly $45-55 million a year sits on top of that. At $8.60 the enterprise is worth about $1.75 billion, or about 11-12x real free cash flow and 15-16x after stock pay, for a company whose revenue has fallen three years running ($2.60 billion in 2023 to a guided $2.39-2.44 billion in 2026). The Integrated Care growth is largely acquired (about 2.1 of the 3.3 points of 2025 growth), and the shift from subscription fees to pay-per-visit is effectively a lasting price cut on the core product, with the promised turn to a tailwind already pushed to the end of 2026. BetterHelp's cash-pay base keeps falling (paying users down 6% in Q4 2025, with US users down low double digits), insurance carries lower gross margins, and the April 2026 outlook was cut only three months later on 2026-07-29, so management's multi-quarter view has not earned trust. The whole $998 million convertible stack is due June 2027 against $850 million of cash; a refinancing in a positive-real-rate market adds interest cost that did not exist at a 1.25% coupon. Insiders sold 194,162 shares on 19 open-market sales with no buys, the finance chief seat was vacant for most of a year, and the company has repeatedly written down goodwill. After a 26% one-day rally on the Q3 beat, the stock sits 80% up its 52-week range and above its 200-day average, so the easy re-rate is already in the price. Confirmation of the bear case: BetterHelp revenue declines that do not narrow in Q4 2026 and Q1 2027 results, an Integrated Care organic decline, or a refinancing that adds equity dilution.
picks.consensus_delta: The street is not badly wrong here, and after the Q3 rally it is roughly right. The thin consensus target of $9.30 (median $9.00, only two new targets last quarter, the latest $11.00 and $9.00 on 2026-11-02) sits close to our $9.0 fair value. Where we disagree is with the screener's own optics, not the analysts: the 5.4x price to free cash flow and the 50% discount-to-value from a discounted-cash-flow model both rest on a trailing free-cash-flow figure of $233 million that omits capitalized software. The company's own guide is $135-165 million for 2026. On that basis the market is pricing Teladoc as a flat-to-shrinking cash stream at a fair multiple, not pricing in terminal decline. The deep-value question - is the street pricing terminal decline into stable earnings power - is answered no: earnings power is stable at best, and the price already credits it.
picks.valley_of_death: The months just ahead carry three risks. First, the June 2027 maturity of about $1.0 billion of 1.25% convertible notes: cash of $850 million plus perhaps $70-100 million of free cash flow by then roughly covers it, but leaves the company with little cash, so a new loan or bond at market rates is likely and any equity-linked refinancing would dilute holders. Second, the Q4 2026 and Q1 2027 results (expected late February and late April 2027) will show whether BetterHelp's cash-pay decline keeps narrowing now that advertising has been cut; a renewed decline would undo the Q3 relief. Third, Integrated Care membership is guided lower in 2026 as Affordable Care Act subsidies and Medicaid changes shrink health-plan enrollment, and Teladoc 1 contributes little revenue before 2028 by management's own account. None of these threatens solvency, but each can push the shares back toward the $6.70 level where they traded in late July 2026.
picks.positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling pressure in view. Teladoc pays no dividend, so there is no yield base to flush; the convertible notes are struck far above the share price, so convert-arbitrage hedging is not a meaningful driver. The realistic seller at our level is a sector or style sell-off in small-cap digital health or a give-back of the 26% post-earnings rally, the same kind of move that took the stock to $6.70 in late July 2026 and to a 52-week low of $4.40. Insider selling (19 open-market sales, no buys) is steady supply rather than a flush.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near $7.45, which a sector-wide sell-off in small-cap digital health, or a give-back of the post-earnings rally, could deliver. The thesis holds: Teladoc is a solvent, cash-generative virtual-care company whose employer and health-plan business is stable and whose consumer therapy arm is being steadied by insurance, and the Q3 2026 results on 2026-10-28 backed that up with adjusted EBITDA up about 14% and insurance revenue ahead of plan. But at $8.60 the price already credits it. Our fair value is about $9.0 a share by its parts (Integrated Care at about 7x adjusted EBITDA, BetterHelp at about 4x, less $185 million of net debt and some refinancing cost), cross-checked at about 11x the company's own free cash flow of roughly $150 million. That is only about 5% above today's price, well short of the 20% discount we require in the current reflation backdrop, while the adverse case of about $6.0 is 30% lower. The main correction to the screener is that its 5.4x price-to-free-cash-flow reading counts $233 million of cash flow the company does not report; after capitalized software and stock pay, the stock is fairly priced for a business whose revenue is still shrinking and whose entire $1.0 billion of convertible debt matures in June 2027. The moat is narrow but stable, and the shift to pay-per-visit pricing is a lasting, material pressure rather than a terminal one. We would buy at $7.45, where the base case offers about 21% upside; until then this is a watch, not a buy.
picks.forcing_function: No single dated event forces a re-rating up. The dated items are the Q4 2026 results (late February 2027), Teladoc 1's broad availability (January 2027) and the June 2027 convertible maturity. A clean refinancing plus a BetterHelp revenue line that stops falling in 2027 results would be the combination that lifts the multiple; a failure on either is more likely to force a re-rating down.

# Teladoc Health (TDOC) - a deep dive on management and the setup

Prepared 2026-11-16. Sources: five earnings calls (Q3 2025 through Q3 2026, the latest on 2026-10-28), the screener's financial block, and the FMP filings feed (quarterly statements through 2026-09-30). Live price used: $8.60 (NYSE, USD, 2026-11-16).

**Takeaway.** Teladoc is a cash-generative but shrinking virtual-care company in the middle of two business-model changes at once: its employer and health-plan business (Integrated Care) is moving from flat monthly subscription fees to paying per visit, and its consumer therapy business (BetterHelp) is moving from cash-pay customers to insurance. Integrated Care is stable and its profit is growing; BetterHelp's cash-pay base is still melting and the insurance replacement, while growing fast, is lower-margin. The screener's headline cheapness (5.4x price to free cash flow) overstates the case: on the company's own definition free cash flow is about $135-165 million this year, not the $233 million the data feed shows, and roughly $1.0 billion of convertible notes come due in June 2027.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-29):** the story was "execution" - revenue and adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, excluding stock pay and one-offs) above the guidance midpoint, the shift to visit-based pricing ("over 50% of our U.S. virtual care revenues" now visit-based), and BetterHelp's brand-new insurance offering, live in 7 states after the UpLift acquisition. CFO Mala Murthy was on her last call.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-26):** full-year 2025 revenue of $2.53 billion, down 1.5%; adjusted EBITDA $281 million; free cash flow $167 million after retiring $550 million of converts in June 2025. The emphasis moved to AI ("Pulse" data platform, "Prism" care platform) and to BetterHelp insurance, guided to $75-90 million of 2026 revenue with a ~$100 million exit run rate. No CFO on the call.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-30):** the most confident call of the set. Insurance "progressing ahead of our expectations", 30 states, a run rate over $75 million, and a raised exit target of "$125 million or more". Management promised subscription-to-visit headwinds would turn into "a net tailwind" by the end of 2026.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-29):** the reversal. BetterHelp's revenue outlook was cut: from mid-May, faster migration of users toward insurance, "provider capacity and network constraints", and "a more accelerated decline in cash pay users" broke the assumptions given just three months earlier. Management pulled advertising and refocused on matching demand to therapist capacity. The new product Teladoc 1 (a whole-person care model for cardiometabolic populations, broadly available January 2027) took center stage.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-28):** stabilization. Revenue near the top of the range, adjusted EBITDA above it ($79 million, up about 14% year over year), BetterHelp insurance revenue $32 million in the quarter, above the range, and an annualized insurance run rate "over $140 million". A new CFO (Mike Grasher, appointed 2026-08-31) joined. Non-US BetterHelp expansion was quietly de-prioritized ("reduce near term emphasis on non US markets") - a growth driver introduced in 2025 and dropped in 2026.

Net arc: from growth-through-innovation, to a guidance cut, to a credible but still early stabilization. The core story has contracted to "Integrated Care holds and grows slowly; BetterHelp shrinks into a smaller, insured, more durable business."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Sustainable underlying growth" in virtual care (Q3 2025) | Consolidated revenue $2.03B (2021) -> $2.60B (2023) -> $2.57B (2024) -> $2.53B (2025) -> guided $2.39-2.44B for 2026, about 4-5% lower. Q3 2026 revenue $605M vs about $626M a year earlier. | Richer than the numbers. Revenue has fallen three years running. |
| Integrated Care grows | 2025 segment revenue +3.3%, but about 2.1 points of that came from acquisitions (Catapult, TeleCare); Q4 2025 +4.7% with ~2.6 points acquired. | Roughly flat organically; profit is improving faster than revenue. |
| Profitability improving | Adjusted EBITDA $281M (2025) -> guided $277-303M (2026); Q3 2026 +14%. GAAP net loss narrowed from -$1.00B (2024) to -$200M (2025) and about -$130M for the first nine months of 2026. | Matches, on an adjusted basis. |
| Strong free cash flow (screener: TTM $233M, 5.4x P/FCF) | The data feed counts only small "capex" lines; Teladoc capitalizes ~$30-42M of software every quarter, booked as "other investing". On the company's own definition, 2026 year-to-date free cash flow is $85.4M (vs $113.5M a year earlier) and full-year guidance is $135-165M. Trailing twelve months is roughly $140M. Stock pay of roughly $45-55M a year is real dilution on top. | The screener's FCF is overstated by about $90M; true price/FCF is about 11x, about 15-16x after stock pay. |
| Strong balance sheet ("net debt to EBITDA under 0.8x") | Cash $850M vs $998M of convertible notes now classified as current (due June 2027) plus $38M of leases. Net debt $185M (ex-lease ~$148M). | True on a ratio basis, but the whole debt stack matures in about 6.5 months and must be repaid or refinanced. |
| BetterHelp insurance "ahead of expectations" (Q1 2026) | The same segment's revenue outlook was cut one quarter later; Q3 2026 insurance revenue $32M did beat its range. | Directionally true on insurance, wrong on the total segment. |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: **Stable, after a dip.** Q1 2026 was the high point ("ahead of our expectations", "net tailwind"). Q2 2026 was defensive and lengthy, explaining that trends were "generally consistent ... through mid May" before they were not. Q3 2026 is measured: "there is more work ahead, but we are encouraged". The language has shifted from offense (new states, new markets, 1-2 new countries) to discipline (lower advertising, "connect the demand generation to the capacity we have", "good financial stewards"). Guidance specificity on BetterHelp insurance has stayed high (sessions per week, run rate), which is a plus.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Quarterly ranges are reliably met, usually above the midpoint (Q3 2025, Q4 2025, Q1 2026, Q3 2026 all beat; the screener shows 4 of 7 quarters beating EPS). The failure is on the medium-range view: the April 2026 BetterHelp outlook lasted three months before being cut in July. The 2026 free cash flow range ($135-165M) was held through Q3. Reliability: **Medium** - good on near-term ranges, poor on the multi-quarter BetterHelp path.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **BetterHelp cash-pay decline** - asked every quarter; management keeps describing it as "ongoing challenges" without quantifying the floor.
- **How long the lower advertising can protect margins** (TD Cowen, Q2 2026): management answered with principles, not a timeline.
- **Therapist capacity** (UBS, Q3 2025; TD Cowen, Q2 2026): first dismissed ("keeping up with the demand"), then it became one of the stated reasons for the Q2 cut.
- **Teladoc 1 revenue** (KeyBanc, Q3 2026): no figures; "some impact on 2027", real selling in 2027 for 2028.
- **Not addressed on any call in the provided material:** the June 2027 convertible maturity and the refinancing plan.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Red flags:
- Q2 2026: BetterHelp outlook cut three months after an "ahead of expectations" call.
- Q3 2025 to Q3 2026: about a 10-month CFO gap (Murthy left late 2025, Grasher started 2026-08-31); the Chief Legal Officer also changed (announced 2026-09-25).
- Insiders: 0 open-market buys against 19 sales (194,162 shares) in the latest window.
- Repeated goodwill impairments ($13.7B in 2022, $1.0B loss in 2024, a further impairment in 2025); book value per share has shrunk about 47% a year over five years.
- Q3 2026: non-US BetterHelp expansion de-prioritized.
- About $1.0B of converts due June 2027 against $850M of cash.

Green flags:
- Q3 2026: adjusted EBITDA up about 14%; Integrated Care margin above guidance; GAAP EPS outlook raised.
- BetterHelp insurance revenue: $13M (2025) -> $32M in Q3 2026 alone; weekly sessions 1,200 per day (Feb) -> 14,000 per week (Apr) -> 27,000 per week (Oct).
- Chronic care enrollment rebounded (Q3 2025, Q4 2025, Q2 2026), helped by multi-condition bundles.
- Gross margin steady near 69-70%; kept margins through the 2021-22 inflation.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "Visit-based arrangements" are, economically, a price cut on the old subscription fee: the client now pays only when used. Management repeatedly calls the shift a coming "net tailwind" but has moved the date out (end-2026).
- The new vocabulary - "accountability for both clinical performance and total cost of care" - signals a move toward outcome-based contracts, which carry risk-sharing.
- On BetterHelp, the CEO now concedes the original cash-pay model met a need "when there was less network access coverage", and that "others have sort of moved in that space" - an admission the consumer moat has narrowed.
- The new CFO comes from insurance and financial services, which fits a refinancing-and-discipline year rather than a growth year.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **PIVOTING** - two business-model shifts at once, with profit stabilizing and revenue still falling.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the real free cash flow is about $140-150M a year, not $233M, and the entire $1.0B convertible stack matures in June 2027.** At $8.60 the equity is worth about $1.57B and the enterprise about $1.75B, so the stock trades near 11x company-defined free cash flow and about 6x adjusted EBITDA - fair, not deep, for a business with falling revenue. The equity case needs BetterHelp to stop shrinking and Integrated Care to grow organically.

Moat: Integrated Care has a **narrow** moat from scale and switching costs (over 100 million covered members, embedded employer and health-plan contracts, 70% gross margin held steady). BetterHelp's brand moat in cash-pay therapy has eroded as in-network competitors arrived. Returns on capital are negative because of goodwill write-downs, so the evidence is margins rather than ROIC; segment margins are stable to improving, so the moat trend is stable rather than widening.

Secular threat: **material, not terminal.** The client shift from subscriptions to pay-per-visit is a lasting pricing compression on the core product, and commoditized telehealth plus AI-native rivals keep pressure on price. But the company's scale, clinical network and stable gross margin argue the base is shrinking slowly rather than melting. The cheapness is mostly a fair price on a low-quality cash stream, not a fear-driven mispricing.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

picks.bull_thesis:
Bytes Technology Group sells Microsoft and other vendors' software licences, cloud subscriptions and security products to UK companies and public bodies, and increasingly delivers its own managed services (work it performs itself for a recurring fee). The bull case is that an exceptionally profitable franchise has come out of a one-year, vendor-imposed stall with growth that is broad, led by the core business, and ahead of its own guidance - and that the profit lag behind that growth is a one-off cost step that unwinds from the year to February 2028.

The evidence is dated. In the half-year results of 13 October 2026 (six months to 31 August 2026), gross invoiced income rose 19.6% to £1.6 billion, gross profit 17.8% to £97.1 million and operating profit 6.6% to £35.3 million, against a May 2026 guide of high single-digit to low double-digit gross-profit growth and flat operating profit. Crucially, software gross profit itself grew 15.8%: the recovery is in the licence engine, not only in services. Public-sector gross profit rose 23.1% and private-sector 14.6%, so the private-sector sales reorganisation did not cost customers. Full-year guidance was raised in September and reiterated: low-to-mid-teens gross-profit growth, low-to-mid single-digit operating-profit growth.

The profit lag has an identifiable cause. Employee costs rose 22.3% to £48.2 million while total headcount rose only 2% to 1,353: the increase is restored bonuses, developer salaries no longer capitalised and platform amortisation - the roughly £4.5 million of cost normalisation flagged in May - not a runaway cost base. The CFO said the 36.4% ratio of operating profit to gross profit is 'a low point this year' and that from the year to February 2028 operating profit should grow 'broadly in line with gross profit'.

Quality is the best in its peer group: returns on equity around 63% and on invested capital around 56%, a free-cash-flow margin near 27% of revenue, capital spending under 1% of revenue, a renewal rate above 115% of prior-year spend, and £68.4 million of net cash with no borrowings at 31 August 2026 after returning £41.3 million in the half. Cash conversion improved to 46% from 34% in the comparable half (109% on a rolling twelve months).

Services are the long-run multiple lever: services invoiced income grew 41%, technical delivery headcount 17.4%, and the CyberOne acquisition (announced 13 October 2026, £19.4 million initial cash plus an earn-out; about £9.5 million of revenue) adds a higher-margin security operations business. If services keep compounding, the share of gross profit nobody else can reprice rises every year.

Conditions: the second half to February 2027 lands at the guided high single-digit gross-profit growth; Microsoft's October 2026 incentive changes prove neutral-to-positive as management claims; and the operating-profit ratio turns up in the year to February 2028.
picks.bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Bytes is a poor business; it is that the shares price the gross-profit recovery while the profit that matters keeps lagging, and that the next twelve months contain both a sharp growth deceleration and a fresh vendor reset.

The conversion arithmetic is now confirmed in audited half-year figures (13 October 2026): gross profit rose about £14.7 million and operating profit about £2.2 million, so each new pound of gross profit converted at roughly 15 pence against a normal 37-40 pence. Operating profit as a share of gross profit has fallen for three reporting periods running - 40.7% for the year to February 2025, 37.5% for the year to February 2026, 36.4% in this half (40.2% a year earlier). The promise that it recovers is for a year that has not started.

Growth is decelerating into the half that matters. Management guided the second half to 'high single-digit' gross-profit growth after 17.8% in the first, and Bytes earns most of its profit in the second half around the February renewal season. The earnings exit rate was also queried on the call: an analyst noted earnings were broadly flat through the first four months of the half.

Vendor risk is live again. Microsoft is about half of group gross profit, and the chief executive confirmed 'the next set of partner incentive changes take effect this month' (October 2026) without quantifying them. The January 2025 change is what caused the 2025 stall and the slide to 248.6p within the last twelve months.

Secondary drags: interest income fell to £4.9 million in the half on lower rates and lower cash, and the CyberOne outlay and buybacks reduce it further; the services gross margin fell from 24% to 19% as capacity was hired ahead of revenue; new-customer gross profit was only £1.8 million in six months; and the CFO warned that 109% cash conversion should not be 'penciled in ever more'. If the second half disappoints or the incentive change bites, the market will re-rate the shares toward the UK channel's historical 12-13x operating profit.
picks.consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market: the market has paid for the gross-profit recovery and is treating the conversion promise as already banked; we treat it as a forward claim for a year that has not started.

For a deep-value lens the question is whether the street is pricing terminal decline into a company with growing earnings power. It is not: at 429.6p the shares trade about 14.5x forward operating profit and about 16-18x free cash flow, roughly 15% below Softcat, after rising from 248.6p within the last twelve months. There is no fear priced in. The assumption the price embeds is that the 17.8% first-half gross-profit growth becomes earnings growth. The audited half says otherwise for now: about £14.7m of new gross profit produced about £2.2m of new operating profit, and the full-year guide is low-to-mid single-digit operating-profit growth on low-to-mid-teens gross-profit growth. The CFO's own bridge says the ratio recovers only from the year to February 2028. At 429.6p the investor is paying a fair price for that recovery in advance, with a fresh Microsoft incentive change (effective October 2026) as the open risk.

Where the market may be too cautious: the core software line grew 15.8%, which answers the September worry that growth was services-led mix. If the second half holds high single digits and the ratio turns, a 16x multiple on about £72m of year-to-February-2028 operating profit plus cash supports the mid-500s. That is the upside we would buy at a better price.
picks.valley_of_death:
The risky window (the months just ahead) carries no solvency risk: net cash £68.4m at 31 August 2026 (about £49m after the CyberOne initial payment), no borrowings, and a seasonal cash peak to come around the February renewals. There is no maturity, covenant or forced-selling trigger that could kill the thesis before the price converges to fair value.

The risks are disclosure and seasonality. First, Microsoft's partner-incentive changes that took effect in October 2026: management has not quantified them, and the January 2025 change is what caused the last stall. Any first read will come in the full-year trading update, around late March 2027. Second, the second half is guided to high single-digit gross-profit growth, about half the first-half pace, and it is where most profit is earned; a miss there would land on a stock priced for delivery. Third, interest income (£4.9m in the half, about 12% of pre-tax profit) is shrinking with lower cash. Fourth, CyberOne integration and the earn-out add modest cost and execution risk. None is fatal; each is a reason not to pay up ahead of the evidence.
picks.positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling pressure in the register. Bytes is a FTSE 250 constituent with a stable domestic institutional base and a sizeable passive holding; the dividend (10.2p for the last full year, interim raised 3.1% to 3.3p) is covered and secure, there is no leverage, and the company itself is a steady buyer (its £25m programme completed in the half, £41.3m returned in six months). The recent slide - from a twelve-month high of 494.2p to 429.6p on 9 November 2026, with no company news found - looks like a drift in UK mid-cap technology and software-reseller names rather than any forced seller. The setup we would buy is a further sector-wide or style-wide sell-off in UK channel and mid-cap technology stocks that takes the shares to about 405p, around their late-summer levels and still well above the 340p adverse case; that would require no change in the company itself.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Wait for a better price: we buy near 405p, which a sector-wide sell-off in UK mid-cap technology and software-reseller shares could deliver.

Bytes is a very good business, and its half-year results of 13 October 2026 confirmed that the thesis holds: gross profit up 17.8%, software up 15.8%, both sectors growing double digits, guidance raised and reiterated, £68.4m of net cash and £41.3m returned to shareholders in six months. Returns on capital around 56% remain the best in its peer group. What the results also confirmed is the weak spot this committee flagged in September: operating profit grew only 6.6%, so new gross profit is converting at well under half the normal rate, and management's promise that profit catches up with gross profit is for the year to February 2028.

On our sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately) the shares are worth about 490p, unchanged from our last look because the interim figures moved both the bull and bear sides about equally; the adverse case is about 340p and the favourable case about 600p. At 429.6p (9 November 2026) the discount to fair value is about 14%, short of the 20% margin of safety this committee requires in today's market backdrop. We would buy at about 405p, where the discount clears that bar and the price still sits far above the adverse case. No dated fact has changed since our 2 November review - the drift from 452p came without company news - so we keep the same answer: wait for a better price, with conviction unchanged at moderate.

The catalyst has already happened (the edge is spent), which is neither a plus nor a minus here: the case is judged on the residual value, and today that residual is too thin to buy. The two things to watch are the full-year trading update around late March 2027, which will show whether Microsoft's October 2026 incentive changes help or hurt, and the May 2027 results, which will show whether profit conversion has turned. A clean read on both, or a price near 405p, would make this a buy.
picks.forcing_function: There is no dated, binding event that forces a re-rating; the event that would have done so - the return to double-digit growth - already happened on 17 September and 13 October 2026. For a deep-value name the re-rating levers are mechanical and continuous: steady buybacks and a covered, growing dividend on a cash-rich balance sheet. The scheduled tests are the full-year trading update (the prior-year equivalent came on 24 March 2026), which covers the February renewal season and the first read on Microsoft's October 2026 incentive change, and the audited full-year results around May 2027, which will give the year-to-February-2028 outlook and therefore the first evidence on the promised recovery in operating-profit conversion. Those dates test the thesis in either direction; they are not catalysts we pay for in advance.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier - Bytes Technology Group plc (BYIT.L)

**Date of review:** 9 November 2026
**Price used:** 429.6 pence (London Stock Exchange, quoted in pence sterling), live quote 9 November 2026, down 2.4% on the day from 440.2p. Market value about £989 million on roughly 230 million shares. Twelve-month range 248.6p to 494.2p; 50-day average about 438p, 200-day average about 370p.
**Evidence base:** one earnings-call transcript - the half-year results presentation for the six months to 31 August 2026, delivered 13-14 October 2026 by the chief executive, Sam Mudd, and the chief financial officer (CFO), Andrew Holden. Bytes reports twice a year and does not hold quarterly calls, so there is no multi-quarter series of calls to compare; the earlier guidance this dossier tests comes from the company's regulatory statements of 12 May 2026 (audited full-year results to 28 February 2026) and 17 September 2026 (half-year trading update), both quoted in this committee's prior work and verified by an independent check on 22 September 2026. The five-year figures come from our screener.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Bytes sells Microsoft and other vendors' software licences, cloud subscriptions and security products to UK companies and public bodies, and increasingly delivers its own technical and managed services (work it performs itself for a recurring fee) on top of them. It reports gross profit as its main measure because the invoiced value mostly passes straight through to the vendor.

The story over the last eighteen months has three chapters. In the year to February 2026 the business stalled: Microsoft changed its partner incentives in January 2025, software gross profit slipped 0.5% to £145.2 million and operating profit fell 5.6% to £62.7 million. In May 2026 a new management team set out a reorganisation of the private-sector sales force, an alignment of the Bytes and Phoenix brands to the public and private sectors, and about £4.5 million of "cost normalisation" (restored bonuses, development salaries no longer capitalised, platform amortisation), guiding to flat operating profit. In September and October 2026 the business reported that the reset had worked: the half-year call opens with "those changes would show through in our performance during this financial year. And I'm pleased to say this morning that they have."

The emphasis has shifted from "software licensing reseller" to "the U.K.'s leading trusted adviser on AI, cloud and cyber", with services and security as the growth vectors, and the first acquisition in some time (CyberOne, a UK cyber-security managed-services firm, £19.4 million initial cash plus a performance earn-out over 16 months, announced 13 October 2026). Importantly the chief executive still anchors the business on licensing: "growth will continue with software licensing at the core."

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management claim (H1 call, Oct 2026) | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Gross profit grew by 17.8%", "broad-based growth" | Software gross profit +15.8%, public sector +23.1%, private sector +14.6%; hardware more than doubled off a small base; services gross profit +12% to £9.3m | Corroborated. The growth was led by the core licence business, not by services. This answers the open question in our September work (whether the growth was services mix): it was not. |
| Operating profit "up 6.6%" against a guide of broadly flat | £35.3m; operating profit as a share of gross profit fell to 36.4% from 40.2% | Corroborated, but it confirms the weak-conversion point: incremental gross profit of about £14.7m produced only about £2.2m of extra operating profit. |
| The 36.4% ratio "a low point this year"; from the year to February 2028 "operating profit to grow broadly in line with gross profit" | Admin costs +24.7%, employee costs +22.3% to £48.2m on headcount up only 2% - the cost rise is pay and normalisation, not headcount, which supports the "one-off step" explanation | Plausible, untested. It is a forward promise for a year that has not started. |
| Cash conversion 46% vs 34%; 109% rolling twelve months | Screener: trailing free cash flow £121m (FMP basis), FCF margin ~27% of revenue, net cash £68.4m after £41.3m of returns | Corroborated, with the CFO's own caveat: "I just want to make sure that we are not penciling in 109% cash conversion ever more." |
| Renewal rate "over 115%" | New-customer gross profit only £1.8m in the half; 97% of gross profit from existing customers in the prior year | Corroborated as share-of-wallet growth; new-logo acquisition remains thin. |
| Services: "capacity ahead of the revenue"; margin 24% to 19% | Technical delivery headcount +17.4% | Plausible. The margin drop is a cost-before-revenue pattern; the second half has to show the utilisation recovery. |

The five-year screener trajectory (revenue £146m to £221m, net income £33m to £51m, EPS 13p to 21p) shows a business that has compounded at roughly 12-13% a year with one flat year, and returns on equity above 60% and on invested capital near 56%. Nothing in the call is richer than the numbers justify; if anything the conversion ratio is a number management chose to confront directly rather than bury.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

Rising, from a defensive base. In May 2026 the language was about cost resets, organisational change and a flat profit year. By October it is offensive: "trading was ahead of our expectations", a guidance upgrade, an acquisition, and an explicit multi-year profit-conversion promise. The guidance is also more specific than before: management gave the second-half gross-profit rate ("high single-digit growth for the second half") and an exit rate ("more like the mid-teens") rather than a single annual phrase. The one defensive note is on cash: the CFO warned of vendor pressure to collect faster as interest rates rise and of slower conversion as services grow.

## 4. Guidance credibility

May 2026 guide: high single-digit to low double-digit gross-profit growth, operating profit broadly flat. Delivered in the half: 17.8% and 6.6%. Upgraded in September to low-to-mid-teens gross profit and low-to-mid single-digit operating profit, and reiterated in October. That is an over-delivery against the company's own bar. The screener's beat rate (2 of 4 periods, 50%) reflects the difficult prior year, when the Microsoft incentive change caught the business out. The implied second half is a deceleration (high single digits after 18%), so the full-year guide looks deliberately reachable rather than stretched - mild conservatism, not sandbagging. Reliability: Medium-to-High, improving.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

- The earnings exit rate: an analyst pointed out that earnings were broadly flat for the first four months, implying a sharp step-up in the last two. The CFO disputed the framing and pointed back to the second-half guide - a fair answer, but it confirms that the half was back-end loaded and that the second half will grow far more slowly.
- Microsoft's new partner incentives, which the chief executive said "take effect this month" (October 2026). Management says it has planned for them and that they "are quite lucrative", but gave no quantification. This is the same mechanism that caused the 2025 stall, and it is not answered with numbers.
- Operating margin with acquisitions: the CFO declined to give a three-year margin target and gave only qualitative "clues" for CyberOne.
- New business: the chief executive conceded new-logo wins are a "ramping effect" that "can take up to a full year".

## 6. Red flags and green flags

- Red: Operating-profit conversion fell for a third consecutive reporting period, to 36.4% of gross profit in H1 FY27 (40.2% a year earlier; 37.5% for FY26; 40.7% for FY25).
- Red: A fresh round of Microsoft partner-incentive changes took effect in October 2026 with no quantified impact; Microsoft is about half of group gross profit.
- Red: The second-half growth guide (high single digits) is about half the first-half rate, and the second half is where Bytes earns most of its profit.
- Red: Interest income (£4.9m in the half) is falling with lower average cash; it was about 12% of pre-tax profit and is shrinking further after the CyberOne cash outlay and buybacks.
- Green: Software gross profit +15.8% - the core business, not just services, re-accelerated.
- Green: Cash conversion 46% vs 34% in the comparable half; £41.3m returned to shareholders in six months; £68.4m net cash and no borrowings.
- Green: Customer continuity through the brand realignment ("every single customer retaining continuity of account manager") and a renewal rate above 115%.
- Green: Headcount up only 2% while gross profit rose 18%: the cost rise is a step, not a run-rate.

## 7. Hidden signals

- The vocabulary has moved from "partner" and "licensing" to "trusted adviser", "managed services" and "AI", but the chief executive pointedly keeps licensing "at the core" - a signal to investors that the services push is additive, not a pivot away from the cash engine.
- The CFO is new to the role's public voice and is noticeably careful about cash ("not ringing alarm bells") - a conservative financial voice, which is a mild positive for credibility.
- Commission plans now pay sellers double on services, which will steer effort toward services; it should help mix over time but adds cost before revenue.
- CyberOne's delivery is partly from the Philippines ("labor arbitrage"), which tells you management is willing to buy lower-cost delivery to protect services margins.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

Trajectory: strengthening. The business came out of a vendor-driven stall with growth that is broad, core-led and ahead of guidance, while returning a large share of its cash. Capital allocation is disciplined: a 2-3% dividend yield, steady buybacks, and a small, bolt-on acquisition at roughly 2% of market value.

The single most important thing for the director: the shares already price the recovery in gross profit; the value case now rests on the promise that operating profit reconnects with gross profit from the year to February 2028. Until that shows up - the first real read is the full-year trading update in late March 2027 and the results in May 2027 - the business is a high-quality franchise at roughly a fair price, not a discount.

Economic moat: narrow, switching-costs type. Vendor accreditations (Microsoft Frontier Partner status), deep public-sector framework positions, and embedded account relationships produce the 99%-plus renewal and returns on invested capital in the 50s. But the moat sits on a vendor's goodwill: Microsoft sets partner economics and has reset them twice in two years. Returns remain very high but profit conversion has drifted down for three periods, so the trend is stable-to-soft rather than widening. Secular threat: manageable. Direct-from-vendor buying and AI-driven procurement could squeeze reseller margins over time, but the base is growing, not shrinking, and the services shift is a hedge. The current price is not a fear-print; it is a fair price on a good business.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: Great Wall is a profitable, net-cash carmaker priced as if its earnings will keep shrinking. At HK$5.785 (about RMB 4.90) the shares trade at roughly 8 times this year's depressed earnings of about RMB 0.62 per share (nine-month profit RMB 3.83 billion plus a normal fourth quarter) and well under half their five-year average earnings power: net profit averaged about RMB 8.9 billion a year from 2021 to 2025 (peak RMB 12.7 billion in 2024). Pricing has held: revenue rose 4.1% in nine months on flat units and third-quarter gross margin recovered to about 17.3% from 15.4% in the second quarter. Conditions: the subsidy receivable is real and collectable, the inventory is overseas pipeline rather than unsold domestic stock, and domestic price competition stabilises.
picks.bear_thesis: The cheapness rests on numbers the business is no longer producing. The screen's 1.5 times price to free cash flow is built on a trailing figure that depends on one seasonal quarter (Q4 2025); the third quarter of 2026 produced negative operating cash flow and negative free cash flow of RMB 2.44 billion while reporting RMB 1.36 billion of profit. Inventory is up 54% to RMB 40.2 billion in nine months. Management partly blames 'accelerated supplier payments' - if regulators have ended the supplier-financed working capital that Chinese carmakers relied on, part of the past cash strength was borrowed. At home the franchise is shrinking: domestic volume is down about a quarter, the high-margin Tank brand fell 13.5% and new-energy volume fell 5.9% while the market electrifies, so the profit mix keeps worsening. Exports depend on decisions by foreign governments (Russian recycling fees and rebates, tariffs elsewhere). The same explanation - delayed subsidies, currency - has been given for three quarters running; if the fourth quarter repeats it, the market will treat it as permanent. The interim dividend was skipped in 2026. Net cash is only RMB 2.44 billion once supplier bills and debt (RMB 52.7 billion) are netted against RMB 55.1 billion of cash. picks.consensus_delta: The market is pricing Great Wall as a shrinking combustion-engine carmaker whose profits will not recover: about 8 times depressed 2026 earnings and well under 5 times its 2021-2025 average profit, with brokers cutting (Citi to sell at HK$7.3 after the first-half warning; Morgan Stanley HK$7.30 on 2026-11-05, headline only). Where we disagree: the export business (476,000 units in nine months, up 42%) and steady pricing (revenue up on flat units, gross margin back to about 17.3% in the third quarter) are a real earnings base that the price does not credit. Where the market is right: the screen's cash-flow cheapness was flattered by a seasonal fourth quarter and possibly by supplier financing, and the 'delayed subsidy' explanation is unproven after three quarters. We do not claim the street is wrong yet; we claim the gap between price and normalised value is large enough to be worth waiting on proof.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window is now through the full-year results by 2027-03-31. Inventory of RMB 40.2 billion must be sold or written down; if it is unsold domestic stock, a fourth-quarter discounting push would cut margins below our 16.5% fail line. Domestic price competition intensified after BYD price cuts in November 2026. Any change in Russian recycling-fee or rebate policy hits the export story directly. Cash is not a solvency risk (RMB 55.1 billion of cash, RMB 2.44 billion net), but weak cash flow could keep the final dividend small or skipped, which removes support from yield-minded holders. There is no debt wall in the sources found.
picks.positioning_washout: The shares are down about 60% this year and sit at their 52-week low, well below their 50-day (HK$7.00) and 200-day (HK$10.02) averages. The yield-oriented holder base has already been hit by the skipped 2026 interim dividend; a further cut to the final dividend in March 2027 could produce another round of selling by income funds. No index deletion or lock-up is identified. Much of the selling to date reads as a sector-wide sell-off in Chinese autos plus company-specific disappointment, not forced selling by holders who must sell regardless of value.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for proof: we buy once the full-year 2026 results show fourth-quarter net profit of RMB 2.0 billion or more with gross margin at or above 18%, due by 2027-03-31. The thesis is in doubt until that test. Our earlier test, the third-quarter 2026 report published 2026-10-30, landed in between: profit of RMB 1.36 billion and gross margin near 17.3% missed the bar we set but did not break the case. What the quarter added is a cash-quality worry - operating cash flow turned negative and inventory rose 54% since the start of the year - so we lowered our fair value from about HK$10.0 to HK$8.80 per share. At HK$5.785 the shares now sit about 50% below that value, with an adverse case near HK$4.85, so the price is attractive if the earnings recover; but the cheapness depends on cash flows the business has not produced this year, and the explanation for weak profit (delayed overseas subsidies and currency) has now been offered for three quarters running. The export growth is real, the home market is shrinking, and the move to electric cars in China works against Great Wall's combustion-heavy line-up. We keep conviction at 3 and keep waiting: buying before the proof would be buying a value case whose central earnings and cash numbers are currently unconfirmed.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Great Wall Motor (2333.HK) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Prepared 2026-11-16. Hong Kong H-share, quoted at HK$5.785 (FMP live quote, 2026-11-16). Company reports in renminbi (RMB); HK$1 = RMB 0.848 (FMP, 2026-11-16).*

**Source note.** No earnings-call transcript is bundled and FMP carries none for this listing. This dossier relies on the company's reported numbers (FMP quarterly statements through 2026-09-30), the third-quarter 2026 report released on 2026-10-30 as summarised by Chinese financial press (10jqka, 2026-11-03; ifeng, 2026-10-30), the first-half 2026 interim report, and dated broker actions found by web search. No management quotes are reproduced because none could be sourced verbatim; management's stated reasons are paraphrased from the press summaries.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
The story over the last four reports has narrowed from "a profitable SUV and pickup maker going global" to "an exporter whose profits are stuck in transit." In 2024 the business earned a record RMB 12.7 billion on RMB 199.6 billion of revenue. Through 2025 and 2026 the emphasis moved overseas: exports passed half of all sales in 2026 (476,000 of 920,300 units in the first nine months, up 42%), and management lifted the 2026 export target from 600,000 to 700,000 vehicles. Meanwhile the home market has been ceded: the Tank off-road brand fell 13.5% and Haval 2.5% in the first nine months, and new-energy volume fell 5.9% while the Chinese market moves steadily to electric. The explanation offered for weak profits has stayed the same for three quarters - delayed overseas tax subsidies (reported by Citi as Russian scrap-tax rebates), exchange-rate losses, and domestic price competition - which is either a consistent truth or a recurring excuse. Q3 2026 did not settle which.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim | What the numbers say | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Overseas growth is the engine | 9M 2026 overseas units +42%, now over 50% of volume | Matches |
| Profit is depressed by timing (delayed subsidies, currency), not by the franchise | Q3 2026 net profit to shareholders RMB 1.36B (-40.8% y/y); excluding one-offs RMB 0.98B (-48.3%). 9M net profit RMB 3.83B (-55.7%) | Partly: the gap is too wide and too persistent for timing alone |
| Pricing holds | Q3 gross margin about 17.3% (FMP: 9.98B / 57.76B), down about 1.1 points y/y, but up from 15.4% in Q2 | Stable-to-softer, not collapsing |
| The business is a cash machine (screen shows 1.5x price to free cash flow) | Q3 2026 operating cash flow -RMB 0.27B, free cash flow -RMB 2.44B; 9M operating cash flow RMB 6.22B, -70.9%. The trailing RMB 16.6B is propped up by Q4 2025 alone (RMB 14.4B) | Diverges - the cheapness on cash flow is a stale, seasonal figure |
| Balance sheet strength | Net cash only RMB 2.44B (cash 55.1B against 52.7B of debt incl. supplier bills); inventory RMB 40.2B, up 54% since year-end 2025 | Thinner than the headline cash suggests; inventory build is the red flag |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Declining. The confident export target raise (to 700,000) sits beside a skipped interim dividend in 2026, a first-half profit warning (net profit down 61%), and a third quarter in which the company again cited delayed subsidies. The language has shifted from growth to explanation.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Medium-to-low. The screen shows 3 of 7 recent quarters beating expectations (43%). Revenue delivery is real (9M revenue +4.1% despite flat units), but the profit recovery repeatedly promised as subsidies "catch up" has not arrived in Q1, Q2 or Q3 2026. Brokers have cut: Citi moved to sell with a HK$7.3 target after the first-half warning, and Morgan Stanley set HK$7.30 on 2026-11-05 (headline only; details unverified).

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- When exactly the overseas subsidy receivable is collected, and how large it is (never quantified in the sources found).
- Why inventory is up RMB 14.7B in nine months - overseas stocking (management's explanation) versus unsold domestic product.
- Accelerated supplier payments (cited for weak cash flow) - a policy change, or the end of supplier-funded working capital that flattered past free cash flow.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red (Q3 2026): operating cash flow negative in a quarter with RMB 1.36B of profit.
- Red (9M 2026): inventory +54% to RMB 40.2B.
- Red (H1 2026): interim dividend skipped; profit -61%.
- Red (9M 2026): domestic volume down about a quarter (derived: about 444,000 units against about 589,000 a year earlier); new-energy volume down while the market electrifies.
- Green (Q3 2026): gross margin recovered to about 17.3% from 15.4% in Q2.
- Green (9M 2026): exports +42%; Ora +100%; Wey +4.7%.
- Green: still net cash, small buybacks continuing (about RMB 0.22B in Q2 2026).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
"Accelerated supplier payments" is the important phrase: Chinese automakers came under regulatory pressure in 2025 to pay suppliers within 60 days. If that is the cause, part of the historic free-cash-flow strength was supplier financing, and the 1.5x price-to-cash-flow screen overstates durable cash earnings. The receding Tank brand (the high-margin product) explains the mix-driven profit squeeze better than subsidies do.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: deteriorating. The single most important thing to weigh: the cheapness rests on cash flow and earnings that Q3 2026 did not reproduce. Until a quarter shows profit back near RMB 2 billion with inventory falling, the low multiple is on an earnings base that is still shrinking.

Moat: narrow, scale-cost plus a brand niche in off-road SUVs and pickups (Tank, Poer). Returns are modest (ROIC 6.9%) and the domestic niche is being eroded by price competition and the shift to electric vehicles, where Great Wall lags. The export franchise is real but exposed to tariff and subsidy decisions in Russia and other markets. Secular threat: material, not terminal - the energy-transition shift erodes the domestic combustion-SUV base, but exports and plug-in hybrids give a credible path. The discount is partly a fear print and partly a shrinking domestic base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory weakening · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat material.
