picks.bull_thesis: JD Logistics is China's largest self-operated warehouse-and-delivery network (about 1,600 warehouses and more than 34 million square metres, end-2025), anchored by JD.com volume and growing fast with outside customers. Revenue rose from RMB 104.7B in 2021 to RMB 217.2B in 2025, and first-half 2026 revenue was RMB 124.7B, up 26.5%. Profit is now catching up. Management promised on 2026-03-05 that 2026 profit would improve, and it delivered: IFRS (reported) net income was RMB 0.88B in Q1 and RMB 2.41B in Q2 2026, and adjusted operating profit rose 39.9% in the half. Cost ratios are falling. In Q2 2026 staff costs were 34.2% of revenue (-1.0 point), rent 5.3% (-1.1 points) and operating expenses 6.4% (-0.5 points), as automation (more than 1,000 driverless delivery vehicles and robot-run warehouses) takes cost out. Deppon, the freight subsidiary that dragged on 2025, is 'on the track of recovery' (2026-08-13), and the CFO guided that operating margin 'will be further improved in the second half'. Overseas warehouses (doubled in 2025 to nearly 2 million square metres) and the JoyExpress delivery brand in Europe and Saudi Arabia add a second growth curve. At HK$10.26 the stock trades on about 7.6 times trailing earnings (about RMB 7.4B over the last twelve months), with about RMB 17.3B of net cash before leases, roughly a third of its RMB 53B market value. It sits near the bottom of its 52-week range (HK$9.51 to HK$16.76). Sell-side targets cluster around HK$18.4, though the snapshots date from mid-2026 and are stale. The case needs three things to hold: the second-half margin improvement shows up, Deppon stops dragging, and revenue growth holds in the high teens.
picks.bear_thesis: The cheapness is in the earnings, not the cash or the returns. Return on invested capital is about 1% and the net margin about 3%, so a scale network that protects volume has not shown pricing power. Gross margin fell 0.9 points to 9.7% in Q2 2026 even as revenue grew 24%. More of the growth now comes from consolidated, low-margin on-demand riders, with outsourcing costs up 40.5% to 37% of revenue, rather than from integrated supply-chain work, where external revenue growth slowed to 12.5%. Free cash flow fell 26.7% in 2025, and the latest trailing figure in our data feed is zero. After about RMB 18.7B of lease liabilities, the 'net cash' becomes about RMB 1.4B of net debt, and automation spending will be 'higher than that of 2025' (2026-03-05) with no payback disclosed. Dependence on the parent is rising, not falling: JD Group supplied RMB 19.88B of RMB 30.17B integrated supply-chain revenue in Q2 2026. # JD Logistics (2618.HK) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*As of 2026-11-16. Transcripts read: Q3 2025 (2025-11-13), Q4/FY 2025 (2026-03-05), Q2 2026 (2026-08-13). Figures in RMB unless stated; the stock trades in Hong Kong dollars (HK$10.26 on 2026-11-16, FMP quote). Third-quarter 2026 results are due 2026-11-17 (FMP earnings calendar).*

**Takeaway:** JD Logistics is a fast-growing, thin-margin logistics network whose profits are now rising again after a soft 2025, and management has broadly done what it said it would on profit. The two things to watch are the quality of the growth (much of the 2026 revenue jump is a consolidated, low-margin on-demand delivery business, not the higher-value supply-chain work) and cash conversion, which the latest data feed reports as roughly zero over the trailing twelve months.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-11-13):** the story was integrated supply chain (ISC - running a customer's warehousing, inventory and delivery end to end) growth of 45.8% to RMB 13.1B, "targeted investments" in overseas and timeliness, and the new full-time food-delivery rider force. Profit was the soft spot: non-IFRS (adjusted, excluding items like share-based pay) net profit RMB 2.02B, attributable profit down about 8% year on year.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-03-05):** the CEO framed 2025 around three differentiators - ISC, customer experience, and automation/AI. Overseas warehouse space was doubled as promised (nearly 200 bonded/overseas warehouses, about 2 million square metres) and the JoyExpress delivery brand launched in Saudi Arabia and Europe. Deppon (the freight subsidiary) was conceded as a 2025 margin drag with "positive improvement" promised for 2026.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-08-13):** the CFO led with profit, not growth: revenue RMB 64.1B (+24.3%), adjusted operating profit +11.6% for the quarter and +39.9% for the half. The emphasis has shifted from "capacity building" to "operating leverage", with overseas now called "an important second growth curve" and the Joybuy European retail venture of the parent JD.com a named driver.

The arc is from investment to harvest - but the headline growth has quietly changed composition: ISC revenue growth slowed to 12.1% in Q2 2026, while "other customers" (express, freight and the newly consolidated on-demand riders) grew 37.6%.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| "High-quality revenue growth" (every call) | Revenue RMB 104.7B (2021) to 217.2B (2025); H1 2026 RMB 124.7B, +26.5% | Corroborated on volume. Quality is mixed: Q2 2026 gross margin 9.7%, down 0.9pp year on year; outsourcing costs +40.5% to 37% of revenue on the on-demand consolidation. |
| 2026 profit would show "positive improvement" (2026-03-05) | IFRS net income Q1 2026 RMB 0.88B, Q2 RMB 2.41B; H1 adjusted operating profit +39.9% | Delivered. Trailing-twelve-month IFRS net income about RMB 7.4B (Q3 25 2.03 + Q4 25 2.04 + Q1 26 0.88 + Q2 26 2.41). |
| Core business margins rising, Deppon the drag (2026-08-13) | Group gross margin fell; management says the "original core business" margin rose | Plausible but unaudited in the transcript - no segment margin given. Cannot verify the split. |
| Overseas warehouse doubling by end-2025 (2025-11-13) | Confirmed achieved on 2026-03-05 | Delivered. |
| Strong cash generation (implied by the cheap price-to-free-cash-flow) | FY 2025 price/FCF about 5x; FMP trailing FCF reported as 0; FCF growth -26.7% in 2025 | Unclear. A "0" trailing figure may be a data gap, but the falling 2025 FCF is real. Lease payments (RMB 18.7B of lease liabilities) sit below operating cash flow and make FCF look better than owner cash. |
| Balance sheet strength | Cash RMB 22.47B vs borrowings RMB 5.17B (2026-06-30) | Corroborated: about RMB 17.3B net cash before leases; about RMB 1.4B net debt once RMB 18.7B of leases are counted. |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable, edging up.** Q3 2025 was defensive on profit ("lay the foundation for long-term business growth"; "In 2026, still I'm not in the right time to make the forecast"). Q4 2025 was more assertive on 2026 profit but vague on numbers. Q2 2026 is the most confident: "The operating margin will be further improved in the second half" and express growth "more than double the industry average". The shift is from offensive investment language to an operating-leverage message - a healthy direction - but specifics remain thin: no margin targets, no capex number, and no Deppon figures.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Management gives qualitative, not numeric, guidance. What they promised, they delivered: the overseas-warehouse doubling (promised 2025-11-13, confirmed 2026-03-05) and the 2026 profit recovery (promised 2026-03-05, H1 operating profit +39.9%). The screener records 4 of the last 5 quarters beating estimates. Because the targets are soft, sandbagging is hard to detect. **Reliability: Medium-High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Deppon's profitability** (asked 2026-03-05 and 2026-08-13): answered only with "on the track of recovery", never numbers.
- **Automation capex and returns** (2025-11-13, 2026-03-05): management says investment will be "higher than that of 2025" but gives no figure or payback.
- **Express industry slowdown** (2026-08-13): answered with relative growth claims, not unit pricing.
- **2026 revenue outlook** (2025-11-13): explicitly declined.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: gross margin down 0.9pp in Q2 2026 even as revenue grew 24%.
- Red: growth mix shifting toward consolidated, low-margin on-demand delivery (outsourcing costs +40.5%, Q2 2026).
- Red: free cash flow fell 26.7% in 2025 and the latest trailing figure is reported as zero; lease burden is large.
- Red: external ISC growth slowed to 12.5% in Q2 2026 from much higher rates in 2025.
- Green: profit recovery delivered on schedule (H1 2026 adjusted operating profit +39.9%).
- Green: cost ratios improving - staff costs 34.2% of revenue (-1.0pp), rent 5.3% (-1.1pp), operating expenses 6.4% (-0.5pp) in Q2 2026.
- Green: about RMB 17.3B of net cash before leases - roughly a third of the market value.
- Green: overseas build-out delivered to target.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The CFO, not the CEO, opened the Q2 2026 call and led with operating profit - a sign the investor message is now about margins.
- "Technology exports" appeared on 2026-08-13: the company now talks of selling its warehouse robots to outside customers - early, unquantified.
- The dependence on the parent is rising, not falling: JD Group ISC revenue RMB 19.88B of RMB 30.17B in Q2 2026, with Joybuy (JD's European retail) named as a driver. Related-party pricing is a governance lever worth watching.
- Energy-cost language ("fluctuation of the energy industry", 2026-08-13) shows management expects input-cost pressure; vehicle costs nonetheless fell 0.2pp as a share of revenue.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Growth is robust and profit is recovering, but margins are not structurally widening yet, and the mix shift toward on-demand delivery offsets the core ISC improvement.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** whether the cheapness is in the earnings or in the cash. On earnings the stock is about 7.6 times trailing profit with a third of its value in pre-lease net cash; on owner cash (after lease payments and rising automation capex) the case is much thinner. The 2026-11-17 third-quarter results are the next read on both.

**Moat:** scale-cost and network (the densest self-operated warehouse network in China, about 1,600 warehouses and 34 million square metres, plus the JD.com anchor volume). Returns are low (ROIC about 1%, net margin about 3%), so the moat protects volume more than pricing - narrow, stable. **Secular threat:** manageable - automation and autonomous delivery are being adopted by the company itself rather than used against it, and e-commerce channel shift is a tailwind for a logistics provider. The cheapness reads as a fear print on China and thin margins, not a shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: The market is pricing Eiffage as if French politics will confiscate the motorway concession and the contracting business were worth little on its own. Neither holds up. First, the works business (construction, infrastructure, energy systems - roughly EUR 22bn of revenue) has a record order book that grew again in every business line at the H1 2026 results (2026-08-26), with long-dated, non-cyclical work: about EUR 5bn of new-nuclear EPR2 contracts (2025-02-27), a 12-year nuclear components partnership with Arabelle Solutions, a 25-year Paris district-heating concession, a 5-year RTE grid programme and EUR 120m of high-voltage work for an AI campus (all 2026-08-26). Management has delivered what it promised - a return to construction growth in 2025, the 2025 outlook, and a confirmed 2026 outlook with reported half-year profit up about 11%. Earning roughly EUR 1bn of operating profit, this business alone justifies most of the share price at a contractor multiple. Second, APRR (the motorway network, about 52% economically owned) remains a legal monopoly with operating margins above 70% and roughly nine years to run. Even after the proposed levy - Morgan Stanley puts the hit at 9-12% of 2027 earnings for the exposed groups - its remaining cash flow is worth tens of euros per share. Third, there are real hidden assets: a stake in Getlink (the Channel Tunnel operator), airports, other concessions and treasury shares. At EUR 99.70 the stock trades at about 9 times 2025 earnings of EUR 11.01 and about 3 times group free cash flow, versus Vinci on a materially higher multiple, and below even the most bearish dated broker target (Goldman, EUR 127, 2026-10-20). Conditions: the levy is passed at or below the proposed scale (not extended to tolls), traffic stabilises as oil normalises, and the works margin holds near 4-4.5%.
picks.bear_thesis: Eiffage's value is concentrated in a wasting, politically exposed asset. APRR and AREA expire in the mid-2030s, management admitted it is 'far too early' to say what replaces their profit (2025-02-27), and the state is visibly treating concession profits as a fiscal reserve: a corporate surtax cost about EUR 200m in 2025 (2025-08-29), and the 2027 finance bill would more than double the infrastructure levy to as much as 12.2% while forbidding toll pass-through (announced 2026-09-29). France has no parliamentary majority; a budget forced through by special constitutional powers can be harsher than the draft, and the next government could revisit the concession contracts themselves. Operationally, light-vehicle traffic is falling on high oil prices tied to the Middle East conflict (2026-08-26) and road-building is down 5% on weaker local-authority spending. Earnings per share were flat in 2025 (+0.6%), free cash flow fell 12.2%, gross margin is contracting (12.9%), return on invested capital is a thin 6.3% and the Altman-Z solvency score is 1.0 because of EUR 10.8bn of net debt (including leases) at 2026-06-30. Group free cash flow flatters: 48% of APRR's cash belongs to minority holders and concession cash runs off at expiry, so the headline 3x price-to-free-cash-flow is an illusion. What would confirm the bear: article 22 passed at or above 12.2%, a second year of surtax, a dividend cut below the 45% payout, or a works margin slipping below 4%.
picks.consensus_delta: The street is not pricing terminal decline - consensus targets sit around EUR 155-158 with a buy rating across about 17 analysts (MarketScreener / ad-hoc-news, October 2026) - but the tape is: the stock sits about 2% above its 52-week low and 22% below its 200-day average. Where we disagree with the market is the size of the political hit. Morgan Stanley's 9-12% cut to 2027 earnings is a one-year earnings figure; for APRR's remaining roughly nine years it is worth about EUR 7 per share in present value on our numbers, against a share-price fall of about EUR 48 from the high. The market is extrapolating the fiscal clawback into the works business, which has no such exposure and a record order book. We also disagree with the bulls: consensus near EUR 155 looks stale on concession value, and Goldman's EUR 127 (2026-10-20) is closer to our EUR 128.
picks.valley_of_death: The next three to nine months: (1) the 2027 finance-law debate - article 22 could be passed at or above 12.2%, by special constitutional powers, possibly with a renewed corporate surtax; (2) Q3 revenue around 2026-11-11/12 could show further light-vehicle traffic declines while oil stays high; (3) full-year results in late February 2027 carry dividend risk - management said the 45% payout is not a floor. There is no liquidity cliff: the debt sits mainly at the concessions and is serviced by toll cash; Altman-Z of 1.0 reflects that structure, not distress. The risk is a lower fair value, not a forced sale.
picks.positioning_washout: Smart-money score 4/100 and the price 2% up its 52-week range show holders have already been selling. The likely remaining sellers are yield and income funds if the dividend is trimmed in February 2027, and European infrastructure funds de-risking French political exposure - a sector-wide or style-wide sell-off rather than forced selling by holders who must sell regardless of value. Much of that is already in the price after a roughly one-third fall from the high.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Buy now. Last time we said Eiffage was a genuinely good business at a modestly good price and that we would wait for a wash-out - a sharp sell-off by forced or non-fundamental sellers. It has arrived: the shares fell 10.8% from EUR 109.20 to EUR 97.42 by 2026-10-23 and trade at EUR 99.70 today, about a third below the 52-week high. The thesis holds. The contracting business keeps winning long-dated nuclear, grid, heating and data-centre work and confirmed its 2026 outlook in August. The pressure is on the motorway concession: falling traffic from high oil and a proposed French levy of up to 12.2% that cannot be passed to tolls. We have taken that out of our numbers, about EUR 7 per share, and still reach a base fair value of about EUR 128 per share by adding up the parts, with an adverse case near EUR 75 and a favourable case near EUR 152. Conviction stays moderate at 3 because French politics now sets part of the value: the levy is undecided, the concession ends in the mid-2030s, and the dividend is not guaranteed. The discount is real, the business is clean, and the risk is a lower fair value rather than a broken company. Size it as a deep-value position with a political tail, and re-check after the finance-law vote and the February 2027 results.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Eiffage (FGR.PA) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-10-26. Live price EUR 99.70 on Euronext Paris (FMP quote, 2026-10-26; previous close EUR 97.42; 52-week range EUR 96.26-147.50). All figures in euros.

Short version: management has done what it said it would for three reporting periods running. Contracting (the "works" side: construction, infrastructure, energy systems) keeps growing its order book and margins hold. The concession side (mainly APRR, the motorway network Eiffage controls with about a 52% economic stake) is where the stress is, and that stress comes from outside the company: high oil prices cutting car traffic, and a French government that wants to more than double a special levy on motorway operators. The share price has fallen by about a third from its 52-week high. That fall is a verdict on French politics and on a concession that ends in the mid-2030s, not on the quality of management's execution.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **FY2024 results call (2025-02-27).** The story was scale and visibility. A record order book, up 11% year on year, strengthened by "the two major contracts of the EPR 2 [and] Line 15 East", about EUR 5 billion of new-nuclear work, more than EUR 1.1 billion of offshore-wind orders at Smulders, and a "total change of scale in Germany" through the Salvia and EQOS acquisitions. Management formalised a 45% dividend payout policy. The concession expiry question (what replaces APRR's profits once the concession ends) got a candid "it's still far too early to be able to say".
- **H1 2025 call (2025-08-29).** Same story, more Europe: revenue up 8.4%, growth in Europe outside France of 17.4%, order book up another 4%. A new theme arrived: the French "exceptional contribution" corporate surtax (EUR 135 million booked in the first half, about EUR 200 million for the year). Management called it "temporary" but conceded that "things are pretty unstable right now".
- **H1 2026 call (2026-08-26).** The framing moves to long-term structural demand: "sovereignty of energy, development of new mobilities, necessary adaptation to the climate change". The works side is still advancing (order book up again "on all of the branches lines of business"). For the first time the concessions are described as a drag: "performance is impacted by the decrease of the motorway traffic of the LVs [light vehicles] given the persistence of the oil price, which is high, direct consequence of the Middle East conflict." Road-building (Eiffage Route) is down 5% on weaker local-authority spending. Data centres are framed with deliberate restraint: one hyperscale project under way, perhaps three at most "on a frame of 6 to 12 months".

Net arc: the contracting growth story widened over the period (Germany, nuclear, grid, offshore wind, data-centre power), while the concession story narrowed from "cash machine" to "cash machine under political and traffic pressure".

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Evidence in the financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Very strong year... dynamic growth" (2025-02-27); revenue growth in 2025 and 2026 | Revenue EUR 19.2bn (2021) to 26.1bn (2025), +8.8% in 2025, 3-year compound growth 7.8% | Matches |
| Construction "back to growth" from 2025 (promised 2025-02-27) | H1 2025 construction +3.6% (2025-08-29); H1 2026 "construction line is back to growth" | Delivered |
| Earnings growth | Net income EUR 753m (2021) to 1.04bn (2024), then 1.02bn (2025): earnings per share +0.6% in 2025 | Poorer than the story. The French surtax (about EUR 200m) explains the 2025 stall; underlying growth continued |
| Margins "of good quality... no notion of impairment of the margin level" (2026-08-26) | Gross margin 12.9% and described as contracting; net margin 3.9%; margin 0.25 standard deviations below its historical peak | Broadly matches. The gross-margin drift is mostly mix (more acquired energy-services revenue), not price erosion, but it is a drift |
| Cash generation "extremely good" | Free-cash-flow margin 10.8%, price-to-free-cash-flow about 3.2x; free cash flow fell 12.2% in 2025 | Strong in level. Note that group free cash flow includes 100% of APRR, of which about 48% belongs to minority holders, and concession cash is a wasting asset that runs off at expiry |
| Balance sheet comfort ("cash available is significant", 2025-08-29) | Net debt EUR 10.80bn including leases (EUR 9.66bn excluding leases) at 2026-06-30, mostly concession debt; Altman-Z (a solvency score) 1.0 | Normal for a concession group, but leverage sits on the asset now under fiscal attack |
| Returns | Return on equity 14.6%; return on invested capital 6.3% | Modest. Capital-heavy concessions dilute the high-return contracting business |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rating: **Stable**, with the confidence shifting from the concessions to the works side.

- 2025-02-27: offensive. "Once again, a very strong year both in terms of earnings as well as order intake."
- 2025-08-29: offensive on operations, defensive on taxation. Results "went very well according to our expectations and confirms our outlook"; on French tax, "we do not have more visibility than you have".
- 2026-08-26: confident on works, matter-of-fact on concessions. Outlook for higher activity and results in 2026 confirmed; organic-growth guidance of 2-3% for energy systems reaffirmed ("the assumption of 2%, 3% organic growth is the right one"). On data centres, notably careful: "do not expect a tremendous jump overnight in activity."

Guidance has stayed qualitative (direction, not numbers) throughout, which is this company's long-standing style rather than a new retreat.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

- Promised a return to construction volume growth in 2025: delivered by H1 2025.
- 2025 outlook "confirmed" in August 2025: full-year revenue +8.8% delivered; net income flat only because of the surtax management had flagged in advance.
- 2026 outlook (growth in activity and results) confirmed on 2026-08-26; press coverage reports half-year profit up 11%.
- Earnings beat rate of 3 of the last 5 quarters (60%): neither sandbagging nor serial misses.

Reliability: **High** on what management controls; it does not and cannot guide French fiscal policy.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **The APRR expiry** (BNP Paribas, 2025-02-27): how will lost concession profit be replaced? The answer was a non-answer ("far too early"), and that remains the single largest unresolved question in the valuation.
- **French tax and the dividend** (Jefferies, 2025-02-27 and 2025-08-29): is the 45% payout a floor? Management: "it's not a floor". The surtax "will have an effect on dividends". Analysts were right to push: French fiscal risk has since escalated (see below).
- **Offshore wind** (Citigroup, 2025-08-29): no US exposure, but caution that European clients are stretched by their US problems.
- **Data-centre opportunity** (2026-08-26): analysts pushed on a large addressable market; management deliberately talked it down.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: Concession traffic falling (2026-08-26) because high oil prices, linked to the Middle East conflict, are cutting light-vehicle trips. Tolls are regulated, so lost volume is lost margin.
- Red: The French 2027 finance bill (article 22, filed at the National Assembly on 2026-10-01 after the government announced it on 2026-09-29) would raise the levy on long-distance transport infrastructure from a flat 4.6% to as much as 12.2% for the most profitable operators, and bars passing it through to tolls. Morgan Stanley estimates a 9-12% hit to 2027 earnings for the exposed groups. As of 2026-10-22 article 22 had not yet been debated.
- Red: The 2025 surtax already showed the state treats concession profits as a fiscal reserve; the dividend policy was explicitly "not a floor".
- Red: Eiffage Route down 5% (2026-08-26) on weaker local-authority orders.
- Green: Order book at a record and growing in every business line (2026-02 and 2026-08-26).
- Green: Long-dated, non-cyclical wins: about EUR 5bn of new-nuclear work (2025-02-27), a 12-year Arabelle Solutions nuclear components partnership, a 25-year Paris district-heating concession, a 5-year RTE grid-buildings contract, EUR 120m of high-voltage work for an AI campus (all 2026-08-26).
- Green: Disciplined mergers and acquisitions in markets it already knows (Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg through Baatz), no adventurism.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary moved from "record order book" to "sovereignty of energy" and "adaptation to the climate change": management is positioning the works business as a European-infrastructure franchise that stands on its own, as it should with APRR's end date approaching.
- The new head of concessions (Camille Bonenfant-Jeanneney, from January 2025, background in EU institutions, RATP and ENGIE) is a regulatory and stakeholder profile, not a traffic engineer: a hint that the next decade of concessions is a negotiation with the state.
- On treasury shares (5.8% of capital in early 2025): "we're not going to cancel". Buybacks are opportunistic and kept as a resource, not returned outright.
- Getlink stake: "prepared to strengthen, but we don't plan to take control". It is a financial option, not an empire-building signal.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: **Stable.** The works franchise is strengthening and the concession franchise is being squeezed from outside; together they net to steady.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **how much of today's discount is a permanent transfer of APRR's cash flow to the French state.** If article 22 passes as drafted and traffic stays weak, the concession's remaining roughly nine years of cash flow shrink by a mid-single-digit euro amount per share in present value. If the levy is softened, much of the 2026 sell-off is overdone. The works business, which carries no such political exposure, is on its own worth a large part of the current share price.

Moat: the concessions hold a regulatory-license moat (a legal monopoly on the motorway network), wide while it lasts but finite (APRR and AREA expire in the mid-2030s) and now visibly subject to fiscal clawback. The works business has a scale-and-capability moat (few European contractors can deliver nuclear, high-voltage and hyperscale work), narrow but real, and widening in energy systems. Returns are modest (return on invested capital 6.3%) and stable rather than falling, so this is not an eroding moat in the sense of a melting franchise. On balance: narrow, stable.

Secular threat: none of the listed structural forces (artificial-intelligence displacement, energy transition and so on) threatens the terminal value; the energy transition is a tailwind for the works side. The real terminal question is the concession end date and the regulatory model that replaces it, a known, dated, political risk that is manageable rather than terminal. The cheapness therefore looks more like a fear print on French politics than a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis:
China Oilfield Services is the dedicated offshore oilfield-services arm of China's state offshore oil company, and at HK$7.165 the Hong Kong line prices it as a melting asset while the numbers show a franchise that is getting steadily better. Four facts carry the case.

First, profitability is expanding, and not because of the oil price. Gross margin has gone from 12.3% in 2022 to 17.4% in 2025 to 20.5% for the nine months to 2026-09-30; operating margin from 8.4% to 13.7% over the same span. Revenue compounded 12.1% a year over three years (RMB 35.66B in 2022 to RMB 50.28B in 2025) and net income rose from RMB 2.36B to RMB 3.84B. Return on equity is 8.1% and return on invested capital 7.5% on a trailing-twelve-month basis, both up sharply from 2022. The trailing EBITDA margin (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, as a share of revenue) of 22.6% is higher than Schlumberger's 19.6%, Halliburton's 18.0% and Baker Hughes's 17.8%.

Second, the fleet is effectively sold out and the market is tightening. On the 2026-03-24 annual call management confirmed that in 2025 'all large-scale equipment have been put into use' and described the large-equipment market as 'a tight balance situation'; on 2026-10-26 the operating rule was 'full utilization of the vessels... without leaving them idle'. Consolidation is doing the work: 'for the large contractors and companies, we can see that the profit margin is rising. However, for the smaller contractors, many of their rigs and platforms have been suspended' (2026-03-24). The company intends to buy that stranded capacity cheaply.

Third, the company is finally getting paid for performance. The new three-year agreement with the parent added a classification-and-reward mechanism - a 'slight increase of day rate for equipment with good operational performance' - and management attributed part of nine-month 2026 drilling revenue growth to ranking high in the parent's assessment (2026-10-26). After a decade of surrendering on price, that is a change in kind. Alongside it the balance sheet is repairing: USD 1B repaid in June-July 2025, high-coupon debt swapped out, interest expense down from RMB 969M (2023) to RMB 636M (2025), and net debt down from RMB 9.71B at 2026-06-30 to RMB 7.58B at 2026-09-30, about 1.0 times EBITDA.

Fourth, the demand driver is policy, not the oil price. Three-quarters of revenue is domestic, supplied to the parent under multi-year agreements, against a national energy-security mandate: China burns 750-760 million tonnes of oil a year, the parent is raising output and capital spending, and a new ten-year production action plan was proposed around 2026-10-23. Management said on 2026-10-26 that the 2026 workload came in 'better than the expectation we set at the beginning of the year'. Meanwhile overseas revenue is 24-25% of the total and management wants it an order of magnitude higher, with dated proof points: locked overseas technical contracts up 47% and bundled services up 255% in the nine months of 2025, a south-Brazil rig operating since September 2025, Norway running all four vessels, and a Kazakhstan framework signed by the chairman.

The flat nine-month profit line is an accounting artefact, not a stall: nine-month 2026 net income of RMB 3.21B is level with 2025's RMB 3.21B only because of a RMB 720M non-operating exchange loss on intercompany balances, which the chief financial officer disclosed against his own interest on the 2026-10-26 call after an analyst offered him the benign version. Strip it and earnings power is up double digits. Management has said since 2026-04-23 that it is examining a change of bookkeeping currency that would remove the line entirely.

Conditions the case needs: the parent's 2027 capital-expenditure budget holds or grows; utilisation stays near full; capital spending does not step up so far that free cash flow halves; and the Hong Kong discount to the Shanghai line (the same shares trade at RMB 12.77, equal to HK$14.99) narrows at least partly rather than widening.
picks.bear_thesis:
The shares are cheap for reasons that are real, durable and largely outside the company's control, and the headline cheapness is partly an illusion.

First, the free cash flow on the screen is not the free cash flow you are buying. The 5.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow headline rests on trailing free cash flow of RMB 5.87B, which exists because the company spent under RMB 3B of capital in nine months against its own RMB 8.4B guidance for the year - a shortfall management volunteered on 2026-10-26 ('we are rather slow in fulfilling the CapEx guidance'). Worse, they told the market the same day that 2026-2030 investment intensity 'will be even more than during the 14th 5-Year Plan period', which itself averaged about RMB 5.9B a year, and that deferred projects are 'incorporated in our future vessel building plans' to be 'gradually released down the road'. A step to RMB 8B of annual capital spending against RMB 5.70B of depreciation takes free cash flow from about RMB 5.4B to roughly RMB 3B and breaks the cheapness screen.

Second, returns are barely at the cost of capital. Return on invested capital is 7.5% and return on equity 8.1%. A business earning 8% on equity is arithmetically worth less than its book value, so 0.60 times book is not automatically a bargain - it may simply be the right price. Halliburton earns 18.5% on equity and Weatherford 22.5%, and both trade above two times book.

Third, pricing power belongs to the controlling shareholder, not to the company. Over 75% of revenue is domestic and most of it goes to the parent; day rates under the new three-year agreement are 'overall maintained steady' (2026-10-26); and management has effectively conceded the marine-support pricing dispute, calling it 'an old issue that has been dwelling for 10-odd years' and resolving it by deciding 'it is better to put higher requirements on ourselves than to making requests with other parties' (2026-03-24). They also conceded on the same call that the North Sea long-term agreements carry no oil-price escalator at all.

Fourth, the company has no inflation protection and a bad precedent. Gross margin fell from 18.8% (year to December 2019) to 12.3% (2022) through the last inflation, and state-set wage rules mean salaries 'would take up a rather big portion of our overall cost' (2025-10-30). The current growth-and-inflation backdrop is exactly the one that hurt them last time.

Fifth, the cash is slow and related-party. Days of sales outstanding are 154, net current assets are negative (RMB -1.35B), and collection is concentrated in the fourth quarter - RMB 9.30B of RMB 11.29B of 2025 operating cash flow arrived in the final quarter, and the first quarter of 2026 burned RMB 3.61B of free cash. There is also RMB 3B of debt maturing in 2027 (2025-10-30), to be refinanced into positive and rising real long rates.

Sixth, the currency loss is unfixed and growing: RMB 303M (first quarter) to RMB 560M (first half) to RMB 720M (nine months), with the renminbi near a 52-week high against the Hong Kong dollar. The promised bookkeeping fix has been 'under examination' since 2026-04-23 with nothing done.

Seventh, and most importantly for a value buyer, there is no mechanism that closes the gap. The same shares are quoted at RMB 12.77 in Shanghai against HK$7.165 in Hong Kong - a 109% premium - so the discount is not a disagreement about the business, it is a Hong Kong access-and-governance discount on Chinese state-owned enterprises that has persisted for years. The only lever that historically narrows it is a bigger payout, and management has answered that question with the identical unquantified formula at three consecutive calls: 'the payout ratio shall be stable with the increase'. Meanwhile they have told the market they are entering a newbuild-and-acquisition cycle - 'we have yet given up plans to buy additional drilling vessels' (2026-10-26) - which is the opposite of a harvest.

What would confirm the bear case: the 2027-03-25 annual results showing 2027 capital-spending guidance of RMB 8B or more with no payout increase; the parent's January 2027 budget flat or down on a weaker oil price; or gross margin rolling back below 17% as wage and input costs bite with no pass-through.
picks.consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market. The Hong Kong line prices this company at 0.60 times book and about 7.6 times trailing earnings while gross margin has gone from 12.3% to 20.5% in four years and operating margin from 8.4% to 13.7%. The only visible street anchor - a Buy initiation with a HK$11 target roughly six weeks ago, citing an underestimation of how durable the offshore cycle is - sits 54% above the price and nobody is paying it. Three specific market assumptions look factually wrong.

(1) That flat nine-month profit means a stalling business. It does not. Nine-month 2026 net income of RMB 3.21B is level with 2025 only because of a RMB 720M non-operating exchange loss on intercompany balances - an accounting translation item management is trying to eliminate by changing its bookkeeping currency. Operating profit rose (first-quarter operating profit was up 22% year on year per the 2026-04-23 call; nine-month operating profit was RMB 4.86B). Strip the currency line and earnings power is up double digits.

(2) That the oil unwind is a demand event here. Brent falling from $116.72 on 2026-10-23 to $92.41 on 2026-11-10 took the Hong Kong line down 10.2% from its 2026-10-26 close, as if this were a price-taking driller. Roughly three-quarters of revenue is domestic, supplied to the parent in the first year of a three-year day-rate agreement, driven by a national energy-security mandate and a newly proposed ten-year production action plan. Management reported workload 'better than the expectation we set at the beginning of the year' on 2026-10-26, and the fleet is fully used. At $92 oil nothing in that demand picture changes - the parent's offshore breakevens sit far below.

(3) That the 5.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow is the earnings power. Here we disagree with the bulls rather than the bears: trailing free cash flow of RMB 5.87B reflects under RMB 3B of nine-month capital spending against an RMB 8.4B guide, and management has told the market 2026-2030 intensity will be higher. Our fair value does not use that number; it uses mid-cycle free cash flow of about RMB 5.2B.

Where we agree with the market, and this is the honest limit on the edge: the Hong Kong discount is real and structural. The identical shares trade at RMB 12.77 in Shanghai, equal to HK$14.99 - a 109% premium. Hong Kong is not mispricing the business relative to Shanghai; it is applying an access-and-governance discount to Chinese state-owned enterprises that has persisted for years and that no event on the calendar forces to close. Our valuation keeps half of that discount in place.
picks.valley_of_death:
The risky window - the months just ahead. For a deep-value name the question is whether anything forces a sale or breaks the cash story before the discount narrows. Six things to survive.

(1) Working capital. The first quarter is reliably cash-negative: the first quarter of 2026 produced negative RMB 2.28B of operating cash flow and negative RMB 3.61B of free cash flow, because collections arrive in a fourth-quarter lump - RMB 9.30B of RMB 11.29B of 2025 operating cash flow landed in the final quarter. Days of sales outstanding are 154 and net current assets are negative RMB 1.35B. Expect an ugly cash statement with the annual results on 2027-03-25 and again in April.

(2) The capital-spending catch-up. Projects deferred in 2026 are 'incorporated in our future vessel building plans' to be 'gradually released down the road', with 2026-2030 intensity above the 2021-2025 period (2026-10-26). A step from about RMB 6B to RMB 8B or more roughly halves free cash flow and will read as a broken cheapness screen.

(3) Debt. RMB 3B of maturities fall due in 2027 (2025-10-30), against RMB 15.05B of total borrowings and RMB 7.48B of cash, about 1.0 times cash earnings. Serviceable rather than a wall, but refinancing into positive and rising real long rates removes the interest-cost tailwind that has driven part of recent profit growth.

(4) Currency. The loss scales with renminbi strength, and the renminbi is at 1.1742 to the Hong Kong dollar, near a 52-week high. There is no hedge; the bookkeeping fix has been 'under examination' since 2026-04-23. Fourth-quarter and full-year reported profit can disappoint on this line alone.

(5) Oil and the parent's budget. Brent has fallen about 21% from its 2026-10-23 peak after the 2026-11-02 Hormuz reopening plan. If it keeps falling and the parent's 2027 capital budget, usually published in January, comes flat or down, the load-bearing domestic-workload assumption is challenged before any re-rating.

(6) Seasonality. Management warned on 2025-10-30 that second-half revenue is hurt by weather and that the fourth quarter carries a heavy state-mandated wage load. Net income in the fourth quarter of 2025 was RMB 632M, about a fifth of a normal quarter. The 2027-03-25 print will have the same shape, and a reader who annualises the third quarter will be disappointed.

What is not in the window: there is no cash-burn hump, no liquidation risk, no covenant cliff and no going-concern question. The solvency score sits in the grey zone (Altman 2.6) and the accounting-quality score is good (Piotroski 7 of 9), with trailing earnings 2.8 times covered by operating cash flow.
picks.positioning_washout:
Forced-selling pressure. There is no pivot and no dividend cut, so no yield-focused or passive holder is being forced out: the company paid HK$0.32349 on 2026-06-30 - a 4.5% yield at today's price and about a third of earnings - and has raised it three years running (HK$0.23059, then HK$0.25056, then HK$0.32349), with management saying the payout 'shall be stable with the increase'. So this is not forced selling by holders who must sell regardless of value.

What has already happened is a sector-wide sell-off instead. As of 2026-11-10 every peer trades below both its fifty-day and two-hundred-day averages - Schlumberger $50.38 against a $52.19 fifty-day, Baker Hughes $48.45 against $56.92, Halliburton $31.88 against $34.10, Valaris $78.55 against $86.45, Transocean $5.17 against $5.74, NOV $17.69 against $19.70 - and this name fell 10.2% from its 2026-10-26 close as the Brent war premium came out after the 2026-11-02 Hormuz reopening plan. The sellers are energy-sector and energy-index money cutting exposure to the whole group, not holders reacting to anything the company did.

Two structural features matter for how this resolves. First, the Hong Kong line has a thin free float (about 2.33 billion shares), so moves are amplified in both directions and there is no large domestic buyer base to absorb selling - domestic money buys the Shanghai line instead, at a 109% premium. Second, and the honest consequence: this name has no marginal buyer of its own. It re-rates when the group re-rates or when the Hong Kong discount to Shanghai narrows, and nothing forces either. That also means the HK$6.09 52-week low set earlier in 2026 is a live reference point rather than a floor, which is why our adverse case sits just above it at HK$6.50. Smart-money and institutional-flow readings are weak (14 of 100 and 50 of 100) and the insider buy ratio is zero - though for a Hong Kong-listed Chinese state-owned enterprise insider buying is effectively never observed, so the zero carries no information either way.
picks.moderator_conclusion:
Buy now. We are the same committee that bought this on 2026-10-26, nothing about the business has changed since, and the price has fallen about 8% from where we last looked - so this is the same case, only cheaper.

What you own at HK$7.165 (the Hong Kong listing; the company reports in renminbi, and the same shares also trade in Shanghai at RMB 12.77, equal to HK$14.99). China Oilfield Services is the dedicated offshore oilfield-services arm of China's state offshore oil company. Three-quarters of its revenue comes from the parent under multi-year agreements, driven by a national energy-security mandate rather than by the oil price. The business is demonstrably improving: gross margin has gone from 12.3% in 2022 to 17.4% in 2025 to 20.5% for the nine months to September 2026, operating margin from 8.4% to 13.7%, the fleet is effectively sold out, net debt fell from RMB 9.71B in June to RMB 7.58B in September, and the interest bill is down a third since 2023 after the company repaid USD 1B in mid-2025. Nine-month profit looks flat only because of a RMB 720M exchange loss on internal balances - an accounting item the chief financial officer disclosed against his own interest when an analyst offered him the softer reading, which is a large part of why we score management's credibility 4 out of 5.

Valuing the business by its parts - well services, drilling, marine support and geophysical, each at a multiple of its own cash earnings, less the RMB 7.58B of net debt, then with an explicit 25% discount for the Hong Kong listing - gives a base fair value of about HK$9.80, which is 0.82 times the HK$11.96 book value and under 9 times normalised earnings. Our favourable case is HK$12.50 and our adverse case HK$6.50, a level that is 0.54 times book and just above the HK$6.09 low the market itself set earlier this year. There is no structural floor underneath: the company carries net debt rather than net cash, there is no deal and no contractual payout, and a 4.5% dividend yield is not a floor. Against the global peer group this is the cheapest name on both cash earnings and book - about 3.1 times enterprise value to cash earnings against a peer median near 9, and 0.60 times book against a median of 2.38 - on a cash margin that is actually higher than Schlumberger's, Halliburton's or Baker Hughes's.

Why this is a modest-conviction buy rather than a high-conviction one, and why the discount is not all ours to collect. First, the free cash flow on the screen is not the free cash flow we are buying. The headline 5.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow rests on under RMB 3B of capital spending in nine months against the company's own RMB 8.4B plan, and management told the market in October that investment intensity through 2030 will run higher than the last five years - so we underwrite mid-cycle free cash flow of about RMB 5.2B, not the trailing RMB 5.87B. Second, returns are only just at the cost of capital: 8.1% on equity and 7.5% on invested capital, which is why 0.60 times book is a discount to fair rather than a free lunch. Third, pricing power sits with the parent, not the company - day rates are held steady, a marine-support pricing dispute has gone unresolved for a decade, and management conceded in March that no oil-price escalator exists in its North Sea contracts. Fourth, and most important for a value buyer: the same shares cost 109% more in Shanghai than in Hong Kong, which tells us the discount is largely a Hong Kong access-and-governance discount on Chinese state-owned companies - a shared factor across that whole market rather than anything specific to this company - and no event on the calendar forces it to close. We keep half of it in our fair value and refuse to call the rest edge.

The catalyst is soft, with no fixed date and no contractual payout: the new five-year and ten-year state energy plans are policy direction with no commitment to this company, the Kazakhstan agreement is a framework at the test-well stage, Brazil is an opportunity the company says it will monitor, and the payout question has drawn the same unquantified formula at three consecutive calls. In this book a spent or undated catalyst is neither a plus nor a penalty, so it neither lifts nor lowers the score. What would re-rate the stock fastest is not an event at all but two or three more quarters of the same margin trend with capital spending held near depreciation and the currency drag removed - and that is already happening.

Timing. The 10% fall from the 26 October close is a sector-wide sell-off, not company news: Brent came off its $116.72 peak of 23 October to $92.41 after the Iran-Qatar plan to reopen traffic through the Strait of Hormuz on 2 November, and every peer in the group now trades below its fifty- and two-hundred-day averages. That cuts both ways. It has handed us a wider discount - about 37% to fair value against 23% in October - which clears the bar this growth-and-inflation backdrop requires. It is also a reminder that the thesis leans on one shared macro driver, which the current market-regime read treats as a reason to keep size modest rather than to add. The near-term risks are known and survivable: a cash-negative first quarter, a seasonally weak fourth quarter reported on 25 March 2027, RMB 3B of 2027 maturities to refinance into positive real rates, and a currency loss that grows while the renminbi is strong. None of them threatens solvency. The moat is narrow - a licensed, scale-based position inside one customer's supply chain - but it is widening, and the energy-transition risk to the long-run value of the business is manageable rather than terminal while China is adding offshore production under an energy-security mandate. Buy here, at a modest size, and let the margin trend do the work.
picks.forcing_function:
The catalyst - what forces the re-rating. The honest answer is that nothing here is hard-dated or binding, which is exactly why we judge the residual value case rather than the event. The candidates, ranked by how much they would actually move the price:

(1) A step-up in the payout ratio, or a buyback authorisation, announced with the 2026 annual results on 2027-03-25 (the one confirmed date on the company's reporting calendar). This is the single lever that converts free cash flow into something a Hong Kong minority holder can collect, and historically it is the main thing that narrows the Hong Kong discount on Chinese state-owned enterprises. Management has promised only 'stable with the increase' at three consecutive calls and has never named a number, so this is a hope with a date attached to the meeting, not to the decision.

(2) Changing the bookkeeping (functional) currency, which would remove the exchange line that is currently masking all of the profit growth. Management has been 'examining... some possible solutions' since 2026-04-23. Undated, and entirely within their control, which makes six months of inaction informative.

(3) The parent's 2027 capital-expenditure budget, usually published in January, plus formal allocations under the 15th Five-Year Plan and the National Energy Administration's new ten-year action plan. Management said on 2026-10-26 that 'we're still discussing the specific arrangements'. Third-party, non-binding, unsized.

(4) A named contract from Brazil - the parent and Sinopec won a deepwater block 70-30 - or from Kazakhstan. The company has committed to nothing beyond monitoring 'relevant opportunities' on 'a market-based principle'.

What would actually re-rate this fastest is none of the above but the simplest thing: two or three more quarters of the margin trend (gross margin 12.3% to 17.4% to 20.5%) with capital spending held near depreciation and the currency line neutralised. That is a compounding re-rate rather than an event, and it is already under way - which is why this is a buy at today's price despite the absence of a hard date.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier — China Oilfield Services Limited (COSL), Hong Kong line 2883.HK

**Prepared 2026-11-10.** Price used throughout: **HK$7.165** (Hong Kong dollars, the 2883.HK listing on the Hong Kong exchange, live quote 2026-11-10). The company reports in Chinese renminbi; one renminbi buys 1.1742 Hong Kong dollars today, so renminbi figures are converted at that rate where a per-share comparison is needed. The same shares are also listed in Shanghai (601808) at RMB 12.77, equivalent to HK$14.99.

Transcripts reviewed: 2025-10-30 (third quarter 2025), 2026-03-24 (2025 annual results), 2026-04-23 (first quarter 2026), 2026-10-26 (third quarter 2026). Financials are from the screener scan plus the company's filed quarterly statements through 2026-09-30.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these four calls the story moves in one clear direction: **from "survive the cycle on cost" to "grow overseas and get paid for performance."**

In the 2025-10-30 call the company is defensive and inward-looking. Management leads with efficiency: the task is "to ensure the high level of efficiency of our operations and at the same time, make effective dynamic adjustments to the use of our equipment in the global front." Oil prices had fallen, global upstream investment was down about 6%, and the well-services business was shrinking 3% at home. The bullish question analysts kept putting to management — six Middle East drilling projects restarting — was politely deflated: "to date, we do not have any well-established demand coming from that region."

By the 2026-03-24 annual results the frame has widened to industry structure. Management argues consolidation is handing pricing to the large operators: the 2025 mergers mean "for the large contractors and companies, we can see that the profit margin is rising. However, for the smaller contractors, many of their rigs and platforms have been suspended." Critically they now describe the equipment market as "a tight balance situation" and confirm that in 2025 "all large-scale equipment have been put into use." The strategy shifts from buying capacity to building it: "productization," "our self-developed design, our own R&D, our self-construction."

The 2026-04-23 first-quarter call is the most confident of the four on operations and the least confident on accounting. Operating profit rose 22% year on year, well-services margin reached 18.2% with domestic above 20%, one domestic deepwater semi-submersible rig hit "almost 100%" use at a materially higher day rate — and yet management spent most of the call explaining a RMB 303M currency loss and conceding they are "even bothered by that."

By the 2026-10-26 third-quarter call internationalization has become the headline strategy rather than a side plan: overseas is "between 24% or 25%" of revenue and management wants to take it "to the next level — next order of magnitude," naming Kazakhstan and Mozambique. Two things were quietly **added**: a performance-based day-rate reward inside the new three-year agreement with the parent, and an explicit warning that capital spending intensity in the 2026-2030 plan "will be even more than during the 14th 5-Year Plan period." Two things were quietly **dropped**: the Middle East recovery narrative, which has simply stopped being mentioned as a driver, and any pretence that the marine-support pricing dispute will be won.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (date) | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "The company presents a high-quality and sustainable development trend" (2025-10-30, repeated 2026-10-26) | Revenue RMB 35.66B (2022) → 44.11B (2023) → 48.30B (2024) → 50.28B (2025); net income RMB 2.36B → 3.84B. Nine months of 2026: revenue RMB 35.35B, up 1.4%; net income RMB 3.21B, level with RMB 3.21B a year earlier | **Supported on the four-year trend, poorer than the story on 2026.** Growth has decelerated hard: +12.1% three-year compound revenue growth, +1.4% for the nine months just reported |
| Margins are improving through cost control and mix | Gross margin 12.3% (2022) → 17.4% (2025) → **20.5% for the nine months of 2026**; operating margin 8.4% → 12.4% → 13.7% | **Richer than the claim.** This is the strongest fact in the file, and it is not an oil-price effect |
| Flat profit is a currency artefact, not an operating problem | Operating profit for the nine months RMB 4.86B against a nine-month net income of RMB 3.21B; disclosed exchange loss RMB 303M (first quarter) → RMB 560M (first half) → **RMB 720M (nine months)** | **Corroborated.** Strip the non-operating currency line and earnings power is up double digits. It is also an admission that reported profit is now hostage to a bookkeeping choice |
| "All large-scale equipment have been put into use" / near-full utilisation (2026-03-24, 2026-10-26) | Revenue per unit of capacity is rising while capital spending falls — consistent. Third quarter 2026 revenue RMB 11.94B on RMB 0.76B of capital spending | **Supported**, and it is the mechanism behind the margin gain |
| Finance costs are coming down through active debt management; USD 1B repaid June-July 2025 (2025-10-30) | Interest expense RMB 969M (2023) → 791M (2024) → **636M (2025)**. Net debt RMB 9.71B (2026-06-30) → **7.58B (2026-09-30)**; total borrowings RMB 15.05B against RMB 7.48B cash; net debt about 1.0x EBITDA | **Delivered, and verifiable.** A real and recurring profit tailwind |
| Overseas is the growth engine (every call) | Overseas is 24-25% of revenue (2026-10-26), up from a smaller base; locked overseas technical contracts +47% and bundled services +255% in the nine months of 2025 (2025-10-30) | **Supported directionally**, but the absolute base is small: well-services overseas scale is "about 5 billion" renminbi against a RMB 50B company |
| "There is no strong correlation between whether we have high or low CapEx vis-a-vis our return to investors" (2026-10-26) | Capital spending RMB 9.47B (2023) → 6.03B (2024) → 5.89B (2025), against depreciation of RMB 5.70B. Free cash flow RMB 3.62B → 4.99B → 5.40B | **Convenient but defensible.** Free cash flow did rise as capital spending fell. The problem is the forward statement, below |
| Capital spending guidance of RMB 8.4B for 2026 | Less than RMB 3B spent in nine months; management now says the year will be "almost on par with the situation last year, but might be slightly less than the guidance" (2026-10-26) | **Missed by a wide margin, and volunteered by management.** The trailing twelve-month free cash flow of RMB 5.87B that underpins the 5.3x price-to-free-cash-flow screen is therefore flattered by an underspend management has promised to reverse |
| "The payout ratio shall be stable with the increase" (2026-04-23, and in substance 2026-03-24) | Dividend HK$0.23059 (2024) → 0.25056 (2025) → **0.32349 paid 2026-06-30**, about a third of earnings; 4.5% yield at today's price | **Delivered so far.** But never quantified or dated — see section 5 |
| Costs are controllable | Gross margin fell from 18.8% in 2019 to 12.3% in 2022 through the last inflation; management conceded on 2026-03-24 that the North Sea long-term agreements carry no oil-price pass-through, and on 2025-10-30 that state wage rules mean salaries "would take up a rather big portion of our overall cost" | **The story is poorer than it sounds.** There is no contractual inflation escalator. The recent margin gain is cost and mix work, which is harder to repeat |

**The one place the numbers are materially worse than the narrative is working capital.** Days of sales outstanding are 154 and net current assets are negative (RMB −1.35B). Cash arrives in a fourth-quarter lump — management said it plainly on 2025-10-30 ("because of the speeding up of account settling in the final quarter") and the statements prove it: of RMB 11.29B of 2025 operating cash flow, RMB 9.30B landed in the fourth quarter, and the first quarter of 2026 produced **negative** RMB 2.28B of operating cash flow and negative RMB 3.61B of free cash flow. This is a related-party receivables structure, not a cash machine that pays monthly.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising, with a clear split between operational confidence (rising) and accounting confidence (falling).**

- **2025-10-30 — defensive.** The vocabulary is efficiency and control: "we need to continuously do our homework," "it is still well under control." Management benchmarks downward rather than upward, citing Halliburton's and Baker Hughes's declines to argue relative outperformance. They refuse the Middle East upside the analyst offers.
- **2026-03-24 — structurally confident but macro-agnostic.** On oil: "we are not an expert in this area." On war: "we don't know how long this war will last." But on their own position: "we have a lot of courage and confidence in achieving this goal," and the equipment market is "a tight balance."
- **2026-04-23 — most offensive on operations.** "On the whole, things are better than expectation in terms of segment breakdown"; all three of drilling's revenue, margin and operating profit improved; well-services margin 18.2%, up two percentage points. Simultaneously the most uncomfortable the company has sounded, on currency: "we are even bothered by that."
- **2026-10-26 — confident and, notably, forward-leaning on investment.** "Our overall workload and utilization rates for major equipment remain high"; 2026 workload "better than the expectation we set at the beginning of the year"; and the first unambiguously expansionary statement in the file: equipment holdings "will increase during the 15th Five-Year Plan period."

**Specificity has increased, not decreased** — a good sign. Early calls gave directional colour; the latest calls give named numbers (24-25% overseas, RMB 720M currency loss, RMB 3B of 2027 maturities, capital spending below guidance). The shift in language is the opposite of the usual deterioration pattern: it runs **from** defensive efficiency **to** offensive investment.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: Medium-High on operations; Low on capital-spending guidance.**

Delivered:
- The 14th Five-Year Plan revenue arc management described on 2026-04-23 — "from CNY 30 billion to CNY 40 billion and to CNY 50 billion, exceeding CNY 50 billion" — is exactly what the statements show (RMB 29.20B in 2021 to RMB 50.28B in 2025).
- The tax-rate call from 2025-10-30 ("our effective tax rate has already returned to the normal level, I do not expect any substantial changes") has held; the trailing tax burden is 25%.
- The 2025-10-30 promise that "for the fourth quarter, I would say all 4 vessels will go into normal operations" in Norway was followed by improved drilling profitability in 2026.
- The dividend has risen three years running, as promised in substance.

Missed:
- **Capital spending, badly.** Guided RMB 8.4B for 2026; under RMB 3B spent in nine months; now guided to roughly the 2025 level. Management disclosed this itself, unprompted in substance, which is why the miss costs them less than it otherwise would.
- **The currency fix.** On 2026-04-23 management said they were "currently examining and looking at some possible solutions," explicitly including "adjusting the functional currency that we use in bookkeeping." Six months later the loss had grown from RMB 303M to RMB 720M and nothing had been changed.

**Sandbagging pattern: none detectable, and arguably the reverse.** The screener records four beats in six quarters (67%), but the pattern is lumpy rather than managed — fourth quarters are structurally weak (net income of RMB 632M in the fourth quarter of 2025, roughly a fifth of a normal quarter) because of weather and a wage-cost load management flagged in advance on 2025-10-30. They warn about the bad quarter before it arrives. That is the opposite of sandbagging.

**The single most credibility-positive moment in the file** is on 2026-10-26, when a Bank of America analyst handed management a benign interpretation — "I personally assume that the gain loss from FX conversion for the third quarter is relatively smaller" — and the chief financial officer corrected him against his own interest: "I'm sorry to say, but the situation for our FX loss was during the third quarter was no better than the first half of the year."

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**1. Shareholder returns — asked at three consecutive calls, never answered with a number.** On 2026-03-24 ("given the decline in your gearing ratio, in the future, are you going to increase dividend payout?"), on 2026-04-23 (Changjiang Securities, directly on the 2026-2030 return plan), and in substance again later. Every answer lands on the same formula: "the payout ratio shall be stable with the increase," prefaced by a long passage about revenue milestones. For a company whose entire investment case rests on converting free cash flow into something a Hong Kong minority holder can collect, **this is the most important non-answer in the file.**

**2. Day rates.** Analysts keep probing whether prices with the parent can rise; management keeps redirecting to utilisation. The clearest instance is 2026-10-26: "I believe that this indicator [full utilisation] will contribute much, much more to our overall operational performance compared with any slight change in the day rate." Translation: they do not expect to win much on price.

**3. Marine-support pricing — pushed on, and effectively conceded.** On 2026-03-24 an analyst asked whether the pricing mechanism would change. The answer: "this has been an old issue that has been dwelling for 10-odd years… we are of the view that it is better to put higher requirements on ourselves than to making requests with other parties." That is a surrender dressed as self-improvement, and management itself called the area one of "the pain points in our operation."

**4. Oil-price pass-through — asked, and denied.** On 2026-03-24: "is there any way that you can pass on such oil price increase impact?" Answer: "if such mechanism can be put in place, it is good. But then right now, we believe that our customers also encounter much difficulty." No escalator exists.

**5. A question that later turned into bad news.** Through 2025 and early 2026 analysts pressed repeatedly on the Middle East restart story. Management refused to endorse it ("we do not have any well-established demand," 2025-10-30), and by 2026-03-24 the conflict had suspended three pieces of integrated equipment in Iraq. The analysts were wrong and management was right — worth weighting.

**6. What analysts are not asking.** Nobody on these calls asks about the 154-day receivable cycle, the negative net current asset position, or why cash collection is concentrated in a single quarter. That is the largest unexamined risk in the file.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The currency loss is growing and unaddressed.** RMB 303M (first quarter 2026) → RMB 560M (first half) → RMB 720M (nine months). It is the sole reason nine-month profit is flat. The fix has been "under examination" since 2026-04-23. The renminbi is near a 52-week high against the Hong Kong dollar, so the drag is live.

🔴 **Free cash flow is flattered and about to be squeezed.** Trailing free cash flow of RMB 5.87B rests on under RMB 3B of nine-month capital spending against an RMB 8.4B guide — and management stated on 2026-10-26 that 2026-2030 investment intensity "will be even more than during the 14th 5-Year Plan period," which averaged about RMB 5.9B a year. Deferred projects are "incorporated in our future vessel building plans" and "will be gradually released down the road."

🔴 **Cash collection is lumpy and related-party.** 154 days of sales outstanding; negative RMB 1.35B of net current assets; RMB 9.30B of RMB 11.29B of 2025 operating cash flow arrived in the fourth quarter; the first quarter of 2026 burned RMB 3.61B of free cash.

🔴 **No inflation pass-through, with a bad precedent.** Gross margin fell 18.8% → 12.3% through 2021-2022. Management conceded on 2026-03-24 that no oil-price escalator exists in the North Sea agreements, and on 2025-10-30 that state-set wage rules dominate the cost base.

🔴 **Pricing power sits with the parent, not the company.** Over 75% of revenue is domestic, the bulk of it to the controlling shareholder; day rates are "overall maintained steady" under a three-year agreement; the marine-support price has been disputed for a decade without resolution.

🔴 **Shareholder-return policy remains a formula, not a number**, after three calls of being asked.

🟢 **Margins and returns are expanding, on evidence.** Gross margin 12.3% → 17.4% → 20.5%; operating margin 8.4% → 13.7%; return on equity 8.1% and return on invested capital 7.5% trailing, both up substantially from 2022. This is a widening, not an eroding, earnings base.

🟢 **The fleet is effectively sold out.** "All large-scale equipment have been put into use" (2026-03-24); "the utilization rate of equipment of Chinese players now is at a relatively high level" and the operating rule is "full utilization of the vessels… without leaving them idle" (2026-10-26).

🟢 **Industry consolidation is on their side.** "For the large contractors and companies, we can see that the profit margin is rising. However, for the smaller contractors, many of their rigs and platforms have been suspended" (2026-03-24). The company intends to buy distressed small-operator equipment.

🟢 **First real evidence of price moving their way.** The new three-year parent agreement added "additional award or reward mechanism… slight increase of day rate for equipment with good operational performance," and management attributed part of nine-month drilling revenue growth to it (2026-10-26). After a decade of price surrender, this is a change in kind.

🟢 **Deleveraging is real and measurable.** USD 1B repaid June-July 2025, high-coupon debt swapped out, interest expense RMB 969M → 636M, net debt down RMB 2.1B in the third quarter of 2026 alone.

🟢 **Internationalisation has dated proof points, not just slides.** Locked overseas technical contracts +47% and bundled services +255% in the nine months of 2025; the south-Brazil semi-submersible rig operating since September 2025; a Kazakhstan framework signed personally by the chairman; thirteen countries and 120 operating sites.

🟢 **Unusual candour.** Correcting an analyst's optimistic currency assumption against interest, volunteering a capital-spending shortfall against their own guidance, and naming their own pain points.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The business model is quietly changing from buying assets to building them.** On 2026-03-24 management listed four ways to add capacity — "leasing, self-construction, transfer, and purchase" — then ranked them: leasing "has to be left for a later stage," self-construction is the priority, purchase only "when we see resources with high value for money." The new vocabulary is "productization," "reliable… highly efficient, intensive," "replicated and… further promoted." Lower cash cost per rig, but a longer payback and more capitalised engineering, which is why the 2026-2030 capital-spending warning matters more than it first reads.

**A terminology shift away from cost.** Through 2025 and early 2026 the standing strategy list led with "cost-oriented" and "cost leadership." On 2026-03-24 management described the change of development method as moving from "major elements input" to "a knowledge-based approach." Cost leadership has stopped being the primary identity.

**A double negative worth reading twice.** On 2026-10-26: "we have yet given up plans to buy additional drilling vessels." Combined with "investment in heavy asset shall be done in areas where there is a high level of certainty," the 2026-2030 plan is a newbuild-plus-acquisition cycle, not a harvest cycle. A deep-value buyer should not assume the current free cash flow is distributable.

**The analyst base has changed what it asks about.** In 2025 the questions were rescue narratives: are the Middle East rigs restarting, will oil go up, is the North Sea idle. On 2026-10-26 four of the questions were capital-allocation questions: why is capital spending below guidance, what happened to the currency loss, how will you prioritise scarce equipment, will the parent's higher capital spending flow to you. The buy side has moved from "is demand coming" to "where does the cash go" — the deep-value question — and management has not yet given it an answer.

**The chairman, not a segment head, signed Kazakhstan** (2026-04-23). Internationalisation is a board-level commitment, which raises both the probability it happens and the probability capital is spent on it.

**One voice, consistently.** The chief financial officer, Qie Ji, answers nearly every substantive question across all four calls. There is no management turnover to read, and no second voice contradicting the first — which is why his willingness to correct an analyst downward carries weight.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

The operating business is demonstrably better than it was three years ago and better than it was a year ago: gross margin from 12.3% to 20.5%, operating margin from 8.4% to 13.7%, the fleet effectively sold out, the interest bill down a third, net debt falling, and the first performance-linked day-rate mechanism the parent has ever granted. The flat nine-month profit line is an accounting translation artefact, disclosed candidly, not an operating stall.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: the free cash flow you are buying is not the free cash flow on the screen.** Trailing free cash flow of RMB 5.87B — the basis of the 5.3x price-to-free-cash-flow headline — reflects under RMB 3B of capital spending in nine months against an RMB 8.4B guide, and management has stated on the record (2026-10-26) that 2026-2030 investment intensity will exceed the 2021-2025 period, which itself averaged about RMB 5.9B a year. Underwrite mid-cycle free cash flow of roughly RMB 5.0-5.4B, and stress it to RMB 3B if capital spending steps to RMB 8B. Second, and nearly as important: there is no dated mechanism that converts that cash into a Hong Kong shareholder's return. Management has answered the payout question with the same unquantified formula three times.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and WIDENING.** The moat type is a combination of **regulatory-licence** and **scale-cost**: COSL is the dedicated offshore services arm of the state offshore oil company, which supplies three-quarters of its revenue under multi-year agreements, and it owns the largest Chinese offshore fleet in a market management itself describes as in "tight balance," where small contractors are stacking rigs. Judged on the evidence rather than the story, the width is narrow, not wide: a 7.5% return on invested capital and 8.1% return on equity sit barely at the cost of capital, and the price-setting power belongs to the controlling shareholder rather than to the company — a decade-old unresolved marine-support pricing dispute and an explicit admission that no oil-price pass-through exists are both moat evidence against. But the **trend is clearly widening**: returns and margins are rising from a low base on every measure, the newly granted performance-linked day-rate mechanism is the first pricing concession in years, and consolidation is removing competing capacity. A 22.6% EBITDA margin that exceeds Schlumberger's 19.6%, Halliburton's 18.0% and Baker Hughes's 17.8% is not the signature of an eroding franchise.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The applicable structural force is the energy transition — long-run displacement of oil and gas demand would ultimately shrink the offshore services pool. Three facts keep it from being terminal inside any horizon this committee underwrites: the demand driver here is a national energy-security mandate rather than the oil price (China consumes 750-760 million tonnes of oil a year against falling domestic conventional output, and a new ten-year production action plan was proposed in October 2026); the parent is growing offshore output and raising its own capital spending; and the fleet is sold out today at near-full utilisation. The risk is cyclical and policy-dependent, not terminal.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a shrinking base?** Predominantly a **fear-print**, with a structural haircut that must be respected rather than wished away. At HK$7.165 the Hong Kong line trades at 0.60 times book and about 3.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA — the cheapest in its global peer group on both measures — on a margin profile at the top of that group and mid-pack returns. The earnings base is growing, not shrinking. But the identical shares are quoted at RMB 12.77 in Shanghai, equivalent to HK$14.99: a 109% premium. That gap is not a judgement about the business; it is a Hong Kong access-and-governance discount applied across Chinese state-owned enterprises, it is shared-factor rather than company-specific, and it has no forcing function. The honest conclusion is that the business is better than the Hong Kong price implies and that part of the discount will not close on anything this committee can name.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend widening · structural threat manageable.
