picks.bull_thesis: ANTA is China's largest sportswear group and one of the best-run consumer franchises in Asia, priced like an ordinary one. In the first half of 2026 (to 30 June) revenue rose 12.9% to RMB43.5B, gross margin rose to 63.9% and operating profit rose 16.1% to RMB11.8B, with an operating margin of 27.0%. Free cash flow was RMB11.6B in six months, and the company pays out about half its underlying profit. Return on equity is about 23% and the screener scores it 8 of 9 on the Piotroski quality test. The growth engine has moved to the premium portfolio - Descente and Kolon Sport grew 44% in the first half and 25-30% in the third quarter - which sells at higher prices and higher margins than the mass ANTA brand. On top of the operating business sit two listed stakes the market barely credits: about a third of Amer Sports (Arc'teryx, Salomon, Wilson; our stake estimate is approximate) worth roughly HK$17 a share at Amer's live price, and 29% of Puma worth about HK$3.50 a share. Strip those and the net cash out of the HK$80.65 price and the operating business trades at about 10-11 times its 2026 earnings, against 12-13 times for the weaker Li Ning. If the third-quarter dip proves to be weather and promotions, as management says, and the core brands steady in 2027 while the premium brands keep growing in the 20s, a re-rating to 18 times underlying earnings plus full credit for the stakes gets to about HK$135. Brokers' targets sit at HK$108-110 (CLSA, 2026-09-25; Citi 2026-06, HK$108.8), which supports a value above today's price.
picks.bear_thesis: The two brands that make up three-quarters of revenue have stopped growing. ANTA brand retail sales went from high-single-digit growth in Q1 2026 to low single digits in Q2 to a mid-single-digit decline in Q3; FILA went from 10-20% growth to a low-single-digit decline over the same three quarters. ANTA-brand operating profit grew just 1.2% in the first half. Management blames weather and promotions, but Xtep and Li Ning reported declines in the same quarter, which says China's mass sportswear market is saturated and fighting on price. Full-year guidance for the two core brands now needs a fourth-quarter rebound. Meanwhile the company is spending its cash on stakes in other people's turnarounds: EUR1.51B for 29% of a loss-making Puma (third-quarter loss of EUR55M, sales down 5%), already worth a quarter less than ANTA paid. Reported earnings are inflated by repeated one-off gains on Amer Sports (RMB1.55B in H1 2026), so the trailing earnings per share of 10.81 in our data overstates the business by about half. The net-cash figure is fuzzy: the company says RMB39B at June, the balance sheet recomputation says RMB11B, and RMB11B of Puma plus the interim dividend have gone out since. If the core brands keep shrinking and margins give back to promotions, the operating business deserves 10-11 times earnings like Xtep's tier, the stakes deserve a holding-company discount, and the value is about HK$66.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market: the street prices ANTA as a mature China-consumer name whose core brands have stopped growing - and on that point the street is right as of the 2026-10-21 update. Where it is looking the wrong way is the parts. At HK$80.65, roughly HK$20-30 a share is the Amer Sports and Puma stakes plus net cash, so the operating business with a 27% operating margin and RMB11.6B of half-year free cash flow is valued at about 10-11 times earnings, cheaper than Li Ning. Broker targets cluster at HK$108-110 (CLSA 2026-09-25, Citi June 2026), above our HK$99, so we are not the optimists; our edge is narrower than consensus and rests on the stakes and cash, not on a core-brand rebound.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the next 3-9 months): the fourth-quarter operating update (around January 2027) could confirm a second quarter of declines at the ANTA brand and FILA and force a guidance cut; full-year 2026 results (around March 2027) will carry Puma's losses through the associates line and may book an impairment on a stake bought above today's market value. China's consumer weakness and promotional price wars across Li Ning and Xtep could pressure margins. There is no debt wall or cash-burn risk: the group is net cash and generates free cash flow every half-year.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure is limited; this is a widely held Hong Kong large cap. The plausible seller to our HK$70 level is a sector-wide sell-off in Chinese consumer and global sportswear stocks - the kind that took the stock to its 52-week low of HK$66.85 - for example on a weak fourth-quarter update across the sector or a broader Hong Kong de-rating. Southbound and index flows add volatility but are not company-specific.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near HK$70, which a sector-wide sell-off in Chinese consumer and global sportswear stocks could deliver. This is the answer we gave on 2026-10-19, and what has happened since does not argue for buying at today's HK$80.65. The thesis holds: ANTA is a high-quality, cash-generative group (first-half 2026 operating margin 27%, gross margin 63.9%, free cash flow RMB11.6B in six months) with a narrow but real moat and no structural threat to its long-run value. But the one new fact, the third-quarter update of 2026-10-21, was negative: the ANTA brand and FILA - three-quarters of revenue - both saw retail sales fall for the first time since 2022, while the smaller premium brands kept growing 25-30%. The Puma stake closed in early October and is already worth about a quarter less than ANTA paid. Our sum-of-the-parts (valuing each piece separately) puts fair value at about HK$99: the operating business at 14 times underlying earnings (HK$77), the Amer Sports stake after a holding-company discount (HK$12.70), Puma (HK$2.80) and net cash (HK$7.60). That leaves about 23% upside, enough to clear our 20% bar on paper, but the adverse case of HK$66 assumes the core brands keep shrinking, and the next two reports could prove it. At HK$70 the upside to fair value is about 41% and the margin over the adverse case is real; that is the price at which we would commit capital. Value conviction stays at 3: a genuine discount on a quality franchise, held back by core-brand momentum turning negative and capital going into Puma's turnaround.
picks.forcing_function: The catalyst that forces a re-rating is not dated. The useful reads are the fourth-quarter operating update (around January 2027), full-year 2026 results with the final dividend (around March 2027), and any buyback or special distribution from the net cash. A clear return to growth at the core brands while premium brands keep growing in the 20s would re-rate the multiple; a sector-wide sell-off would give us our entry price.

# ANTA Sports Products (2020.HK) - a deep dive on management and the setup
*Prepared 2026-11-16. Live price HK$80.65 (Hong Kong listing, HKD; FMP quote 2026-11-16). Company reports in Chinese yuan (RMB); RMB 1 = HK$1.176 (FMP, 2026-11-16).*

**Source note.** FMP holds no earnings-call transcript for this Hong Kong listing, and no transcript was bundled. This dossier is built from the company's own dated releases: the 2026 interim results (published 2026-08-26 on the ANTA investor-relations site), the third-quarter 2026 operating update (2026-10-21, as reported by SGI Europe, 10jqka, Jiemian and Eastmoney), the Puma stake completion (reported 2026-10-08), and the screener's financial trajectory. No call quotes are reproduced because none could be sourced; where we describe management's tone we cite the written releases.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
The story has shifted from "ANTA the brand" to "ANTA the brand portfolio." Through 2023-24 the growth engine was the ANTA brand and FILA together, with Descente and Kolon Sport as add-ons. In 2026 that order flipped. In the first half of 2026 (six months to 30 June) group revenue rose 12.9% to RMB43.5B, but the ANTA brand grew only 4.8% (RMB17.8B) and FILA 6.1% (RMB15.1B), while "all other brands" grew 44.2% to RMB10.7B. The third-quarter operating update (2026-10-21) then showed the two big brands' retail sales falling year on year: ANTA brand down by a mid-single-digit percentage and FILA down by a low-single-digit percentage, against other brands up 25-30%. Quarter by quarter the ANTA brand went from high-single-digit growth (Q1 2026) to low-single-digit growth (Q2) to a decline (Q3); FILA went from 10-20% growth to low single digits to a decline. Press reports note the last quarterly retail decline at the ANTA brand was during the 2022 pandemic lockdowns.

The second new chapter is global: ANTA closed its EUR1.51B purchase of a 29.06% stake in Puma in early October 2026 (approved unconditionally by China's market regulator on 2026-09-11), on top of its large stake in Amer Sports (Arc'teryx, Salomon, Wilson). The company has said it will not bid for the rest of Puma.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)
| Claim (source, date) | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-brand strategy keeps group growth in double digits (interim results, 2026-08-26) | H1 2026 revenue +12.9%; operating profit +16.1% to RMB11.76B; operating margin 27.0% (+0.7 points) | Corroborated for H1 |
| Gross margin is stable and high | Gross margin 63.9% in H1 2026 (+0.5 points); screener shows 62% for FY2025, "stable" | Corroborated |
| Cash generation is strong | H1 2026 free cash flow RMB11.63B (+54.2%); FY2025 FCF margin 22.8%; Piotroski 8/9 | Corroborated; the 54% jump partly reflects working-capital timing |
| Profit growth is clean | H1 2026 profit excluding a one-off RMB1.55B gain from the dilution of its Amer Sports stake rose 12.9% to RMB7.94B. Reported EPS is flattered by repeated Amer one-offs (FY2024 profit of RMB15.6B vs FY2025 RMB13.6B is the same artifact reversing) | Clean only on the adjusted basis; the trailing EPS of 10.81 in the metrics block should not be capitalised |
| The core ANTA brand is still growing | ANTA brand segment operating profit grew only 1.2% in H1 on 4.8% sales growth, then Q3 retail sales fell | Narrative is now richer than the numbers for the core brand |
| Net cash is large | Company: about RMB39.1B net cash at 2026-06-30; the screener's balance-sheet recomputation shows only RMB11.07B (cash RMB44.06B minus debt RMB32.99B incl. leases). The gap is mostly long-term deposits and other treasury assets the company counts. Since then: Puma (about RMB11.3B) and the interim dividend (HK$1.51 a share, about HK$4.2B) have been paid out | Treat as roughly RMB0-24B pro forma; we use about RMB18B in the base case |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Stable to slightly declining. The interim release (2026-08-26) was confident - record revenue, record profit, margin expansion. The Q3 update (2026-10-21) is more defensive: the official wording described the two main brands as seeing "slight fluctuation," while the company pointed to a tougher consumer backdrop than in the first half, intense promotional price competition and extreme weather (rainstorms and typhoons) hurting store traffic. Offence has moved from the domestic core to the portfolio and to Puma.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Medium-high. The screener shows 7 of 7 recent periods beating expectations. Full-year 2026 retail-sales guidance (ANTA brand low-single-digit growth, FILA mid-single-digit, other brands above 20%) was set early in the year. Other brands are well ahead of it (25-30% in Q3, above 30% year to date). The ANTA brand and FILA now need a fourth-quarter rebound to hit their guidance; we could not find a dated revision of it, so it is at risk rather than missed. Score: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- Whether the ANTA-brand and FILA slowdown is weather and promotions (temporary) or saturation in China's mass sportswear market. Peers Xtep and Li Ning also reported retail declines for the same quarter, which points to an industry-wide slowdown.
- Capital allocation: paying EUR1.51B for 29% of Puma, a loss-making turnaround (Puma reported a EUR55M third-quarter loss and a 5% sales drop). At Puma's live price (EUR25.94, market value EUR3.82B) the stake is worth about EUR1.11B - roughly a quarter below what ANTA paid. Broker Guangfa flagged a near-term profit drag.
- The press has reported talks about Castore; nothing confirmed.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red: two core brands turned negative in Q3 2026 for the first time since 2022.
- Red: the ANTA brand's operating profit has stalled (+1.2% in H1 2026).
- Red: a mark-to-market loss on the Puma stake within weeks of closing, and a growing reliance on associates whose profits are lumpy.
- Green: H1 2026 gross margin of 63.9% and operating margin of 27.0% (both up) despite price competition.
- Green: other brands (Descente, Kolon Sport) grew 44% in H1 and 25-30% in Q3 - a real second engine.
- Green: free cash flow of RMB11.6B in H1 alone; a payout of about 50% of underlying profit.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
The language has moved from "single focus, multi-brand" to global platform-building (Amer, Puma). Reporting "slight fluctuation" when media read the figures as declines is soft framing, though not misleading - the disclosure is by range, as always. Profit excluding one-offs is now the headline number, which is the honest choice given the Amer gains.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)
Trajectory: stable. Group economics are intact, but growth has migrated from the core brands to the portfolio and to associates. The single most important thing to weigh: whether the Q3 2026 decline at the ANTA brand and FILA is a cyclical consumer-and-weather dip or the start of saturation. The group's numbers to June 2026 say the franchise is healthy; the fourth quarter (reported around January 2027) and the FY2026 results (around March 2027) will tell.

Moat: intangible brand plus scale-cost (China's largest sportswear distribution and supply chain). Return on equity of about 23% and return on invested capital of about 14%, with gross margin steady around 62-64%: a narrow but real moat, stable rather than widening. Secular threat: manageable - competition from domestic brands and channel promotions is cyclical and competitive, not terminal; no structural force (AI, channel extinction) impairs terminal value. The cheapness (about 14x underlying earnings) is a China-consumer fear print, not a shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: Sprouts is a 504-store natural and organic grocer that grew revenue from $6.1B (2021) to $8.81B (2025) and earnings per share from $2.10 to $5.31, with a gross margin near 38% that conventional grocers do not reach. At $49.58 the market value is about $4.6B; excluding leases the company holds about $0.1B of net cash, so the operating business trades at roughly 7.5 times this year's guided operating profit of about $605M and about 10 times trailing free cash flow of $336M. The growth engine still works: the 2026 store class is 'outperforming our expectations' and recent vintages comp positively (Q3 2026 call, 2026-10-28), the pipeline holds more than 105 signed leases and 160 approved sites, and 42 net new stores are planned for 2026, close to 9% unit growth. Sprouts Brand (26% of sales) and e-commerce (16% of sales, +12%) keep growing. The Q3 2026 reset is deliberate: management is putting price into the customers it lost, committing to keep the operating margin above 5%, and a new CEO (Nick Konat) has every reason to set a low bar he can beat. If traffic stabilizes in the first half of 2027, the 2027 operating margin can hold 5.5-6%, earnings can rebuild toward $5 a share with buybacks ($537M authorization left) shrinking the count, and a grocer with high-single-digit unit growth deserves 15-17 times earnings, putting the shares at $75-85. The stock sits about 4% above its 52-week low and 35% below its 200-day average, and Street targets were already cut to $49-74, so expectations are low. Conditions: Q4 2026 comps inside the -2% to -4% guide, transactions improving, and the 2027 margin guide at or above 5.5%.
picks.bear_thesis: On 2026-10-28 management itself said the traffic loss is 'not cyclical' - transactions fell 3.3% in Q3 even against easier comparisons, and Walmart's better produce execution and 'intensifying competition' in conventional produce are hitting the category Sprouts is built on. Guidance credibility is poor: the 2026 EPS outlook was raised to $5.32-5.48 in April and cut to about $4.80 six months later. The fix is a price investment of unknown size and duration (about 90 basis points of Q4 gross-margin deleverage and about 170 basis points of expense deleverage), and the only floor offered is an operating margin 'above 5%'. A grocer that must buy traffic with price while carrying $2.12B of store leases has high operating leverage on the way down: every point of negative comps hits a fixed-cost base. If 2027 margins land near 4.5-5% and comps stay negative, EPS falls to about $4.00-4.40, consensus already sees forward EPS down about 12%, and the stock re-rates to a conventional-grocer 9-10 times, or $38-44. Insiders sold 56 times on the open market with zero purchases, the CEO is changing mid-reset, and past buybacks were done at prices well above today's, destroying value. What would confirm it: Q4 2026 comps worse than -4%, or a 2027 margin guide below 5%.
picks.consensus_delta: The question for a cheap grocer is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a business with durable earnings power. Partly yes: at about 10-11 times this year's reduced EPS and about 7.5 times operating profit excluding leases, the price implies the 2025 earnings peak ($5.31) was a one-off and margins keep sliding. Our base case agrees the peak was inflated by a 2024-25 customer surge, but sees a floor near a 5.4% operating margin supported by new stores that comp positively. Where we do not disagree with the Street: the newest targets (Wells Fargo $60, Barclays $65, Roth $56 on 2026-10-29) already discount a reset, and consensus forward EPS down about 12% is reasonable. Our edge is not a different 2027 number but a valuation that already sits below a reasonable base - which only matters once the 2027 guide removes the open-ended price-investment risk.
picks.valley_of_death: The next three to four months are the risky window: Q4 2026 is guided to comps of -2% to -4% with about 260 basis points of operating-margin pressure, the holiday quarter will show whether price cuts move traffic, and the new CEO may 'kitchen-sink' the 2027 guide. There is no debt wall (borrowings $119M, revolver to July 2030) and free cash flow stays positive, so there is no liquidation or financing risk - the danger is a further de-rating if the 2027 margin guide lands below 5%, which would take the stock toward the $40 bear value.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure is moderate and mostly done. Growth and momentum holders who owned Sprouts for its 2024-25 share gains have been exiting since the 2026-10-28 results (about a 20% one-day drop, then a further slide from about $55 to $49.58 by 2026-11-09); fund filings show trimming (Boston Trust Walden cut 5.1%, reported 2026-11-05). There is no index deletion, lock-up or dividend-cut holder base to force mechanical selling. Insiders sold 56 times on the open market with zero purchases. Smart-money score 34/100.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for proof: we buy once the 2027 outlook, due with Q4 2026 results around 2027-02-25, shows an operating-margin guide of 5.5% or better and fourth-quarter comparable-store sales land at or better than -3%. The thesis is in doubt until that test. Nothing new happened at the company between our 2026-11-02 look and today; the stock simply fell another 10% to $49.58 as holders kept exiting after the 2026-10-28 guidance cut. Management called the traffic loss 'not cyclical', has missed its own outlook once this year, and is changing CEO mid-reset, so buying before the 2027 guide would be buying an open-ended margin cut. The business case is real - about 9% unit growth from stores that beat plan, a 38% gross margin, net cash outside leases and steady free cash flow - and the price is cheap versus grocery peers, so we keep conviction at 3 and keep the wait. Downside if the test fails is about $40; upside if it passes is the mid-$60s, with $85 if margins rebuild toward 6%.

# Sprouts Farmers Market (SFM) - a deep dive on management and the setup
As of 2026-11-09. Price used: $49.58 (Nasdaq, US dollars, FMP live quote). Transcripts read: five calls, Q3 2025 (2025-10-29) through Q3 2026 (2026-10-28).

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC
The story has moved in four steps from "health-and-wellness share gainer" to "a grocer that must buy back its own customers with lower prices."

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-29):** comparable-store sales (sales at stores open more than a year, "comps") up 5.9%, traffic positive, gross margin 38.7%. The first crack appeared: management "underestimated the impact of lapping strong numbers from last year."
- **Q4 2025 (2026-02-19):** comps slowed to +1.6% and traffic turned "slightly negative after a disappointing holiday season." The problem was framed as the lower-engaged customer "visiting less often" - a lapping issue, not a franchise issue.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-29):** comps -1.7%, yet management raised the earnings-per-share outlook to $5.32-5.48 and promised that comparisons would "improve in the back half." First "selective price adjustments" appeared.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-29):** comps -1.0%, results "in line with our outlook," July "improved in line with expectations."
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-28):** the turn. Comps -0.9% (about 0.6 points from a cyclospora food-safety disruption), transactions -3.3%. The chief financial officer said traffic, units and frequency "are not recovering, even against easier compares," which is "an important signal that the pressure on the business was not cyclical." The full-year EPS outlook was cut to about $4.80 (52-week basis), the fourth quarter was guided to comps of -2% to -4% with roughly 260 basis points of operating-margin deleverage, and the CEO handed over to Nick Konat, with Jack Sinclair moving to executive chairman. The only margin commitment left is an operating margin (EBIT, earnings before interest and taxes, as a share of sales) "above 5%."

What stayed constant: new stores (the 2026 vintage "outperforming our expectations"), Sprouts Brand at about 26% of sales, e-commerce at about 16%, self-distribution in meat and produce, and the buyback.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS
| Claim | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| New-store engine drives growth | Revenue $6.1B (2021) to $8.81B (2025); 504 stores at Q3 2026 vs 464 a year earlier; 42 net new planned in 2026 | Matches |
| Margins are structurally higher (shrink, self-distribution) | Gross margin 38.8% in FY2025 (+70 basis points); but 38.2% in Q3 2026 (-50 basis points) and about 90 basis points of planned Q4 deleverage | Was true; now reversing |
| Earnings power of $5+ per share | FY2025 EPS $5.31 (+42%); Q1 2026 guide raised to $5.32-5.48; now about $4.80; trailing-twelve-month EPS $5.21 | Peak of the cycle, not the base |
| Cash generation funds growth and buybacks | Operating cash flow $555M year to date, net capex $275M, buybacks $299M; trailing free cash flow $336M | Matches, but buybacks were done at much higher prices |
| Balance sheet is strong | Borrowings only $119M, cash $229M (net cash about $110M excluding leases); with $2.12B of capitalized leases, net debt is $2.01B | Clean ex-leases; leases are a real fixed cost when comps fall |
| Customer gains of 2024 retained | Transactions -3.3% in Q3 2026 | Did not hold up |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY
Declining. From "surging interest in health and wellness" (Q3 2025) to "uneven" operating environment (Q2 2026) to "our recent performance needs to improve" and "we have work to do to strengthen our execution and customer proposition" (Q3 2026). Language moved from offense (unit growth, innovation) to defense (affordability, "deeper investments" in price, cost discipline). Guidance became less specific: a range for EBIT was replaced by a floor ("above 5%") and a promise to "assess customer response and refine the scale and pace of our investments."

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY
Medium-low. Management beat 6 of 7 quarters on EPS historically, but in 2026 the full-year outlook went from raised (Q1: EPS $5.32-5.48, EBIT $675-695M) to cut by about 10% (Q3: EPS about $4.80, EBIT about $605M). The Q1 promise of easier back-half comparisons was explicitly wrong. The pattern is not sandbagging; it is persistent over-optimism on the lapping thesis, followed by a large reset. The reset may now be conservative (the new CEO has an incentive to set a low bar), but that is a hypothesis.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS
- Produce competition: R5 Capital pointed to Walmart's improved produce execution and "inconsistency" in Sprouts' stores. Management conceded "intensifying competition" in conventional produce.
- How deep and how long the price investment runs: management would not size 2027 beyond "EBIT margins to remain above 5%."
- Core-store productivity: older stores are being refreshed; new stores comp positively while the core declines - a sign that the base, not the format, is leaking.
- Agentic (AI-agent) shopping: dismissed as no visible impact so far.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS
- Red: Q3 2026 - transactions -3.3% with management calling the pressure "not cyclical."
- Red: Q3 2026 - guidance cut about 10% six months after a raise.
- Red: Q3 2026 - CEO transition during a reset.
- Red: insiders - 56 open-market sales and zero purchases over the window in our data.
- Red: Q4 2026 guide - comps -2% to -4% and about 260 basis points of EBIT-margin pressure.
- Green: new-store vintages outperform and comp positively (Q3 2026).
- Green: still a 38% gross-margin grocer with Sprouts Brand at 26% and e-commerce up 12%.
- Green: about $0.1B net cash excluding leases; $537M left on the buyback; Altman-Z of 3.7.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS
"Health enthusiasts" with "not the highest incomes" is a new target-customer framing - the company is moving down-market to defend traffic, which is a margin trade-off. "Affordable entry points" and "conventional produce" signal a partial retreat from the organic premium. Shipt as a fourth delivery platform shows a push for reach. The incoming CEO is the operator who ran the past four years of strategy, so this is continuity, not a clean outsider reset.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT
Trajectory: deteriorating. The single thing the director must weigh: whether the operating margin settles near 5.5% (the business is then worth roughly $60-65 a share) or slides toward 4.5% as price investments fail to restore traffic (roughly $40). The 2027 outlook, expected with Q4 results around late February 2027, settles which.

Moat: narrow, built on a differentiated assortment and private-label brand (an intangible-brand moat) plus format economics. Its width is being tested: gross margin and transactions are both falling while a large rival competes harder in produce. That is erosion of the trend, not proof of terminal decline - the new-store results argue the format still works. Secular threat: manageable; this is competitive and consumer-cyclical pressure, not a structural force that removes the business. The cheapness is mostly a fear-print over a reset, with a real risk that the reset runs longer.

picks.bull_thesis: The bull case is that Gubra is a validated obesity-drug discovery engine trading for less than its pipeline is worth. AbbVie licensed Gubra's long-acting amylin candidate (now ABBV-295) in the first half of 2025, paying roughly DKK 2.4bn of licence income that passed through that half-year's accounts; that deal is outside proof that the peptide-discovery platform produces assets big pharma will pay for, and it leaves Gubra with future development milestones and royalties it did not have to fund. Amylin (a gut hormone that slows eating, now one of the most contested next-generation obesity targets) is a field where a successful long-acting drug could be worth many billions in sales, so even a modest royalty stream can dwarf today's market value. Around that option sit a services business with roughly DKK 250-270m of revenue a year and high gross margins (about 76% in the first half of 2026), a balance sheet with about DKK 715m of net cash (about DKK 43 a share, 30 June 2026) and no bank debt, and a management team that returned about DKK 1.0bn to shareholders in 2025 instead of squandering the windfall. If ABBV-295 advances cleanly through mid-stage trials and the internal pipeline produces a second partnering deal, the parts can sum to well above DKK 400 a share. Conditions: AbbVie keeps prioritising the asset, clinical data show competitive weight loss and tolerability, and Gubra's own spending converts into another licence before the cash runs low.
picks.bear_thesis: The bear case is that the stock arrived here on a measurement error and is not cheap on anything that recurs. The screen's 2.9x price-to-free-cash-flow and 64% net margin come entirely from the first half of 2025's licence income. In the first half of 2026 Gubra reported revenue of DKK 126m, an operating loss of DKK 123m, a net loss of DKK 110m and free cash flow of minus DKK 187m; the twelve months to 30 June 2026 show about DKK 271m of revenue and a net loss of roughly DKK 182m. Net cash fell from about DKK 976m to about DKK 715m in six months, as operating costs nearly doubled from the 2024 run-rate and the company took on a larger leased facility. Services revenue has been flat for two years, so the profitable base is not growing. At DKK 297.20 the market pays about DKK 4.2bn after net cash for that loss-making business plus a pipeline whose lead asset sits in AbbVie's hands, in an amylin field crowded with programmes from Novo Nordisk, Zealand Pharma with Roche, Eli Lilly and others. Any slip in ABBV-295's timeline, an unfavourable tolerability readout from a rival amylin programme that de-rates the class, or AbbVie deprioritising the asset would leave Gubra burning about DKK 350-380m a year with roughly two years of cash. What would confirm it: another half-year of flat services revenue and a further DKK 180m-plus cash decline at the next report, with no milestone payment.
picks.consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is narrower than the screen suggests. Quantitative screens show Gubra at three times free cash flow with a discounted-cash-flow value of DKK 493.50; that view is simply wrong, because it capitalises the 2025 licence cheque as if it recurs. The market itself does not appear to make that error - the share price has fallen from a 52-week high of DKK 557.50 to DKK 297.20, about 15% below its 200-day average - and is now valuing Gubra as a pipeline company. We find no analyst price-target coverage for this listing in FMP and could not search for one this run, so we cite none. Our disagreement with the price is in the other direction: even as a pipeline company, we value the parts at about DKK 238, below the market.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) is quiet but costly. The next scheduled report is the full-year 2026 results around early March 2027; until then, the stock has no company-controlled catalyst and the business spends roughly DKK 30m a month. Risks that could hit before any re-rating: data from rival amylin programmes at much larger companies that either raise the bar for ABBV-295 or de-rate the whole class; AbbVie reprioritising its obesity portfolio; and a full-year report showing a further fall in net cash below DKK 600m with flat services revenue. With no debt, there is no maturity wall and no liquidation risk in the next two years.
picks.positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure is limited. There is no dividend left to cut (the 2025 payout was a one-off return of licence cash), so no yield-focused holder base is forced out. Some quantitative value funds may have bought on the 2.9x free-cash-flow screen and could exit as trailing figures roll off the licence year in the full-year 2026 accounts, which could add selling around March 2027. The register is thinly traded (about 38,000 shares on 2 November 2026), so modest selling moves the price, but we cannot name a mechanical seller with a date.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Pass for now. Nothing dated has changed since our 26 October look, so we keep the committee's answer and update only the price. The thesis has broken in the sense that matters for this book: Gubra came to us as a deep-value company at three times free cash flow, and that cheapness came entirely from a one-off licence payment from AbbVie in the first half of 2025. The recurring business - preclinical contract research plus a growing discovery effort - lost DKK 110m in the first half of 2026 on DKK 126m of revenue, and net cash fell to about DKK 715m. Valued by its parts (the services arm, the net cash less two years of spending, the risk-adjusted AbbVie amylin economics and the internal pipeline), we reach about DKK 238 a share, below today's DKK 297.20, with an adverse case near DKK 120 and a favourable case near DKK 439. That favourable case is a real biotech option, but it is a long-dated story in a debt-cycle backdrop that rewards cash now, and it is not a discount. Conviction stays low; the value case on its own also rates low, because the only value is in pipeline options we cannot underwrite at this price.
picks.forcing_function: The catalyst - what forces the re-rating - is clinical progress on ABBV-295 and the milestone payments it would trigger, plus any second licensing deal from Gubra's internal pipeline. Neither has a verified date; both depend on AbbVie or on a counterparty. The one fixed date is the full-year 2026 report, expected around early March 2027, which will show the first full year of the post-licence cost base.
picks.interrogator_dossier:
# Gubra A/S (GUBRA.CO, Copenhagen) - deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-03. Price used: DKK 297.20 (FMP quote, Copenhagen listing, 2 November 2026 session; previous close DKK 297.80). All figures in Danish kroner.

Source note, stated up front: no earnings-call transcript exists in our data feed for this listing (FMP carries none), and this run's web-search budget was exhausted before any new search could be made, so no fresh management commentary could be retrieved. Gubra reports half-yearly. Everything below is built from the reported half-year statements in FMP (through 30 June 2026), the screener's multi-year trajectory, and this committee's own prior work (7 September and 26 October 2026). No management quotes are given because none could be sourced; none are invented.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Gubra began as a contract research organisation (a CRO - a company paid to run preclinical experiments for drug makers) specialising in obesity and metabolic disease models, and built a peptide-discovery engine on top of that know-how. For years the services arm carried the company: revenue of roughly DKK 200-265m a year from 2021 to 2024, with small profits turning into losses as discovery spending grew.

The story changed in the first half of 2025, when AbbVie licensed Gubra's long-acting amylin candidate (now ABBV-295). Roughly DKK 2.4bn of licence income passed through the first-half 2025 income statement, producing a reported half-year net profit of DKK 1.76bn and full-year 2025 earnings per share of about DKK 103. Gubra then paid out about DKK 1.0bn as a dividend in the second half of 2025 and has since stepped up its own spending: operating costs in the first half of 2026 were DKK 219m against DKK 117m in the second half of 2024.

So the narrative has pivoted from "profitable niche CRO" to "obesity-drug discovery company with a validating big-pharma partner, funded by one large licence cheque." The screener sees the old cheque; the business today is the new, cash-consuming shape.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| What the screen implies | What the reported numbers show | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Price/free cash flow of 2.9x, 64% net margin | Both come from the first half of 2025 (licence income). First half 2026: revenue DKK 126m, operating loss DKK 123m, net loss DKK 110m, free cash flow minus DKK 187m | Artifact of a one-off |
| "TTM free cash flow DKK 1.48bn" in the bundle | The two half-years that make up the twelve months to 30 June 2026 show free cash flow of about minus DKK 605m (second half 2025, which includes tax and working-capital outflows tied to the licence year) and minus DKK 187m (first half 2026) | The bundle's figure is stale; the true trailing number is negative |
| Model fair value DKK 493.50 (discounted cash flow) | Extrapolates licence-year cash flow | Not usable |
| Net cash | Cash and short-term investments DKK 901m, debt including leases DKK 187m: net cash about DKK 715m (about DKK 43 a share) at 30 June 2026, down from about DKK 976m six months earlier | Real, but shrinking at roughly DKK 180-190m per half-year |
| Services revenue base | First half 2024 DKK 121m; second half 2024 DKK 145m; second half 2025 DKK 145m; first half 2026 DKK 126m | Flat, not growing |

The core forensic point: the company is honest in its accounts - the licence income is real cash that was really received and largely paid out - but the scan's headline cheapness measures a payment that will not recur.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Cannot be rated from transcripts (none available). The behavioural signal in the numbers is offensive, not defensive: a near doubling of the operating cost base and a larger leased facility (lease liabilities rose from DKK 107m to DKK 158m in six months; property and equipment from DKK 132m to DKK 230m). Management is investing for a bigger discovery business. Trajectory read from actions: rising ambition.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

No guidance history could be retrieved. The screener records 0 of 3 periods as earnings beats, but with no analyst coverage of note on this listing that statistic carries little information. Reliability: unscored (Medium by default, neither corroborated nor contradicted).

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without transcripts, the questions an analyst must press are clear from the numbers: (1) the timing and size of the next AbbVie development milestone; (2) how long the DKK 715m of net cash lasts at the current run-rate (about two years); (3) whether the services arm can grow again or is being run for capability rather than profit; (4) how Gubra's amylin asset is positioned against a crowded field of amylin and amylin-combination programmes at much larger companies.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: First half 2026 operating loss DKK 123m on DKK 126m of revenue - the company now loses about a krone for every krone of sales.
- Red: Net cash fell by about DKK 260m in six months (31 December 2025 to 30 June 2026), partly capital spending on facilities.
- Red: Services revenue flat for two years; the profitable base the stock was once valued on is not expanding.
- Red: The quantitative screen is badly mis-specified for this name (2.9x free cash flow is a one-off artifact), which is how it arrived here as "deep value."
- Green: A clean balance sheet with no bank debt and about DKK 43 a share in net cash.
- Green: AbbVie's licence is third-party validation of the discovery engine and leaves Gubra with future milestone and royalty rights.
- Green: Roughly DKK 1.0bn returned to shareholders in 2025 rather than spent - a shareholder-friendly use of a windfall.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The cost-base expansion and the larger lease are the most important quiet signals: Gubra is choosing to become a more R&D-heavy biotech rather than a services company that banks royalties. That raises the cash burn and makes the equity more dependent on the pipeline - including ABBV-295 milestones that Gubra does not control.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: turning - from a services company into a discovery biotech with a partnered lead asset.

The single most important thing to weigh: the stock is not cheap on any recurring number. At DKK 297.20 the market value is about DKK 4.9bn and, after net cash, the market pays about DKK 4.2bn for a business with DKK 271m of trailing revenue and operating losses. The investment case is a bet on pipeline value (chiefly the AbbVie amylin economics), not on the cash flow the screener shows.

Moat: a narrow but real moat - an intangible, know-how moat in metabolic disease models and peptide engineering, validated by a big-pharma licence; there is no evidence it is widening (services revenue is flat) or eroding (gross margin on services remains high, around 76% in the first half of 2026). Secular threat: manageable - the risk is competitive crowding in amylin and obesity drugs rather than a structural force destroying the business. The cheapness on the screen is neither a fear-print nor a value trap in the classic sense: it is a measurement artifact.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory turning · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

picks.bull_thesis: Adobe is a cash machine priced like a shrinking one. picks.bear_thesis: The cheap multiple may be the market correctly pricing the end of Adobe's pricing power in creative software. picks.interrogator_dossier:
# 4imprint Group plc (FOUR.L) - a deep dive on management and the setup

As of 2026-11-16. No earnings-call transcript is available from our data provider (FMP) for this London listing. This dossier is built from the company's own trading statements and results as reported on the dates shown (20 January 2026 full-year 2025 trading update, 20 May 2026 annual-meeting trading update, 5 August 2026 half-year results, 10 November 2026 ten-month trading update), FMP's reported half-year statements, and the screener's multi-year figures. No management quotes are reproduced because no transcript was read; paraphrases are attributed to the dated statement they come from.

4imprint is a US-centred direct marketer of promotional products (branded pens, drinkware, apparel and bags for businesses). It reports in US dollars and its shares trade in pence in London (live price 4,110p on 2026-11-16, about $54.2 at $1.319 to the pound). The screener files it under advertising agencies; it is really a catalogue-and-online distributor whose edge is a marketing machine and fulfilment network.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- 2021-2024 was a post-pandemic recovery and share-gain story: revenue rose from $787m (2021) to about $1.37bn (2024), and earnings per share from about $0.80 to $4.15. Management's story then was market-share gain from a fragmented distributor base and operating leverage on a brand-marketing (TV, "brand awareness") spend.
- 2025 turned defensive. Revenue slipped to about $1.35bn (20 January 2026 trading update) as US small-business customers ordered less; new-customer orders were down about 13% in the ten months to October 2025 (November 2025 update). The narrative shifted from growth to "resilience" and margin protection.
- 2026 is a stabilisation story with a tariff overlay. Four-month orders were down about 2%, new-customer orders down about 7% (20 May 2026). At the half (5 August 2026) revenue was up about 1% to $666m but adjusted profit before tax fell about 12% to $64.8m as gross margin fell from 32.8% to 31.5% on tariff-related product costs. Management nonetheless raised full-year guidance to revenue slightly above $1.35bn and adjusted profit before tax of about $130m. On 10 November 2026 it reaffirmed that guidance: ten-month revenue up 2%, order intake down 1%, average order value up 3%, new-customer orders down 5% year to date with the decline narrowing every quarter (minus 9% in the first quarter, minus 5% in the second, minus 3% in the third).

The arc is: growth compounder (2021-24), demand stall (2025), tariff-squeezed stabilisation with improving order momentum (2026).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim (dated statement) | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue "slightly above $1.35bn" in 2026 (5 Aug, reaffirmed 10 Nov) | H1 revenue $661-666m, ten months +2% | Matches. |
| Adjusted profit before tax about $130m (5 Aug, reaffirmed 10 Nov) | H1 adjusted $64.8m (reported $59.6m); ten-month operating margin just above 9% | Achievable; implies a second half of about $65m, similar to the first. Note it is down from about $149m+ in 2025 (20 Jan 2026 update) - a 12-13% profit decline. |
| Gross margin pressure is tariff-driven and manageable | Gross margin 32.8% (H1 2025) to 31.5% (H1 2026) to "just above 31%" (ten months) | Consistent; the squeeze is real and still building into the second half. |
| Strong cash generation | Cash $152m at end-October 2026 after $68m of dividends and a ~$10m office project; FMP shows half-year free cash flow of $51.6m (H1 2026) and $54.4m (H2 2025) | Matches. Trailing free cash flow is about $106m, not the $229m in the screener's trailing block. |
| Screener trailing earnings per share $7.78, free cash flow $229m | FMP half-years: earnings per share $2.07 (H2 2025) + $1.53 (H1 2026) = $3.60 | The screener's trailing figures double-count half-yearly reports. True trailing earnings per share is about $3.60. The headline 69% margin of safety is a data artefact. |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Stable. The tone through 2025 was cautious (demand softness among small US businesses, tariff uncertainty). In 2026 it firmed: a guidance raise at the half (5 August) despite lower margins, and a clean reaffirmation with improving new-customer trends on 10 November. Guidance remained specific (revenue level plus a profit-before-tax number), which is a sign of confidence rather than hedging.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

High. The 2025 full-year outcome (about $1.35bn revenue, profit before tax of at least $149m) was flagged early and delivered. The 2026 guidance was raised at the half and held at ten months. The screener shows earnings beats in three of the last three reported periods. No sandbagging pattern of note; management tends to guide once and hit it.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- How far tariffs compress gross margin in the second half of 2026 and in 2027, and how much can be passed on (average order value up about 3% suggests partial pass-through).
- Whether the brand-marketing spend still buys new customers efficiently: new-customer orders fell about 13% in 2025 and about 5% in 2026 to date.
- Capital allocation: a large net cash pile (about $152m) and whether special dividends continue (2025 included a large payout; $119.9m of dividends in H1 2025 per FMP).
- Broker coverage is thin (about five analysts). Published targets found range from about 3,500p (Deutsche Bank, March 2026) to 5,140p (Berenberg, March 2026) and about 5,300p (Peel Hunt, undated); consensus averages of roughly 4,650-4,950p were reported by aggregators around mid-2026. None was found dated after the 10 November update.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: profit before tax down about 12-13% in 2026 on flat revenue; gross margin down about 1.5 points since H1 2025 (tariffs); operating margin fallen from about 10.8% (2024-25) to just above 9% (ten months 2026); new-customer acquisition shrinking two years running.
- Red (data, not company): the screener's trailing earnings and cash-flow figures are inflated roughly 2x, which is what made the stock screen as deep value.
- Green: net cash about $152m (end-October 2026), essentially no debt; return on invested capital above 50%; free cash flow about $106m trailing; new-customer decline narrowing each quarter of 2026; average order value rising; guidance raised (5 August) and reaffirmed (10 November).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The emphasis has moved from "share gain" to "average order value" and "existing customers" - a defensive, retention-led framing typical of a mature franchise.
- A roughly $10m office relocation in Oshkosh, Wisconsin is being treated as an adjusting item; the gap between adjusted and reported profit (H1: $64.8m vs $59.6m) should be watched so that recurring costs do not migrate into adjustments.
- The interim dividend was held at 80.0 cents (5 August 2026) rather than raised - consistent with a flat-earnings year.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: stable. This is a high-quality, cash-generative, debt-free business going through a flat year with tariff margin pressure and improving order trends. The single most important thing to weigh: the cheapness the screen reported is not real. On true trailing earnings of about $3.60 per share (about 273p) the shares trade at about 15 times earnings, or about 13.5 times after stripping out net cash of about 411p a share - a fair, not a cheap, price for a no-growth year.

Moat: scale-cost and marketing-machine (customer-acquisition engine plus supplier scale in a fragmented industry). Width is narrow but real: returns on capital remain above 50%, but operating margin has fallen about 1.5-2 points since 2025 and new-customer acquisition has weakened two years running, so the trend is softening rather than widening; part of that is tariffs (policy, potentially cyclical) rather than structural. Secular threat: manageable - marketplace and online competition and changes in how small businesses find suppliers (search and AI-assisted buying) could raise acquisition costs, but promotional products remain a physical, fragmented, relationship-light category where 4imprint is the scale leader. The price is not a fear-print; it is roughly fair value for a stable base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

Return on tangible equity (profit divided by shareholders' equity excluding goodwill) was 19.2% in 2025 and 20.2% for the first nine months of 2026, and management has met or beaten every dated guide across the last five calls: 2025 income of £16.4bn against about £16.3bn guided, a 19.2% return against more than 18%, and impairments of 16bp against below 20bp. Earnings per share rose from 27p in 2021 to 67p in 2025, a 25% compound annual rate, helped by a share count that fell from over 11bn to under 8bn. The bank generates more than 200bp of core capital a year (252bp in 2025, 208bp in 9M 2026) and paid out £4.1bn for 2025, about 75% of profit. At today's market value of about £47bn, that is a cash yield to shareholders near 8-9% a year from dividends plus buybacks. Three supports run into 2027-28. First, the Bank of England is now expected to raise rates to 4% (Q3 2026 call), and the structural hedge (swaps that lock in yields on stable deposits) reinvests at higher swap rates; management accelerated it in Q1 2026 'to accelerate the increase in our structural hedge'. Second, cost/income is down to 45.7%, near the below-45% target, with £420m of gross savings this year. Third, Evelyn Partners doubled assets under management to £132bn, adding a fee engine that uses little capital. The October 2026 budget fear (a surcharge back to 8%) resolved milder than feared, at 6% for 15 months only (Budget, 2026-10-28). Yet the shares sit about 24% below the 52-week high of 788p, at about 7.8x 2026 earnings and about 1.6x tangible book. For the bull case to work, returns of 19-20% must be sustained, the margin must hold at about 250bp, and credit must stay prime-quality (cost of risk below 25bp).
picks.bear_thesis: The 2023-25 earnings engine (margin expansion from the hedge and rate rises) has stopped accelerating. Net interest margin was 'broadly stable at 250 basis points' in Q3 2026, and attributable profit was £1.5bn against £1.6bn a year earlier; Reuters called it a flat quarter, and the screener shows latest-quarter EPS down 5% year on year. The CFO conceded that 'we will start to issue more wholesale funding to support loan growth' (2026-10-30): the deposit surplus is used up, so growth now costs more to fund. Analysts noted that the new deposit growth is all in more expensive term deposits. 2027 brings three headwinds at once. The bank surcharge rises from 3% to 6% from 2027-01-01 for 15 months (about 3-4% of EPS). Basel 3.1 adds about £10bn of risk-weighted assets on 2027-01-01 (about 70bp of core capital). And the Evelyn goodwill has already diluted tangible book per share, which grew 9.4% only 'excluding Evelyn Partners'. Cost of risk is drifting up, from 15bp in Q3 2025 to 24bp in Q3 2026, and there is about £20bn of fund lending; a severe-downside scenario implies a £1.7bn credit hit. UK banks also carry recurring political risk, with windfall-tax talk returning almost every budget. If returns settle at 15-16% with a 13% cost of equity, a fair multiple is about 1.3x tangible book, or roughly 470p. The bear case is confirmed if 2027 guidance (FY results, about February 2027) points to returns below 17%, the margin falls below 240bp, or the buyback is cut.
picks.consensus_delta: The market is pricing NatWest as a bank whose earnings peaked with the margin, at about 7.8x 2026 earnings and 1.6x tangible book after a fall from 788p to 595p. We think that read is partly right. Margin expansion is over: management now guides a stable margin of about 250bp, and Q3 profit was flat. Where we disagree is the durability of returns. Returns of 19-20% with more than 200bp of annual capital generation, a falling share count and cost/income moving below 45% support compounding of about 9-10% a year in tangible book plus distributions, without any margin help. Rates rising to 4% (Q3 2026 guidance) are a modest tailwind the market is not crediting after the stable-margin guide. The disagreement is moderate, not deep: our base case sits about 18% above the price, just short of the 20% bar we require for a buy at today's price.
picks.valley_of_death: The risky window over the next 3-9 months has four parts. First, 2027-01-01 brings both Basel 3.1 (about £10bn of risk-weighted assets, about 70bp of core capital) and the higher 6% surcharge. Together these could lead management to guide a smaller 2027 buyback at FY results (expected around February 2027), the main near-term disappointment risk. Second, the margin guide could slip below 250bp if term-deposit migration and wholesale funding costs rise faster than lending yields. Third, credit costs are drifting up (24bp in Q3 2026 against 15bp a year earlier) under a macro overlay tied to Middle East conflict and sticky inflation. Fourth, UK political noise around bank taxes recurs every budget. There is no funding cliff or debt-maturity wall: the liquidity coverage ratio is 140%, the loan-to-deposit ratio is 90%, and the only near-term capital instrument call is a £1bn AT1 in May 2027.
picks.positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling pressure. The government sell-down ended with the return to full private ownership in May 2025, so that overhang is gone. The holder base is income and value funds that are paid well (about 8-9% total distribution yield) and have no reason to sell mechanically. The realistic route to a lower price is a sector-wide de-rating of UK domestic banks on rates, tax or a UK growth scare, the same factor that took the shares from about 662p (2026-10-16) to under 600p. Our entry level of 580p sits inside that sector-wide range.
picks.moderator_conclusion: Wait for a better price: we buy near 580p, which a sector-wide sell-off in UK domestic banks could deliver. The thesis holds. NatWest is a high-return (about 20% on tangible equity), low-cost, well-capitalised UK bank, and management has delivered every target it set over the past year. We put fair value at about 700p (roughly 1.9x tangible book of about 370p, or 9x 2027 earnings of about 79p). From 595.4p that is about 18% upside, just under the 20% margin we require before buying at today's price in a reflationary backdrop. Our adverse case is about 470p, if returns settle near 16%, and our favourable case is about 820p. The pause is about price, not the business. Margin growth has stopped (Q3 2026 profit was flat, and the margin is guided stable at about 250bp), and 2027 brings Basel 3.1 and a higher bank surcharge, so we would rather be paid a little more for those headwinds. The recent fall came from a UK bank sector move on tax fears and the stable-margin guide, not from a company-specific problem. Conviction is moderate. On value alone the business qualifies; only the size of the discount is short.
picks.forcing_function: No single hard-dated event forces a re-rating. The nearest checkpoint is the FY2026 results and capital-return announcement, customarily mid-February 2027. That release will give 2027 guidance after Basel 3.1 and the higher surcharge, and the size of any buyback. A buyback of about £750m or more with a return guide of 19% or better would confirm the compounding case. The Private Banking and Wealth spotlight (November 2026) adds detail on Evelyn but is unlikely to move the stock.

# NatWest Group (NWG.L) - a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 2026-11-16 from five calls: Q3 2025 (2025-10-24), full-year 2025 (2026-02-13), Q1 2026 (2026-05-01), the H1 2026 fixed-income call (2026-07-31) and Q3 2026 (2026-10-30), checked against the screener's financial history. Price used: 595.4p on the London listing (FMP live quote, 2026-11-16).*

**Bottom line:** NatWest is a well-run, highly profitable UK bank whose management has hit or beaten almost every target it set over the past year. The open question is not credibility but the earnings slope: the margin tailwind from its interest-rate hedges is flattening, profit in Q3 2026 was flat year on year, and a higher UK bank tax starts in January 2027. The stock has fallen from about 788p at its 52-week high to about 595p.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-24):** the story is recovery plus the "structural hedge". The hedge is a rolling book of interest-rate swaps that locks in yields on stable deposits, and management said it would add "greater than GBP 1 billion" of income into 2026. Income guidance was raised to about £16.3bn and the return target to above 18%. Acquisitions faced "the financial high bar".
- **FY 2025 (2026-02-13):** the bank returned to full private ownership (May 2025), set targets for 2028 (customer balances growing more than 4% a year, cost/income below 45%, more than 200bp of capital generated a year, return on tangible equity above 18%) and announced the Evelyn Partners wealth acquisition. The story widened from "hedge-driven income" to "three growth engines".
- **Q1 2026 (2026-05-01):** the tone turned more defensive. Conflict in the Middle East led to a £140m macro provision, and rates were assumed to hold at 3.75% ("higher for longer"), which management framed as income-positive. There was a new emphasis on AI productivity ("over 40% of our code is now written by AI") and on resilience in the Bank of England stress test ("the lowest stress drawdown of any U.K. bank").
- **H1 2026 (2026-07-31):** Evelyn completed. Return guidance was raised to above 19% and income guidance to about £17.9bn including Evelyn. Capital headroom was the theme: operate at around 13% CET1 (common equity tier 1, the core capital ratio), with Basel 3.1 adding about £10bn of risk-weighted assets on 2027-01-01.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-30):** the story is now growth by volume, not margin. Net interest margin (NIM, the spread earned on loans and deposits) was "broadly stable at 250 basis points". The Bank of England is now expected to raise rates to 4% in Q4 2026. Analysts pushed hard on why the margin has stopped rising.

The arc runs from margin expansion (2025) to volume growth with a stable margin (late 2026). That shift is the main reason the shares de-rated.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Claim (quarter) | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| FY25 income about £16.3bn (Q3 25) | Delivered £16.4bn (FY25) | Beat |
| FY25 return on tangible equity above 18% (Q3 25) | 19.2% (FY25) | Beat |
| FY25 loan impairment below 20bp (Q3 25) | 16bp (FY25) | Beat |
| 2026 income £17.2-17.6bn (FY25) | Top end (Q1), then about £17.9bn including Evelyn (H1), reaffirmed (Q3) | Delivered, with Evelyn flattering the number |
| 2026 return above 19% (H1 26) | 20.2% for the first nine months (Q3 26) | On track |
| EPS growth | Screener: EPS 0.27 (2021) to 0.67 (2025), a 25% compound annual rate; 57.4p for 9M 2026, up 13.2% | Corroborated, but slowing |
| Quarterly profit | Q3 2026 attributable profit £1.5bn vs £1.6bn in Q3 2025; the screener shows latest-quarter EPS down 5% year on year | Momentum stalled. Reuters called it "flat third-quarter profit". |
| Capital generation above 200bp (FY25) | 252bp (FY25); 208bp in 9M 2026 | Corroborated |
| Share count falling | "from over 11 billion to just under 8 billion" (FY25); market cap of £46.98bn at 595.4p implies about 7.89bn shares | Corroborated |

Screener caveats: the P/FCF, DCF and free-cash-flow lines are meaningless for a bank, because deposits and loans flow through operating cash flow. The "net debt £10.17bn" is funding, not leverage in the industrial sense. The ROIC of 1.7% is also not meaningful; return on tangible equity is the relevant return.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY - Stable (high, but more defensive on margin)

- Q3 25: confident and upgrading ("we are revising our full year guidance for income").
- FY25: expansive ("we're ambitious for the business").
- Q1 26: considered ("sentiment is now more considered"), provisions taken, guidance held.
- H1 26: confident; return guidance upgraded.
- Q3 26: guidance unchanged, but the CFO was defending the margin. She pointed analysts to "one of my favorite slides... slide 30". Citi's Andrew Coombs opened by noting "the magnitude of the share price move". The tone remains specific and numeric, with no hedging on targets.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY - High

Every dated numeric guide tracked across the five calls was met or beaten: income, returns, impairments, capital generation and costs (£8bn for FY25, about £8.5bn for 2026 including Evelyn). The screener shows a 6-of-7 quarter earnings beat rate (86%). There is a mild sandbagging pattern (guide, then nudge up), but nothing evasive. The one area where guidance moved against investors is cost of risk: below 20bp in 2025, now below 25bp in 2026. That came alongside a macro overlay, not realised losses (21bp for the first nine months).

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Margin ceiling (Q3 26).** Rob Noble asked whether the bank is "bound by liquidity" and now has to issue wholesale funding to grow. The CFO conceded "we will start to issue more wholesale funding to support loan growth". This marks the end of the surplus-deposit era: growth now costs more to fund.
- **Deposit mix.** Coombs noted that all the interest-bearing deposit growth was in term deposits, which cost more than current accounts. Management said the mix was stable at about 30% non-interest-bearing, but conceded the market is "competitive".
- **Hedge duration (Q3 25).** Analysts asked why the product hedge is 2.5 years when peers use 3.5. Management cited behavioural evidence. A shorter hedge means income reprices faster in both directions.
- **Risk appetite and private credit (Q1 26).** Exposure to fund lending is about £20bn: roughly £17bn of subscription lines and £3-4bn of lending against fund net asset values, at loan-to-value ratios of about 30% and with no historical losses. KBW's Ed Firth asked whether the bank takes "enough" risk. A severe-downside scenario implies a £1.7bn credit hit.
- **AI cost claims (FY25).** Firth challenged whether AI will ever lower the absolute cost base. Management conceded "the absolute cost base has gone up a little bit".

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Red flags:**
- Q3 2026 profit was flat to down year on year (£1.5bn vs £1.6bn), with the margin plateauing at about 250bp (Q3 26).
- Growth needs wholesale funding from here (Q3 26), so the deposit surplus is used up.
- The UK bank surcharge rises from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 2027-01-01 (Budget, 2026-10-28), a small headwind to 2027 EPS, roughly 3-4%.
- Basel 3.1 adds about £10bn of risk-weighted assets on 2027-01-01 (H1 26), roughly 70bp of CET1.
- The Evelyn deal adds goodwill, which dilutes tangible book: tangible NAV per share rose 9.4% only "excluding Evelyn Partners" (Q3 26).
- Cost of risk is drifting up (24bp in Q3 26 vs 15bp in Q3 25).

**Green flags:**
- Return on tangible equity has been above 18% for many quarters running (19.2% FY25, 20.2% 9M 2026).
- Capital generation is above 200bp a year, and 2025 distributions were £4.1bn (about 75% of profit).
- The share count fell from over 11bn to under 8bn.
- Cost/income fell to 45.7% (Q3 26), close to the 2028 target of below 45%.
- The bank showed the lowest Bank of England stress drawdown of any UK bank (Q1 26).
- Rates rising to 4% (Q3 26), plus a hedge that reinvests at higher swap rates, supports income into 2027-28.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The Q3 2026 CEO script leads with "customer assets and liabilities" (CAL) growth of 14.2%. That figure is inflated by Evelyn's assets under management, a softer metric than lending or income. Leading with the broadest growth number is typical when margin growth fades.
- "Most efficient large bank in the U.K." has replaced "hedge tailwind" as the core claim.
- The capital language has moved from "surplus capital distribution" (2025) to "flexibility to invest" (2026). After Evelyn, the CET1 target of around 13% leaves less room for large buybacks in 2027, given Basel 3.1.
- The CFO's line "we will start to issue more wholesale funding" is the most important new sentence of 2026.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: Stable.** Returns are high and steady and guidance is reliable, but the growth engine has shifted from margin to volume, and profit growth stalled in Q3 2026.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** whether returns of about 19% are durable enough to justify paying roughly 1.6x tangible book while profit growth flattens and 2027 brings both Basel 3.1 and a higher bank surcharge. Price the stock on a stable-margin, 18-19% return case, not on the 2025 growth rate.

**Moat:** the moat is narrow but real. It rests on scale and low cost (the lowest cost/income among large UK banks) and on a sticky commercial deposit franchise (it is the leading UK business bank, about 30% of its deposits pay no interest) behind a regulatory licence. The returns evidence is stable to rising (return on tangible equity: 19.2% FY25, 20.2% 9M 2026), so the moat is not eroding. It is not wide: UK mortgages are commoditised, and deposit pricing is competitive.

**Secular threat: manageable.** Fintech, stablecoin and AI-agent deposit mobility could raise deposit betas (the share of rate rises passed on to savers) over time. Today, however, non-interest-bearing balances are stable at about 30% and the bank is itself an AI adopter. The cheapness looks like a fear-print over UK tax, politics and a margin plateau, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

# EEFT - Euronet Worldwide - Forensic Dossier (Interrogator, 2026-11-02)

Live price used: $66.16 (NASDAQ: EEFT, USD, FMP quote 2026-11-02; +4.8% on the day; 52-wk range 57.48-83.97). Market cap ~$2.47bn -> ~37.4m shares.

## 1. What changed since the last committee read (2026-10-12)
- 2026-10-27 Q3 2026 results: revenue ~$1.2bn, adj. EPS $3.55 (-2% y/y; Zacks consensus $3.63 - a miss), adj. EBITDA $226.1m.
- Full-year 2026 guidance cut: revenue ~$4.375bn, adj. EBITDA ~$725m, adj. EPS growth ~10% (low end of the 10-15% band given in Feb-2026 / the May Investor Day framework). CFO: 2027 "on the lower end" of 10-15%.
- Stock fell to ~$59 on 2026-10-28 (below the committee's $62.50 wait level) on company news (the guidance cut), then recovered to $66.16 by 2026-11-02.
- Street PTs reset 2026-10-28: 84 / 80 / 63 (vs 94 in July).

## 2. Segment truth (Q3 2026, constant currency)
- Payments infrastructure (ex-EFT): revenue +9% (merchant acquiring + CoreCard), adj. OI flat, adj. EBITDA +4% (cost inflation; +$4.7m CoreCard PPA amortization).
- epay: revenue +5%, OI +5%, adj. EBITDA +6%. Q4 headwind: Steam gift-card removal, backfill uncertain.
- Cross-border (Ria/Xe/Dandelion): revenue -4%, OI -35%, adj. EBITDA -32% (US immigration policy, FX, ~$6m extra digital advertising). Digital transactions +34%; ~3/4 of digital customers new to the franchise. Sequential cc revenue decline improved (-5% Q2 -> -4% Q3); management calls US outbound "stabilizing to subtle improvement".
- Digital accelerators +30% in Q3, +33% YTD, ~26% of revenue.

## 3. Earnings quality
- Adjusted earnings (2025: $408m) run well above GAAP NI ($310m) - gap = amortization, share comp, non-cash items. TTM GAAP diluted EPS $6.15 vs adjusted run-rate ~ $10.5.
- FCF is the weak spot: TTM FCF $95m (scan), FCF -33% y/y, 3-yr FCF CAGR -14%. Euronet's reported FCF swings with ATM cash and settlement working capital, so single-period FCF understates owner earnings, but the persistent gap between adjusted EPS and cash conversion is the main forensic discount. Q3 operating cash flow $139m.
- Piotroski 5/9, Altman-Z 1.5 (depressed by settlement liabilities typical of payments companies - not a true distress signal, but not a clean bill either).

## 4. Balance sheet
- 2026-09-30: unrestricted cash ~$955m-1.0bn, total debt $2.18bn (incl. $1bn 0.625% 2030 convert), capitalized leases $142m. Net debt $1.36bn incl. leases ($1.22bn ex-leases). $913m of cash sits inside the ATM network (operational, not counted as cash here). Investment-grade target maintained.

## 5. Capital allocation
- Buybacks ~85% of earnings over 4 years; Q3 2026 $50m (~690k shares at ~$72). Buying back at higher prices than today; the stock now ~6x adj. EPS makes continuing buybacks accretive.
- M&A: CoreCard (closed Oct-2025), Kyodai, Credia Bank merchant acquiring. Diebold Nixdorf LOI (2026-10-26), Fireblocks stablecoin card issuing (2026-10-19), OLON launch (2026-10-21) - optionality, no near-term P&L.

## 6. Insider / positioning
- Open-market insider: 2 buys (3,781 sh) vs 10 sells (182,255 sh) - no insider conviction signal.
- Smart-money 34/100; PT velocity -15% vs year-ago. Positioning is washed but not capitulated.

## 7. Management credibility

- European travel/discretionary spend (ATM withdrawals), FX translation.

- Cash conversion vs adjusted EPS.

picks.interrogator_dossier:
# JD Sports Fashion (JD.L) — a deep dive on management and the setup

*Prepared 2026-11-09. Sources: half-year results calls of 2023-09-21, 2024-10-02, 2025-09-24 and 2026-09-23, plus the screener's fiscal-year financials. Prices are in pence on the London listing (JD.L); the live quote used is 96.28p (FMP, 2026-11-09).*

**Bottom line:** JD is a highly cash-generative retailer whose earnings have been sliding for three years while its balance sheet has been getting steadily stronger. Management is credible on cash and costs and less credible on the top line: each year the story of a "structural growth market" has been replaced by a little more "controlling the controllables". The cash is real; the growth is not, for now.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **September 2023 (H1 FY24):** a governance and expansion story. The chairman talks about a new CFO, CTO and legal counsel, disposing of the fashion brands, buying out minorities in Iberia, Germany and Central Europe, and the pending Courir acquisition in France. Growth is the theme.
- **October 2024 (H1 FY25):** still a growth story — revenue "breaking the £5 billion milestone", JD-brand organic growth of 9%, double-digit organic growth in North America and Europe, and the Hibbett acquisition just closed. Nike's "stumble" is acknowledged as a headwind but framed as diversifiable ("if Nike is a little bit off form, we have New Balance and Adidas").
- **September 2025 (H1 FY26):** the tone shifts to discipline. Priority three of the April 2025 strategy update is "cash generation and shareholder return". Like-for-like sales fall 2.5% and growth comes from acquisitions (Hibbett, Courir) and new space.
- **September 2026 (H1 FY27):** fully defensive. "Our response to a maturing market and challenging trading conditions is to control the controllables." Organic sales fall 0.7%, like-for-like sales (sales at stores open in both years) fall 2.8%, and the store count is 106 lower. The proud line is now cash: net cash before leases of £168m, up almost £300m year on year, and "cash is king and cash is real."

The growth drivers introduced in 2023-24 (US expansion through acquisitions, the "structural growth market") have quietly given way to store productivity, apparel mix and buybacks. The phrase "maturing market" appears for the first time in 2026.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Highly cash-generative business" (every call) | FCF margin 7.9%, FCF up 40% in the latest year; net cash before leases swung from £125m net debt to £168m net cash (Aug 2025 to Aug 2026) after returning £260m | Matches |
| Market-share gains in North America and Europe (2025) | Revenue grew from £10.5bn (FY24) to £12.7bn (FY26), but mostly acquired (Hibbett, Courir); like-for-like negative in 2025 and 2026 | Richer than the numbers |
| Gross margin "maintained through trading discipline" | Gross margin steady around 47-48% for years; the 2026 call admits a 50bp underlying hit from price investment, offset by supplier marketing money | Broadly matches |
| Operating discipline protecting profit | Net income fell from £539m (FY24) to £490m (FY25) to £436m (FY26); H1 FY27 operating profit fell 19.5% and margin 120bp | Diverges — costs are controlled, but margins are not |
| Buybacks create value per share | Adjusted EPS fell 13.7% in H1 FY27 against a steeper fall in pre-tax profit; the share count is shrinking | Matches |

The headline earnings trajectory (EPS 0.10 in FY24 to 0.085 in FY26, down 10% in the latest year) is poorer than a "resilient" narrative implies. The cash trajectory is better than the earnings trajectory, which is the core of the bull case.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining on growth, stable on cash.**
- 2023: expansive ("the pace at JD is quite extraordinary").
- 2024: confident but with caveats (the "legendary UK summer", Nike's stumble).
- 2025: defensive ("a tough couple of years", national insurance rises, governance clean-up).
- 2026: defensive and specific — guidance is given as a fixed range (£700m-£800m pre-tax profit before adjusting items, £460m-£520m free cash flow after leases) and language centres on cost, capital and cash. The CEO concedes "heat created by the market leader... is not today the case", a direct admission that the Nike product cycle still drives the business.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Management held its full-year guidance range at the 2024 half year and kept the FY27 range "unchanged from the Q2 trading statement" in September 2026. That FY27 range sits well below the prior year's profit, so the expectation was reset during 2026 rather than met. The screener shows earnings beats in only 3 of the last 7 quarters (43%). There is no clear sandbagging pattern: guidance is reset downward when trading turns, then held. **Reliability: Medium.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **The footwear cycle and Nike:** analysts asked in 2025 and again in 2026 what it takes for footwear to return to growth. The answer was qualitative (end promotions, wait for new franchises such as the Adidas Samba, On, Salomon). There is no dated recovery marker.
- **Inventory:** management says it is "comfortable" while noting the industry may be too heavy, which is why the market stays promotional.
- **Mexico franchise and US womenswear (2026):** management frames franchising as capital-light growth. It is real but small.
- **Dividend cover:** the CFO signals a progressive dividend toward a yield "around 2-plus percent". The interim dividend was raised 21% to 0.40p.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: like-for-like sales negative in both H1 FY26 (-2.5%) and H1 FY27 (-2.8%).
- Red: three years of falling net income despite revenue up about 20%, so acquisitions have bought revenue but not profit.
- Red: heavy dependence on Nike, about half of revenue by Barclays' estimate, where brand heat is still weak (CEO, 2026-09-23).
- Red: North America operating margin down 220bp in H1 FY27, with the standalone Finish Line business being wound down.
- Green: net cash before leases up almost £300m year on year to £168m (Aug 2026), even after £260m of shareholder returns.
- Green: online sales up 5.2%, apparel up 4% to 36% of the mix, and like-for-like operating costs flat (H1 FY27).
- Green: adjusting items have shrunk to mainly the amortisation of acquired intangibles, so statutory and adjusted profit are converging. This marks the governance clean-up as done.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "Fewer, bigger, better stores" has replaced store-count growth as the space story. It signals saturation in mature markets.
- Capital-allocation language has moved from acquisitions (2023-24) to buybacks and dividends (2025-26). This is a classic sign that management sees fewer high-return reinvestment options.
- The CFO now quotes free cash flow after leases as a headline metric, a more conservative and more honest measure than in 2023.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Earnings are drifting lower, but cash generation, the balance sheet and governance are all improving, and capital returns are rising.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** the stock has already re-rated from about 64p to 96p over the past year and now trades near the top of its 52-week range. At roughly 9 times this year's guided earnings and a free-cash-flow yield of about 10%, it is cheap in absolute terms. Most of the discount to peers is explained by negative like-for-like sales and the Nike dependence, and the recovery in the Nike product cycle has no date.

**Moat:** a narrow scale and brand moat. JD is the preferred wholesale partner of Nike and Adidas for premium allocations, with a multi-brand, multi-country store estate that brands need for reach. The width is modest: return on invested capital is 8%, gross margin is steady around 47-48%, and operating margin is under pressure. Gross margin is not eroding, so the moat is stable rather than shrinking. **Secular threat:** manageable. Brand direct-to-consumer selling (the retail channel shift) was the structural fear, but Nike's partial return to wholesale has eased it. The cheapness reflects a cyclical earnings trough plus supplier concentration, not a structurally shrinking base.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory steady · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.
